a1701: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Managed LLM Platforms — Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI Lesson 17.1 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Name the three platform strategies (marketplace vs exclusive vs Gemini-first) and match each to a product use case. Explain what Provisioned Throughput Units (PTUs) buy you in Azure OpenAI and why on-demand Bedrock typically reads ~25 ms slower at the 405B scale. Diagram the FinOps attribution surface for each platform (Bedrock Application Inference Profiles vs Vertex project-per-team vs Azure scopes + PTU reservations). Write down a "two-provider minimum" policy and explain why single-vendor lock-in is the expensive mistake in 2026. Before you start Needs : Phase 11 (LLM Engineering), Phase 13 (Tools & Protocols) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy cost-and-latency comparator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Three hyperscalers, three distinct strategies. AWS Bedrock is a model marketplace — Claude, Llama, Titan, Stability, Cohere behind one API. Azure OpenAI is an exclusive OpenAI partnership plus Provisioned Throughput Units (PTUs) for dedicated capacity. Vertex AI is Gemini-first with the best long-context and multimodal story. In 2026 Artificial Analysis measures Azure OpenAI at ~50 ms median and Bedrock at ~75 ms on Llama 3.1 405B equivalents — PTUs explain the gap because dedicated capacity beats shared on-demand. The decision rule Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Bedrock "AWS LLM service" Model marketplace across Claude, Llama, Titan, Mistral, Cohere Azure OpenAI "Azure's ChatGPT" Exclusive OpenAI models in Azure datacenters with enterprise controls Vertex AI "Google's LLM" Gemini-first platform with Model Garden for third-party models PTU "dedicated capacity" Provisioned Throughput Unit — reserved inference GPUs, priced per hour Application Inference Profile "Bedrock tagging" Per-product cost/usage profile with tags, CloudWatch-native Model Garden "Vertex catalog" Vertex AI's third-party model section, separate from Gemini Two-provider minimum "LLM redundancy" Policy of running every critical LLM path across ≥2 hyperscalers BAA "HIPAA paperwork" Business Associate Agreement; required for PHI; provided by all three Abuse monitoring "the log watcher" Provider-side safety scan on prompts/outputs; opt-out in enterprise The problem In plain words first A managed LLM platform is a cloud service that runs models for you, so you send a request and pay for the tokens instead of renting GPUs yourself. The three big clouds each sell one, and they made different bets. AWS Bedrock is a shop with many brands of model behind one API. Azure OpenAI sells OpenAI's models only, inside Azure. Vertex AI is built around Google's Gemini models. You pay in one of two ways. On-demand means you share capacity with everyone else and pay per token. Provisioned throughput (Azure calls a unit of it a PTU ) means you rent a reserved slice of capacity by the hour, used or not. This lesson shows how to choose a platform and a payment mode from the facts you have: which models you need, how fast the first token must arrive, how steady your traffic is, and how clearly you need to see who spent what. You picked Claude 3.7 Sonnet for your product. Now you need to serve it. You can call the Anthropic API directly, or you can call it through AWS Bedrock, or you can go through a gateway. The direct API is the simplest; Bedrock adds BAAs, VPC endpoints, IAM, and CloudWatch attribution. The gateway adds failover, unified billing, and rate limits across providers. The deeper question is catalog. If you need Claude and Llama and Gemini in the same product, you cannot buy them all from one place unless that place is Bedrock plus Vertex plus Azure OpenAI simultaneously. The hyperscalers are not interchangeable — they each made a different bet on who owns the model layer. This lesson maps the three bets, the latency gap, the FinOps gap, and the lock-in risk. Idea 1 · Three strategies AWS Bedrock — the marketplace. Claude (Anthropic), Llama (Meta), Titan (AWS first-party), Stability (image), Cohere (embeddings), Mistral, plus image and embedding sub-catalogs. One API, one IAM surface, one CloudWatch export. Bedrock's bet is that customers want optionality more than they want a single model. Azure OpenAI — the exclusive partnership. You get GPT-4 / 4o / 5 / o-series, DALL·E, Whisper, and fine-tuning of OpenAI models in Azure datacenters. No non-OpenAI models in the "Azure OpenAI Service" catalog — those go to Azure AI Foundry (separate product). Azure's bet is that OpenAI remains the frontier and customers want enterprise controls on that specific relationship. Vertex AI — Gemini first, everything else second. Gemini 1.5 / 2.0 / 2.5 Flash and Pro, plus Model Garden (third-party). Vertex's bet is multimodal long-context — 1M-token Gemini context is the differentiator. Idea 2 · Latency gap at scale Artificial Analysis runs continuous benchmarks. On equivalent Llama 3.1 405B deployments, Azure median first-token latency is around 50 ms with PTUs; Bedrock on shared on-demand is around 75 ms. The gap is not an AWS failure — it is a capacity model difference. Azure sells PTUs (Provisioned Throughput Units), which reserve GPU capacity for your tenant. Bedrock's equivalent (Provisioned Throughput) exists but starts around $21/hour per unit, and most customers stay on shared on-demand. On-demand shared capacity competes with every other customer's traffic. Dedicated capacity does not. If your product SLA is TTFT < 100 ms at P99, you either buy PTUs on Azure, buy Bedrock Provisioned Throughput, or accept the default variance. Idea 3 · Provisioned Throughput economics Azure PTUs: a reserved block of inference compute. Up to ~70% savings vs on-demand for predictable workloads. Costs fixed per hour regardless of traffic — you pay for the reservation even when idle. The break-even is usually around 40-60% sustained utilization. Bedrock Provisioned Throughput: $21-$50 per hour depending on model and region. Similar math — break-even is around half peak utilization. Monthly commitment required. Vertex provisioned capacity is sold per Gemini SKU; pricing varies by model and region and is less publicly advertised. Idea 4 · FinOps surface — the real differentiator Bedrock Application Inference Profiles are the cleanest attribution in the marketplace. Tag a profile with team , product , feature ; route all model invocations through it; CloudWatch breaks out cost per profile without post-processing. Added 2025, still the most granular hyperscaler native. Vertex attribution is project-per-team plus labels-everywhere. You model each team as a GCP project, put labels on every resource, and use BigQuery Billing Export + DataStudio for rollups. More work, but BigQuery gives you arbitrary SQL on the cost data. Azure relies on subscription/resource-group scopes plus tags, with PTU reservations as a first-class cost object. Tags are inherited from resource groups, not requests, so per-request attribution requires Application Insights custom metrics or a gateway that stamps headers. The pattern: Bedrock is cleanest native, Vertex is most flexible via BigQuery, Azure is most opaque unless you instrument. Idea 5 · Lock-in is the 2026 risk Single-hyperscaler commitment was fine when one model dominated. In 2026 the frontier moves monthly — Claude 3.7 one quarter, Gemini 2.5 the next, GPT-5 the quarter after. Locking to one platform locks you out of two-thirds of the frontier. The pattern working teams adopt: two-provider minimum for any product-critical LLM call. Bedrock plus Azure OpenAI is the common pair — Claude from one, GPT from the other, failover between them, same gateway. Cost uplift is negligible because gateway routes optimal; availability uplift during outages (like the Azure OpenAI January 2025 incident, the AWS us-east-1 outage) is decisive. Idea 6 · Data residency, BAAs, and regulated industries Bedrock: BAAs in most regions; VPC endpoints; guardrails. Common fintech default. Azure OpenAI: HIPAA, SOC 2, ISO 27001; EU data residency; the enterprise-regulated default. Vertex: HIPAA, GDPR, data residency per region; Google Cloud's compliance stack. All three meet the basic checkbox. The differences are in data retention policies, how logs are handled, and whether abuse-monitoring reads your traffic (default opt-in on most; opt-out available for enterprise). Idea 7 · Numbers you should remember Azure OpenAI median TTFT on Llama 3.1 405B equivalents: ~50 ms (with PTUs). Bedrock median TTFT on-demand: ~75 ms. Bedrock Provisioned Throughput: $21-$50/hr per unit. Azure PTU break-even: ~40-60% sustained utilization. PTU savings vs on-demand at high utilization: up to 70%. The same idea as a formula When does reserved capacity pay off? Let a reservation cost dollars per hour and serve at most tokens per hour. On-demand costs dollars per token. If your traffic fills a fraction of the reservation on average, on-demand would cost per hour, so the reservation wins when = C ⋅ p R ​ The break-even utilization is the reservation's price divided by what its full capacity would cost on demand. Worked example Where a reservation starts to pay A reservation costs R = $10 an hour and can produce C = 2 million output tokens an hour. On-demand output costs p = $10 per million tokens. Full capacity on demand would cost 2 × $10 = $20 an hour. Break-even: = 10/20 = 0.5 . Below 50% average utilization, on-demand is cheaper. At 80% utilization, on-demand costs 0.8 × $20 = $16 an hour against the reservation's $10: you save $6 an hour, about $4,300 a month. At 30%, on-demand costs $6 an hour, and the reservation wastes $4 an hour. The same arithmetic explains the "40–60% band" quoted for PTUs: real prices put somewhere in that range. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✗ Azure is faster than Bedrock because its GPUs are better. The roughly 50 ms against 75 ms gap comes from reserved capacity against shared on-demand capacity, not from the hardware. ✓ A reservation costs the same per hour whether you send traffic or not. ✗ Reserving capacity always saves money on a busy product. It saves money only when the average utilization is above break-even. A product that is busy for two hours a day can still lose money on a reservation. ✓ Running each critical call on two providers costs little and protects you during a regional outage. Predict before you run Your traffic peaks at 100% of one reservation for 4 hours a day and sits at 20% the rest of the time. The reservation's break-even is 50%. Before you run the code below, guess: does the reservation pay off over a whole day? The four busy hours do not decide it; the twenty quiet ones do. If you still need fast first tokens in the busy window, the usual answer is a small reservation for the steady base load plus on-demand for the peaks. Recap What to keep from this lesson The three platforms differ in catalog : Bedrock is a marketplace, Azure OpenAI is OpenAI-only, Vertex is Gemini-first. Latency gaps between them come mostly from reserved versus shared capacity . A reservation pays off when average utilization is above , usually 40–60%. Solutions Solution P1 · Where does a reservation beat on-demand? In code/main.py the reservation costs $10 an hour and serves 2 million tokens an hour, against $10 per million on demand. Full capacity on demand is $20 an hour, so break-even is 50% utilization. The sweep shows the tie at 50% and the reservation winning from 60%. That sits in the middle of the advertised 40–60% band. Cheaper reservations or pricier tokens move it lower. Solution P2 · Claude plus GPT-4o Put Claude on Bedrock and GPT-4o on Azure OpenAI, with one gateway in front (LiteLLM, Portkey or similar) that holds both credentials. Route each feature to its primary model. On a 5xx error, a timeout or a regional outage, fail over to the other provider's closest model, using prompts tested on both. Log which provider served each request, so cost and quality can be compared. Solution B1 · The 50 ms figure The 50 ms median belongs to Azure with PTUs , which is reserved capacity. On demand, Azure shares capacity like everyone else, and its tail latency is no better than Bedrock's. A P99 target needs reserved capacity on whichever platform hosts the model, or a gateway that sends overflow elsewhere. They also compared medians, while their target was a P99. a1702: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Inference Platform Economics — Fireworks, Together, Baseten, Modal, Replicate, Anyscale Lesson 17.2 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Name the three market segments (custom silicon, GPU platforms, API-first) and map each vendor to a segment. Explain why the "per-token" API pricing model compresses toward the serving engine's cost curve, not the hardware's. Compute effective cost per request across at least three vendors and explain when per-minute (Baseten, Modal) beats per-token. Identify which platform is the right default for a given workload (serverless bursty, steady high-throughput, fine-tuned variants, multimodal). Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 01 (Managed LLM Platforms), Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy per-call economics comparator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The 2026 inference market is no longer GPU time rental. It bifurcates into custom silicon (Groq, Cerebras, SambaNova), GPU platforms (Baseten, Together, Fireworks, Modal), and API-first marketplaces (Replicate, DeepInfra). Fireworks raised price $1/hr per GPU on May 1, 2026, and $4B valuation on 10T+ tokens/day tells you the volume-driven model works. Baseten closed $300M Series E at $5B in January 2026. The competitive positioning rule is simple: Fireworks optimizes latency, Together optimizes catalog Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Custom silicon "non-GPU chips" Groq LPU, Cerebras WSE, SambaNova RDU — optimized for decode FireAttention "Fireworks engine" Custom attention kernel; marketed at 4x lower latency than vLLM Truss "Baseten's format" Model packaging manifest; dependencies + secrets + serving config Per-token "API pricing" Charge by tokens consumed; pay for no idle Per-minute "dedicated pricing" Charge by wall-clock GPU time; wins at high utilization Per-prediction "Replicate pricing" Charge per model invocation; common for image/video RayTurbo "Anyscale engine" Proprietary inference on Ray; competes with vLLM on Ray clusters Batch tier "50% off" Non-interactive queue at reduced rate; common on Fireworks, OpenAI Fine-tuned at base rate "Fireworks LoRA" Charge LoRA-served requests at base model's rate (differentiator) The problem In plain words first Below the big clouds sits a layer of inference platforms : companies whose whole business is running models fast and cheaply. Some build their own chips (Groq, Cerebras), most rent NVIDIA GPUs and tune the software (Fireworks, Together, Baseten, Modal, Anyscale), and some are marketplaces with thousands of models (Replicate). They price in different units. Per-token pricing charges for what you generate, so idle time is free. Per-minute or per-second pricing rents you a GPU, so you pay for idle time too but nothing extra for each token. To compare them you convert everything to one unit, usually dollars per day or dollars per million tokens, for your traffic. This lesson does that conversion and finds where one pricing model overtakes the other. You evaluated managed hyperscaler platforms. You decided you need a narrower, faster provider — Fireworks for latency, Together for breadth, Baseten for a fine-tuned custom model. Now you have six real choices and the pricing pages do not line up. Fireworks shows $/M tokens; Baseten shows $/minute; Modal shows $/second; Replicate shows $/prediction. You cannot compare them head-to-head without modeling the workload. Worse, the business model behind each pricing page is different. Fireworks runs its own custom engine (FireAttention) on shared GPUs; the per-token rate reflects their utilization curve. Baseten gives you Truss + dedicated GPUs; per-minute reflects exclusivity. Modal is true Python serverless — per-second billing with sub-second cold starts. Same output (an LLM response), three different cost functions. This lesson models the six and tells you when each wins. Idea 1 · The three segments Custom silicon — Groq (LPU), Cerebras (WSE), SambaNova (RDU). Typically 5-10x faster decode than a GPU-based cluster on the same model. Higher per-token price (Groq was ~$0.99/M on Llama-70B late 2025) but unbeatable for latency-sensitive use cases. Groq is the production pick for voice agents and real-time translation. GPU platforms — Baseten, Together, Fireworks, Modal, Anyscale. Run on NVIDIA (H100, H200, B200 in 2026) or sometimes AMD. The economic layer between "raw GPU rental" (RunPod, Lambda) and "hyperscaler managed service" (Bedrock). API-first marketplaces — Replicate, DeepInfra, OpenRouter, Fal. Broad catalog, pay-per-prediction or pay-per-second, emphasize time-to-first-call. Idea 2 · Fireworks — latency-optimized GPU platform FireAttention engine (custom); marketed as 4x lower latency than vLLM on equivalent configs. Batch tier at ~50% of serverless rate for non-interactive workloads. Fine-tuned model served at the same rate as the base model — a real differentiator versus providers that charge a premium for your LoRA. Mid-2026: raised on-demand GPU rental $1/hour effective May 1, 2026. Volume pricing negotiable at scale. Financial signal: $4B valuation, 10T+ tokens/day handled. Idea 3 · Together — breadth-optimized 200+ models including open-source releases within days of upstream publication. 50-70% cheaper than Replicate on equivalent LLM models — the "AI Native Cloud" positioning is volume and catalog. Inference + fine-tuning + training in one API. Idea 4 · Baseten — enterprise-polish-optimized Truss framework: model packaging with dependencies, secrets, serving config in one manifest. GPU range from T4 through B200. Per-minute billing with reasonable cold-start mitigation. SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA-ready. Common fintech and healthcare pick. $5B valuation, January 2026 Series E ($300M from CapitalG, IVP, NVIDIA). Idea 5 · Modal — Python-native-optimized Infrastructure-as-code in pure Python. Decorate a function with @modal.function(gpu="A100") and deploy with one command. Per-second billing. Cold starts 2-4s with pre-warming; <1s for small models. $87M Series B at $1.1B valuation (2025). Strongest developer experience score in independent surveys. Idea 6 · Replicate — multimodal breadth Pay-per-prediction. The default platform for image, video, and audio models. Integration ecosystem (Zapier, Vercel, CMS plugins). Less competitive on LLM per-token rates but wins on multimodal variety. Idea 7 · Anyscale — Ray-native Built on Ray; RayTurbo is Anyscale's proprietary inference engine (competes with vLLM). Best for distributed Python workloads where the inference step is one node in a larger graph. Managed Ray clusters; tight integration with Ray AIR and Ray Serve. Idea 8 · Per-token versus per-minute — when each wins Per-token makes sense when the workload is latency-insensitive and bursty — you only pay for what you use. Per-minute makes sense when utilization is high and predictable — you beat per-token once you're saturating the GPU. Rough rule: for workloads above ~30% sustained utilization of a dedicated GPU, per-minute (Baseten, Modal) starts to beat per-token (Fireworks, Together). Below that, per-token wins because you avoid paying for idle. Idea 9 · Custom engine is the real moat Every platform above vLLM and SGLang claims a custom engine. FireAttention, RayTurbo, Baseten's inference stack. Custom-engine claims shade marketing — the honest framing is that vLLM + SGLang represent about 80% of production open-source inference, and the differentiators at the platform layer are DX, attribution, and SLAs. Idea 10 · Numbers you should remember Fireworks GPU rental: $1/hr raise effective May 1, 2026. Fireworks claim: 4x lower latency than vLLM on equivalent configs. Together: 50-70% cheaper than Replicate on LLMs. Baseten valuation: $5B (Series E, Jan 2026, $300M round). Modal valuation: $1.1B (Series B, 2025). Per-minute beats per-token above ~30% sustained utilization. The same idea as a formula Per-token against a rented GPU. A rented GPU costs dollars per minute and can produce tokens per minute. Per-token pricing costs dollars per token. At average utilization , renting wins when m ​ The crossover depends on how fast the GPU runs your model ( ), not on a universal rule. A faster engine lowers the crossover. Worked example The crossover in `code/main.py` The script uses a per-minute GPU at $0.55 a minute that produces 900,000 tokens a minute, against per-token pricing of $0.90 per million tokens. Full use of the GPU for a minute on per-token pricing: 0.9 million × $0.90 = $0.81. Crossover: 0.55 / 0.81 ≈ 0.68. The rented GPU wins only above about 68% average utilization. The lesson's rule of thumb says about 30%. Both are right for their inputs: with a slower model (say 400,000 tokens a minute), the crossover is 0.55 / 0.36, above 100%, so renting never wins; with a cheaper GPU or pricier tokens it drops towards 30%. The lesson: do the division for your model, your throughput and your quotes. Solutions Solution P1 · Baseten against Fireworks With the script's numbers, $0.55 a minute against $0.90 per million tokens at 900,000 tokens a minute, the crossover is 0.55 / 0.81 ≈ 68% utilization. Solution P3 · Batch tier after a price rise If 40% of traffic moves to a batch tier at half price, the blended rate is 0.6 × 1 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.8 of the old rate. That 20% saving usually outweighs a $1 an hour rise on the remaining on-demand capacity unless the volume is small. Solution B1 · Busy hours are not utilization "Busy from 9 to 5" means traffic for a third of the day, and even then a GPU is rarely saturated. Average utilization over the 24 hours they pay for was probably under 15%, far below the crossover. They should have divided daily tokens by the GPU's daily capacity before switching, or rented only for the busy window. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off Two inference platforms quote you for the same open model. One bills per million tokens. The other rents a dedicated GPU by the minute. Your traffic is steady through the working day and near zero at night. Which pricing wins, and what number decides it? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Sustained utilization decides it. Per-token billing charges only for what you use, so it wins when traffic is bursty or low and a dedicated GPU would sit idle. Per-minute billing charges for wall-clock time, so it wins once you keep the GPU busy, and the lesson's rule of thumb puts the crossover near 30 percent sustained utilization. A load that runs only in the daytime sits near that line, so measure your utilization over a full week before you sign. Two cost functions for one output. Per-token pricing reflects the platform's own utilization curve across all of its customers, and you pay for no idle time. Per-minute or per-second pricing reflects exclusivity: the GPU is yours, and the bill runs whether or not a request arrives. The output, a model response, is the same. The crossover. The economics lesson states the rule: above about 30 percent sustained utilization of a dedicated GPU, per-minute starts to beat per-token. Below it, per-token wins because you are not paying for idle. The lesson on managed platforms shows the same shape for reserved capacity on a hyperscaler: the break-even sits around 40 to 60 percent sustained utilization, savings reach up to 70 percent at high utilization, and the reservation is billed when idle. Compute it for your own traffic. Take the request count per hour of the day for a week, and the tokens per request. The per-token bill is the token total times the rate. The per-minute bill is the rented hours times the rate. That is every hour unless you scale to zero at night, which brings a cold start every morning. Utilization is the busy time divided by the rented time. Compare it with the crossover. What the price does not show. Dedicated capacity avoids queueing behind other tenants. The lesson on managed platforms measures a lower first-token median on reserved capacity than on shared on-demand for the same model class. A fine-tuned model can change the per-token price. One platform in the lesson serves a fine-tune at the base model's rate, which is a differentiator. A dedicated GPU serves it at the same hourly price either way. Non-interactive work has a third option: a batch tier at about half the serverless rate. A mixed answer. Rent dedicated capacity for the daytime floor, and send the overflow and the overnight batch to per-token or batch pricing. The utilization of the dedicated part then stays high, and the bursts never pay for an idle GPU. Plausible wrong answers. "Per-token is always cheaper because you never pay for idle." Above the utilization crossover, the per-token rate carries the platform's idle and margin, and your own GPU is cheaper. "Dedicated is always cheaper at scale." Only when you keep it busy. A daytime-only load leaves it idle half the time. "Compare the headline prices." The two prices have different units. Only your traffic profile turns them into a bill. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does per-token pricing cost more per token than your own GPU time at high utilization? Expected: the platform's margin and its idle time are built into the per-token rate. At high utilization you pay for idle that you do not have. (level 2) What changes when you scale the dedicated GPU to zero at night? Expected: you stop paying for the night and buy a cold start every morning, so the first requests of the day pay in latency. (level 3) Why is the dedicated option faster at the tail? Expected: shared on-demand capacity competes with every other customer's traffic, and dedicated capacity does not. That is the gap the lesson on managed platforms measures between reserved and on-demand first-token latency. (level 3) How does a fine-tuned model change the comparison? Expected: a per-token platform may serve the fine-tune at the base rate or charge a premium for it. A dedicated GPU serves it at the same hourly price either way. Where it is taught. The inference platform economics lesson gives the per-token against per-minute crossover, and the managed platforms lesson gives the break-even for reserved capacity. a1703: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production GPU Autoscaling on Kubernetes — Karpenter, KAI Scheduler, Gang Scheduling Lesson 17.3 75 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Diagram the three autoscaling layers (node provisioning, gang scheduling, application-level) and name the tool used at each layer. Explain why DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL is the wrong HPA signal for vLLM and name two replacements (queue depth, KV cache utilization). Describe gang scheduling and the partial-allocation failure mode KAI Scheduler prevents (7 of 8 GPUs idle). Name the Karpenter consolidation policy ( WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized ) that terminates running GPU jobs and state the 2026 safe alternative. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 02 (Inference Platform Economics), Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy queue-depth autoscaler simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Three layers, not one. Karpenter provisions nodes dynamically (under one minute, 40% faster than Cluster Autoscaler). KAI Scheduler handles gang scheduling, topology awareness, and hierarchical queues — it prevents the 7-of-8 partial allocation trap where seven nodes wait and burn on one missing GPU. Application-level autoscalers (NVIDIA Dynamo Planner, llm-d Workload Variant Autoscaler) scale on inference-specific signals — queue depth, KV cache utilization — not CPU/DCGM duty cycle. The classic HPA trap is that `D Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Karpenter "the node provisioner" Kubernetes node autoscaler; sub-minute provisioning Cluster Autoscaler "the old scaler" Kubernetes node autoscaler predecessor; slower, group-based KAI Scheduler "the GPU scheduler" Secondary scheduler for gang + topology + queues Gang scheduling "all or nothing" Schedule N pods atomically or defer all of them Topology awareness "rack-aware" Place pods based on NVLink/IB/rack placement DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL "GPU utilization" Duty-cycle metric; NOT a scaling signal for LLMs Queue depth "waiting requests" Correct HPA signal for prefill-bound scaling KV cache utilization "memory pressure" Correct HPA signal for decode-bound scaling Consolidation "Karpenter consolidation" Node termination to cheaper instance type WhenEmpty + 1h "safe consolidation" Policy that doesn't evict running GPU jobs The problem In plain words first Autoscaling means adding or removing capacity as traffic changes. On Kubernetes, a GPU model server scales at three levels. Nodes are the machines with GPUs; a tool such as Karpenter adds one when work is waiting. Scheduling decides which machine each piece of work runs on; a big model may need 8 GPUs that must all start together, which is called gang scheduling . Replicas are copies of the model server; something must decide how many to run. The common mistake is to scale replicas on "GPU utilization", which only says whether the GPU did any work in each sample. A busy GPU reads 100% with one request or a hundred. Better signals measure the work itself: how many requests are queued, how full the KV cache is, how slow the first token has become. Your team ships an LLM-serving service on Kubernetes. You set up HPA with DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL as the signal. The service pins at 100% utilization during business hours. HPA never scales up — it already thinks you're full. You add a replica manually; TTFT drops. HPA still doesn't scale. The signal is lying to you. Separately, you use Cluster Autoscaler for nodes. A 1M-token prompt arrives at 2 a.m.; the cluster spends 3 minutes provisioning a node, and the request times out. Separately again, you deploy a 70B model requiring 8 GPUs across 2 nodes. The cluster has 7 GPUs free, scattered across 3 nodes, and needs 1 more. Cluster Autoscaler provisions a node for the 1 missing GPU. The 7 reserved GPUs sit idle for 4 minutes burning money while Kubernetes gets the last GPU up. Three layers, three different failure modes. GPU-aware autoscaling in 2026 is not "turn on HPA." It's composing node provisioning, gang scheduling, and application-signal autoscaling. Idea 1 · Layer 1 — node provisioning (Karpenter) Karpenter watches pending pods and provisions nodes within ~45-60 seconds (Cluster Autoscaler typically takes 90-120 seconds for GPU nodes). It picks instance types dynamically per the NodePool constraint — if your pod needs 8 H100s and the cluster has no matching node, Karpenter provisions one directly instead of scaling an existing group. The consolidation trap : Karpenter's default consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized is dangerous for GPU pools. It will terminate a running GPU node to migrate pods to a cheaper right-sized instance. For inference workloads that means evicting running requests and reloading a 70B model on the new node. Loss is minutes of capacity plus request failures. Safe setting for GPU pools: Copy Lets Karpenter consolidate truly empty nodes after an hour but never evict a running job. Idea 2 · Layer 2 — gang scheduling (KAI Scheduler) KAI Scheduler (project "Karp" then renamed) handles what default kube-scheduler does not: Gang scheduling — schedule all-or-nothing. A distributed inference pod requiring 8 GPUs either all 8 start together or none do. Without this, you get the partial-allocation trap: 7 of 8 pods start, wait indefinitely, burn money. Topology awareness — know which GPUs share NVLink, which sit on the same rack, which have InfiniBand between them. Place pods accordingly. A DeepSeek-V3 67B tensor-parallel workload must stay on one NVLink domain; KAI Scheduler respects that. Hierarchical queues — multiple teams compete for the same GPU pool with priority and quota. Team A's production pinch gets preempted by Team B's training job only if priority rules allow. KAI is deployed alongside kube-scheduler as a secondary scheduler; you annotate workloads to use it. Ray and vLLM production-stack both integrate. Idea 3 · Layer 3 — application-level signals The HPA trap : DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL is a duty-cycle metric — it measures whether the GPU was doing work at each sampling interval. 100% utilization could mean 10 concurrent requests or 100; the GPU was busy either way. Scaling on duty cycle is scaling blindly. Worse, vLLM and similar engines pre-allocate KV cache memory (up to --gpu-memory-utilization ). Memory usage stays near 90% even at one request. Memory-based HPA never scales down. 2026 replacement signals : Queue depth (number of requests waiting for prefill). KV cache utilization (what fraction of blocks are allocated to active sequences). Per-replica P99 TTFT (your SLA signal). Goodput (requests meeting all SLOs per second). NVIDIA Dynamo Planner and llm-d Workload Variant Autoscaler consume these signals and scale replicas. They replace HPA entirely for LLM serving. Idea 4 · When to use what Scale decision Tool Add/remove nodes Karpenter Schedule multi-GPU jobs KAI Scheduler Add/remove replicas Dynamo Planner / llm-d WVA (or custom HPA on queue depth) Choose GPU type Karpenter NodePool Preempt low-priority KAI Scheduler queues Idea 5 · Disaggregated prefill/decode complicates everything If you run disaggregated prefill/decode (Phase 17 · 17), you have two pod classes with different scaling triggers: prefill pods scale on queue depth, decode pods scale on KV cache pressure. llm-d exposes these as separate Services with per-role HPA. Do not try to put a single HPA in front of both. Idea 6 · Cold start matters here too Cold-start mitigation (Phase 17 · 10) is where node provisioning time becomes user-visible. Karpenter's 45-60 second warm-up plus a 20GB model load plus engine init means a from-zero request takes 2-5 minutes. Keep a warm pool ( min_workers=1 ) for SLO-critical paths, or use Modal-style checkpointing at application layer. Idea 7 · Numbers you should remember Karpenter node provisioning: ~45-60s vs Cluster Autoscaler ~90-120s (GPU nodes). KAI Scheduler prevents partial-allocation waste — 7-of-8 trap. DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL as HPA signal: broken; use queue depth or KV utilization. Karpenter WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized : terminates running GPU jobs. Use WhenEmpty + consolidateAfter: 1h for inference. Worked example Why "100% busy" says nothing about load Two replicas each report a GPU utilization of 100%. Replica A has 2 requests in flight and 0 queued. Its first token arrives in 300 ms. Replica B has 40 requests in flight and 120 queued. Its first token arrives in 9 s. The duty-cycle metric is identical, so an autoscaler that targets 70% utilization treats them the same: it adds replicas for both, or for neither. A queue-depth rule ("add one replica per 5 queued requests") leaves A alone and adds 24 replicas' worth of demand signal for B, capped by the cluster's limit. The duty-cycle metric saturates as soon as a GPU is used at all, which is exactly where scaling decisions start to matter. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✗ Memory-based autoscaling works for vLLM because memory grows with load. vLLM reserves most of the GPU memory for KV cache at start-up, so memory reads about 90% even with one request. ✓ Gang scheduling stops 7 of 8 GPUs from sitting idle while the 8th is found. ✓ Karpenter's WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized consolidation can evict a running model to save money. ✗ One autoscaler can serve prefill and decode pods of a disaggregated deployment. They bottleneck on different things: prefill on the queue, decode on KV cache pressure. Predict before you run code/main.py runs a one-hour bursty workload under three scaling rules. The duty-cycle rule dropped 1 request but left GPUs idle for 266 minutes: once any request runs, utilization reads above 70%, so it keeps adding replicas and rarely removes them. The queue-depth rule used about a fifth of the idle time but dropped 64 requests, because it removes replicas the moment the queue empties and cannot bring them back fast enough when the next burst arrives. Neither is right as written. A production rule scales up on queue depth or TTFT, keeps a warm floor, and waits several minutes before scaling down. Break it on purpose A team sets HPA to keep DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL at 70% for its vLLM service. In the morning rush it never scales up, and TTFT climbs to 10 seconds. What is HPA seeing, and what should it watch instead? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this lesson Three layers: Karpenter for nodes, KAI Scheduler for gang and topology-aware placement, an application signal for replicas. GPU duty cycle and GPU memory are poor scaling signals for LLM servers. Scale on queue depth, KV cache use, P99 TTFT or goodput. Keep a warm floor and a slow scale-down; new GPU capacity takes minutes. Do not let Karpenter consolidate running GPU nodes. Solutions Solution P1 · Duty cycle against queue depth In this simulation the duty-cycle rule drops 1 request and the queue-depth rule 64, the opposite of the lesson's claim, while duty cycle wastes about five times more idle GPU time. The difference comes from the scale-down logic: queue depth removes a replica whenever the queue is empty, so each burst meets too few warm replicas. Add a cooldown or a higher warm floor and queue depth keeps its low idle time without the drops. Solution P4 · Signals for prefill and decode Scale prefill pods on queue depth (requests waiting for their first forward pass), because prefill is compute-bound and its symptom is waiting. Scale decode pods on KV cache utilization, because decode is memory-bound and runs out of room for sequences before it runs out of compute. Solution B1 · Busy is not overloaded HPA sees 100% duty cycle from the first request onwards, which it reads as "above target", but once the replica count reaches its maximum or the metric is averaged across replicas, it cannot tell a slightly busy fleet from a drowning one. a1704: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Serving Engine Internals — PagedAttention, Continuous Batching, Chunked Prefill Lesson 17.4 75 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain PagedAttention as a KV cache allocator: blocks, block tables, and why fragmentation stays under 4% at production load. Diagram continuous batching at the iteration level: how finished sequences leave the batch and new ones join without draining. Describe chunked prefill in one sentence and name which latency metric it protects (hint: it is the ITL tail of concurrent decodes, not mean throughput). Check a vLLM feature combination against the compatibility matrix for your version before enabling every optimization at once. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 01 (Model Serving), Phase 11 (LLM Engineering) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy continuous batching scheduler). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Modern serving-engine throughput rests on three compounding defaults, not a single trick. PagedAttention is always on. Continuous batching injects new requests into the active batch between decode iterations. Chunked prefill slices long prompts so decode tokens never starve. Turn all three on and a Llama 3.3 70B FP8 on one H100 SXM5 pushes 2,200-2,400 tok/s at 128 concurrent — roughly 25% above vLLM's own default and 3-4x a naive PyTorch loop. This lesson reads the scheduler and attention kernel of vLLM — the Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means PagedAttention "the KV trick" Fixed-size block allocator for KV cache; fragmentation <4% Block table "the page table" Per-sequence map from logical token position to physical KV block Continuous batching "dynamic batching, but right" Admit/release decisions made every decode iteration Chunked prefill "prefill splitting" Break long prefill into 512-token slices interleaved with decode TTFT "first token time" Prefill + queue + network; dominated by prefill at long prompts ITL "inter-token latency" Time between consecutive decode tokens; dominated by batch size Goodput "throughput that meets SLO" Requests/sec that still hit TTFT and ITL targets (Phase 17 · 08 reports it as the share of requests) V1 scheduler "the new scheduler" vLLM's 2026 scheduler; runs continuous batching with chunked prefill --gpu-memory-utilization "the memory knob" Fraction of HBM reserved for KV blocks after weights and activations The problem In plain words first A model server answers many users at once by putting their requests into one batch and running them through the model together. The hard part is that requests have different lengths and arrive at different times. vLLM, the most used open-source server, does three things to keep the GPU full of useful work. PagedAttention stores each request's KV cache (the keys and values the model remembers for earlier tokens) in small fixed-size blocks, the way an operating system pages memory, so little is wasted. Continuous batching lets requests join and leave the batch after every generated token instead of waiting for the slowest one. Chunked prefill cuts a long prompt into slices so it does not freeze everyone else's output while it is read. A naive PyTorch serve loop runs one request at a time: tokenize, prefill, decode until EOS, return. At one user this works. At one hundred, it is a queue of patient people. The obvious fix — static batching — pads every request to the longest prompt in the window, pads every decode to the longest expected output, and stalls the whole batch on the slowest sequence. You pay for padding you never use, and fast requests wait for slow ones. vLLM solves three problems at once. PagedAttention stops KV cache fragmentation from eating 60-80% of GPU memory the way classic contiguous allocation does. Continuous batching lets requests join and leave the batch between each decode iteration, so the batch is always full of real work. Chunked prefill breaks a 32k-token prompt into ~512-token slices that interleave with decode, so a long prompt does not freeze every decode token on the GPU. The 2026 production default is all three on. You need to understand what each one does because the failure modes are all on the scheduler, not the model. Idea 1 · PagedAttention as a virtual memory system A KV cache is num_layers × 2 × num_heads × head_dim × seq_len × bytes_per_element per sequence. For Llama 3.3 70B at 8192 tokens, that is roughly 1.25 GB per sequence in BF16. If you pre-reserve 8192 slots for every request but the average request only uses 1500 tokens, you waste roughly 82% of the HBM you reserved. Classic batching pays this waste. PagedAttention borrows the idea from OS virtual memory. KV cache is not contiguous per sequence. It is allocated in fixed-size blocks (default 16 tokens). Each sequence has a block table that maps its logical token positions to physical block IDs. When a sequence grows past its allocated blocks, one more block is added. When it finishes, its blocks return to the pool. Fragmentation drops from 60-80% (classic) to under 4% (PagedAttention). You do not enable PagedAttention with a flag — it is the only allocator vLLM ships. The knob is --gpu-memory-utilization (default 0.9), which tells vLLM how much HBM to reserve for KV blocks after loading weights and activations. Idea 2 · Continuous batching at the iteration level The old "dynamic batching" waited for a window (say 10 ms) to fill a batch, then ran prefill + decode + decode + decode until every sequence finished. Fast sequences left early and sat idle while the GPU finished the slow ones. Continuous batching operates between each decode step. Call the set of running sequences the RUNNING list. At each iteration: Any sequence in RUNNING that just hit EOS or max_tokens is removed. The scheduler looks at the waiting queue. If there are free KV blocks, it admits new sequences (prefill or resumed). The forward pass runs on whatever is now in RUNNING , emitting one new token per sequence. The batch size is never padded to a fixed number. Sequences at different positions in their output share one fused forward. In 2026 vLLM this is called the V1 scheduler . The key invariant: the scheduler runs once per decode iteration, not once per request. Idea 3 · Chunked prefill protects the ITL tail Prefill is compute-bound. A 32k-token prompt on Llama 3.3 70B takes ~800 ms of pure prefill on one H100. While prefill runs, decode tokens for every other sequence in the batch wait. In a serving loop, the first-token latency (TTFT) of one long prompt becomes the inter-token latency (ITL) blip for dozens of other users. Chunked prefill splits prefill into fixed-size chunks (default 512 tokens) and schedules each chunk as a unit. Between chunks the scheduler can advance decode sequences by one token. You trade a small absolute prefill latency hit (a few ms per chunk) for much lower decode-time jitter. P99 ITL under mixed load drops from ~50 ms to ~15 ms in published benchmarks. Idea 4 · The three defaults interact All three features assume each other. PagedAttention gives the scheduler a fine-grained KV resource to trade against. Continuous batching needs that fine-grained resource so admitting a new sequence does not force a global reshuffle. Chunked prefill is a decision the scheduler makes on the same RUNNING list — it is one more scheduler policy, not a separate system. You do not need to know every flag. You need to know what the scheduler optimizes: goodput under KV-block budget, subject to chunked prefill slicing. Idea 5 · Check the compatibility matrix Check every feature combination against the compatibility matrix for your exact vLLM version before enabling all of them at once, because what composes changes between releases. In v0.18.0 the feature matrix marks speculative decoding as compatible with chunked prefill and prefix caching, and the speculative-decoding page lists two known incompatibilities: pipeline parallelism through v0.15.0, and draft-model speculation through v0.10.0. For the draft method itself, the 2026 default is often EAGLE-3 ( "method": "eagle3" ), covered in Phase 17 · 05. Idea 6 · Numbers you should remember Llama 3.3 70B FP8, H100 SXM5, 128 concurrent, all three on: 2,200-2,400 tok/s. Same model, default vLLM (no chunked prefill): ~1,800 tok/s. Same model, naive PyTorch forward loop: ~600 tok/s. KV fragmentation waste under PagedAttention at production load: <4%. P99 ITL under mixed load: ~15 ms with chunked prefill, ~50 ms without. Idea 7 · What the scheduler looks like Copy code/main.py is exactly this loop in stdlib Python with fake token counts and fake forward latency. Running it shows how chunked prefill keeps decode sequences alive during a long prefill. The same idea as a formula KV cache per sequence. For a model with layers, ​ key-value heads of size , stored in bytes per number, a sequence of tokens needs ​ ⋅ d ⋅ n ⋅ b The 2 counts keys and values. Reserving ​ tokens per request when it uses only wastes the fraction ​ of that reservation. Worked example Waste from reserving the maximum Llama 3.3 70B has 80 layers and 8 KV heads of size 128. In BF16 ( ), one token needs 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes, about 0.33 MB. Reserving 8,192 tokens per request: 8,192 × 0.33 MB ≈ 2.7 GB per request. A request that really uses 1,500 tokens fills 1,500 / 8,192 ≈ 18% of it; 82% is wasted. With 16-token blocks, the same request takes ⌈1500 / 16⌉ = 94 blocks = 1,504 slots: 4 slots of waste, about 0.3%. That difference in waste is the room continuous batching uses to fit more requests on one GPU. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Continuous batching runs the scheduler once per generated token, not once per request. ✗ Chunked prefill makes each long prompt finish faster. It makes the long prompt slightly slower; what it protects is everybody else's inter-token latency. ✓ --gpu-memory-utilization sets how much GPU memory vLLM reserves for KV blocks. ✗ Every vLLM feature can be switched on together in every version. Check the compatibility matrix for your version first. Predict before you run On a GPU, one decode step for 64 sequences takes barely longer than for 1, because reading the model's weights from memory dominates. Before you run the code below, guess how much more throughput a batch of 64 gives than a batch of 1. Batching pays because the dominant cost, reading the weights, is shared. Keep this in mind when you read the toy scheduler below: it charges a fixed 0.5 ms for every token in the batch, so batching cannot pay there the way it does on a GPU. Break it on purpose An engineer turns off chunked prefill because "it makes TTFT worse for our long prompts". Recap What to keep from this lesson PagedAttention allocates KV cache in 16-token blocks, cutting waste from most of the reservation to a few per cent. Continuous batching admits and releases requests after every token. Chunked prefill slices long prompts so decode keeps moving: better P99 ITL, not better throughput by itself. Batching pays because a decode step's cost is dominated by reading weights, shared by the whole batch. KV bytes per token = 2 · layers · KV heads · head size · bytes per number. Solutions Solution P1 · STATIC against CONTINUOUS In this toy the gap goes the wrong way: STATIC reaches about 4,000 tokens/s, CONTINUOUS under 900, because each decode step costs 0.5 ms per sequence and continuous mode is also capped by the KV block budget. On a real GPU, with near-constant step cost, continuous batching wins on decode efficiency: finished sequences leave immediately and new ones take their place instead of padding. Solution P4 · Fragmentation waste (a) Contiguous allocation at 8,192 tokens with a mean use of 1,500 wastes about 1 − 1,500 / 8,192 ≈ 82% of reserved KV memory. (b) With 16-token blocks, each request wastes on average half a block, 8 tokens of about 1,500, roughly 0.5%. Solution B1 · Stalls mid-sentence Without chunked prefill, each long prompt's prefill runs as one large step, and every decode sequence waits for it. Short chats see their tokens stop for hundreds of milliseconds whenever a long prompt arrives: the P99 inter-token latency jumps. Turn chunked prefill back on and, if long-prompt TTFT matters, raise the chunk size a little. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism Most explanations of continuous batching describe a prefill phase and a decode phase that take turns on the GPU. Describe what the vLLM scheduler does in one step instead. Where does chunked prefill come from in that design, and where do you read the value that controls it? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The scheduler asks the same question of every request: how many tokens does it still need to compute? Each step has a budget of tokens, set by --max-num-batched-tokens , and the running requests take their next token first. Waiting prompts fill the rest of the budget, so a long prompt is split over several steps, and chunked prefill needs no extra mechanism. One question for every request. A new request needs all of its prompt tokens. A running request needs one token, or more with speculative decoding. No prefill phase and no decode phase exist in the code, only a count of tokens still to compute. The order inside a step. Each running request gets the tokens it needs, up to the budget. Waiting requests are admitted while budget and room remain. --max-num-seqs caps the running requests. A prompt that does not fit the rest of the budget gets a part now and the rest in later steps. That is chunked prefill, and it is on by default because the budget design needs nothing else to support it. The default depends on the memory that vLLM reads. GPU memory that vLLM reads Budget, vllm serve Budget, LLM class --max-num-seqs , both 160 GiB or more 16,384 16,384 1,024 70 GiB or more, but not an A100 8,192 16,384 1,024 less, or unknown 2,048 8,192 256 The unified-memory machine in the manual has 121.69 GiB that the CPU and the GPU share, and its log still shows 2,048, the value for a small or unknown GPU. Read the value that your server uses before you change it. At 0.31.0 the log does not print the budget under its own name; find compile_ranges_endpoints in the engine config line, and the largest number in that list is the budget. Why decode goes first. Running requests come first so that a user who already sees a stream keeps seeing it. A new prompt waits for what is left. A smaller budget gives a smoother stream; a larger one gives a faster first token for long prompts. The small default of 2,048 is a choice for the stream. Why one budget. One budget for every kind of work keeps the scheduler simple. Prefix caching only lowers the count of tokens to compute. Speculative decoding only raises the count for a running request. The same loop serves all of them. The cost is that one number decides the balance between the first token and the stream, and no single value suits every workload. The lesson's toy scheduler uses a fixed 512-token chunk. The real engine has no separate chunk size at 0.31.0: the chunk is what is left of the budget in that step. Plausible wrong answers. "Chunked prefill is a flag you turn on." It follows from the budget: a prompt that does not fit the rest of the budget gets part now and the rest later, so it is on by default and has no separate mechanism. "New prompts go first so that the first token comes fast." Running requests take their tokens first so that a user who sees a stream keeps seeing it; a new prompt waits for the budget that is left. "The budget is 2,048 on every GPU." It depends on the memory that vLLM reads: 2,048 below 70 GiB, 8,192 at 70 GiB or more, and 16,384 at 160 GiB or more, and the offline LLM class uses larger values. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Prefix caching is on, and a request with a 2,048-token prompt finds 1,024 tokens in the cache. What does the scheduler count for it? Expected: 1,024 tokens still to compute; the cache only lowers the count, and the same loop serves the request. (level 3) A server with 121.69 GiB of unified memory logs a budget of 2,048. Why not 8,192? Expected: the default comes from the memory that vLLM reads, and the unified machine reads as small or unknown, so it gets the small value; read compile_ranges_endpoints before you change it. (level 4) Speculative decoding is on with three draft tokens. How does the budget rule change? Expected: it does not; a running request now needs more than one token per step, so its count rises, and the budget is spent in the same order. Where it is taught. Why one token budget replaces a prefill phase and the long prompts section give the rule and the defaults, and the serving engine internals lesson has the toy scheduler. Explain the mechanism Explain how vLLM keeps the KV cache in GPU memory. Why does it not give each request its own buffer, how does it recognize a prompt it has seen before, and what happens when the memory runs out? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The KV cache is one pool of 16-token blocks, and a request takes blocks one at a time as it grows, mapped by a small block table. A buffer per request wastes memory twice: on length that the request never reaches, and on gaps between requests of different sizes. Each full block gets a hash that is chained with the hash of the block before it, so one hash names a whole prefix, and a new request walks its chain and stops at the first miss. When no block is free, the scheduler preempts the newest request and computes it again later. Blocks, not buffers. At startup vLLM splits the cache into blocks of 16 tokens and keeps all of them in one pool. The blocks of a request do not need to be next to each other. A block table maps the token positions of the request to block numbers. The original paper called this PagedAttention, after the way an operating system pages memory. The lesson gives the size of the waste that this removes. A classic allocator that reserves the full length for every request loses 60 to 80 percent of the memory to fragmentation. With blocks the waste stays under 4 percent. For a 70B model at 8192 tokens, one reserved sequence is about 1.25 GB in BF16, and a request that uses 1500 tokens wastes about 82 percent of it. The hash chain. When a block fills, vLLM hashes its tokens together with the hash of the block before it. The chain means that one hash names a whole prefix, not only 16 tokens. The hash also covers the other inputs that change the keys and values: the LoRA adapter, the images in the prompt, and an optional salt for each request. A new request computes the same chain over its prompt and looks each hash up in a map. Every block before the first miss is a hit and needs no compute. Only full blocks are cached, so the tail of a prompt below 16 tokens is always computed. Since version 0.11 the hash is SHA-256 by default. A faster hash exists, and the documentation warns that a collision could return the wrong blocks or leak data between tenants. Eviction. A block that no request uses goes to a free list and keeps its hash. A later request with the same prefix can still use it. When vLLM needs a new block, it takes the head of the free list, the block unused the longest. Only then does the old content go away. So the cache is the pool: no separate cache memory exists, and a busy server keeps fewer old prefixes than an idle one. When memory runs out. A running request needs a new block every 16 tokens. If none is free, the scheduler preempts a request. Under the default first-come policy it picks the newest running request, frees all of its blocks, and puts it back at the head of the waiting queue. When the request runs again, vLLM computes its tokens again from the start. Older versions could also copy blocks to CPU memory and back; the current engine only recomputes, because the documentation judges that cheaper. The cost shows as a longer time for the preempted request and in the vllm:num_preemptions counter. Hybrid models. A model with sliding-window or state-space layers does not keep one entry per token in every layer. Each kind of layer gets its own group with its own page size and its own rule for a hit. The groups share one pool. Plausible wrong answers. "vLLM swaps preempted requests to CPU memory." Older versions could; the current engine only recomputes, because the documentation judges the recompute cheaper, and the cost shows in the time of that request and in the preemption counter. "The prefix cache has its own memory budget." The cache is the pool; a freed block keeps its hash on the free list until a new block is needed, so a busy server keeps fewer old prefixes than an idle one. "A block hash covers only its own 16 tokens." It is chained with the hash of the block before it, so one hash names a whole prefix, and it also covers the adapter, the images and the salt. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Every request starts with the same 25 tokens. How many of them come from the cache? Expected: 16, one full block; the last 9 tokens are computed on every request because only full blocks are cached. (level 3) Two tenants send the same system prompt. What can one learn about the other, and what field stops it? Expected: they share blocks, so the timing of one tenant can reveal what the other sent; a cache_salt per tenant goes into the hash, so the two never share a block. (level 4) Under the default policy, which request does vLLM preempt when no block is free, and what does it cost? Expected: the newest running request; all of its blocks are freed, it goes to the head of the waiting queue, and its tokens are computed again from the start, which the preemption counter records. Where it is taught. How the block pool manages KV memory explains the pool, the token budget section covers preemption, and the serving engine internals lesson gives the fragmentation numbers. Explain the mechanism A user sends a chat request to a serving engine and the answer streams back, slowly at first and then word by word. Describe what the GPU does from the moment the request arrives until the last token. Name the phases, and name the numbers you would put on a dashboard for each of them. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A request has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values into the KV cache, so the GPU is busy with math. Decode then writes one token per request per step, and each step reads all the weights to do it, so the GPU waits for memory. Four numbers measure them: TTFT for the wait before the first token, TPOT and ITL for the stream, and output tokens per second for the whole server. Prefill. Prefill handles many prompt tokens in one step. The keys and values of every prompt token go into the KV cache. The step does a lot of math for each byte it reads, so it is compute bound. A long prompt makes the first token late. Decode. Decode makes one new token for each running request in each step. The step reads all the model weights once to do that, whatever the batch size. The step moves many bytes for little math, so it is memory bound. This is why a bigger batch is almost free per step on a dense model: the weights are read once for all the requests in the step. The four numbers. Number What it measures Who feels it TTFT the wait from the request to the first token, mostly queue time and prefill the person who waits for the answer to start TPOT the mean time between tokens after the first one the person who reads a long answer ITL each gap between two tokens; its P99 shows the worst stalls the person who sees the stream stop and start Throughput output tokens per second for all users together the person who pays for the GPU Report the four together. A throughput number alone hides the latency that the users feel. What load does to them. The manual measured Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B with vLLM 0.31.0 from one user to 64 users at once: Users at once Median TTFT Median TPOT Output tokens per second 1 257 ms 32.3 ms 29.5 64 965 ms 243.8 ms 239.3 With 64 users the server wrote about eight times as many tokens per second. Each user waited almost four times as long for the first token, and each token took about 7.5 times longer. A busy server is cheaper per token and slower for each user. Every tuning choice moves one of these four numbers and costs another. One scheduler, not two stages. The engine does not run the two phases as separate stages. In vLLM, each scheduler step has one token budget. Running requests get their next decode token first. The rest of the budget goes to prompt tokens, in chunks. A prefill is only a request with many tokens left to compute. Plausible wrong answers. "Throughput is the number to optimize, and the rest follows." Throughput is what the GPU owner pays for; the users feel TTFT and the gaps between tokens, and at 64 users the manual's server wrote eight times the tokens while each user waited about 7.5 times longer per token. "Prefill and decode run as two separate stages inside the engine." The vLLM scheduler has one token budget per step; running requests get a decode token first and prompt chunks fill the rest, so the two phases mix in one step. "TPOT and ITL are the same number." TPOT is the mean time per output token for one request; ITL is each gap between two tokens, and its P99 shows the stalls that the mean hides. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which of the four numbers matters most to someone who reads a long answer? Expected: TPOT, the mean gap between tokens, together with the P99 ITL for the worst stalls. (level 2) Why is decode bound by memory and prefill by math? Expected: a decode step reads every weight to make one token per request, so the bytes moved dominate; a prefill step handles hundreds of prompt tokens per pass, so the math per byte is high. (level 3) In the manual's run, 64 users got about eight times the output of one user. Why do the cost per token and the wait per user move in opposite directions? Expected: each decode step reads the weights once for all running requests, so more requests share one read; each request then waits for a longer step. (level 4) The lesson describes a prefill phase and a decode phase. What does the vLLM scheduler have instead? Expected: one token budget per step; running requests take their next token first and prompt chunks fill the rest, so a prefill is a request with many tokens left to compute. Where it is taught. The request flow is in the vLLM 101 section on what happens to your request and in the serving engine internals lesson. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy acceptance-rate simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Speculative decoding pairs a fast draft model with the target model. The draft proposes K tokens; the target verifies in a single forward; accepted tokens are free. In 2026, EAGLE-3 is the production-grade variant — it trains a draft head on the target model's hidden states rather than on raw tokens, pushing acceptance rate alpha into the 0.6-0.8 band on general chat. The right question is not "how fast is the draft" but "what is alpha on my traffic?" If alpha drops below ~0.55, speculative decoding is net negative at high concurrency because eve Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Speculative decoding "draft plus verify" Propose K tokens with a cheap model, verify all K in one target forward Acceptance rate alpha "spec accept rate" Fraction of draft tokens accepted by the target; the only metric that matters Draft length K "spec k" How many tokens the draft proposes per target forward; typical 4-8 Verify overhead epsilon "spec overhead" Extra cost to verify-and-reroll vs a plain target forward; grows with batch EAGLE-3 "latest EAGLE" 2025-2026 variant; trains draft head on multiple target layers; alpha 0.6-0.8 on general chat speculative_config "vLLM spec config" The explicit opt-in in vLLM V1; no default means no acceleration N-gram spec decode "N-gram draft" GPU-side draft using N-gram lookups in the prompt; chunked-prefill-compatible Break-even alpha "no-op alpha" Alpha at which spec decode gives zero speedup; watch this at production concurrency Rejected-draft two-pass "reroll cost" Two target forwards when drafts reject; drives P99 tail The problem In plain words first When a model generates text, each new token needs one full pass through the model, and on a GPU that pass is slow mainly because all the weights must be read from memory. Speculative decoding uses that waiting time. A small, cheap draft guesses the next few tokens, and the big target model checks all the guesses in one pass. Every guess it agrees with is a token you got almost for free; at the first disagreement it writes the correct token and the round ends. The output is exactly what the target alone would have produced. How much you gain depends on the acceptance rate , the chance that a draft token is accepted. EAGLE-3 is a draft head trained on the target model's own internal states, which pushes up. Decode is memory-bound. On an H100 running Llama 3.3 70B FP8, each decode step reads all ~70 GB of weights from HBM and emits one token per sequence. The GPU compute is almost idle during decode — the bottleneck is HBM bandwidth, not matmul throughput. Speculative decoding exploits the gap. Generate K candidate tokens with a cheap draft model, then ask the target model to verify all K in a single forward pass. Each verified token is effectively free (amortized into a batch-of-K forward the target would have had to do anyway). The classic draft-model approach uses a smaller model of the same family (Llama 3.2 1B drafting for Llama 3.3 70B). It works but acceptance rate is mediocre — the smaller model distribution diverges from the target. EAGLE, then EAGLE-2, then EAGLE-3 train a light draft head directly on the target model's internal states, so the draft's distribution tracks the target much more closely. That is why alpha goes from 0.4 with draft-model to 0.6-0.8 with EAGLE-3. The catch: EAGLE-3 is opt-in in vLLM 2026. speculative_config must be set explicitly. No flag, no acceleration. Teams that flip it on without measuring alpha on their real traffic often see tail latency get worse, not better. Idea 1 · What speculative decoding actually buys Without spec decode, per-token cost is one target forward. With spec decode at draft length K and acceptance alpha, expected tokens per target forward is 1 + K * alpha . The speedup is (1 + K * alpha) / (1 + epsilon) where epsilon is draft-plus-verify overhead. For K=5, alpha=0.7: (1 + 5*0.7) / (1 + 0.1) = 4.5 / 1.1 = 4.1x . Real-world numbers cluster around 2-3x because alpha is rarely that high on production traffic and epsilon grows at high batch size. Idea 2 · Why alpha is the only metric that matters Rejected tokens do not disappear — they force a second target forward for the first rejected token. On a workload where alpha drops to 0.4, you pay draft overhead plus verification plus re-roll. At high concurrency (say 256 concurrent), the decode batch is already large enough that the memory-bandwidth gap between "target alone" and "target with verify" shrinks. Below alpha 0.55 on most 2026 hardware, spec decode is net negative. Alpha varies by workload. On ShareGPT-style general chat, EAGLE-3 trained on ShareGPT hits 0.6-0.8. On domain-specific traffic (code, medical, legal) the draft head trained on general data drops to 0.4-0.6. Training a domain-specific draft head recovers alpha — it is a light, quick training job compared to target finetuning. Phase 7 · 16 and Phase 10 · 15 quote higher values (0.85 and above). Those are per-token rates on chat benchmarks that match the draft's training data. Plan with the bands on this page and measure alpha on your own traffic. Idea 3 · EAGLE generations at a glance Classic draft model : small model of same family. Alpha 0.3-0.5. Infrastructure simple — two models loaded, draft runs K forwards per target forward. EAGLE-1 (2024) : single draft head trained on target hidden states (last layer). Alpha ~0.5-0.6. Small param overhead on top of target. EAGLE-2 (2025) : adaptive draft length and tree-based drafts (verify multiple branches in one target pass). Alpha ~0.6-0.7. More complex draft scheduler. EAGLE-3 (2025-2026) : draft head trained on multiple target layers (not just last), better alignment. Alpha ~0.6-0.8 on general chat. Idea 4 · The 2026 production recipe Ship target model plain. Measure baseline TTFT, ITL, throughput at target concurrency. Enable EAGLE-3 draft via vLLM speculative_config . Re-run the benchmark. Log acceptance rate alpha. vLLM V1 reports this as spec_decode_metrics.accepted_tokens_per_request . Divide by requested draft length to get alpha. If alpha < 0.55 on production traffic distribution, disable spec decode or train a domain-specific EAGLE-3 draft. At production concurrency, re-run. Confirm P99 ITL did not get worse. Idea 5 · The production pitfall: P99 tail Mean ITL drops with spec decode. P99 can get worse if you do not tune. Rejected drafts trigger a two-pass sequence (draft + verify-fail + reroll). Under full batch, those two passes serialize. Watch P99 ITL, not P50. Idea 6 · Where EAGLE-3 is already deployed Google deployed speculative decoding in AI Overviews in 2025 (same quality, faster response). vLLM V1 ships speculative_config as the documented interface, and its feature matrix marks speculative decoding as compatible with chunked prefill. SGLang supports EAGLE-3 as the recommended draft path for prefix-heavy workloads. Idea 7 · Break-even math in one line Expected speedup: S(alpha, K) = (1 + K*alpha) / (1 + verify_overhead) . Setting S = 1 solves for alpha: alpha_breakeven = verify_overhead / K . For typical verify_overhead ~0.15 and K=5: alpha_breakeven = 0.03 . But that is the raw decode math. At high concurrency the verify overhead rises and the decode batch already amortizes memory reads across sequences, so effective alpha_breakeven climbs to ~0.45-0.55 in practice. Idea 8 · When not to use speculative decoding Batch-1 offline generation where latency does not matter. Use plain target. Very short outputs (under 50 tokens). Draft overhead and verify cost dominate. Specialized domains without a domain-trained draft head. Alpha too low. Assuming every feature pair composes. Draft tokens; each is accepted with probability , and the round stops at the first rejection, where the target supplies one token itself. The expected number of tokens per target pass is + ⋯ + α K = 1 − α 1 − α K + 1 ​ The lesson's shortcut assumes every draft token is judged independently of the ones before it. Because one rejection discards everything after it, the true figure is lower. Worked example K = 5, α = 0.7 Shortcut: 1 + 5 × 0.7 = 4.5 tokens per pass. Correct: (1 − 0.7⁶) / (1 − 0.7) = (1 − 0.118) / 0.3 ≈ 2.94 tokens per pass. With a verify overhead of 15%, speedup ≈ 2.94 / 1.15 ≈ 2.6×, not the 3.9× the shortcut gives. That is why the lesson says to switch off below α ≈ 0.55 on real traffic: the gain shrinks fast and the tail gets worse.
