Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism Speculative decoding promises several tokens per step with no change to what the model writes. Explain how the engine keeps that promise, where the speedup comes from, and why the gain shrinks as more users share the server. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A cheap proposer guesses the next few tokens, and the target model runs once over all the guesses and computes its own distribution at every position. A rejection sampler keeps each guess that the target supports, samples a correct token from the target at the first rejection, and stops, so one pass gives at least one token and at most the number of guesses plus one, with the same output distribution as plain decoding. The gain comes from idle GPU time: a small decode batch waits for memory, and as the batch grows that idle time goes away, so the checks of rejected guesses start to cost real compute. Guess, then check. A decode step on a small batch reads all the weights to produce one token per request, and most of the GPU sits idle while it waits for memory. Speculation uses that idle time. With greedy sampling a guess stays only if it equals the top token of the target at that position. With random sampling the rejection rule keeps the output distribution equal to the target's distribution. In SGLang the accept thresholds default to 1.0, so a greedy request produces the same tokens it would produce without speculation. The acceptance length is the number of tokens committed per verify pass: the accepted drafts plus one bonus token from the target. One real Qwen3-8B request on our L4 got about 1.8 tokens per pass. The proposers. Method Where the guesses come from ngram earlier text in the same request that matches the last few tokens suffix a suffix tree over earlier prompts and answers eagle , eagle3 a small draft head that reads the hidden states of the target *_mtp extra prediction heads that come with some models draft_model a separate small model N-gram costs almost nothing and needs no extra weights. It pays when the answer copies the prompt: an edit of a document, a summary that quotes the source, a code change that keeps most lines, extraction from a long input. On our L4 with random prompts it cut the time per token from 241.7 to 76.6 ms at one user, and at four users the P99 ITL rose from 290 to 1,691 ms. It also turns off async scheduling, with only a warning in the log. An EAGLE3 head needs training for your target; the public head for Qwen3-8B has one layer and a draft vocabulary of 32,000 tokens. Why the gain falls with load. The idle time exists only while the step reads more memory than it computes. As the batch grows, the step does more compute for each byte, and the idle time goes away. The checks of rejected guesses then cost real compute. One report shows both ends on the same GPU and model: at batch 1 output went from 42.0 to 92.5 tokens per second, and at concurrency 20 it fell from 217.8 to 164.4. The maintainer's answer was that speculation is meant for small batches. The dynamic mode follows from this rule: it sets the number of guesses from the batch size and stops guessing for large batches. The lesson's arithmetic. Expected tokens per target forward are 1 + K x alpha, with K the draft length and alpha the acceptance rate. For K of 5 and alpha of 0.7, with about 10 percent verify overhead, that is 4.5 divided by 1.1, about 4.1 times. Real gains cluster around 2 to 3 times, because alpha is rarely that high on production traffic and the overhead grows with the batch. The lesson puts the break-even alpha at high concurrency near 0.45 to 0.55. What to watch. The engine exports the proposed and the accepted tokens. Divide accepted by proposed for the acceptance rate, and read the mean tokens per step. A high acceptance rate with no gain in the time per token means the batch is already compute bound. Plausible wrong answers. "Speculation changes the output a little, so you trade some quality for speed." With greedy sampling a guess stays only if it equals the target's top token, and with random sampling the rejection rule keeps the output distribution equal to the target's, so the quality does not change, although one sampled run can differ from a run without speculation. "The draft is where the speed comes from, so a faster draft always helps." The gain comes from idle GPU time in a small batch; a fast draft with low acceptance adds checks that cost compute, and at concurrency 20 one report lost a quarter of its throughput. "Turn it on for the stress test too." At batch 1 one report more than doubled its speed and at concurrency 20 it was slower; the maintainer's answer was that speculation is for small batches. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which proposer needs no extra model, and when does it pay? Expected: n-gram, which matches the last tokens of the output against earlier text in the request; it pays for edits, quotes, code changes and extraction, and fails on open chat. (level 3) Acceptance is high but the time per token did not fall. What does that tell you? Expected: the batch is already compute bound; the idle memory time that speculation uses is gone, so the checks cost as much as they save. (level 3) With greedy sampling, how does the check decide at each position? Expected: a guess stays only if it equals the top token of the target there; the first mismatch is replaced by the target's token and the rest are dropped. (level 4) Why can one verify pass never commit more tokens than the draft length plus one? Expected: the target computes a distribution at every draft position and one past the last guess, so when all guesses pass the sampler still draws one bonus token from that last distribution; at a rejection it samples a correct token there and stops. Where it is taught. a1706: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Prefix-Cache Serving — RadixAttention and KV Reuse Lesson 17.6 75 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Diagram RadixAttention: how prefixes are stored in a radix tree and how KV blocks are shared across sequences rooted at the same branch. Explain cache-aware scheduling and why FCFS is wrong for prefix-heavy traffic. Compute expected speedup for a workload given prefix-cache hit rate and prompt length distribution. Name the prompt-ordering discipline that makes the 6.4x number real vs a lost upside. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals), Phase 14 (Agentic RAG) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy radix-tree cache + cache-aware scheduler). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Treat the KV cache as a first-class, reusable resource stored in a radix tree, and scheduling changes with it: instead of FCFS (first-come, first-served) as vLLM schedules, a cache-aware scheduler prioritizes requests with longer shared prefixes — effectively a depth-first radix traversal so hot branches stay resident in HBM. SGLang is the engine that built serving around this idea. On Llama 3.1 8B with ShareGPT-like 1K prompts, SGLang hits ~16,200 tok/s to vLLM's ~12,500, a ~29% edge. On prefix-heavy RAG workloads the advantage reaches 6 Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means RadixAttention "the SGLang thing" KV cache indexed as a radix tree so shared prefixes reuse blocks Radix tree "compact trie" Tree where each node owns a token range and its KV blocks Cache-aware scheduler "hot-branch-first" Scheduler that prefers requests sharing the resident branch Prefix-cache hit rate "how much of your prompt was free" Fraction of prompt tokens served from reused KV blocks FCFS "first-come first-served" Default scheduling that breaks prefix locality Branch-level LRU "evict the leaf" Eviction policy matched to radix shape Prompt template ordering "the cache key" The prompt's component order determines what the tree can share System prompt pinning "resident prefix" Keep the immutable system portion pinned to avoid eviction thrash The problem In plain words first Many requests to the same model start with the same text: the same system prompt, the same tool descriptions, the same retrieved document. Reading that shared beginning (the prefix ) costs the same work every time. Prefix caching keeps the KV cache computed for a prefix and reuses it, so only the new part of each prompt needs reading. SGLang's RadixAttention stores cached prefixes in a radix tree , a tree where each path from the root spells out a sequence of tokens. A new request walks down the tree as far as its tokens match and reuses everything on that path. Two things decide how much you save: whether your prompts put the shared parts first in a fixed order, and whether the scheduler serves requests that share a branch together, so that branch stays in memory. Classic serving treats each request's prompt as opaque. Even when 5,000 RAG requests all start with the same 2,000-token system prompt plus same retrieval preamble, vLLM prefills that 2,000-token prefix 5,000 times. The GPU does the same work over and over. The observation: prompts in agentic and RAG workloads share long prefixes almost always. System prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples, retrieval headers, conversation history — all repeat across requests. If you stored the KV cache for that prefix once and reused it, you would not prefill it again. RadixAttention does exactly this. Tokens are indexed in a radix tree; each node owns KV blocks for the token sequence on its path from root. A new request walks the tree: any node whose token matches re-uses that node's KV blocks. Prefill cost becomes proportional to the "new" suffix, not the full prompt. The challenge is scheduling. If two requests share a 2,000-token prefix and a third shares only 200 tokens of the same prefix, you want to serve the two long-shared requests together so the long prefix stays in HBM. FCFS does the opposite — it serves whoever arrived first, potentially evicting the hot branch before the next long-prefix request hits. Idea 1 · The radix tree as a KV index A radix tree (compact trie) stores token sequences. Each node owns a token range and the KV blocks computed for that range. Children extend the sequence one or more tokens. Copy A new request comes in with system prompt + "Context: " + "Question: Carol". The scheduler walks: system prefix matches (124 blocks reused), doc-A branch matches (31 blocks reused), then allocates fresh blocks only for "Question: Carol" (4 blocks). Prefill cost: 4 blocks of new tokens. Without the tree: 160 blocks. ~40x savings on prefill. Idea 2 · Cache-aware scheduling Radix-tree-backed reuse is pointless if the cache churns. Two key policies: Depth-first dispatch . When picking the next request from the queue, prefer requests rooted at the same branch as the current running set. This keeps the hot branch pinned. LRU at branch level, not block level . Evict whole branches (starting from shortest-used leaves) rather than individual blocks, so cache shape matches radix shape. FCFS violates both. A request sharing 2,000 tokens sits behind a request sharing 50, then the 2,000-token branch gets evicted to admit the 50-token one. Idea 3 · Benchmark numbers you should memorize Llama 3.1 8B, H100, ShareGPT 1K prompts: SGLang ~16,200 tok/s vs vLLM ~12,500 (~29% edge). Prefix-heavy RAG (same system + same doc, varying question): up to 6.4x on SGLang. Voice cloning workloads: 86.4% prefix-cache hit rate. Production hit rates across SGLang customers: 50-99% depending on prompt discipline. Deployed on 400,000+ GPUs in 2026. Idea 4 · The ordering gotcha The 6.4x number relies on consistent prompt-template ordering. If your client constructs prompts as [system, tools, context, history, question] in some requests and [system, context, tools, history, question] in others, the tree cannot find the shared prefix. What looks like a shared prefix to a human is two distinct sequences to the radix tree. Engineer's lever: your prompt template is a cache key. Fix the order. Put everything immutable (system, tools, schemas) first. Put retrieval context next. Put user question last. Do not interleave dynamic content into the prefix. Real case from the research: moving dynamic content out of the cacheable prefix took one deployment from 7% to 74% cache hit rate in one change. Idea 5 · Where RadixAttention wins and loses Wins: - RAG (same retrieval preamble, varying question). - Agents (same tool schemas, varying query). - Chat with long system prompt. - Voice / vision workloads with repeated preambles. Loses (returns to vLLM-level throughput): - Single-shot generation with unique prompts (code completion, open-ended chat without system prompt). - Dynamic prompts where every request interleaves unique content into the prefix. Idea 6 · Why this is a scheduler problem, not just a kernel problem You can implement KV reuse as a kernel trick. SGLang's insight is that reuse only pays if the scheduler keeps the hot branch resident. A naive "reuse if available" policy will churn the cache under mixed load. The radix-tree-indexed scheduler is what turns the kernel trick into a 29% production edge. Idea 7 · Interplay with vLLM The two systems are not strict competitors. In 2026 vLLM added prefix caching ( --enable-prefix-caching ) and a cache-aware router (vLLM Router in Rust). The gap closed but did not fully disappear — SGLang's whole stack is radix-first; vLLM grafted it on. For workloads dominated by prefix reuse, SGLang remains the default. For general-purpose serving without strong prefix patterns, vLLM remains equal or better. Worked example What a 2,000-token shared prefix saves A RAG service sends 5,000 requests. Each prompt is a 2,000-token system prompt, a 500-token document (one of 10 documents) and an 80-token question. Without caching: 5,000 × 2,580 = 12.9 million prompt tokens to prefill. With a radix cache that keeps everything resident: the system prompt once (2,000), each document once (10 × 500 = 5,000), every question (5,000 × 80 = 400,000). About 407,000 tokens. Saving: 1 − 0.407 / 12.9 ≈ 97% of prefill work. If half the clients put the document before the system prompt, those requests share nothing with the others, and the saving for them drops to the document alone. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Your prompt template is a cache key: the order of its parts decides what can be shared. ✗ Prefix caching helps code completion with unique prompts. With no shared beginning there is nothing to reuse. ✓ Evicting whole branches keeps the cache shaped like the tree. ✗ Prefix reuse only needs a fast kernel. It pays only if the scheduler keeps hot branches resident instead of churning them. Recap What to keep from this lesson Shared prefixes are common in RAG, agents and chat; reusing their KV cache skips most prefill. RadixAttention indexes cached prefixes in a radix tree and reuses the longest match. Fixed template order, immutable parts first, is the biggest lever. Cache-aware scheduling and branch-level eviction keep hot prefixes resident. vLLM's prefix caching narrows the gap; SGLang is radix-first throughout. Solutions Solution P1 · FCFS against cache-aware On the fixed-order workload there is no delta: both reach 69.1%, because the whole working set fits in the toy cache. The delta appears only under pressure, on the scrambled workload (8.4% against 26.5%), and it comes from prefill savings: cache-aware scheduling serves requests from a branch while that branch is resident. Solution P5 · An 8% hit rate Three likely causes: (1) dynamic content at the start of the prompt (timestamps, request IDs, user names), found by diffing two prompts token by token; (2) inconsistent ordering of system, tools and context between clients, found by grouping prompts by their first 200 tokens; (3) cache too small for the working set, found by checking eviction counts against the number of distinct prefixes. Solution B1 · A timestamp first The timestamp changes every second, so no two requests share even their first token, and everything after it, system prompt and tools included, cannot be reused. Move the timestamp to the end, next to the user's question, or drop seconds. The fixed parts then form a shared prefix again. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A team runs long agent sessions on SGLang with hierarchical caching on. Their dashboards show #cached-token: 0 on requests that resend a long history. They have tuned the cache tiers and the write policy, and the hit rate barely moves. The prompt template looks stable to them. Where do you look first, and what do you expect to find? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Look at the first tokens of the request as the server sees them, not at the template. A relay or a chat template often adds something that changes on every request near the start, such as a request ID, a session hash or the date, and the tree matches from the first token and stops at the first difference. In the manual's incident a random hash in the system prompt cost 27.6 points of hit rate, and removing it moved the engine hit rate from 66.8 to 94.4 percent. Reproduce it with one identifier in three places. The manual's capture kit sends one 2,999-token system prompt and a short question, five times in each of three forms, with --enable-cache-report on so that each response reports its cached tokens: Form Cached tokens Prompt tokens Median TTFT stable system prompt 2,998 2,999 45.1 ms random ID at the start 5 3,034 1,255.3 ms the same ID at the end 2,985 3,028 88.2 ms The ID at the start made the first token 28 times slower. The ID at the end cost 43 ms. The tokens are almost the same in the three forms; only their order differs. The ID at the start matched the 5 tokens before the random hex digits and nothing after them. Why nothing after a change can match. The attention values of every later token depend on every earlier token. A cache that reused the later tokens would return wrong answers. So the tree is exact, and a change in the system prompt invalidates everything behind it, while a change in the newest message invalidates only that message. The incident behind the question. The reporter found three causes stacked on each other: The relay put a per-session random hash and a rotating system message into every request. Removing them moved the engine hit rate from 66.8 to 94.4 percent. The client wrote its task-list snapshot at the end of the system prompt. Every task update changed the system prompt and invalidated more than 100,000 tokens of history behind it. Hierarchical cache load-back, when it found no room, evicted the prefixes of other sessions. The reporter counted 250,000 evict calls against 376 completed load-backs. The first fix was a prompt edit. No cache flag could have recovered the 27.6 points that the hash cost. The lesson tells the same story from another deployment, where moving dynamic content out of the cacheable prefix took the hit rate from 7 to 74 percent. The order of checks. Dump the exact token sequence of two consecutive requests and compare them from the first token. Include what the relay and the chat template add. Read cached_tokens in the usage block with --enable-cache-report , or in meta_info of the native /generate route. Read #new-token and #cached-token in the Prefill batch lines. Read sglang:cache_hit_rate from /metrics . With several servers, check routing. A request that lands on a server without its prefix misses whatever the prompt looks like. One report moved from 64.7 to 92.1 percent by routing each conversation to the same server. Two server settings look like prompt problems. A request for prompt log probabilities from position k can reuse only the first k tokens. Different LoRA adapters never share tree nodes, because the adapter is part of the tree key. Plausible wrong answers. "Raise the hierarchical cache ratio until the hit rate recovers." No cache flag can recover a miss that starts at token 5; the first fix was a prompt edit, worth 27.6 points of hit rate. "The template is stable, so the prompt is stable." The template is not what the server sees; a relay, a gateway or the chat template can insert a hash, a date or a snapshot, so compare the token sequences of two consecutive requests from the start. "A changed field in the middle only costs the tokens of that field." Every token after the change is a different branch of the tree, because the attention values of later tokens depend on every earlier token. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) The same random ID moves behind the fixed text instead. What does it cost now? Expected: about 45 tokens of prefill instead of about 3,027; in the experiment that was 43 ms more than the stable prompt instead of 28 times longer. (level 3) After the prompt fix, one server hits well and the fleet still misses. What next? Expected: routing; a request that lands on a server without its prefix misses, and routing each conversation to the same server moved one report from 64.7 to 92.1 percent. (level 4) The host tier still hurts other sessions after the prompt fix. What did the incident count, and what does it mean? Expected: 250,000 evict calls against 376 completed load-backs; a load-back that finds no room evicts other sessions from the GPU pool, so the pool size and the write policy need a look only after the prompt is fixed. Debug a failure Every request to your service starts with the same long system prompt, and the prefix cache is on. The server reports almost no cached tokens, and the first token is slow. Last week a teammate added a request ID to the start of the system prompt for tracing. What happened, and what do you change? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The prefix cache matches a prompt from its first token and stops at the first token that differs. A new ID at the start makes every later token a miss, so the server computes the whole prompt again on each request. Move the parts that never change to the front and put the ID after them. Then prove the fix with the cached-token counters. Why the position matters. The attention values of each token depend on every token before it. So a cache can reuse a token only when the whole prefix before it is the same. The SGLang radix tree compares tokens from the first one and stops at the first difference. vLLM does the same with blocks of 16 tokens. It caches only full blocks and stops at the first block that differs. What it costs. The SGLang manual measured one system prompt of 2,999 tokens in three layouts: Layout Median TTFT Median cached tokens The same prompt every time 45.1 ms 2998.0 A random ID at the start 1255.3 ms 5 The same ID at the end 88.2 ms 2985 With the ID at the start, only the 5 tokens before the random digits matched. The first token took 28 times longer. With the ID at the end, the cost was 43 ms. The fix. Put the parts that never change first: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the fixed instructions. Put the parts that change rarely next, such as the documents of one session. Put the parts that change on every request last: the user question, the time and the request ID. Send the trace ID in a header or a request field, not in the prompt text. Check the chat template too. Some templates put the date into the system prompt. The proof. On vLLM, read vllm:prefix_cache_hits and vllm:prefix_cache_queries from /metrics . The hits divided by the queries is the hit rate. On SGLang, start the server with --enable-cache-report and read usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens in each response. A good layout shows almost every prompt token as cached after the first request. Plausible wrong answers. "Give the cache more memory." A bigger pool keeps more blocks, but a prompt that differs at the first tokens has no block to reuse. "The cache matches the longest shared part anywhere in the prompt." The cache matches only from the first token, so a shared part after a difference never hits. "Turn on hierarchical caching." A second tier stores more prefixes. It cannot match a prefix that is different on every request. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) The hit rate is still low after the fix. What is the next cause to check? Expected: a full pool, because the cache keeps old blocks only until a running request needs the memory. (level 2) Where in a chat request does a change cost the least? Expected: in the newest message, because the template puts it last, so only that message is computed again. (level 3) Two tenants send the same system prompt. What is the risk, and what is the control in vLLM? Expected: one tenant can learn from timing what the other sent. Send a different cache_salt for each tenant, so that their requests never share blocks. (level 3) A team tunes the cache tiers and the eviction policy, and the hit rate does not move. What do you check first? Expected: the prompt text, for a value that changes on each request near the start, such as a random hash or a timestamp. Where it is taught. Explain the mechanism Every request to your chat service repeats the same long system prompt, and the engine has prefix caching on by default. What decides whether the next request reuses the work of the last one? How would you lay out the prompt, and how do you show a hit with a number instead of a guess? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The cache matches tokens from the first one onward and stops at the first difference, so a hit needs the same tokens in the same order at the start of the prompt. Put the parts that never change first, the parts that change per session next, and the question, the time and any request ID last. Prove the hit from the server: the cached_tokens field in the usage block, the #cached-token count in the prefill log line, or the prefix cache counters in /metrics . What a hit saves. On our L4 with Qwen/Qwen3-8B, vLLM 0.31.0 ran 4 groups of 16 prompts at 8 users. The prompts in a group shared a system prompt of the length in the table, then added a 128-token question and asked for 64 tokens back. Shared prompt tokens Median TTFT, cache on Median TTFT, cache off none 408 ms 392 ms 256 488 ms 753 ms 1,024 396 ms 1,213 ms 2,048 410 ms 2,550 ms 4,096 375 ms 13,353 ms With the cache on, the first token took about 400 ms at every length. Without it, the first token grew with the shared part, because every request computed the whole prompt again. The 1,024 row is the cleanest comparison, because both runs held 1,410 MHz or more; there the cache cut the first token about 3 times and gave 50 percent more output. SGLang on the same card gave the same shape: 479 ms against 14,706 ms at 4,096 shared tokens, with the cache-off run throttled to 930 MHz. Why the order decides. The attention values of every token depend on every earlier token. A cache that reused tokens after a change would return wrong answers, so prefix caching is exact by design and unforgiving by the same design. In vLLM the match runs one 16-token block at a time and only full blocks are cached: a shared part of 20 tokens gives one cached block, and the last 4 tokens are computed every time. In SGLang the radix tree matches token by token, and the last prompt token always goes through prefill, because the model needs its logits to sample the first output token. A 2,999-token prompt reported 2,998 cached tokens. The order. The parts that never change: the system prompt, the tool definitions in a fixed order, the fixed instructions. The parts that change rarely: the documents of one session, the earlier turns, sent unchanged. The parts that change on every request: the user question, the time, the request ID. Check the chat template too. Some templates put the date into the system prompt. A JSON object whose keys change order is a different token sequence. Prove the hit. vLLM: vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total divided by vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total from /metrics , and the log line that prints Prefix cache hit rate , which read 87.2 percent in the middle of the shared-prefix run. SGLang: start with --enable-cache-report and read cached_tokens in the usage block, read #cached-token and #new-token in every Prefill batch line, or read the sglang:cache_hit_rate gauge, which read 0.94 after the shared-prefix benchmark and 0.0 with the cache off. If the hit rate is low, the prompt order is almost always the cause. A full pool is the next cause, because the cache keeps old blocks only until a running request needs the memory. Routing is the third: with several servers, a request that lands on a server without its prefix misses whatever the prompt looks like, and one report moved its hit rate from 64.7 to 92.1 percent by routing each conversation to the same server. Keep tenants apart. Two users with the same prefix share blocks, and the timing of one can reveal what the other sent. A cache_salt field per tenant goes into the block key, so different salts never share. The LoRA adapter is part of the key too. Plausible wrong answers. "The cache is on, so repeated prompts hit it." The match is exact from the first token; a timestamp, a request ID or a reordered tool list near the start makes every later block miss, and one random ID at the start matched only 5 tokens of a 3,034-token prompt. "Put the user question first so the model reads it first." The question changes on every request, so the shared system prompt behind it never matches; put the fixed part first and the question last. "Turn the cache off for a fair benchmark." The cache is on in production, so the test must reset it between runs, not remove it; with it off the first token at 4,096 shared tokens took 13,353 ms on vLLM and 14,706 ms on SGLang. "Measure the hit rate from the response time of the client." Read it from the server, in the usage block, the prefill line or the counters; a faster second response can also come from a warmer GPU. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) On vLLM every request starts with the same 20 tokens. How many come from the cache? Expected: 16, one full block; the last 4 are computed each time because only full blocks are cached. (level 3) The prompt is stable, one server hits well, and the fleet still misses. Name two causes outside the prompt. Expected: a full pool that drops blocks before the next request arrives, and a router that sends a session to a server which never saw its prefix; sticky routing moved one report from 64.7 to 92.1 percent. (level 3) Why does SGLang report 2,998 cached tokens for a 2,999-token prompt and never 2,999? Expected: the last prompt token always goes through prefill, because the model needs its logits to sample the first output token. (level 4) A client writes a task-list snapshot at the end of the system prompt and updates it on every turn. What does the tree do? Expected: every update changes the system prompt, so every token after it misses, including the whole history behind it; in the manual's incident that invalidated more than 100,000 tokens per turn, and the fix is to move the snapshot behind the history or into request metadata. Where it is taught. Make repeated prompts hit the prefix cache, Prefix-friendly prompts and RadixCache measure the cache on both engines, and the RadixAttention lesson gives the ordering rule. Compute the HBM footprint of a frontier model under BF16, FP8, and NVFP4 and reason about where the savings come from. Name the Blackwell-specific features TRT-LLM exploits (day-0 FP4, MTP, disaggregated serving, all-to-all primitives). Decide when TRT-LLM's NVIDIA-lock is worth the 7x cost gap vs vLLM on Hopper. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals), Phase 10 · 13 (Quantization) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy FP8/NVFP4 memory and cost calculator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Hardware-specialized inference compilation trades portability for throughput, and TensorRT-LLM — NVIDIA-only, tuned for Blackwell — is the clearest example of the trade paying off. On GB200 NVL72 with Dynamo orchestration, SemiAnalysis InferenceX measured $0.012 per million tokens on a 120B model in Q1-Q2 2026, against $0.09/M on H100 + vLLM — a 7x economic gap. The stack compounds two floating-point formats with two serving techniques: FP8 stays critical for KV cache and attention kernels because it has the dynamic r Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means FP8 "eight-bit float" 8-bit floating point; used for KV cache and attention due to dynamic range NVFP4 "four-bit micro" NVIDIA's 4-bit microscaling FP format; weights and activations on Blackwell MXFP8 "MX eight" Microscaling FP8 variant; hardware-accelerated on Blackwell Tensor Cores Day-0 FP4 "ship FP4 weights" Model providers release weights already in FP4; no post-train conversion step MTP "multi-token prediction" TRT-LLM's integrated speculative-decoding draft (Phase 17 · 05) Disaggregated serving "split prefill/decode" Prefill and decode on separate GPU pools; KV transferred over NVLink/IB All-to-all "MoE expert comm" Communication pattern routing tokens to expert GPUs; NVLink 5 cuts 3x InferenceX "SemiAnalysis inference bench" The 2026 industry-accepted cost-per-token benchmark The problem In plain words first The cost of each generated token depends on four choices stacked on top of each other: the GPU generation (NVIDIA's Hopper H100/H200 or the newer Blackwell B200/GB200), the precision the numbers are stored in (16-bit, 8-bit FP8 or 4-bit NVFP4), the serving engine (vLLM, SGLang, or NVIDIA's own TensorRT-LLM), and the orchestration around it (NVIDIA Dynamo splits work across GPUs). Each choice multiplies the others. Fewer bits per weight means less memory to read for every token, and reading memory is what limits generation speed. The catch: the cheapest combination only exists on NVIDIA hardware with NVIDIA's closed software, and 4-bit weights can hurt quality on reasoning tasks, so you trade portability and some accuracy for price. The frontier of inference economics in 2026 is "how many tokens per dollar". The answer depends on four stacked choices: hardware generation (Hopper H100/H200 vs Blackwell B200/GB200), precision (BF16 → FP8 → NVFP4), serving engine (vLLM vs SGLang vs TRT-LLM), and orchestration (plain vs disaggregated vs Dynamo). On Hopper with vLLM, a 120B MoE runs at ~$0.09 per million tokens. On Blackwell with TRT-LLM + Dynamo, the same model runs at ~$0.012 — 7x cheaper. Some of that gap is hardware (Blackwell is 11-15x per-GPU LLM throughput vs Hopper). Some is the stack: FP4 weights, MTP draft, disaggregated prefill/decode, and NVLink 5 all-to-all for MoE expert communication. You cannot replicate this outside NVIDIA's stack. That is the tradeoff — portability for economics. Understanding which stack choices give which share of the gap is the point of this lesson. Idea 1 · Why FP8 is still the floor for KV cache A common mistake in 2026: assuming NVFP4 applies everywhere. It does not. KV cache needs FP8 (8-bit floating point) because it stores attention keys and values that span a wide dynamic range. Quantizing KV to FP4 causes catastrophic accuracy loss — the tail of the distribution drops off and attention scores collapse. FP8's exponent bits give KV cache the range it needs. NVFP4 (2025-2026) applies to weights and activations. Microscaling: each block of weights has its own scale factor so small blocks can span different dynamic ranges without per-tensor scale loss. For activations, FP4 holds up because activations are small-range within a layer. The typical Blackwell config: Weights: NVFP4 (4-bit microscaling). Activations: NVFP4. KV cache: FP8. Attention accumulator: FP32 (softmax stability). Idea 2 · The Blackwell-specific primitives TRT-LLM uses Day-0 FP4 weights : model providers ship FP4 weights directly; TRT-LLM loads without post-training conversion. No AWQ / GPTQ step for FP4. Multi-token prediction (MTP) : same idea as EAGLE (Phase 17 · 05) but integrated into the TRT-LLM build. Disaggregated serving : prefill and decode on separate GPU pools, KV cache transferred over NVLink or InfiniBand. Same idea as Dynamo (Phase 17 · 20). All-to-all communication primitives : NVLink 5 cut MoE expert communication latency by 3x vs Hopper. TRT-LLM's MoE kernels are tuned for this. NVFP4 + MXFP8 microscaling : hardware-accelerated scale-factor handling on Blackwell Tensor Cores. Idea 3 · The numbers you should memorize HGX B200 at $0.02/M tokens on GPT-OSS-120B via TRT-LLM. GB200 NVL72 at $0.012/M tokens via Dynamo (orchestrating TRT-LLM). H100 + vLLM ≈ $0.09/M tokens on comparable workload. 2.8x throughput gain in three months of TRT-LLM updates (2026). 11-15x per-GPU LLM throughput, Blackwell vs Hopper. MLPerf Inference v6.0 (April 2026): Blackwell dominates every submitted task. Idea 4 · What FP4 actually costs in quality NVFP4 is aggressive. On reasoning-heavy workloads (chain-of-thought, math, code-gen with long context), FP4 weights degrade visibly. Per-block calibration mitigates but does not eliminate. Teams shipping reasoning models often use FP8 weights + FP4 activations as a compromise, or stick to H200 with FP8 throughout. The rule: always validate task quality on your eval set before committing to NVFP4 weights. Idea 5 · Why this is an NVIDIA-lock decision TRT-LLM is C++ + CUDA + closed-source kernels. Models need to be compiled for a specific GPU SKU. No AMD, no Intel, no ARM. If your infra strategy is multi-vendor, TRT-LLM is a non-starter for the TRT-LLM-served tier — you can still serve from vLLM on mixed hardware. If you are NVIDIA-only, the 7x gap pays for the lock. Idea 6 · 2026 practical recipe For a $100M+ annual inference bill, running on Hopper + vLLM leaves 7-10x on the table. Migrate cost-dominant workloads to Blackwell + TRT-LLM + Dynamo. Keep experimentation tier on H100 + vLLM for model iteration speed. Validate quality on each NVFP4-converted model before production. Idea 7 · The disaggregation bonus TRT-LLM's disaggregated serving (separate prefill and decode pools) is covered in depth in Phase 17 · 20. On Blackwell, the multiplier stacks: FP4 weights × MTP speedup × disaggregated placement × cache-aware routing. The 7x number assumes this full stack. The same idea as a formula The memory-bandwidth ceiling for decode. At batch size 1, generating a token reads every active weight once. With ​ active parameters stored at bytes each and memory bandwidth bytes per second, ​ ⋅ b B ​ Halving (16-bit → 8-bit → 4-bit) doubles the ceiling; a mixture-of-experts model reads only its active experts, so ​ is what counts, not the total. Worked example A 70B dense model, one request at a time H100, BF16: bandwidth about 3.35 TB/s; weights 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB, more than one 80 GB GPU holds, so it needs at least two, but the per-token read is still 140 GB. Ceiling ≈ 3,350 / 140 ≈ 24 tokens/s. H100, FP8: 70 GB per token. Ceiling ≈ 48 tokens/s. B200, NVFP4 weights: about 8 TB/s and 35 GB per token. Ceiling ≈ 8,000 / 35 ≈ 229 tokens/s. So precision gives 2× twice over, and the hardware another 2.4×. The rest of the "7×–15×" figures quoted for Blackwell come from batching, multi-token prediction and disaggregated serving on top. Solution P5 · 405B at 128k context Weights: 405B × 0.5 bytes ≈ 203 GB. KV cache for Llama 3.1 405B (126 layers, 8 KV heads of 128) in FP8: 2 × 126 × 8 × 128 × 1 byte ≈ 258 KB per token, so 128k tokens ≈ 33 GB per sequence. About 236 GB for one sequence, well within a GB200 NVL72 rack (72 GPUs, about 13 TB of HBM), and even within two B200s. a1708: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Inference Metrics — TTFT, TPOT, ITL, Goodput, P99 Lesson 17.8 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Define TTFT, TPOT, ITL, E2E, throughput, and goodput precisely and name the component each one measures. Explain why mean is the wrong statistic for LLM serving and how to read P50/P90/P99. Construct an SLO multi-constraint (e.g. TTFT<500 ms AND TPOT<15 ms AND E2E<2 s) and compute goodput against it. Name two benchmark tools that disagree on TPOT for the same run and explain why. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy percentile calculator and goodput reporter). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Five metrics decide whether an inference deployment is working. TTFT is prefill plus queue plus network. TPOT (often reported as ITL, though tools disagree on whether ITL counts the first token) is the memory-bound decode cost per token. End-to-end latency is TTFT plus TPOT times output length. Throughput is tokens per second aggregated across the fleet. But the one that matters for product is goodput — the fraction of requests that met every SLO simultaneously. High throughput at low goodput means you are processing tokens that never reac Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means TTFT "time to first token" Queue + network + prefill; dominated by prefill at long prompts TPOT "time per output token" Memory-bound decode cost per token after first ITL "inter-token latency" Same as TPOT in most tools (not all — see GenAI-Perf) E2E "end to end" TTFT + TPOT * output_len; response-side network on top Throughput "tok/s" Fleet efficiency; useless without latency percentiles Goodput "SLO-met rate" Fraction of requests meeting every SLO constraint simultaneously P99 "tail" 1-in-100 worst-case latency; the user experience metric SLO multi-constraint "the joint" AND of all three latency bounds; a request fails if any one is violated GenAI-Perf vs LLMPerf "the tool trap" Tools disagree on whether ITL includes TTFT The problem In plain words first "How fast is the model?" has several answers, and each one hides different problems. TTFT (time to first token) is how long a user waits before anything appears; long prompts and queues make it worse. TPOT or ITL (time per output token, inter-token latency) is the gap between streamed tokens once they start. E2E latency is the whole request. Throughput is tokens per second across all users, which says the fleet is busy but not that anyone is happy. Goodput is the share of requests that met every target at once: first token fast enough, tokens steady enough, whole answer quick enough. Latency is uneven, so you describe it with percentiles : P50 is the typical request, P99 the slowest 1%, and P99 is what users remember. "Our throughput is 15,000 tokens per second." So what? If 40% of requests blew past 2 seconds end-to-end, users abandoned the session. Throughput alone does not tell you whether the product works. Inference has multiple axes of latency and each one fails differently. Prefill is compute-bound and scales with prompt length. Decode is memory-bound and scales with batch size. Queuing delay is an operational problem. Network is a physical-distance problem. You need distinct metrics for each, and you need percentiles, and you need a single composite that says "did the user get what they expected" — that is goodput. Idea 1 · TTFT — time to first token TTFT = queue_time + network_request + prefill_time Prefill dominates when prompts are long. On Llama-3.3-70B FP8 on H100, a 32k prompt takes ~800 ms of pure prefill. Queue time is scheduler behavior under load. Network request is wire time including TLS. TTFT is the latency the user sees before anything streams back. Idea 2 · TPOT / ITL — inter-token latency Many names for one quantity. TPOT (time per output token), ITL (inter-token latency), decode latency per token — all the same. It is the time between consecutive streamed tokens after the first. TPOT = (decode_forward_time + scheduler_overhead) / tokens_produced On the same Llama-3.3-70B H100 stack with chunked prefill, TPOT mean ~7 ms. Without chunked prefill, during a long prefill on a neighboring sequence, TPOT can spike to 50 ms. Watch P99, not mean. Idea 3 · E2E latency E2E = TTFT + TPOT * output_tokens + network_response For long outputs (>500 tokens), E2E is TPOT-dominated. For short outputs with long prompts, E2E is TTFT-dominated. Report output-length-conditioned E2E. Idea 4 · Throughput throughput = total_output_tokens / elapsed_time Aggregate metric. Tells you fleet efficiency. Does not tell you individual-request health. Idea 5 · Goodput — the metric you actually care about goodput = fraction of requests meeting (TTFT <= a) AND (TPOT <= b) AND (E2E <= c) The SLO is a multi-constraint. A request is "good" only if every constraint held. Goodput is the share. Some papers and dashboards report goodput as a rate instead: requests per second that meet every SLO. Multiply the share by the request rate to convert. High throughput at 60% goodput is failure. Lower throughput at 99% goodput is the target. In 2026, goodput is the metric used in MLPerf Inference v6.0 submissions and in internal SLA tracking at AI platform providers. Idea 6 · Why mean is the wrong statistic LLM latency distributions are right-skewed. A decode batch with one long-prefill neighbor can ship 500 tokens with TPOT ~7 ms and 20 tokens with TPOT ~60 ms. Mean TPOT is 9 ms. P99 TPOT is 65 ms. Users hit the P99 regularly — that is why they leave. Always report the triple (P50, P90, P99). For user experience, P99 is the one you optimize. Idea 7 · Reference numbers — Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on TRT-LLM, 2026 mean TTFT: 162 ms mean TPOT: 7.33 ms mean E2E: 1,093 ms P99 TPOT: varies 10-25 ms depending on chunked-prefill configuration. These are the published NVIDIA reference points. They change with model size (70B would show 3-5x), hardware (H100 vs B200 ~3x), and load. Idea 8 · The measurement trap Two of the most-used 2026 benchmark tools disagree on TPOT for the same run: NVIDIA GenAI-Perf : excludes TTFT from the ITL calculation. ITL starts from token 2. LLMPerf : includes TTFT. ITL starts from token 1. For a request with TTFT 500 ms and 100 output tokens in 700 ms total decode, GenAI-Perf reports ITL = 700/99 = 7.07 ms , LLMPerf reports ITL = 1200/100 = 12.00 ms . Tool choice changes the number. Always state which tool. Always publish the definition. Idea 9 · Constructing an SLO A reasonable consumer-facing SLO for a 70B chat model in 2026: TTFT P99 <= 800 ms. TPOT P99 <= 25 ms. E2E P99 <= 3 s for <300-token outputs. Goodput target >= 99%. Enterprise SLOs tighten TTFT (200-400 ms) and loosen E2E. The point is to write them down, measure all three, and track goodput as a single composite. Idea 10 · How to measure Run real traffic or realistic synthetic (LLMPerf with --mean-input-tokens 800 --stddev-input-tokens 300 --mean-output-tokens 150 ). Target 2x peak concurrency for the benchmark run. Run 30-50 iterations, take percentiles of the combined sample. Publish with tool name, tool version, model, hardware, concurrency, prompt distribution. The same idea as a formula Goodput. With SLO limits , , , # { r : TTFT r ​ ≤ a ∧ TPOT r ​ ≤ b ∧ E2E r ​ ≤ c } ​ and ​ − 1 ) + network . Worked example One request, two tools A request has TTFT = 500 ms, then 99 more tokens over 700 ms (100 output tokens, 1,200 ms in total). GenAI-Perf measures from the second token: ITL = 700 / 99 ≈ 7.07 ms. LLMPerf spreads the whole time over all tokens: 1,200 / 100 = 12.00 ms. Same request, 70% apart. A dashboard that switched tools would show a "regression" that never happened. Check E2E: 500 + 7.07 × 99 ≈ 1,200 ms. Both tools agree on E2E; they disagree on how to split it. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Throughput can be high while most users have a bad experience. ✗ Mean TPOT is a good summary for a dashboard. Latency is right-skewed; a 7 ms mean can sit next to a 65 ms P99. ✓ A request counts towards goodput only if every SLO held for it. ✗ Benchmark tools agree on what ITL means. GenAI-Perf excludes the first token, LLMPerf includes it. Solutions Solution P1 · Tightening the TPOT limit In the visual above, tightening the TPOT limit from 30 to 15 ms changes nothing: the healthy 99% sit near 7 ms and the slow 1% near 63 ms, so goodput stays at 99% either way. In the script, the "target" profile tightens TTFT, TPOT and E2E together and goodput falls to about 76%, mostly from the TTFT and E2E limits. Tightening one limit only matters if requests sit between the old and new values. Solution B1 · Three mistakes (1) 50 requests cannot give a meaningful P99: that is the single slowest request. Use thousands, over 30–50 runs. (2) Identical 100-token prompts hide the real mix: long prompts cause the prefill stalls users see. Use a realistic distribution of input and output lengths. (3) Production load is higher: benchmark at about twice peak concurrency. Also say which tool and which ITL definition the number uses. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A teammate posts in the team channel that the server does 255 tokens per second. Is that a result? What would you ask for, and what single number tells you where to stop adding users? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. It is a slogan, not a result, because a throughput number without the latency that came with it describes nothing a user feels. Ask for the concurrency, the median and P99 first token and time per token at that concurrency, the client and the temperature, and the clock. Goodput is the number that sets the limit: the requests per second, or the share of requests, that met every latency target at once, and on the manual's GB10 the BF16 server's goodput was highest at a cap of 4 while its throughput kept rising to a cap of 64. The same server, two loads. The 255 came from the manual's own capture. The same server gave that throughput with a median time to first token of 0.8 s at one load and 3.9 s at another: Cap Output tok/s Median TTFT P99 TTFT Median TPOT 1 175.15 162.98 ms 270.18 ms 4.38 ms 8 255.63 785.79 ms 2180.87 ms 22.52 ms 32 252.74 3917.54 ms 8262.86 ms 93.61 ms From a cap of 8 to 32 the throughput fell about 1 percent, the median first token got 5 times slower, and the median time per token got 4.2 times slower. The server had no idle compute left to give; new users only waited for a share of the same steps. Goodput. Goodput is the share of requests, or the rate of requests per second, that met every latency bound at the same time: the first token under a limit, the time per token under a limit, and the end-to-end time under a limit. A request that misses any one of them is not good. The lesson's rule: high throughput at 60 percent goodput is failure, and lower throughput at 99 percent goodput is the target. The manual's target was a first token under 1 s and a mean time per token under 100 ms. On the GB10 with Qwen3-30B-A3B: Cap BF16 goodput BF16 median TPOT FP8 goodput FP8 median TPOT 4 0.44 req/s 71.01 ms 0.80 req/s 38.60 ms 8 0, up to 0.04 in one seed 102.21 ms 1.07 req/s 54.96 ms 16 0 154.24 ms 1.10 req/s 81.90 ms 32 0 201.91 ms 0 104.12 ms BF16 goodput was highest at a cap of 4. At a cap of 8 the median request took longer than 100 ms per token, so at least half of the requests missed the target, and goodput was 0, up to 0.04 in one seed, while throughput at that cap was 74.11 tokens per second and still rising. FP8 held the target up to a cap of 16. Choose the cap from goodput at your own target, and use the throughput curve only to explain it. Why the mean is the wrong statistic. The lesson gives the shape: a decode batch with one long prefill neighbour can ship most tokens near 7 ms per token and a few near 60 ms, so the mean reads 9 ms while the P99 reads 65 ms, and users hit the P99 regularly. Report the median, the P90 and the P99 together. The tools also disagree on the definition: for a request with a 500 ms first token and 100 output tokens over 700 ms of decode, one tool that excludes the first token reports 7.07 ms per token and one that includes it reports 12.00 ms. State the tool and the definition with every number. Where the knee is, and who enforces it. A closed loop never falls behind, because each client waits for its answer before it sends the next request. A fixed arrival rate does not wait. Under a fixed rate the GB10 BF16 server already had a median time per token of 177.5 ms at 0.5 requests per second and met the target for only 0.07 requests per second, while FP8 met the target for every request up to 1 per second and fell to 0.17 at 2. Enforce the knee outside the engine, in the client or the gateway, because the engine's own admission limit comes from memory and sat at 4096 running requests on that server, far above the knee. The floor behind one number. The lesson shows where the time per token comes from on an L4: one decode step reads 16.41 GB of weights, which takes at least 54.7 ms at 300 GB/s, and the measured step took 60.16 ms. A target of 100 ms per token leaves little room on that card for an 8B model in BF16, which is why the pool and the precision matter before the scheduler does. Plausible wrong answers. "255 tokens per second is the capacity of the server." The same server gave that throughput with a median time to first token of 0.8 s at one load and 3.9 s at another; the number without its latency is not a result. "Add users until throughput stops rising, then stop." On the GB10 the BF16 throughput kept rising to a cap of 64 while goodput was 0 or close to it from a cap of 8; the latency target, not the throughput curve, sets the limit. "Report the mean time per token." The distribution is right-skewed, so a mean of 9 ms can hide a P99 of 65; report the median, P90 and P99. "The engine's own admission limit protects the users." The engine's limit comes from memory, which runs out long after latency is unacceptable; enforce the knee in the client or the gateway. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which numbers go next to a throughput figure? Expected: the concurrency or request rate, and the median and P99 of the first token and of the time per token at that point, with the client, temperature and clock as context. (level 2) Goodput fell to zero at a cap of 8 while throughput still rose. How can both be true? Expected: the server wrote more tokens per second, but the median request took longer than 100 ms per token, so at least half of the requests missed the target and almost none met every bound; throughput counts tokens and goodput counts requests that arrived on time. (level 3) Why is the mean the wrong statistic for the time per token? Expected: the distribution has a long right tail; a batch with one long prefill neighbour can ship most tokens near 7 ms and a few near 60, so the mean reads 9 ms while the P99 reads 65, and users hit the P99 regularly. (level 4) Two tools report different time per token for the same run. Why, and what do you do? Expected: one excludes the first token from the inter-token calculation and the other includes it, 7.07 against 12.00 ms in the lesson's example; state the tool and the definition with every number, and keep one tool for every run you compare. Weigh a trade-off You serve a chat model on one GPU. A load sweep shows output throughput that still rises at a cap of 64 concurrent requests, so the team wants to set the cap to 64. The product needs the first token in under one second and a steady stream of text after it. Which cap do you pick, and how do you defend it? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Pick the cap from goodput, not from throughput. Goodput counts only the requests that meet every latency target, so it falls to zero long before throughput stops rising. On the sweep in the SGLang manual, BF16 goodput was highest at a cap of 4 and was 0 from a cap of 8. Use the throughput curve only to explain the choice. Why throughput hides the knee. A large KV pool lets the server admit more requests. On the GB10 in the manual, the pool held 234,600 tokens, so BF16 throughput still rose at a cap of 64. More admitted requests share each decode step, so each request gets fewer tokens per second. Throughput measures the server. Latency measures the user. Define the target first. The manual counts a request as good when its first token comes in under 1 s and its mean time per token is under 100 ms. Write the target down before the sweep. A goodput number without its target means nothing. Read the sweep. Cap BF16 goodput BF16 median TPOT FP8 goodput FP8 median TPOT 4 0.44 req/s 71.01 ms 0.80 req/s 38.60 ms 8 0 102.21 ms 1.07 req/s 54.96 ms 16 0 154.24 ms 1.10 req/s 81.90 ms 32 0 201.91 ms 0 104.12 ms At a cap of 8, the median BF16 request already takes more than 100 ms per token. Throughput at that cap is 74.11 tok/s and still rising. FP8 holds the target up to a cap of 16. So the answer depends on the build: about 4 for BF16 and about 16 for FP8 on this machine. Defend it. Run three seeds per point and show the band, so that a reviewer can see the gaps are real. Reset the prefix cache before each run. A warm cache makes the first token look fast. A cap is a closed loop. Real users arrive on their own clock, so also run an open-loop sweep with a request rate and check goodput there. Plausible wrong answers. "Set the cap where throughput peaks." The throughput curve had no peak inside the sweep, and every BF16 request missed the target from a cap of 8. "Use the median TTFT alone." A median can hide a slow half of the requests, and the time per token can fail while the first token is fast. "Report goodput from one run." One run can be wrong for reasons you never see, so use three seeds and report the range. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What is the difference between throughput and goodput? Expected: throughput counts all tokens or requests per second; goodput counts only the requests that met every latency target. (level 3) Why can a closed-loop cap never show a growing queue? Expected: each client waits for its answer before it sends the next request, so the server never receives more work than it finishes. (level 3) FP8 holds the target at a cap of 16 and BF16 does not. What do you check before you switch the build? Expected: output quality on your own eval, and the KV pool size, because FP8 frees memory for a larger pool. (level 4) The GPU gets hot at high load. How does that change your sweep? Expected: record the GPU clock and the thermal state with every run, and let the GPU cool to a fixed temperature before each run. Where it is taught. Before you start Needs : Phase 10 · 13 (Quantization foundations), Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy memory and throughput comparison across formats). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Quantization format is not a universal choice — it is a function of hardware, serving engine, and workload. GGUF Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M owns CPU and edge, delivered through llama.cpp and Ollama. GPTQ wins inside vLLM when you need multi-LoRA on the same base. AWQ with Marlin-AWQ kernels delivers ~741 tok/s on a 7B class model with the best Pass@1 at INT4 — the 2026 default for datacenter production. FP8 stays the middle ground on Hopper, Ada, and Blackwell — near-lossless and widely supported. NVFP4 and MXFP4 (Blackwell micros Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means GGUF "llama.cpp format" File format bundling K-quant variants; CPU/edge default Q4_K_M "Q4 K M" 4-bit K-quant medium; the production GGUF default GPTQ "gee pee tee q" Post-train INT4 with calibration; supports LoRA in vLLM AWQ "a w q" Activation-aware INT4; Marlin kernels; best Pass@1 at INT4 Marlin kernels "fast INT4 kernels" Custom CUDA kernels for INT4 on Hopper; 10x speedup FP8 "eight-bit float" Safe precision default on Hopper/Ada/Blackwell MXFP4 / NVFP4 "microscaling four" Blackwell 4-bit FP with per-block scale factors Calibration dataset "cal data" Input text used to pick quantization parameters; must match domain KV cache quantization "KV INT8" Separate choice from weights; affects attention accuracy The problem In plain words first Quantization stores a model's numbers with fewer bits: 8 or 4 instead of 16. Fewer bits mean a smaller model, less memory to read for each token and so faster generation, at some cost in accuracy. There are several formats, each made for a different place. GGUF files are for laptops and CPUs (llama.cpp, Ollama). AWQ and GPTQ are 4-bit formats for GPU servers; they look at sample data (a calibration set ) to decide which weights matter most. FP8 is an 8-bit format that newer NVIDIA GPUs run natively, with almost no quality loss. NVFP4 and MXFP4 are 4-bit formats for Blackwell GPUs. Two traps catch most teams: quantizing the weights does not shrink the KV cache, and 4-bit models lose more on reasoning tasks than on chat. Quantization reduces memory and HBM bandwidth, which is exactly what decode needs. An FP16 70B model is 140 GB of weights. Quantize weights to INT4 (AWQ or GPTQ) and the model is 35 GB — fits in one H100 with room for KV cache, which matters because at 128 concurrent sequences with 2k context, KV cache alone is 20-30 GB. But quantization is not free. Aggressive quantization degrades quality, especially on reasoning-heavy tasks. Different formats work with different engines. Different hardware supports different precisions natively. The 2026 format zoo is real and you cannot copy someone else's choice — you have to pick based on your stack. Idea 1 · The six formats Format Bits Sweet spot Engines GGUF Q4_K_M / Q5_K_M 4-5 CPU, edge, laptops llama.cpp, Ollama GPTQ 4-8 Multi-LoRA on vLLM vLLM, TGI AWQ 4 Datacenter GPU production vLLM (Marlin-AWQ), TGI FP8 8 Hopper/Ada/Blackwell datacenter vLLM, TRT-LLM, SGLang MXFP4 4 Blackwell multi-user TRT-LLM NVFP4 4 Blackwell multi-user TRT-LLM Idea 2 · GGUF — the CPU/edge default GGUF is a file format, not a quantization scheme per se — it bundles K-quant variants (Q2_K, Q3_K_M, Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q6_K, Q8_0) in one container. Q4_K_M and Q5_K_M are the production defaults — near-BF16 quality at 4-5 bits. Best choice for CPU or edge serving because llama.cpp is by far the fastest CPU inference engine. Throughput penalty in vLLM: ~93 tok/s on 7B — the format is not optimized for GPU kernels. Use GGUF when the deployment target is CPU/edge. Not otherwise. Idea 3 · GPTQ — multi-LoRA in vLLM GPTQ is a post-training quantization algorithm with a calibration pass. Marlin kernels make it fast on GPU (2.6x speedup vs non-Marlin GPTQ). ~712 tok/s on 7B. The unique win: GPTQ-Int4 supports LoRA adapters in vLLM. If you are serving a base model plus 10-50 fine-tuned variants (each as a LoRA), GPTQ is your path. NVFP4 does not support LoRA yet as of early 2026. Idea 4 · AWQ — the datacenter GPU default Activation-aware Weight Quantization. Protects the ~1% most-salient weights during quantization. Marlin-AWQ kernels: 10.9x speedup vs naive. ~741 tok/s on 7B, best Pass@1 among INT4 formats. Pick AWQ for new GPU serving unless you need multi-LoRA (GPTQ) or aggressive Blackwell FP4 (NVFP4). Idea 5 · FP8 — the reliable middle 8-bit floating point. Near-lossless. Widely supported. Hopper Tensor Cores accelerate FP8 natively. Blackwell inherits. FP8 is the safe 2026 default when quality is non-negotiable (reasoning, medical, code-gen). Memory savings are half of INT4 but quality risk is far lower. Idea 6 · MXFP4 / NVFP4 — Blackwell aggressive Microscaling FP4. Each block of weights has its own scale factor. Aggressive but hardware-accelerated on Blackwell Tensor Cores. Halve the bytes per token versus FP8 — the economic win in Phase 17 · 07. Caveats: - No LoRA support yet (early 2026). - Quality drop visible on reasoning-heavy workloads. - Validate on your eval set per model. Idea 7 · The calibration trap AWQ and GPTQ require a calibration dataset — typically C4 or WikiText. For domain models (code, medical, legal), calibrating on generic web text lets the algorithm make wrong decisions about which weights to protect. Pass@1 on HumanEval can drop several points. The fix: calibrate on in-domain data. Hundreds of domain samples is usually enough. Test on the eval set before shipping. Idea 8 · The KV cache trap AWQ shrinks weights to 4 bits. KV cache is separate and stays at FP16/FP8. For a 70B model with AWQ: Weights: ~35 GB (INT4 from 140 GB). KV cache at 128 concurrent × 2k context: ~20 GB. Activations: ~5 GB. Total: ~60 GB — fits on H100 80GB. Naively "I quantized my model to 4 GB" forgets the other 30-50 GB. Budget HBM holistically. Separately, KV cache quantization (FP8 KV or INT8 KV) is a different choice with its own tradeoffs — it affects attention accuracy directly and is not a free win. Idea 9 · AWQ INT4 is hazardous for reasoning Chain-of-thought, math, code-gen with long context — these suffer visibly from aggressive quantization. AWQ INT4 loses ~3-5 points on MATH. For reasoning-heavy workloads, ship FP8 or BF16; accept the memory cost. Idea 10 · 2026 picking guide CPU/edge serve: GGUF Q4_K_M. Done. GPU serve, routine chat, no LoRA: AWQ. GPU serve, multi-LoRA: GPTQ with Marlin. Reasoning workload: FP8. Blackwell datacenter, validated quality: NVFP4 + FP8 KV. Ambiguous: run a 1,000-sample eval on each candidate format. Worked example Does a 4-bit 70B model fit on one H100? Llama-style 70B: 80 layers, 8 KV heads of size 128. Serve 128 users with 2,048 tokens each. Weights in AWQ INT4: 70B × 0.5 bytes = 35 GB. KV cache per token in BF16: 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes ≈ 0.33 MB. For 128 × 2,048 = 262,144 tokens: about 86 GB. Total with a few GB of activations: about 125 GB. It does not fit on an 80 GB H100, even though the weights alone use less than half of it. With an FP8 KV cache the KV halves to about 43 GB: total about 82 GB, still just over. Cut concurrency to about 100, or use an H200 (141 GB). The lesson's figure of "~20 GB of KV" is too low for this shape; do this arithmetic for your own model before choosing hardware. FP8 is; 4-bit formats lose several points on maths and long code. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A teammate says: we quantized the 70B model to 4-bit, so it is 35 GB now and it fits on one 80 GB card with room to spare. What is missing from that sentence? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The KV cache. Weight quantization shrinks the weights, and the cache for the running requests is a separate budget that stays in BF16 or FP8 and grows with every token in flight; at 128 concurrent requests with a 2k context the lesson puts it near 20 GB for a 70B model, plus about 5 GB of activations, so the total is about 60 GB on the 80 GB card. That 20 GB is the lesson's rough figure, so check it against the config: Llama-3.1-70B keeps 320 KiB per token in BF16, and 128 full 2k-token requests then need about four times the lesson's figure, which does not fit beside the weights on one 80 GB card. Count the weights, the cache at your peak concurrency and context, and the activations together, and read the pool size in the startup log after the start. The budget has three parts. The lesson's own count for a 70B model with 4-bit weights: Part Size Weights, 4-bit from 140 GB in FP16 about 35 GB KV cache at 128 concurrent requests with a 2k context about 20 GB Activations about 5 GB Total about 60 GB The sentence "it is 35 GB now" forgets the cache and the activations. Budget the card as a whole, and count the cache from the config of your model: Llama-3.1-70B keeps 320 KiB per token in BF16, so at full 2k contexts its cache alone is about four times the 20 GB in the table. Where the cache goes. Every token in a running request keeps its keys and values in GPU memory until the request ends. The bytes per token come from four numbers in the model config: layers times KV heads times head size times 2 for the key and the value, times the bytes per value. Qwen3-8B keeps 144 KiB per token in BF16 and Qwen3-30B-A3B keeps 96 KiB, because the KV heads decide the number and the parameter count does not. The engine gives the cache what is left after the weights and the startup profile, and the users that fit are the pool divided by the context that one user holds, prompt plus output. On the GB10 the weights of the 30B model took 56.93 GiB, 31.32 GiB was left for the cache, and at 96 KiB per token that is about 342,000 tokens. KV quantization is its own decision. An FP8 cache halves the bytes per token, which doubles the users at the same length. It is a separate choice from the weight format, with its own scales and its own effect on the attention values, so it needs its own accuracy check. Quantizing the weights does not shrink the cache. How to fit more, in order of cost. Lower the maximum model length to the longest real request. This does not grow the pool, but it stops one request from claiming all of it. Use an FP8 KV cache. Use FP8 or 4-bit weights, which free memory for the cache. Use a GPU with more memory, or split the model. Read the log. Read two lines after every start: the weight load line and the available KV cache memory line. The pool line then gives the tokens and the maximum concurrency at the full length, which assumes that every user fills the maximum; real users hold less, so more fit. Plausible wrong answers. "The model is 35 GB, so the rest is free for users." The KV cache and the activations take their share first; at 128 concurrent requests with a 2k context the lesson puts the cache near 20 GB and the total near 60 GB. "Quantizing the weights also shrinks the cache." The cache stays in its own dtype; it halves only if you quantize the cache, which is a separate choice with its own accuracy effect. "The cache is small because the model is small." The bytes per token depend on the layers and the KV heads; a 30B expert model keeps 96 KiB per token and an 8B dense model 144 KiB. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which three things take memory on a serving GPU? Expected: the weights, the KV cache for the tokens in flight, and the activations with the startup working memory; the engine gives the cache what is left after the other two. (level 2) What does the KV cache grow with? Expected: the number of running requests and the context that each one holds, prompt plus output, so it grows with concurrency and with length, not with the weights. (level 3) Quantizing the weights to 4-bit and quantizing the cache to FP8 are different decisions. Why? Expected: the weights are a fixed cost and their quantization changes the matrix math; the cache is per token and its quantization changes the attention values directly, so it needs its own accuracy check and its own scales. (level 4) Where in the startup log do you confirm that the budget held? Expected: in the weight load line, the available KV cache memory line and the pool size line with its maximum concurrency; divide the pool by prompt plus output per user rather than by the maximum length. Where it is taught. The production quantization lesson names the trap, and Count the memory before you pick a GPU counts the cache. Defend a design You have twenty fine-tunes of one base model, each a LoRA adapter, and you want to serve them from one vLLM server. What do you set, what decides the cost, and what else in the server changes when LoRA is on? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Turn LoRA on at startup with --enable-lora , name the adapters with --lora-modules , and let each request pick one in its model field. Three limits set the cost: --max-loras , which defaults to 1 and caps the adapters that run in one batch, --max-lora-rank , which defaults to 16 and reserves memory for the largest rank, and --max-cpu-loras for adapters kept in CPU memory ready to load. LoRA also changes the prefix cache, because the adapter is part of every block key, so two adapters never share cached blocks, and it adds CUDA graphs per adapter, so startup takes longer and uses more memory. Start it. Copy Each path is a folder in the PEFT format that most training libraries write: adapter_config.json and the weights in adapter_model.safetensors , or adapter_model.bin . A request picks an adapter by its name in the model field, and /v1/models lists the base model and each adapter. Requests for different adapters can run in the same batch. The manual ran this with Qwen3-0.6B and two public adapters of rank 8 and rank 64, and a chat request to each adapter returned HTTP 200. Size the three limits. Flag Default What it limits --max-loras 1 adapters that can run in one batch on the GPU --max-lora-rank 16 the largest adapter rank the server accepts --max-cpu-loras not set adapters kept in CPU memory, ready to load The default of one adapter per batch is low for a server with many adapters. Requests for a second adapter wait until the batch of the first adapter is done. Raise --max-loras to the number of adapters that are busy at the same time. Set --max-lora-rank to the largest rank of your adapters and not higher: the server reserves memory for the largest rank it accepts, and the documentation advises against a large default such as 256. Adapters in CPU memory load fast when a request names them, so size --max-cpu-loras for the adapters that are warm. Load adapters while the server runs. With VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=True you can post to /v1/load_lora_adapter with a name and a path, and to /v1/unload_lora_adapter to remove it. Turn this on only when you trust every caller of the server, because the route loads files from a path that the caller gives. What changes elsewhere. The prefix cache. The adapter is part of each block key in vLLM and of the tree key in SGLang. Two adapters never share cached blocks, even for the same prompt. A shared system prompt is cached once per adapter, not once. CUDA graphs. vLLM captures separate graphs for batches with an adapter. More adapters and more graph sizes add startup time and memory. Names. Since 0.31 an adapter cannot have the name of a served model. The manual did not measure the cost of the adapter count or the rank on its hardware. Pick the base format with LoRA in mind. The lesson's picking guide says that a 4-bit GPTQ base supports LoRA adapters in vLLM, with the fast Marlin kernels, while the microscaling 4-bit formats did not support LoRA at the start of 2026. For a base model plus many fine-tuned variants, GPTQ is the 4-bit path; AWQ is the pick when there is no LoRA, and FP8 when quality must not move. Plausible wrong answers. "One server per adapter is simpler." Each server would hold its own copy of the base model and its own pool; one base with adapters per request shares both, and requests for different adapters can run in the same batch. "The default limits are fine." One adapter per batch makes requests for a second adapter wait, and a rank limit of 16 rejects a rank-64 adapter; set both from the adapters you serve. "Enable runtime adapter loading so that operators can add adapters without a restart." The load route reads files from a path that the caller gives, so turn it on only when you trust every caller of the server. "LoRA is free for the prefix cache because the base model is the same." The adapter changes the keys and values, so it is part of the block key, and two adapters never share cached blocks. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Two tenants send the same long system prompt through two different adapters. Does the second request hit the cache? Expected: no; the adapter is part of the block key in vLLM and of the tree key in SGLang, so two adapters never share blocks even for identical tokens. (level 3) Requests for the second adapter wait although the GPU is idle. Why? Expected: the adapter cap defaults to 1, so only one adapter runs in a batch and requests for another adapter wait until that batch is done; raise it to the number of adapters that are busy at the same time. (level 3) Why not set the rank limit to 256 to be safe? Expected: the server reserves memory for the largest rank it accepts, so a high limit takes memory from the KV pool for adapters you do not have; set it to your largest rank. (level 4) You also want 4-bit weights for the base model. Which format, and what does it rule out? Expected: a GPTQ 4-bit base, because it supports LoRA adapters in vLLM with the Marlin kernels; the microscaling 4-bit formats did not support LoRA at the start of 2026, so they are out until they do. Where it is taught. Serve many fine-tunes with multi-LoRA gives the flags and limits, Prefix-friendly prompts notes the tree key, and the production quantization lesson pairs a 4-bit base with adapters. Explain why live migration transfers input tokens (KB) not KV cache (GB) and what the penalty is (recomputation).
