Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 02 (Inference Platform Economics), Phase 17 · 03 (GPU Autoscaling) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy cold-start path simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A large model takes minutes to go from cold to serving: a 70B model on a fresh node needs roughly 3-8 minutes before the first token. In a true serverless world, that is not a warm-up — it is an outage. Mitigations operate at five layers: pre-seeded node images (Bottlerocket on AWS, dual-volume arch), model streaming (NVIDIA Run:ai Model Streamer, native in vLLM), GPU memory snapshots (Modal checkpoints, up to 10x faster restart), warm pools ( min_workers=1 ), tiered loading (ServerlessLLM's NVMe→DRAM→HBM pipeline, 10-200x latency reduction), plus Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Cold start "the big pause" Time from request to first token on a fresh replica Warm pool "always-on minimum" min_workers >= 1 to keep at least one replica ready Pre-seeded image "baked AMI" Node image with container weights pre-resident Bottlerocket "AWS node OS" AWS container-optimized OS with dual-volume snapshot support Model streamer "streaming load" Overlap weights I/O with compute setup GPU snapshot "checkpoint to HBM" Serialize post-load GPU state; deserialize on restart Tiered loading "NVMe + DRAM + HBM" Hierarchy of storage tiers; load on demand Live migration "move tokens" Transfer input (KB), recompute KV on destination min_workers "warm replicas" Serverless minimum keep-alive count Scale-to-zero "full serverless" No cost when idle; accept full cold-start tax The problem In plain words first A cold start is the wait when a request arrives and no copy of the model is running: a GPU machine must be found, the software image downloaded, tens of gigabytes of weights loaded into GPU memory and the engine started. For a 70B model that can take several minutes. Scaling to zero (running nothing when nobody is using the model) saves money but makes the next user pay that wait. The fixes attack each step: machine images with the model already on disk, streaming weights onto the GPU while loading, GPU snapshots that restore a running model in seconds, and warm pools , which keep one copy always running at the cost of paying for it all day. Your serverless LLM endpoint scales to zero overnight. At 8 a.m. traffic spikes. The first request waits while: Karpenter provisions a GPU node: 45-60s. The container pulls a 30 GB image with weights: 120-300s. The engine loads weights into HBM: 45-120s depending on model size and storage speed. vLLM or TRT-LLM initializes CUDA graphs, KV cache pool, tokenizer: 10-30s. Total: 220-510s (roughly 3-8 minutes) before one token comes back. Your SLA is 2s. You ship a warm-pool ( min_workers=1 ) and the problem seems to vanish — but now you pay for one idle GPU 24x7. If your service has 5 products each with one warm replica, that's 5 × 24 × 30 = 3,600 GPU-hours/month whether or not a single user called. Cold-start mitigation is how to keep the serverless economics while approximating the latency of always-on. Idea 1 · Layer 1 — pre-seeded node images (Bottlerocket) On AWS, Bottlerocket's dual-volume architecture separates OS from data. Snapshot the data volume with your container image pre-pulled; reference the snapshot ID in your EC2NodeClass . New nodes boot with weights already on local NVMe — steps 2 and part of 3 vanish. Works with Karpenter natively. Typical savings: 2-4 minutes per cold start for large models. Equivalent on GCP: custom VM images with pre-baked container layers. On Azure: managed disk snapshots with the same pattern. Idea 2 · Layer 2 — model streaming (Run:ai Model Streamer) Instead of loading the full file before answering the first request, stream weights into GPU memory layer-by-layer and start processing as soon as the first transformer block is resident. The NVIDIA Run:ai Model Streamer ships native in vLLM 2026. Works with S3, GCS, and local NVMe. Cuts weight-load time roughly in half for large models by overlapping I/O with compute setup. Idea 3 · Layer 3 — GPU memory snapshots (Modal) Modal takes a checkpoint of the GPU state (weights, CUDA graphs, KV cache region) after first load. Subsequent restarts deserialize directly into HBM — 10x faster than re-initializing. This is the closest thing to "boot a warm GPU in 2 seconds." Trade-off: snapshots are per-GPU-topology, so if Karpenter migrates you to a different SKU, you re-checkpoint. Idea 4 · Layer 4 — warm pools (min_workers=1) Simplest mitigation: keep one replica always ready. Cost is one GPU's hourly rate 24x7. The arithmetic is brutal on small models (you pay $0.85-$1.50/hr to avoid a 30s cold start) and kind to large ones (pay $4/hr to avoid a 5-minute cold start). The SLA threshold where warm pools become mandatory: typically TTFT P99 < 60s on a 70B+ model. Idea 5 · Layer 5 — tiered loading (ServerlessLLM) ServerlessLLM treats storage as a hierarchy: NVMe (fast but big), DRAM (medium but tiered), HBM (tiny but instant). Weights are pre-loaded to DRAM; load-on-demand into HBM. Paper reports 10-200x latency reduction on cold loads versus naive disk-to-HBM. Production adoption is early but integrations with vLLM exist. Idea 6 · Layer 6 — live migration (bonus pattern) When a node becomes unavailable (spot eviction, node drain), traditional pattern is cold-start another replica and drain request queue. Live migration moves the input tokens (kilobytes) to a destination that has the model loaded and recomputes KV cache on the destination. Recomputation is cheaper than transferring GB of KV cache over the network. Applicable to disaggregated deployments. Idea 7 · The warm-pool math For a service with P99 TTFT SLA of 2s, the question is not "warm pool yes/no" but "how many warm replicas, and which paths get them." High-value interactive paths (live chat, voice agent): min_workers=1-2 . Background batch paths (nightly classification): scale-to-zero accepted, 5-10 minute cold start tolerable. Premium tier: min_workers per tenant with dedicated capacity. Idea 8 · Measure before optimizing Cold-start anatomy for a 70B model on a fresh node (illustrative): Phase Time Mitigation Node provision 50s Bottlerocket + pre-seeded image, warm pool Image pull 180s Pre-seeded data volume (eliminate) Weights to HBM 75s Model streamer (halve); GPU snapshot (eliminate) Engine init 20s Persistent CUDA graph cache First forward 3s Min inherent latency Total cold 328s Total with mitigations ~15s 22x reduction Idea 9 · Numbers you should remember Modal cold start: 2-4s (with GPU snapshots). Baseten default cold start: 5-10s; sub-second with pre-warming. Raw 70B cold start: 3-8 minutes. Run:ai Model Streamer: ~2x weight-load speedup. ServerlessLLM tiered loading: 10-200x latency reduction (paper numbers). Worked example Is one warm replica worth it? A warm H100 replica costs $4.50 an hour, $3,240 a month. Without it, every request that arrives after the model has scaled down waits 328 s (5.5 minutes). At 1 request an hour, the model is cold for almost every request: about 20 cold starts a day. With a budget of 5 tolerated slow requests a day, 15 are over budget; at a premium product, each is a lost user. The warm replica is worth it. At 10 requests an hour, the model rarely scales down: about 2 cold starts a day, under budget. The warm replica buys little. The decision is about how often traffic gaps are longer than the scale-down timer, not about average traffic. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Pre-seeded node images remove the image pull, the largest step for big models. ✗ A warm pool is free once the model is popular. You pay for the warm replica every hour; popularity only means it is rarely idle. ✓ GPU memory snapshots can restore a loaded model in a few seconds. ✗ Cold-start time is mostly the GPU node starting up. For a 70B model, image pull and weight loading take most of the time. Recap What to keep from this lesson A raw 70B cold start is 3–8 minutes: node, image pull, weight load, engine init. Measure the anatomy, then fix the longest step first. Pre-seeded images, streaming, GPU snapshots and tiered loading each remove a step. Warm pools buy latency with 24×7 cost; give them to the paths whose users will not wait. Pick the minimum mitigation stack (fewest layers) that achieves it. Bottlerocket pre-seeding eliminates image pull but weights still load from snapshot to HBM. Solutions Solution P1 · Break-even request rate In code/main.py the warm replica costs $3,240 a month. At 1 request an hour there are about 20 cold starts a day, 15 over the drop budget, so the warm replica wins; from about 5 requests an hour the model rarely goes cold and the drops stay within budget. The break-even sits between 1 and 5 requests an hour for this scale-down timer. Solution P3 · Weights from NVMe 70B in BF16 is 140 GB. At 7 GB/s: 140 / 7 = 20 s to read, plus GPU transfer and allocation, so roughly 25–30 s. In FP8 (70 GB) about 10–15 s. Streaming overlaps this with the first forward passes. Solution B1 · Twelve warm replicas Most of those tools have long idle gaps, so a warm replica each is paid for and unused. Better: group the tools onto one shared server (several small models, or LoRA adapters on one base), keep one warm replica for the few latency-critical ones, and let the rest scale to zero with pre-seeded images and a GPU snapshot so their cold start is seconds, not minutes. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Your model service runs as a plain Deployment with an autoscaler on CPU use. During a traffic spike the autoscaler added replicas late, kept adding them while the new pods were still loading weights, and a liveness probe restarted the busiest pod in the middle of the spike. Redesign the scaling and the probes. Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Scale on the engine's own signals, not on CPU: the count of waiting requests and the KV cache usage say that a server is saturated long before CPU does. Give the startup probe a window longer than your measured cold start, so that a loading pod is neither sent traffic nor restarted, and make the liveness probe cheap, so that a busy server does not lose its busiest pod to a probe that waited in the queue. Keep the weights and the compile cache on persistent storage, so that a new replica is ready in a fraction of the time. Why CPU is the wrong signal. GPU load is not CPU load. A saturated engine shows waiting requests above zero and cache usage near one while the CPU looks calm. The vLLM manual says this directly about the plain Deployment: it routes at random and scales on the wrong signal. The routing layers that the manual lists read vllm:num_requests_waiting , vllm:num_requests_running and vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc to pick a replica, and an autoscaler should read the same series. Read the signals in pairs. Reading Meaning waiting above 0, cache usage below 0.9 the batch size or the token budget limits admission, not memory waiting above 0, cache usage near 1 the pool limits admission, so add memory or replicas slow first token with nothing waiting long prompts or a slow tokenizer, not a capacity problem preemptions with long answers running requests grow until the pool runs out The second row is a reason to add a replica, because the pool is full. On the first row, raise the batch limit or the token budget first, while the pool has room. If the queue stays after that, or the limit is already where the latency target needs it, add a replica, because each replica brings its own batch limit and token budget. Probes that match a slow start. The manual's example gives the startup probe 90 checks at 10 second intervals, which is 15 minutes, and notes that its own machine took about 8 minutes for a first start. Set the window from your measured cold start. For readiness, send one short real request, which proves the engine can generate, or use the ready endpoint on an engine that has one. For liveness, use a cheap health path. The SGLang manual turns generation off in the health endpoint, because a probe that generates waits in the queue under load, times out after 20 seconds, and marks a busy server unhealthy. In one incident each failed probe also left an orphan request in the scheduler, so the probes added to the load they were meant to detect. Stop the overshoot. New pods take minutes to load. The autoscaler sees the signal still high and adds more. Give it a stabilization window at least as long as the cold start, cap the replicas added per step, and shorten the cold start itself: weights on local disk, the compile cache on a persistent volume, and a preload before the server takes traffic. The cold start lesson adds the warm pool for the interactive path, so that the first replica is never a cold one. Scale down without losing work. Remove the pod from the load balancer, send SIGTERM to the main process only, and set a grace period at least as long as the longest request at the output cap. A forced kill, or a signal to the whole process group, drops every running request. Plausible wrong answers. "Scale on GPU utilization instead of CPU." Utilization can read high while requests wait and low while the pool is full. The queue and the cache usage are the signals the engine exposes for this. "Make the liveness probe stricter so that bad pods restart faster." Under load a strict probe restarts healthy, busy pods. The fix is a cheap probe and a long startup window. "Add replicas faster to beat the spike." Replicas that take minutes to load add nothing during the spike and cost money after it. Shorten the cold start and keep a warm margin. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which pair of readings says the pool is the bottleneck, not the batch limit? Expected: waiting requests above zero with cache usage near one. With cache usage below 0.9, the batch size or the token budget limits admission instead. (level 3) Why does a generating health probe hurt under load? Expected: its request waits in the queue like any other, times out, and marks a busy server unhealthy. In one incident each failed probe also left an orphan request behind. (level 4) How do you keep the autoscaler from overshooting during a cold start? Expected: a stabilization window at least as long as the measured cold start, a cap on replicas added per step, and a shorter cold start from persistent weights and compile caches. (level 4) What does a scale-down need so that no request is lost? Expected: remove the pod from the load balancer, send SIGTERM to the main process only, and a grace period at least as long as the longest request at the output cap. Where it is taught. The Kubernetes section of vLLM 101 sets the probes and names the wrong scaling signal, the production watching section reads the metrics in pairs, the operating section of SGLang 101 explains the health probe incident and the drain, and the cold start lesson sizes the warm pool. Estimate it A pod serving an MoE model on a unified-memory machine took about eight minutes from start to ready. Break that time into its parts, say which parts a restart can skip, and estimate what a warm restart looks like on the same machine. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Most of the time was the weight load. The manual's log shows about 330 seconds to copy 57 GiB of weights into memory on that machine, one tensor at a time from a file-backed page. The engine init took 127.54 seconds, and it holds the two CUDA graph captures of 39 and 38 seconds and a compile share of 18.67 seconds. A restart reuses the compile cache and nothing else, so a warm restart on that machine is only a little shorter than the cold one, unless the weights are staged in host memory or a process snapshot exists, which a field report took from a cold start of 695 seconds to 9.6 seconds. The parts, from the startup log. Phase Measured Where it is logged weight load 56.93 GiB in about 330 seconds the model loading line engine init, profile, KV cache, warmup, with both graph captures 127.54 seconds, of which compilation 18.67 the init engine line first graph capture, inside engine init 39 seconds, 1.17 GiB the first graph capturing line second graph capture, inside engine init 38 seconds, 0.31 GiB the second graph capturing line The two captures finish before the init line, so they are part of its 127.54 seconds. Do not add them to it. The server reported ready about eight minutes after it read its arguments. The load alone is more than two thirds of it. Why the load is slow on this machine. Each tensor is copied from the memory-mapped weights file into the GPU allocation. On this platform an open issue measured about 1.7 ms per tensor copied from the file view, against about 0.2 ms for a copy that starts in host memory. The release that the manual pins saved about 25 seconds with an indexed lookup of expert names, and the per-tensor copy cost stays. The manual's advice: keep the weights on local NVMe, not on a network mount, and start the server once and keep it running. What a restart skips. The compile cache lives under the engine's cache directory. Keep it on a persistent volume, and a later start reads it, so the compile share shrinks. SGLang points all of its kernel caches into one directory for the same reason, and the manual mounts it on a volume that survives the pod. The graph captures and the weight load repeat on every start. So the honest estimate for a warm restart on this machine is the cold start minus the compile share, which is still several minutes. Getting under a minute. The lesson on cold starts maps each phase to a layer: a pre-seeded image removes the image pull, model streaming roughly halves the weight load, and a GPU memory snapshot restores the loaded state about ten times faster than a reload. The SGLang manual quotes a field report with the same shape on a different engine and eight GPUs: a cold start of 695 seconds with 531 of them in weight loading, 88 seconds with kernel caches kept, and 9.6 seconds with a process checkpoint and the weights staged in host memory. Below a minute means a snapshot or staged weights, not a faster disk. What the number sets. The Kubernetes example in the vLLM manual gives the startup probe checks at 10 second intervals across a 15 minute window, and tells you to set the window from your own measured cold start. An autoscaler needs a stabilization window at least as long, and the interactive path needs a warm replica, because no scale-out helps inside an eight-minute window. Plausible wrong answers. "The compile is the slow part, use eager mode." The compile share was 18.67 seconds of an eight-minute start, and eager mode costs decode speed on every request afterwards. "A faster GPU loads faster." The load was bound by the copy path from the file view, not by the GPU. "Restart often to pick up configuration changes." Each restart pays the full load. The manual's advice is to start once and keep the server running. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which phase dominates on this machine, and why? Expected: the weight load at about 330 seconds, because each tensor is copied from a file-backed page, which is slow on this platform. (level 3) What does a persistent compile cache save on a restart? Expected: the compile share of the engine init, 18.67 seconds here. The weight load and the graph captures remain. (level 4) How do you get the restart under a minute? Expected: a process checkpoint or GPU memory snapshot with the weights staged in host memory, which the field report took to 9.6 seconds. A faster disk alone does not get there. (level 4) What does an eight-minute start imply for the probes and the autoscaler? Expected: a startup probe window longer than eight minutes, a stabilization window at least as long, and a warm replica for the interactive path. Where it is taught. The unified memory section of vLLM 101 explains the slow weight load, the compile section reads the capture and compile times, the production section keeps the compile cache, the operating section of SGLang 101 reports the warm and checkpointed starts, and the cold start lesson maps each phase to a mitigation. Defend a design You run three tiers on a serverless GPU platform: paid users on a live chat, trial users on the same chat, and a nightly batch pipeline. Design the warm-pool policy per tier, show the arithmetic behind it, and say what you would measure after a month to revisit it. Level 4 of 4 · about 18 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Give the paid chat one or two warm replicas, because its first-token target cannot absorb a cold start of minutes on a large model. Give trial users a smaller margin, or let them ride on the paid pool's spare capacity, and let the batch pipeline scale to zero, because it tolerates a cold start of several minutes. The arithmetic is the hourly GPU price times the idle hours against the requests that would miss the target during a cold start, and after a month you compare the measured utilization, the cold-start count and the missed-target count per tier. The arithmetic the lesson gives. A warm replica costs one GPU hour every hour. One replica per product is a full month of GPU hours whether anyone calls, and the lesson's example of five products with one warm replica each comes to 3,600 GPU-hours a month idle. The lesson calls the trade brutal on small models, where you pay 0.85 to 1.50 dollars an hour to avoid a 30 second start, and kind on large ones, where about 4 dollars an hour avoids a 5 minute start. Its threshold for a mandatory warm pool: a first-token target at P99 under 60 seconds on a model of 70B or more. The policy per tier. Tier Policy Why paid live chat one to two warm replicas the lesson's high-value interactive path, where a cold start is an outage trial chat zero warm, or overflow into the paid pool at lower priority the loss is a conversion, which you can measure, against a month of GPU hours nightly batch scale to zero the lesson accepts a cold start of 5 to 10 minutes on background paths The lesson's exercise asks exactly this split and asks for the math. The paid tier is decided by the SLA. The batch tier is decided by its tolerance. The trial tier is the real decision, and it is an experiment: the conversion loss from a cold start on the first session against the price of an idle GPU. Make the policy cheaper by shrinking the start. Every mitigation layer moves a tier toward zero. A pre-seeded node image removes the image pull, model streaming halves the weight load, a GPU memory snapshot restores the loaded state in a fraction of the time, and tiered loading keeps weights in host memory. The lesson's table takes a cold start of 328 seconds to about 15 seconds. With a 15 second start, the trial tier can scale to zero with a small loss, and the paid pool can hold one replica instead of two. Match the billing to the tier. The warm replicas run at high utilization, which is where per-minute billing beats per-token, above about 30 percent sustained utilization in the economics lesson. Trial bursts and the overnight batch sit below that line, so per-token or a batch tier at about half the serverless rate fits them. What to measure after a month. Utilization per tier, hour by hour. Cold starts per day and their duration. Requests that missed the first-token target, and whether they fell inside a cold start. Trial conversions for sessions that hit a cold start against sessions that did not. The break-even request rate per tier from the lesson's simulator, against the measured rate. Plausible wrong answers. "Warm replicas for every tier, the cost is small." One replica per product is a month of GPU hours each. Five products idle come to thousands of hours. "Scale trial to zero, those users are free." A cold start of minutes on the first trial session is a lost conversion. Measure it before you decide. "Keep the batch pipeline warm so that it finishes earlier." Batch tolerates minutes. A warm GPU for it is paid idle time for the rest of the day. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why not give trial users the same warm pool as paid users? Expected: a warm replica costs a month of GPU hours whether trial traffic arrives or not. The decision is the conversion loss from a cold start against that cost, and the month of measurement answers it. (level 4) How does a 15 second cold start change the policy? Expected: tiers that tolerate seconds scale to zero, so the warm pool shrinks to the paths with targets of a second or two. (level 4) Which signal says a warm replica count is too low? Expected: the share of requests that miss the first-token target during scale-outs, together with the cold-start count per day. Where it is taught. The cold start lesson gives the warm-pool arithmetic and the tiered policy exercise, and the inference platform economics lesson gives the per-minute against per-token crossover. Weigh a trade-off Your serverless endpoint scales to zero overnight. The first request in the morning waits minutes while a 70B model loads, and the product wants the first token within two seconds. One engineer wants a replica that never sleeps. Another calls that a GPU burning money all night. Settle it. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Both are right, and the decision is arithmetic per path. A warm replica costs one GPU hour every hour whether anyone calls or not, and it removes a cold start of several minutes for a large model. An interactive path with a tight first-token target on a large model needs the warm replica, while a small model with a cold start of seconds, or a background path that tolerates minutes, scales to zero. Then shrink the cold start itself, so that fewer paths need a warm replica at all. What a cold start is made of. The lesson's anatomy for a 70B model on a fresh node: node provision 45 to 60 seconds, image pull 120 to 300 seconds, weights into GPU memory 45 to 120 seconds, engine init 10 to 30 seconds. The sum is 220 to 510 seconds, which is 3 to 8 minutes before one token. The vLLM manual measured one part of that on its own machine: 330 seconds to load 57 GiB of weights. The warm-pool arithmetic. The lesson calls the arithmetic brutal on small models and kind on large ones. You pay 0.85 to 1.50 dollars an hour to avoid a 30 second start on a small model, and about 4 dollars an hour to avoid a 5 minute start on a large one. Five products with one warm replica each are 3,600 GPU-hours a month, called or not. The lesson's threshold: a warm pool becomes mandatory when the first-token target at P99 is under 60 seconds on a model of 70B or more. Tier the paths. Path Policy live chat, voice agent one or two warm replicas nightly classification, batch scale to zero, a cold start of minutes is fine premium tenant dedicated warm capacity Shrink the cold start. Five layers, each removing a phase: a pre-seeded node image removes the image pull, model streaming halves the weight load, a GPU memory snapshot restores the loaded state in a fraction of the time, warm pools hide the rest, and tiered loading keeps weights in host memory. The lesson's table takes a 328 second cold start to about 15 seconds with the layers stacked, a reduction of 22 times. The vLLM manual adds the operational half: keep the weights on local disk, keep the compile cache on a persistent volume, and measure a cold and a warm start for every new image. Plausible wrong answers. "Keep one warm replica everywhere, it is the simple answer." It is one GPU hour every hour per product. Five products idle all night cost thousands of GPU hours a month. "Scale to zero everywhere and let the first user wait." A first-token wait of minutes on an interactive path is an outage, not a wait. "A bigger GPU loads faster." The load is bound by the storage and the copy path. The fix is where the weights live and whether a snapshot exists. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which paths get a warm replica first? Expected: the interactive ones with a tight first-token target on a large model, such as live chat or a voice agent. (level 2) Whose cold start is cheaper to hide, a small model's or a large one's? Expected: in proportion, the large one's. For a small model you pay a full GPU hour to avoid seconds, and for a large one the same hour avoids minutes. (level 3) Name two mitigations that remove whole phases of the cold start. Expected: a pre-seeded node image removes the image pull, and a GPU memory snapshot removes most of the weight load and the init. (level 3) What is the break-even request rate for a warm replica? Expected: the rate above which the cost of cold starts, in requests that miss the target, exceeds the hourly price of the idle GPU. The lesson's simulator computes it. Where it is taught. The cold start lesson gives the cost of a warm replica and the five mitigation layers, and the production section of vLLM 101 measures the weight load and keeps the compile cache. a1711: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Multi-Region LLM Serving and KV Cache Locality Lesson 17.11 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why round-robin load balancing breaks cached inference and quantify the TTFT penalty. Diagram a cache-aware router: inputs (KV-cache events), algorithm (prefix-hash match), tie-breaker (GPU utilization). Name the 32% DR failure driver for LLMs (missing tokenizer files / quantization configs) and state a three-file DR checklist. Distinguish commercial cross-region offerings (Bedrock CRI, GKE Multi-Cluster Gateway) from KV-aware routing. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (vLLM Serving), Phase 17 · 06 (SGLang RadixAttention) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy prefix-cache-aware router simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Round-robin load balancing is actively harmful for cached LLM inference. A request that does not land on the node holding its prefix pays full prefill cost — roughly 800 ms at P50 on a long prompt versus ~80 ms with a cache hit. In 2026 the production pattern is a cache-aware router (vLLM Router in Rust, llm-d router) that consumes KV-cache events and routes on prefix-hash match. Recent research (GORGO) makes cross-region network latency an explicit term in the routing objective. Commercial "cross-region inference" offerings (Bedrock cross-re Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Cache-aware routing "smart LB" Route on prefix-hash match to KV-cache-holding replica KV-cache events "cache pub-sub" Replicas publish block add/evict; router indexes Prefix hash "cache key" Hash of first N tokens used as router lookup GORGO "cross-region routing research" arXiv 2602.11688; network latency as explicit term Cross-region inference "Bedrock CRI" AWS product; availability failover, not TTFT awareness DR manifest "the backup list" Every file needed to restore — not just weights Data residency "GDPR boundary" Legal constraint on which region sees user data RTT "round-trip time" Network latency; 75 ms US-EU, 220 ms US-APAC LLM-aware LB "cache-hit LB" Cache-aware router as a product category The problem In plain words first When the same model runs in several cloud regions (say Virginia, Oregon and Ireland), a router decides which copy answers each request. A normal load balancer spreads requests evenly, which is right for stateless web servers. Model servers are not stateless: each one holds a prefix cache , the KV cache of prompt beginnings it has already read. A request sent to a replica that has its prefix cached skips most of the prefill and gets its first token about ten times sooner. Cache-aware routing sends each request to a replica that already holds its prefix. Across regions you must weigh that saving against the network round trip, and some data (such as EU health data) must never leave its region. The lesson also covers disaster recovery : a backup that holds the weights but not the tokenizer or the configs cannot start. Your service runs in us-east-1, us-west-2, and eu-west-1. You put an ALB in front with round-robin. Prefix cache hit rate in production drops to 8%. TTFT P50 triples. Your vLLM logs show every request is paying full prefill cost. Round-robin is optimal for stateless services. LLM inference is stateful by design — the KV cache encodes everything the model has seen. Routing blind is routing into the wrong cache. Separately, your team has a DR plan. You back up model weights to S3 cross-region. A regional outage hits; you attempt failover; the replica refuses to start. You forgot tokenizer.json, the quantization config, and the RoPE scaling config were in a separate bucket you didn't sync. Multi-region LLM serving is a cache problem, a routing problem, and a DR-hygiene problem — not a load-balancer problem. Idea 1 · Cache-aware routing Request arrives with a prompt. Router hashes the prefix (say, first 512 tokens); it asks each replica "do you have this prefix cached?". Replicas publish KV-cache events on a pub/sub channel as they allocate and evict blocks. Router picks the replica with the match, falls through to GPU-util-based tie-breaker if no one does. vLLM Router (Rust, 2026 production-stack): subscribes to kv.cache.block_added events, maintains a prefix-hash → replica index, routes with lookup. Falls through to least-queue-depth when no match. llm-d router : same pattern, Kubernetes-native. Publishes events via the ControlPlane API. SGLang RadixAttention (Phase 17 · 06) is the intra-replica equivalent. Cross-replica routing is strictly upstream. Idea 2 · Numbers TTFT P50 on a 2K-token prompt, Llama 3.3 70B FP8, H100: - Cache hit (same replica, prefix resident): ~80 ms. - Cache miss (cold prefill): ~800 ms. 10x gap. If your router hits 60-80% of prefix cache across replicas, you approximate single-replica performance at N-replica capacity. If it hits 10%, you approximate naive scaling. Idea 3 · Cross-region has a new constraint — network latency Inter-region RTT: - us-east-1 ↔ us-west-2: ~65 ms. - us-east-1 ↔ eu-west-1: ~75 ms. - us-east-1 ↔ ap-southeast-1: ~220 ms. If routing takes a request from us-east-1 to a hot prefix in ap-southeast-1, the saved prefill (800 → 80 ms, so 720 ms) shrinks to about 500 ms once the ~220 ms RTT is paid, and the margin disappears if the remote region queues the request or has already evicted the prefix. GORGO (2026 research) makes this explicit — minimize prefill_time + network_latency jointly, not prefill alone. Often the answer is to keep routing regional except on massive multi-MB prefixes where prefill dominates. Idea 4 · Commercial "cross-region inference" does not help here AWS Bedrock cross-region inference automatically routes requests to other regions during capacity pressure. It optimizes availability, not TTFT, and treats inference as opaque. GKE Multi-Cluster Gateway is the same — service-level failover, no awareness of KV cache. You still need an app-layer cache-aware router even when using these. They handle the "us-east-1 is on fire" case. Cache-aware routing handles the TTFT case. Idea 5 · DR hygiene — the 32% missing-files problem Widely cited 2026 stat: 32% of LLM DR failures happen because teams backed up weights but forgot: tokenizer.json or tokenizer.model Quantization configs ( quantize_config.json , AWQ scales, GPTQ zero-points) Model-specific configs (RoPE scaling, attention masks, chat templates) Engine config ( vllm_config.yaml , sampling defaults, LoRA adapter manifests) The fix is a three-file minimum DR manifest: All files under the HF model repo (weights + configs + tokenizer). Engine-specific serving config. Deployment manifest (K8s YAML, Dockerfile, dependency lock). Plus: run a DR drill quarterly. The JPMorgan us-east-1 drill hit 22 minutes recovery in Nov 2024 only because the playbook was rehearsed. Idea 6 · Data residency is orthogonal EU customer PHI cannot leave EU. If your cache-aware router sends a Paris-originated request to us-east-1 for a prefix match, you have violated GDPR regardless of TTFT gain. Partition routers by residency boundary before optimizing for cache. Idea 7 · Numbers you should remember Cache hit vs miss TTFT gap: ~10x (80 ms vs 800 ms on 2K prompt). Inter-region RTT US-EU: ~75 ms. DR failure: 32% miss tokenizer/quant configs. JPMorgan us-east-1 failover Nov 2024: 22 minutes (30-min SLA). The same idea as a formula When is a remote cache hit worth it? A local miss costs the full prefill ​ . A hit in another region costs ​ + RTT + q , where is any extra queueing there. Route remotely only when ​ + RTT + q < t miss ​ Prefill time grows with prompt length, so long shared prompts make remote hits pay; short prompts rarely do. Worked example Virginia to Ireland A 2,000-token prompt on Llama 3.3 70B FP8: a hit costs about 80 ms, a miss about 800 ms. The round trip from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 is about 75 ms. Remote hit: 80 + 75 = 155 ms, against a local miss of 800 ms. Remote wins by 645 ms. If the Irish replica has a 400 ms queue: 80 + 75 + 400 = 555 ms. Still better. A 200-token prompt: miss about 80 ms, hit about 15 ms. Remote: 15 + 75 = 90 ms, worse than the local miss. If the request carries EU personal health data and originates in Paris, it must stay in the EU whatever the numbers say. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Round-robin routing ignores which replica holds which prefix. ✗ Bedrock cross-region inference gives you cache-aware routing. It reroutes for capacity during pressure; it does not know about your prefixes. ✓ A DR backup must include the tokenizer, quantization configs and the engine's serving config. ✗ Routing to the region with the best cache hit is always allowed. Data-residency rules come first; partition routers by residency boundary. Regional routing keeps traffic home with no cross-region cost and a modest gain. Which one you ship depends on prompt length, RTT and residency rules, not on the hit rate alone. Break it on purpose During a regional outage, a team fails over to its backup region. The replica starts, loads the weights from S3, and then crashes on the first request. The backup was complete as far as they knew: every .safetensors file was there. What was probably missing? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this lesson Model servers are stateful: route to the replica that holds the prefix. A cache hit is about 10× faster than a miss on long prompts. Across regions, take a remote hit only if hit + RTT + queue < local miss. Residency boundaries come before latency. DR backups need weights, tokenizer, configs and the serving manifest, and a rehearsed drill. Diagnose three possible causes and the observables that would confirm each. Design a DR manifest for a 70B AWQ-quantized model served in vLLM with 5 LoRA adapters. List every file and config. Argue whether Bedrock cross-region inference is "enough" for a fintech with strict TTFT SLOs. Cite specific behaviors. A Paris-origin request matches a prefix in us-east-1. Do you route it? Write the policy. Solutions Solution P1 · Prompt length for cross-region routing With a miss costing about 0.4 ms per token, a hit about 0.04 ms per token and a 75 ms round trip, a remote hit wins when 0.36 × tokens > 75, so above about 210 tokens. Queueing at the remote region raises that threshold; measure your own per-token prefill cost. Solution P2 · Hit rate from 70% to 12% (1) The prompt template changed and dynamic content now leads the prompt: compare first tokens of two requests. (2) The router lost its KV-event feed (subscriber down or lagging): check that the event stream is current. (3) A scaling event added many cold replicas or caches were flushed: check replica count and eviction counts around the drop. Solution B1 · Weights are not enough Most likely the tokenizer files ( tokenizer.json or tokenizer.model ), the quantization config (AWQ scales or GPTQ zero-points) or the model's RoPE and chat-template settings. The engine loads weights, then fails on the first request. Back up the whole model repository plus the serving config and deployment manifest, and run a failover drill every quarter. a1712: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Edge Inference — Apple Neural Engine, Qualcomm Hexagon, WebGPU/WebLLM, Jetson Lesson 17.12 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why mobile LLM inference is memory-bandwidth-bound and compute is secondary. Enumerate the four edge targets (Apple ANE, Qualcomm Hexagon, WebGPU/WebLLM, NVIDIA Jetson) and match each to a use case. Name the 2026 WebGPU coverage gap (Firefox Android catching up) and the Safari iOS 26 landing. Pick a quantization format per target (Core ML INT4 + FP16 for ANE, QNN INT8/INT4 for Hexagon, WebGPU Q4 for browser, NVFP4 for Jetson Thor). Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals), Phase 17 · 09 (Production Quantization) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy bandwidth-bound decode simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The core edge constraint is memory bandwidth, not compute. Mobile DRAM sits at 50-90 GB/s; datacenter HBM3 clears 2-3 TB/s — a 30-50x gap. Decode is memory-bound so the gap is decisive. In 2026 the landscape splits four ways. Apple M4/A18 Neural Engine peaks at 38 TOPS with unified memory (no CPU↔NPU copy). Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite / 8 Gen 4 Hexagon hits 45 TOPS. WebGPU + WebLLM runs Llama 3.1 8B (Q4) at ~41 tok/s on M3 Max (roughly 70-80% of native); 17.6k GitHub stars, OpenAI-compatible API, ~70-75% mobile Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means ANE "Apple neural engine" On-device NPU in M-series and A-series; unified memory Hexagon "Qualcomm NPU" Snapdragon NPU; QNN SDK for access WebGPU "browser GPU" W3C-standardized browser GPU API; Chrome/Safari 2026 WebLLM "browser LLM runtime" MLC-LLM project; Apache 2.0; OpenAI-compatible JS Jetson "NVIDIA edge" Orin Nano / AGX / Thor / T4000 family TRT Edge-LLM "edge TensorRT" 2026 edge port of TensorRT-LLM; EAGLE-3 + NVFP4 Unified memory "shared pool" CPU and NPU see same RAM; no copy overhead Bandwidth-bound "memory limited" Decode gated by bytes/sec reading weights Core ML "Apple conversion" Apple framework for ANE-native models QNN "Qualcomm stack" Qualcomm Neural Network SDK The problem In plain words first Edge inference means running the model on the user's own device: a phone, a laptop, a browser tab or a small board such as NVIDIA Jetson. It keeps data private, works offline and removes network delay. The limit is memory bandwidth , how fast the device can read memory. Every generated token reads all the model's weights once, so a phone that reads 60 GB a second can never generate more than 60 GB ÷ model size tokens a second, whatever its chip's TOPS rating says. Each platform has its own route to its fastest unit: Core ML for Apple's Neural Engine, Qualcomm's QNN for Snapdragon, WebGPU for browsers, TensorRT for Jetson. Small, 4-bit models and short contexts are the rule. A customer wants an on-device chatbot: voice-first, private-by-default, works offline. On a MacBook Pro M3 Max, Llama 3.1 8B Q4 runs at ~55 tok/s — fine. On an iPhone 16 Pro, the same model runs at 3 tok/s — not fine. On a mid-range Android with Snapdragon 8 Gen 3, 7 tok/s. In the browser via WebGPU on Chrome Android v121+, 4-8 tok/s depending on the device. The throughput variance is not a porting issue. It is the bandwidth gap times the quantization format times whether the NPU is accessible from user-space. Edge inference in 2026 is four different problems with four different solutions. Idea 1 · Bandwidth is the real ceiling Decode reads the full set of weights for every token. One 7B model in Q4 is 3.5 GB. Reading 3.5 GB at 50 GB/s takes 70 ms — a theoretical ceiling of ~14 tok/s. At 90 GB/s (high-end mobile DRAM) the ceiling moves to ~25 tok/s. No amount of compute helps below this number. Datacenter HBM3 at 3 TB/s clears the same 3.5 GB in 1.2 ms — ceiling is 830 tok/s. Same model, same weights. Different memory subsystem. Idea 2 · Apple Neural Engine (M4 / A18) Up to 38 TOPS. Unified memory (CPU and ANE share the same pool) — no copy overhead. Access via Core ML + .mlmodel compiled models, or via Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) through PyTorch. Llama.cpp Metal backend uses MPS, not ANE directly; native ANE requires Core ML conversion. Best practical path for iOS apps in 2026: Core ML with INT4 weights + FP16 activations. Idea 3 · Qualcomm Hexagon (Snapdragon X Elite / 8 Gen 4) Up to 45 TOPS. Integrated with CPU and GPU in the SoC but separate memory domain. QNN (Qualcomm Neural Network) SDK and AI Hub provide conversion from PyTorch/ONNX. Chat templates, Llama 3.2, Phi-3 all ship as first-class artifacts on AI Hub. Idea 4 · Intel / AMD NPUs (Lunar Lake, Ryzen AI 300) 40-50 TOPS. Software lags behind Apple/Qualcomm; OpenVINO is improving but niche. Best for Windows ARM copilot apps; native on AMD/Intel desktops for local-first. Idea 5 · WebGPU + WebLLM Run models in the browser via WebGPU compute shaders; no install. Llama 3.1 8B Q4 at ~41 tok/s on M3 Max — roughly 70-80% of native via same backend. 17.6k GitHub stars on WebLLM; OpenAI-compatible JS API; Apache 2.0. 2026 coverage: Chrome Android v121+, Safari iOS 26 GA, Firefox Android still catching up. Overall ~70-75% mobile coverage. Idea 6 · NVIDIA Jetson family Orin Nano Super (8GB): fits Llama 3.2 3B, Phi-3 at good tok/s. AGX Orin: runs gpt-oss-20b via vLLM at ~40 tok/s. Thor / T4000 (JetPack 7.1): 2x AGX Orin performance, EAGLE-3 and NVFP4 supported. TensorRT Edge-LLM (2026) supports EAGLE-3 speculative decoding, NVFP4 weights, chunked prefill — the datacenter optimizations ported to edge. Idea 7 · Quantization choice per target Target Format Notes Apple ANE INT4 weights + FP16 activations Core ML conversion path Qualcomm Hexagon QNN INT8 / INT4 AI Hub converters WebGPU / WebLLM Q4 MLC (q4f16_1) Use mlc_llm convert_weight + compiled .wasm ; GGUF is not supported Jetson Orin Nano Q4 GGUF or TRT-LLM INT4 Memory-bound Jetson AGX / Thor NVFP4 + FP8 KV Edge-LLM path Idea 8 · The long-context trap on edge Llama 3.1's 128K context is a datacenter feature. On a phone with 8 GB RAM, 4 GB model + 2 GB KV cache for 32K tokens + OS overhead = OOM. Edge deployments keep context at 4K-8K unless aggressive KV quantization (Q4 KV) is accepted. Idea 9 · Voice is the killer app Voice agents are latency-sensitive (first token < 500 ms). Local inference eliminates network latency entirely. a1713: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production LLM Observability Stack Selection Lesson 17.13 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish development platforms (bundled: evals + prompts + sessions) from gateway/telemetry tools (traces + metrics only). Map six major tools (Langfuse, LangSmith, Phoenix, Arize AX, Helicone, Opik) to their licensing, pricing, and sweet-spot use cases. Explain the OpenTelemetry-glue pattern that lets you combine a gateway tool with a separate eval platform. Name the 2026 cost differentiator (Arize AX's zero-copy approach vs monolithic ingest) and state the rough 100x multiplier. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 08 (Inference Metrics), Phase 14 (Agent Engineering) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, toy trace-sampling simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line The 2026 observability market splits into two categories. Development platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Comet Opik) bundle monitoring with evals, prompt management, session replays. Gateway/instrumentation tools (Helicone, SigNoz, OpenLLMetry, Phoenix) focus on telemetry. Langfuse is MIT-licensed core with strong OSS balance (50K events/month free cloud). Phoenix is OpenTelemetry-native under Elastic License 2.0 — excellent for drift/RAG visualization, not a persistent production backend. Arize AX uses zero-copy Iceberg/Parquet integration claiming 100x che Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means OpenLLMetry "OTel for LLMs" Open-source OpenTelemetry instrumentation for LLMs GenAI conventions "OTel attributes" Standard OTel attribute names for LLM calls LangSmith "LangChain observability" Commercial platform bundled with LangChain ecosystem Langfuse "OSS LangSmith" MIT OSS with similar feature set Phoenix "Arize dev tool" OpenTelemetry-native dev/eval platform Arize AX "scale observability" Commercial zero-copy Iceberg/Parquet observability Helicone "proxy observability" HTTP proxy collecting LLM telemetry + gateway features Opik "Comet LLM" Apache 2.0 OSS dev platform from Comet Session replay "trace rerun" Replay a full agent session with tool calls Eval "offline test" Running candidate model/prompt over labeled dataset The problem In plain words first Observability means being able to see what your system did and why. For an LLM feature that means recording, for every call, the prompt, the answer, the tokens, the latency, the cost and the model, and linking calls that belong to one user action into a trace . Tools split into two kinds. Development platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Opik) add evaluations, prompt versions and datasets, so you can test a new prompt against old cases. Telemetry and gateway tools (Helicone, Phoenix, SigNoz) focus on recording calls and dashboards. OpenTelemetry is the open standard for sending this data, and its GenAI conventions name the fields ( gen_ai.request.model , gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and so on), so one instrumentation can feed several tools. Because traces are big, production systems keep only a sample , chosen so that errors and expensive calls are never thrown away. You shipped an LLM feature. It works. You have no visibility into prompt failures, tool loops, latency regressions, cost spikes, or prompt-cache hit rate. You Google "LLM observability" and get eight tools all claiming they solve the same problem at three different price points. They don't solve the same problem. LangSmith answers "why did this LangGraph run fail?" Phoenix answers "is my RAG pipeline drifting?" Helicone answers "which app is burning tokens?" Langfuse answers "can I self-host the whole thing?" Different tools, different audiences. Picking involves four axes: stack (LangChain? raw SDK? multi-vendor?), license tolerance (MIT only? Elastic OK? commercial fine?), budget (free tier? $100/mo? $1000/mo?), and self-host (must? nice-to-have? never?). Idea 1 · Two categories Development platforms bundle observability with evals, prompt management, dataset versioning, session replay. You run experiments, see which prompt worked, dataset-regression a new prompt against old winners. LangSmith, Langfuse, Comet Opik. Gateway/telemetry tools instrument inference calls — prompt, response, tokens, latency, model, cost. Helicone, SigNoz, OpenLLMetry, Phoenix. Minimalist. Can be combined with a separate eval tool via OpenTelemetry. Idea 2 · Langfuse — OSS balance Core Apache / MIT licensed; self-host via Docker. Cloud free tier: 50K events/month. Paid: $29/mo for team. Evals, prompt management, traces, datasets. Reasonable coverage of all four dev-platform features. Sweet spot: you want LangSmith-class features but must self-host or stay on OSS license. Idea 3 · Phoenix (Arize) — telemetry-first, OpenTelemetry-native Elastic License 2.0; self-host trivial. Excellent at RAG and drift visualization. Embedding-space scatter plots shipped as first-class. Not designed as persistent production backend — primarily development-time observability. Sweet spot: RAG pipeline development, drift debugging, pairs with a separate gateway for production. Idea 4 · Arize AX — the scale play Commercial. Zero-copy data lake integration via Iceberg/Parquet. Claims ~100x cheaper than monolithic observability (Datadog-class) at scale. The math: you store traces in your own Parquet on S3; Arize reads directly. Sweet spot: >10M traces/day, existing data lake, want LLM-specific dashboards without Datadog pricing. Idea 5 · LangSmith — LangChain/LangGraph first Commercial, $39/user/month. Self-host only on Enterprise. Best-in-class for LangChain and LangGraph stacks. If you are not on either, it is less compelling. Sweet spot: team committed to LangChain, willing to pay. Idea 6 · Helicone — proxy-based minimum viable 15-30 minute setup by swapping your OPENAI_API_BASE to Helicone proxy. MIT licensed; 100K req/mo free, paid $20/mo+. Includes failover, caching, rate limits — acts as a gateway too. Less depth on agent / multi-step traces. Sweet spot: quick start, single-stack app, need gateway + observability in one. Idea 7 · Opik (Comet) — OSS dev platform Apache 2.0, fully OSS. Similar feature set to Langfuse with Comet heritage. Sweet spot: ML teams already on Comet, want LLM observability in the same pane. Idea 8 · SigNoz — OpenTelemetry-first full APM Apache 2.0. Handles general APM plus LLM via OpenTelemetry. Sweet spot: unified observability across services and LLM calls. Idea 9 · The glue: OpenTelemetry + GenAI semantic conventions OpenTelemetry published GenAI semantic conventions in late 2025 ( gen_ai.system , gen_ai.request.model , gen_ai.usage.input_tokens ). Tools that consume OTel can interoperate. The production pattern emerging: Emit OTel with GenAI conventions from every LLM call. Route to gateway (Helicone / Portkey) for day-to-day. Dual-ship to eval platform (Phoenix / Langfuse) for regressions. Archive in data lake (Iceberg) for long-term analysis via Arize AX or DuckDB. Idea 10 · The trap: instrumenting at the wrong layer Instrumenting inside your agent framework (e.g., adding LangSmith traces) couples you to that framework. Instrumenting at the HTTP/OpenAI-SDK layer (via OpenLLMetry or your gateway) is portable. Idea 11 · Sampling — you can't keep everything At >1M requests/day, full-trace retention costs more than the LLM calls. Sample by rules: 100% errors, 100% high-cost, 5% success. Keep aggregates always; keep raw for the long tail. Idea 12 · Numbers you should remember Langfuse free cloud: 50K events/month. LangSmith: $39/user/month. Helicone free: 100K req/month. Arize AX claim: ~100x cheaper than monolithic at scale. OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions: 2025 shipping, 2026 widely adopted. Worked example What a sampling policy keeps A service handles 1,000,000 traces a day. 3% are errors and 1% are unusually expensive (over $0.10). Keep everything: 1,000,000 traces. Random 10%: 100,000 traces, but only about 3,000 of the 30,000 errors. Most failures you will need to debug are gone. "5% of successes + all errors": 0.05 × 970,000 + 30,000 ≈ 78,500 traces, every error kept. Add "all expensive calls": about 10,000 more, so about 88,000 traces, under 9% of the volume, with every error and every cost outlier. Sample by what you will ask later , not uniformly. Rare is exactly why random sampling loses them; keep 100% of errors. ✓ OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions let several tools read the same traces. ✗ LangSmith is the best choice for every stack. It is strongest on LangChain and LangGraph; elsewhere, other tools fit better. Emit OpenTelemetry with GenAI conventions; send it to a gateway, an eval platform and an archive. Instrument at the SDK or HTTP layer, not inside one framework. Sample: all errors, all expensive calls, a few per cent of the rest. Pick by stack, licence, budget and whether you must self-host. Solutions Solution P1 · Sampling cost in code/main.py At 1M traces a day, keeping everything costs about $67.50 a day on a Datadog-class backend; "5% of successes + all errors + high-cost" costs about $5.30 and keeps the signal you debug with. On a data-lake pattern (Arize AX reading your own Parquet) even full retention costs well under a dollar a day, which is why large teams store everything there and sample only the expensive backend. Solution B1 · Framework-coupled tracing Instrument at the model-call layer, through OpenTelemetry with the GenAI conventions (OpenLLMetry or the gateway), so every framework's calls produce the same spans. Framework-specific traces can be added on top for detail, but the baseline must not depend on one framework. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Your service makes more than a million model calls a day. Keeping every trace now costs more than the model calls themselves. Design a retention policy that keeps the traces you will need during an incident and drops the rest. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Sample by rule, not by a flat rate. Keep every errored trace and every high-cost trace, keep a small share of the successes, and keep the aggregates always. Make the decision at the collector with a tail sampler after the trace completes, so that the rule can see the status and the cost. The capstone keeps all errored traces and 10 percent of the successes. Why a flat rate fails. A flat 5 percent keeps 5 percent of the errors too. The trace you need in an incident is the one you dropped, and the aggregate error count tells you only that it existed. The rules. Class Keep errored traces all of them high-cost traces, long outputs or expensive models all of them successes 5 to 10 percent aggregates always, from every request The observability lesson states the rule as 100 percent of errors, 100 percent of high cost and 5 percent of successes. Aggregates do not need traces: counters and histograms count every request even when the trace is dropped. Decide at the tail. Head sampling decides when the trace starts, before anything knows whether it will fail. Tail sampling at the collector decides after the trace completes, so it can read the status, the cost and the eval score. The price is buffer memory at the collector, because whole traces wait until the decision. Stratify, and know the bias. The capstone's exercise keeps every trace with a toxicity score above 0.5 plus a 10 percent stratified sample of the rest, and asks you to measure the bias that the sampling adds. Any analysis over sampled traces overweights the classes you kept in full. Weight by the inverse of the sampling rate, or run the per-trace evals on the stratified share only. Tier the storage. Spans go to a columnar store for queries, and raw events go to object storage for the long tail. The archive is cheap, and long-term analysis runs there. Plausible wrong answers. "Sample 5 percent of everything." Most of the errors you need in an incident are gone, and the aggregate tells you only that they happened. "Keep everything for a week, then delete it." A week of full traces at this volume is the cost you are trying to remove. "Traces are enough, drop the metrics." A percentile over an hour needs every request, which only a histogram gives. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does head sampling lose the errors? Expected: it decides before the span ends, so it cannot see the status. (level 2) What survives from a dropped trace? Expected: the metrics. Counters and histograms count every request, whether or not its trace is kept. (level 3) Your eval jobs run over the sampled traces. What bias do they inherit? Expected: a sample that keeps all errors overweights failures, so weight by the inverse sampling rate or evaluate the stratified share only. (level 3) The collector runs out of memory during a burst. Why, and what do you change? Expected: tail sampling buffers whole traces until they complete. Cap the buffer, shorten the decision wait, and shed with a head rule under pressure. Where it is taught. The observability stack lesson gives the sampling rules, and the dashboard capstone configures the tail sampler and measures its bias. a1714: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Prompt Caching and Semantic Caching Economics Lesson 17.14 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Distinguish L2 prompt/prefix caching (KV reuse at provider) from L1 semantic caching (LLM bypass on similar prompts). Explain Anthropic's cache_control explicit marking and the two TTL options (5-min vs 1-hour) with their price multipliers. Compute expected monthly savings given hit rate, prompt/response mix, and token prices. Name the parallelization anti-pattern that inflates bills by 5-10x and the dynamic-content anti-pattern that collapses hit rate. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals), Phase 17 · 06 (SGLang RadixAttention) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, toy two-layer cache simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Pricing snapshot dated 2026-04. Numeric claims below reflect vendor rate cards captured at this lesson's publication; verify against the linked docs before quoting them downstream. Caching happens at two layers. L2 (provider-level) prompt/prefix caching reuses attention KV for repeated prefixes — Anthropic's prompt-caching docs advertise up to 90% cost reduction and 85% latency reduction on long prompts; for Claude 3.5 Sonnet cache reads are $0.30/M vs $3.00/M fresh with a 5-minute TTL and a 2x write premium for the 1-hour TTL option (d Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means L2 prompt cache "prefix cache" Provider stores KV for repeated prefix cache_control "Anthropic cache marker" Explicit attribute marking cacheable blocks Cache write premium "write tax" Extra cost for first miss-to-cache (1.25x or 2x) L1 semantic cache "embedding cache" App-level hash-and-embed before calling LLM GPTCache "LLM caching lib" Popular OSS L1 cache library Cache hit rate "hits / total" Fraction of requests served from cache Parallelization anti-pattern "the N-write trap" N parallel requests miss cache N times Dynamic content trap "the time-in-prompt trap" Dynamic bytes in prefix kill hit rate RadixAttention "intra-replica cache" SGLang's prefix-cache implementation The problem In plain words first There are two kinds of caching for LLM calls. Prompt caching (the provider's, also called prefix caching) stores the work done reading the start of a prompt; when the next request starts with exactly the same text, that part is billed at about a tenth of the price and starts faster. Writing the cache costs a little extra once. Semantic caching (your application's) stores whole answers: before calling the model, you look for an earlier question that means nearly the same thing and, if you find one, return its answer without calling the model at all. Both only pay if your requests are built for them: the fixed parts of a prompt must come first and stay byte-for-byte identical, and parallel requests must not all race to write the same cache. You add prompt caching to your RAG service. The bill stays flat. You measure the hit rate; it is 7%. Your prompts look static but they are not — the system prompt includes the current date formatted to the minute, a request ID, and a randomized example reorder for diversity. Every request writes a new cache entry, reads zero. Separately, your agent runs ten parallel tool calls per user question. All ten arrive at the provider before the first cache write completes. Ten writes, zero reads. Your bill is 5-10x what "with caching" was supposed to cost. Caching is a protocol, not a flag. Two layers, two different failure modes. Idea 1 · L2 — provider prompt/prefix caching Provider stores the attention KV for a cacheable prefix and reuses it on the next request that matches the prefix. You pay a write cost once, reads nearly free. Anthropic (Claude 3.5 / 3.7 / 4 series) : explicit cache_control marker in the request. You tag which blocks are cacheable. TTL: 5-minute (write costs 1.25x base) or 1-hour (write costs 2x base). Cache reads: $0.30/M on Claude 3.5 Sonnet vs $3.00/M fresh — 10x cheaper (docs.anthropic.com, as of 2026-04). Rates differ per model (Opus/Haiku published separately); always cross-check the live pricing page. OpenAI : automatic caching for prompts ≥1024 tokens (platform.openai.com, 2026-04). No explicit flag. Cached input is roughly 10x cheaper than fresh on current gpt-4o/gpt-5 rate cards. Neither docs nor release notes publish an official hit-rate baseline; community reports cluster around 30–60% with careful prompt design. Monitor usage.cached_tokens to measure your own. Google (Gemini) : context caching via explicit API; 1M-token context means caching pays even more. Self-hosted (vLLM, SGLang) : Phase 17 · 06 covers RadixAttention — same pattern at your own compute. Idea 2 · L1 — app-level semantic caching Before calling the LLM at all, hash the prompt, embed it, and look for a similar cached request (cosine similarity above threshold, typically 0.95+). On hit, return the cached response. On miss, call LLM and cache the result. Open-source: Redis Vector Similarity, GPTCache, Qdrant. Commercial: Portkey Cache, Helicone Cache. Vendor accuracy claims refer to how often the returned cached response was semantically appropriate — not how often you hit. Production hit rates: Open-ended chat: 10-15%. Structured FAQ / support: 40-70%. Code questions: 20-30% (small variants kill hits). Voice agents repeating prompts: 50-80% (voice normalization fixed set). Idea 3 · The parallelization anti-pattern Your agent makes 10 tool calls in parallel. All 10 have the same 4K-token system prompt. Anthropic cache writes are per-request; the first cache-write completes around 300 ms after the provider sees the prompt. Requests 2-10 arrive in the same millisecond window and each sees cache miss. You pay 10 write premiums, 0 read discounts. Fix: batch with sequential-first — make request 1 alone, then fire 2-10 once 1's cache has populated. Adds 300 ms to the first tool call; avoids the 5-10x bill inflation. Idea 4 · The dynamic content anti-pattern Your system prompt looks like: Copy Every request is unique. Every request writes. Zero hits. Fix: move everything truly static to the cacheable prefix; append dynamic content after the cache boundary: Copy ProjectDiscovery moved from 7% to 74% cache hit rate this way and published the anatomy. Idea 5 · Stack batch + cache for overnight workloads Batch APIs (Phase 17 · 15) give 50% discount at 24-hour turnaround. Cached input on top gets you ~10x on top of that. Overnight classification, labeling, and report generation workloads can drop to ~10% of synchronous-uncached cost by stacking. Idea 6 · Numbers you should remember Pricing points are captured 2026-04 from the linked vendor docs and drift every few months — re-check before relying on them. Anthropic cached read: $0.30/M on Claude 3.5 Sonnet, roughly 10x cheaper than fresh input (docs.anthropic.com). Anthropic cache write premium: 1.25x (5-min TTL) or 2x (1-hour TTL). OpenAI auto-cache: applies to prompts ≥1024 tokens; cached input priced at roughly 10% of fresh input on current rate cards (platform.openai.com). Semantic cache hit rate (community-reported): ~10% open chat; up to ~70% structured FAQ; 50-80% for voice agents on a fixed prompt set. Not a vendor-documented baseline. ProjectDiscovery: 7% → 74% hit rate by moving dynamic out of prefix (project blog, 2025-11). Parallelization anti-pattern: typical reports of 5–10x bill inflation when N parallel requests miss the first cache write. The same idea as a formula Cost of a cached prefix over requests. With a prefix of tokens, base input price , write multiplier (1.25 for a 5-minute cache) and read multiplier (about 0.1): Caching pays from the second request on: . Worked example Ten parallel tool calls with a 4,000-token prompt Base price $3 per million input tokens; cache write 1.25×, cache read 0.1×. No caching: 10 × 4,000 × $3/M = $0.120. Fired all at once, before the first write lands: 10 writes at 1.25× = $0.150. Caching made it more expensive. First call alone, then the other nine: 1 write + 9 reads = 4,000 × $3/M × (1.25 + 9 × 0.1) = $0.0258. About a fifth of the uncached cost. The price of the fix is about 300 ms extra on the first call. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A timestamp at the top of the system prompt makes every request a cache miss. ✗ A semantic cache's "95% accuracy" means 95% of requests hit it. It means 95% of the answers it returned were appropriate; hit rates are often 10–30% for open chat. ✓ Batch APIs and prompt caching stack: the discounts multiply. ✗ OpenAI requires you to mark cacheable blocks. OpenAI caches long prompts automatically; Anthropic uses explicit cache_control markers. Predict before you run Before running the code below: for 10 parallel requests sharing a 4,000-token prefix, how much does "first call alone, then nine" save against firing all ten together? See it drawn Parallel against first-then-parallel Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output Firing in parallel costs 25% more than not caching at all, at every size, because every request pays the write premium. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Debug a failure A dashboard panel shows the prefix cache hit rate of a self-hosted server at 94 percent. Over the same run, the server's counters say that it computed 104,057 prompt tokens and took 182,079 from the cache. Both readings come from one scrape of the same endpoint. Which one do you trust for a cost decision, and why do they differ? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Trust the counters. The gauge holds the hit rate of the last prefill interval that the scheduler logged, and at idle it keeps the value from the last batch, which was a shared-prefix benchmark. The counters add up every prefill token since the server started, and their ratio over the whole run is 0.636, not 0.942. For a cost decision, compute the rate from the counters over a time window. Three kinds of series. A gauge is a value the scheduler overwrites on each log interval. A scrape sees the latest value only. A counter is a total that only grows, and you read it as a rate over a window. A histogram is a set of counters, one per bucket, and you read percentiles from it over a window. The two hit rates. The gauge divides the hit tokens of one log interval by the hit tokens plus the computed tokens of that interval. When nothing runs, it keeps its last value. The counters carry the same two quantities since startup, split by mode: input for computed tokens, and device, host and storage hits for cached tokens. Over the whole run, 182,079 cached tokens against 286,136 prefill tokens in total give 0.636. The gauge at 0.942 describes the shared-prefix benchmark that ran last. Both are correct, and they answer different questions. The windowed rate. The HELP text of the counter gives the formula, and in PromQL it reads: Copy One caveat from the code: the hit modes add raw hit counts, so after a retraction the same tokens can count twice. The input mode excludes the re-count. The manual's run had no retractions, so its numbers are exact. Why this is a cost question. A hit rate decides whether you restructure prompts, add a cache-aware router or buy memory. A gauge from the last benchmark says the prompts are fine. The counters say that more than a third of the prompt tokens over the run were computed. The lesson on caching economics says the same for provider caches: measure your own hit rate from the usage fields on every response, and do not take a published figure as yours. What to alert on. Alert on counters and histograms over a window. Alert on a gauge only when the condition lasts for several minutes, such as queued requests above zero or token usage near one. Read the HELP text and the code before you build a panel on a metric. The manual found one utilization gauge that stays at zero at the version it pinned. Plausible wrong answers. "The gauge is the newest value, so it is the most accurate." It is a snapshot of one interval, and it keeps its last value at idle. "Average the two numbers." They answer different questions, and the counters already contain the whole run. "The real rate is lower, so turn the cache off." A rate of 0.636 means a third of the prompt tokens were computed. The fix is the prompt layout or the routing, not the cache. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does a gauge answer, and what does a counter answer? Expected: a gauge answers what happened in the last interval. A counter answers how much happened since the start, and a rate over a window turns it into a trend. (level 3) Why can the counter-based rate overstate the hits after retractions? Expected: the hit modes add raw hit counts, so a retracted request that runs again counts its cached tokens twice, while the input mode excludes the re-count. (level 3) Which gauges may page you, and under what rule? Expected: queued requests above zero and token usage near one, only when the condition holds for several minutes, never on one scrape. (level 4) A panel on this server shows utilization at zero during an outage. Why? Expected: that gauge stays at zero at the pinned version because of a known regression, so the panel shows an idle fleet. Read the HELP text and the code before building on a metric. Where it is taught. The metrics endpoint section of SGLang 101 measures the two hit rates on one server, and the caching economics lesson tells you to compute the rate from your own usage fields.
