Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 14 (Prompt & Semantic Caching) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, toy batch-vs-sync cost simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Every major provider ships an async batch API with a 50% discount and ~24-hour turnaround. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and most of the inference platforms (Fireworks batch tier, Together batch) implement the same pattern. Stack batch with prompt caching and overnight pipelines drop to ~10% of synchronous-uncached cost. The rule is brutally simple: if it tolerates hours of latency, it belongs on batch. Content generation pipelines, document classification, data extraction, report generation, bulk labeling, catalog tagging — anything toleran Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Batch API "async discount" 50% off with 24h turnaround JSONL "batch format" One JSON request per line; OpenAI/Anthropic standard Message Batches "Anthropic batch" Anthropic's batch API product name Batch prediction "Vertex batch" Vertex AI's batch API product Turnaround SLA "24h promise" Guarantee, not typical; typical is 2-6h Workload triage "interactivity decision" Interactive / semi / batch routing decision Output schema "response format" Per-provider JSONL layout; not portable Stacked discount "batch + cache" ~10% of uncached sync bill when both apply The problem In plain words first A batch API lets you upload many requests at once, usually as a file with one request per line, and collect the answers later. The provider promises results within 24 hours (often a few hours) and charges half price , because it can run your work when its GPUs would otherwise sit idle. Batch suits anything whose real deadline is "by morning": nightly summaries, labelling, classification, report drafts. It stacks with prompt caching : a system prompt shared by every request is billed at the cache-read rate, and then halved again. The hard part is not technical. Teams call a workload "real-time" because it runs in production, when its users would never notice a delay of hours. Your team ships a nightly report generation pipeline. 50,000 documents, summarize each, cluster the summaries, draft an executive brief. Running synchronously it takes 4 hours at $2,000/night. You hear about batch APIs. The batch gets you 50% off. You also enable prompt caching on the system prompt (shared across all 50k calls). Stacked, the bill drops to $180/night — ~9% of baseline. Same pipeline, three config changes. Batch is the cheapest lever in the LLM cost toolkit that nobody pulls. The reason is mostly organizational: teams think "real-time" when the SLA actually is "by morning." This lesson is about not leaving 90% of the bill on the table. Idea 1 · The three batch APIs OpenAI Batch API : JSONL file upload with a list of requests. Promised 24-hour turnaround (usually ~2-8 hours in practice). 50% discount on input and output tokens. /v1/batches endpoint. Cache-eligible inputs also get cached-input pricing on top. Anthropic Message Batches : JSONL upload. 24-hour turnaround. 50% discount. Supports cache_control — cache writes are explicit, reads happen automatically within the batch. Google Vertex AI Batch Prediction : BigQuery or GCS input. Similar 50% discount for Gemini. Integrates with Vertex pipelines. Idea 2 · Semantic: asynchronous, not slow Batch is "I promise to return within 24 hours" — not "this will take 24 hours." Typical P50 is 2-6 hours. Provider schedules your batch during off-peak windows when GPU inventory is underutilized. Idea 3 · Stack with caching A 50k-document summarization with the same 4K-token system prompt: Synchronous uncached: 50000 × ($input × 4000 + $output × 200) at full rates. Synchronous cached: system prompt cached after first write; remaining 49999 get 10x cheaper input. Batch cached: all of the above plus 50% discount on both read and write. The stack: batch + cache = ~10% of sync uncached bill. Any workload that runs overnight and has a shared system prompt should use this. Idea 4 · Workload triage Interactive — user waits for the response. TTFT matters. Synchronous call with prompt caching. Cannot batch. Semi-interactive — user submits a task, checks back in minutes. Async queue with fallback to sync if batch not available. Think moderate-volume RAG indexing. Batch — user expects results "by morning" or "by end of day." Content pipelines, classification at scale, offline analysis. Always batch, always stack caching. Common mistake: classifying everything as interactive because the pipeline is production. Production is not a latency spec — SLA is. Idea 5 · The partial-interactivity trap Some features look interactive but tolerate 5-10 minutes. Example: a nightly customer health report with "refresh" button. User clicks refresh; wait 10 minutes is fine. Team ships it as synchronous. 50 concurrent refreshes cost 10x what batched-and-delivered-via-email would cost. The question to ask: "What does 24-hour mean for this user?" If the answer is "they wouldn't notice," batch it. Idea 6 · The output-schema trap Batch file formats differ per provider: OpenAI: JSONL, one request per line. Anthropic: JSONL, one message per line; response format embedded. Vertex: BigQuery table or GCS prefix with TFRecord. Writing "one batch client" across providers means adapter code per provider. Gateways that advertise multi-provider batch (Portkey, LiteLLM some tiers) still thin-wrap the raw format. Idea 7 · Numbers you should remember Batch discount across providers: 50% flat on input + output. Turnaround SLA: 24 hours guaranteed, 2-6 hours typical P50. Stacked batch + cached input: ~10% of sync uncached cost. Workload triage rule: if 24h latency acceptable, always batch. Worked example Where the "10% of the bill" comes from, and when it does not 50,000 documents. Each request: a 4,000-token shared system prompt, 2,000 tokens of document, 200 output tokens. Input $3/M, output $15/M, cached input 0.1×, batch 0.5×. Synchronous, no cache: input 50,000 × 6,000 × $3/M = $900; output 50,000 × 200 × $15/M = $150; total $1,050. Cache the 4,000-token prefix: prefix input falls from $600 to about $60, so the total is about $510 (49%). Batch on top halves everything: about $255, or 24% of the original. The "~10%" figure needs the shared prefix to be most of every request. With a 4,000-token prefix and a 2,000-token document, a third of the input stays at full rate, so 24% is the floor here. Your own ratio of shared to unique tokens decides the saving. Production is not a latency requirement; the user's real deadline is. ✓ Batch and prompt-caching discounts multiply. ✗ One batch client works for every provider without adapters. OpenAI, Anthropic and Vertex use different file formats and result shapes. Explain the mechanism A team runs its nightly report pipeline through the same synchronous endpoint as the chat product, because the pipeline is production. How do you classify model workloads, and where does this one belong? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Sort every workload by the latency its user accepts, not by where it runs. Interactive work has a user waiting for the first token and stays synchronous with prompt caching, and semi-interactive work returns in minutes through an async queue. Anything whose user can wait for the full promise belongs on the batch API, which gives a 50 percent discount with a return promised within 24 hours and typical in a few hours. The nightly report is batch when a return at the 24-hour limit still meets its deadline, or when a synchronous fallback covers a late batch. The three lanes. Lane The user The path interactive waits for the first token synchronous, with prompt caching semi-interactive submits and checks back in minutes async queue, with a synchronous fallback batch expects the result by morning or end of day batch API, with cached input stacked on top The misclassification. The lesson's rule is blunt: production is not a latency spec, the SLA is. The common mistake is to call everything interactive because it runs in production. Its cousin is the partial-interactivity trap: a report with a refresh button that users happily wait ten minutes for, shipped as a synchronous call. The lesson puts 50 concurrent refreshes at 10x the cost of the same report batched and delivered by mail. What batch promises. A return within 24 hours, with a typical return of a few hours, because the provider runs the batch when its capacity is idle. The lesson calls this asynchronous, not slow. Stack it with caching. A nightly pipeline shares one system prompt across every call. Cache that prefix, run the pipeline on batch, and the lesson's arithmetic lands near 10 percent of the synchronous uncached cost. Its opening example takes a nightly pipeline from a four-hour synchronous run to a batch run at about 9 percent of the bill with three configuration changes. The other trap. Batch file formats differ per provider, so one batch client needs an adapter per provider, and a gateway that advertises multi-provider batch still wraps the raw formats. Plausible wrong answers. "It runs in production, so it is interactive." Production is where it runs. The lane comes from the latency the user accepts. "Batch means the answer takes a day." The promise is within a day. The typical return is a few hours. "A 50 percent discount is not worth the complexity." On a shared prefix it stacks with caching to about a tenth of the synchronous cost, which the lesson calls the cheapest lever that nobody pulls. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which question sorts a workload into a lane? Expected: what a wait of a day means to this user. If they would not notice, it is batch. (level 2) A user clicks refresh on a health report and waits ten minutes without complaint. Which lane? Expected: semi-interactive at most, and batch if the report can arrive by mail. Shipping it synchronous is the partial-interactivity trap. (level 2) Why does the lesson call batch asynchronous rather than slow? Expected: the promise is a return within a day, and the typical return is a few hours, because the provider runs it when capacity is idle. (level 3) What breaks when you write one batch client for two providers? Expected: the file formats differ, so you need an adapter per provider. Where it is taught. The batch APIs lesson defines the three lanes and the two traps. Estimate it A nightly pipeline summarizes 50,000 documents, and every call opens with the same system prompt. It runs synchronously against a provider for four hours and costs about 2,000 dollars a night. Estimate what the same job costs on the batch API with the system prompt cached, and say when you would move it onto your own GPU instead. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Batch gives a flat 50 percent discount on input and output tokens, and the cached system prompt makes the repeated input about ten times cheaper after the first write. Stacked, the lesson's worked example lands at about 180 dollars a night, near 9 percent of the synchronous bill, from three configuration changes. Move the job to your own GPU when it runs every night at high utilization and the shared prefix is short, so that neither discount has much to work on, and size that run by raising concurrency until the output stops growing. The three bills. The lesson writes the synchronous uncached bill as the document count times the input and output tokens of each call at full rates, with a shared prompt of about 4000 tokens and an output of about 200 tokens per document. Synchronous, uncached. Every call pays for the full prompt and the full output. Synchronous, cached. The system prompt is written once, and the remaining 49999 calls read it at about a tenth of the input price. Batch, cached. Everything above, plus the 50 percent discount on the reads, the write and the output. The lesson's conclusion: batch plus cache comes to about 10 percent of the synchronous uncached bill, and its worked pipeline goes from 2,000 dollars a night to about 180. What the estimate hides. Output tokens take the batch discount only. Caching reuses the prompt's attention state and does nothing for generated tokens, so a job with long outputs and a short prompt saves much less. The first call of a batch pays the cache write premium. Against tens of thousands of reads, it is noise. If the batch runs longer than the cache lifetime, the one-hour variant with its 2x write is worth it once the reads pass five. Check the usage fields on a sample of the results. A batch whose requests all missed the cache shows writes and no reads, and then the second discount never happened. The return is promised within 24 hours and typical within a few hours. A night is shorter than the promise, so the morning deadline holds only on the typical return. Submit the batch a day ahead, or keep a synchronous fallback for a late batch. When your own GPU wins. The lesson's exercise asks for the shared-prefix length at which batch plus cache beats a reserved GPU running overnight. Your own GPU wins when three things hold: the job keeps a reserved GPU busy every night, the shared prefix is short, so there is little to cache, and the outputs are long, so the batch discount is the only lever on the provider side. Data residency can decide it on its own. How to size the self-hosted run. The vLLM manual's recipe for an offline job: pass the whole prompt list to the offline engine class in one call, or run the batch command on a file of requests, and raise the concurrency until the output stops growing. On its card, the output grew to 273.9 tokens per second at 32 concurrent requests and fell to 241.4 at 64, because the pool filled and the GPU throttled. Raise the token budget above 8,192 for throughput, because a slow first token costs nothing when nobody waits, and watch the running count against the cache usage to see which limit binds. Plausible wrong answers. "Batch alone gets you to a tenth of the cost." Batch alone halves the bill. The other factor is the cached shared prompt. "Caching saves the same on output as on input." The cache reuses the prompt's attention state. Every output token is generated and billed in full, less the batch discount. "Batch is too slow for a nightly job." The promise is a day and the typical return is hours. Submit a day ahead, or keep a synchronous fallback for the rare late batch. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Which of the two discounts applies to output tokens? Expected: only the batch discount. Caching lowers the price of repeated input and does nothing for generated tokens. (level 3) The first call in each batch pays a cache write premium. Does that change the estimate? Expected: not at this volume. One write at a quarter more, against tens of thousands of reads at a tenth of the price. (level 4) When does a reserved GPU beat batch plus cache? Expected: when the job keeps the GPU busy every night, the shared prefix is short and the outputs are long, so the two discounts have little to work on. The lesson's exercise computes the break-even prefix length. (level 4) How do you find the right concurrency for the job on your own GPU? Expected: pass the whole list to the offline engine or the batch command, raise concurrency until the output tokens per second stop growing, and raise the token budget. The manual's card peaked near 32 concurrent requests. Where it is taught. The batch APIs lesson stacks the two discounts on the nightly pipeline, the caching economics lesson gives the cache write and read prices, and the batch jobs section of vLLM 101 finds the throughput ceiling of a self-hosted run. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 01 (Managed LLM Platforms), Phase 17 · 19 (AI Gateways) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, toy cascading router simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A dynamic broker evaluates every request (task type, token length, embedding similarity, confidence) and sends simple queries to a cheap model, escalating complex ones to a frontier model. Also called model cascading. Production case studies show 20-60% cost reduction at iso-quality across US/UK/EU deployments; a 30% routing efficiency improvement on high-volume SaaS turns into six-figure annual savings. The 2026 context is that LLM inference prices for a fixed capability level have dropped about 10x per year (a16z LLMflation estimate); at the G Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Model routing "cost broker" Dynamic choice of model per request Model cascade "cheap-first escalate" Run cheap, fall through to frontier on low confidence Pre-route "classify first" Classifier up front; no re-run Ensemble route "parallel pick" Run multiple, reward-model picks best Escalation rate "uprouted %" Fraction of cascade requests that escalated RouteLLM "LMSYS router" OSS router library Not Diamond "commercial router" SaaS model-routing product Drift "cheap creep" Distribution shift without router noticing Online quality gate "live check" Automated LLM-judge sampling live traffic The problem In plain words first Model routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can answer it well. Most traffic is easy (rephrase this, what time is it in Paris) and a small model handles it at a few per cent of a frontier model's price; the rest needs the big model. There are three patterns. A pre-route classifier looks at the request and picks a model before calling anything. A cascade tries the cheap model first and escalates to the expensive one when the answer looks weak: low confidence, a refusal, hedging. An ensemble runs both and picks the better answer, used only for tests. The risk is quiet: as users change what they ask, a router tuned on last quarter's traffic starts sending hard questions to the small model, and quality drops without an error anywhere. Your service costs $80k/month on GPT-5. Your analytics show 70% of queries are simple: "what time is it in Paris?" "rephrase this sentence." A Haiku-class model handles those perfectly at 3% of the cost. 30% need GPT-5's reasoning — coding, math, multi-step planning. If you route the 70% to cheap and 30% to expensive, your bill drops ~65% at the same product quality. This is routing. The trick is building the broker without regressing quality. Idea 1 · Four routing signals Task classification : simple/complex/codegen/math/chat. Can be a rules-based classifier, a small LLM (Haiku-class at $0.25/M), or embedding similarity to labeled buckets. Output: route = cheap / balanced / frontier. Prompt length : prompts >4K tokens often need frontier for coherence. Prompts <500 tokens usually don't. Embedding similarity to known-hard set : if the query is close (cosine > 0.88) to a known-hard bucket, escalate to frontier directly. Self-confidence from first-pass : send to cheap; if model's log-probs show low confidence OR it refuses OR outputs hedging language, retry on frontier. Adds P95 latency on ~10% of traffic but saves 50%+ on the other 90%. Idea 2 · Three patterns Pre-route (classifier up front): ~5-10ms latency added; fastest overall. Cascade (cheap-first, escalate on low confidence): ~1.2x median latency (cheap run plus verify), ~2x on escalated. Best quality floor. Ensemble route (run cheap and frontier in parallel for a sample, reward-model pick): highest quality, highest cost; use only for critical A/B. Idea 3 · Implementation AI gateways (Phase 17 · 19) expose routing. LiteLLM has router config with fallback and cost-routing. Portkey has guards + routing. Kong AI Gateway has plugin-based routing. OpenRouter's model marketplace exposes a recommendation API. Open-source: RouteLLM (LMSYS), Prompt Mule. Commercial: Not Diamond. Idea 4 · The 2026 price curve Model class Late 2022 2026 Change GPT-4-level quality ~$20/M ~$0.40/M 50x cheaper Frontier (GPT-5, Claude 4) — ~$3-10/M new tier Most of the improvement is serving efficiency — the core lessons in Phase 17 · 04-09 turned into provider-side cost drops. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals), Phase 17 · 08 (Inference Metrics) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy disaggregated-vs-colocated simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Prefill is compute-bound; decode is memory-bound. Running both on the same GPU wastes one resource. Disaggregation splits them onto separate pools and transfers KV cache between them over NIXL (RDMA/InfiniBand or TCP fallback). NVIDIA Dynamo (GTC 2025 announce, 1.0 GA) sits above vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM — its Planner Profiler + SLA Planner auto-rate-match prefill:decode ratios to meet SLOs. NVIDIA publishes throughput gains in this ballpark — developer.nvidia.com (2025-06) shows a ~6x improvement for DeepSeek-R1 MoE on GB200 NVL72 + Dynam Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Disaggregated serving "split prefill/decode" Separate GPU pools for each phase NIXL "NVIDIA transport" Dynamo's inter-node KV transfer (RDMA/TCP) NVIDIA Dynamo "the orchestrator" Stack-above coordinator for vLLM/SGLang/TRT-LLM llm-d "Kubernetes native" Red Hat + AWS K8s disaggregated stack Planner Profiler "Dynamo auto-config" Measures workload, configures pool ratios SLA Planner "Dynamo policy" Auto-rate-matches prefill:decode to meet SLOs packDomain: rack "llm-d topology" Pack prefill+decode on same rack for fast KV UCCL "unified collective" llm-d 0.5 networking layer for scale-to-zero MoE expert routing "expert per token" DeepSeek-V3 pattern; disaggregation helps The problem In plain words first Serving a request has two phases with opposite needs. Prefill reads the whole prompt in one pass; it is a big block of matrix maths, limited by the GPU's compute . Decode then writes the answer one token at a time; each step reads all the weights from memory, so it is limited by memory bandwidth . On the same GPU they get in each other's way: a long prefill stalls everyone's decoding, and a decode-heavy batch leaves compute idle. Disaggregated serving runs them on separate pools of GPUs, each sized for its own bottleneck, and ships each request's KV cache from the prefill pool to the decode pool over a fast link. NVIDIA Dynamo and llm-d are the two main systems that orchestrate this. The transfer costs tens of milliseconds, so short requests can lose. You run Llama 3.3 70B on 8 H100s. Under mixed workload (long prompts + short outputs), GPUs idle during decode because most of the compute was spent on prefill. Under different workload (short prompts + long outputs), the opposite happens. Colocated prefill + decode means you over-provision both. Budget impact: 20-40% of GPU time is wasted on the wrong resource. You are buying H100 compute to run memory-bound decode, or buying H100 HBM bandwidth to run compute-bound prefill. Both are expensive waste. Disaggregation splits prefill and decode onto separate pools sized for each's bottleneck. KV cache transfers from prefill pool to decode pool via high-bandwidth interconnect. Idea 1 · Why the bottlenecks differ Prefill — run the transformer over the full input prompt in one forward. Matrix multiplications dominate; compute-bound. H100 FP8 gives ~2000 TFLOPS of useful throughput. Batch efficiency is good — one forward processes many tokens. Decode — generate one token at a time, reading the full weights each iteration. Memory-bandwidth-bound. HBM3 gives ~3 TB/s. Batch efficiency is good only at high concurrency — the weights read amortizes across the batch. Colocating them: you buy GPUs optimized for both. H100 is good at both but costs the same either way. At scale, you want prefill pool on H100 / compute-heavy; decode pool on H200 / memory-heavy, or with aggressive quantization. Idea 2 · The architecture Copy NIXL is NVIDIA's inter-node transport. Uses RDMA/InfiniBand when available, TCP fallback otherwise. Transfer latency is real — typically 20-80 ms for KV cache of a 4K-token prompt on 70B FP8. This is why short prompts don't justify disaggregation: the transfer tax exceeds the savings. Idea 3 · Dynamo vs llm-d NVIDIA Dynamo (GTC 2025 announce, 1.0 GA): - Sits above vLLM, SGLang, TRT-LLM as an orchestrator. - Planner Profiler measures workload, SLA Planner auto-configures prefill:decode ratios. - Rust core, Python extensibility. - Throughput gains: NVIDIA reports 6x for DeepSeek-R1 MoE on GB200 NVL72 + Dynamo in the medium-latency regime (developer.nvidia.com, 2025-06); community reports of "up to 30x" on full Blackwell + Dynamo + DeepSeek-R1 stacks lack a single primary source and should be treated as directional. - GB300 NVL72 + Dynamo: up to 50x MoE throughput vs Hopper per the Dynamo product page (developer.nvidia.com, undated). llm-d (Red Hat + AWS, Kubernetes-native): - Prefill / decode / router as independent Kubernetes Services. - Per-role HPA with queue depth (prefill) / KV utilization (decode) signals. - topologyConstraint packDomain: rack packs prefill+decode cliques on the same rack for high-bandwidth KV transfer. - llm-d 0.5 (2026): hierarchical KV offloading, cache-aware LoRA routing, UCCL networking, scale-to-zero. Use Dynamo if you want a managed stack-above orchestrator. Use llm-d if you want Kubernetes-native primitives and are committed to the CNCF ecosystem. Idea 4 · Economics Internal composite (not a single published case study — order-of-magnitude anchor): $2M/year inference spend on colocated serving. Switched to disaggregated with Dynamo. Same request volume, same P99 latency SLA. Reported savings: $600K–$800K/year (30–40% reduction). No new hardware. We synthesize this figure from multiple customer disclosures rather than a single citable case study; closest published data point is Baseten's 2x faster TTFT / 61% higher throughput with Dynamo KV routing (baseten.co, 2025-10), and VAST + CoreWeave's projection of 60–130% more tokens/$ at 40–60% KV hit rate (vastdata.com, 2025-12). The savings come from right-sizing each pool; prefill-heavy workloads (RAG with 8K+ prefixes) benefit more than balanced ones. Team cannot operate two GPU pools with per-role scaling: Dynamo helps but not trivially. No RDMA fabric: TCP transfer tax is heavier. Idea 6 · The router integrates with Phase 17 · 11 Disaggregated routers are KV-cache-aware (Phase 17 · 11). A request lands on the decode pool holding its prefix — if no match, it flows prefill → decode. Hit rate and disaggregation compound — the cache-aware router determines whether a new prefill is even needed. MoE expert routing is compute-heavy on prefill but memory-heavy on decode (expert caches), so disaggregation is a double win. 2026 frontier model serving is MoE-dominant (DeepSeek-V3, future GPT-5 variants). Disaggregation saves time ​ (the interference removed) and decode speed-up on a memory-optimised pool, but pays a KV transfer ​ that grows with prompt length: ​ + Δ decode ​ > t k v ​ ≈ link bandwidth n prompt ​ ⋅ KV bytes per token ​ + setup Worked example The transfer tax for a 4,000-token prompt Llama 3.3 70B in FP8 stores about 0.16 MB of KV per token (80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 × 2 × 1 byte). 4,000 tokens × 0.16 MB ≈ 655 MB to move. Over RDMA at about 25 GB/s (200 Gbit/s): 655 / 25,000 s ≈ 26 ms, plus setup. Over TCP at about 5 GB/s: about 130 ms. A 256-token prompt moves only about 42 MB (2 ms on RDMA), but its whole prefill takes maybe 20 ms, so there is little interference to remove: the gain is small and the fixed setup cost dominates. That is the lesson's "do not disaggregate below about 512 tokens". a1718: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Production Serving Stack — KV Offloading and Cache-Aware Routing Lesson 17.18 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Diagram the vLLM production-stack layers: router, engines, KV offload, observability. Explain the KV Offloading Connector API (v0.9.0+) and how the 0.11.0 asynchronous path hides offload latency. Quantify when LMCache CPU-DRAM helps (KV > HBM) vs adds overhead (KV small enough to fit HBM). Pick between native vLLM CPU offload and LMCache connector given deployment constraints. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 04 (Serving Engine Internals), Phase 17 · 06 (SGLang/RadixAttention) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy KV-spill simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A production serving stack wires router, engines, and observability into one Kubernetes deployment — and treats KV cache as a resource that can leave the GPU. KV offloading extracts KV cache out of GPU memory and reuses it across queries and engines (CPU DRAM, then disk/Ceph). vLLM's production-stack is the reference deployment; LMCache is the offloading layer. The vLLM 0.11.0 KV Offloading Connector (January 2026) makes this asynchronous and pluggable via the Connector API (v0.9.0+). The offload path is usually hidden from Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Production-stack "the reference deployment" vLLM's Kubernetes Helm chart + operator Connector API "KV backend interface" vLLM 0.9.0+ pluggable KV store interface Native CPU offload "engine-local spill" Store KV in host RAM of same engine LMCache "cluster KV cache" Cross-engine KV cache server on CPU DRAM + disk 0.11.0 async "non-blocking offload" Offload hidden behind engine stream Preemption "evict to make room" KV cache shuffle when HBM full Prefix reuse "same system prompt" Multiple queries share beginning; cache hit Ceph tier "disk tier" Durable storage below DRAM in the cache hierarchy The problem In plain words first A GPU's own memory (HBM) is fast but small. When many users hold long conversations, their KV caches fill it, and the server preempts some requests: it throws away their cache and later reads their prompt again from scratch. Ordinary computer memory (CPU DRAM) is slower but much larger and cheaper. KV offloading moves cache blocks that do not fit into DRAM, so they can be copied back instead of recomputed. vLLM can do this per engine ( native CPU offload ). LMCache goes further: a shared cache server that several engines can read, so a prompt prefix computed on one engine can be reused by another. The vLLM production stack bundles the router, the engines, LMCache and monitoring for Kubernetes. Offloading costs a few per cent when memory is not under pressure. Your vLLM serving shows GPUs at 100% HBM with preemption events whenever concurrency climbs. Requests get evicted, requeued, and you re-prefill the same 2K-token prompt four times in a minute. GPU compute is spent on redundant prefills; goodput is well below raw throughput. Adding more GPUs costs linearly. Adding more HBM is not possible. But CPU DRAM is cheap — one socket has 512 GB+ at latency orders of magnitude worse than HBM but fine for "temporarily warm" KV cache. LMCache extracts KV cache to CPU DRAM so preempted requests recover fast, and repeated prefixes across engines share cache without each engine re-prefilling. Idea 1 · vLLM production-stack github.com/vllm-project/production-stack is the reference Kubernetes deployment: Router — cache-aware (Phase 17 · 11). Consumes KV events. Engines — vLLM workers. One per GPU or per TP/PP group. KV cache offload — LMCache deployment or native connector. Observability — Prometheus scrape, Grafana dashboards, OTel traces. Control plane — service discovery, config, rolling updates. Shipped as Helm chart + operator. Idea 2 · The KV Offloading Connector API (v0.9.0+) vLLM 0.9.0 introduced a Connector API for pluggable KV cache backends. Your engine offloads blocks to the connector; connector stores them (RAM, disk, object storage, LMCache). Request needs a block, connector loads it back. vLLM 0.11.0 (January 2026) adds an asynchronous offload path — offload can happen in the background so the engine does not block on it in the common case. End-to-end latency and throughput still depend on workload shape, KV cache hit rate, and system pressure; vLLM's own notes call out that custom-kernel offload can degrade throughput at low hit rates and that async scheduling has known interaction issues with speculative decoding. Idea 3 · Native CPU offload vs LMCache Native vLLM CPU offload : engine-local. Stores KV blocks in host RAM. Fast to implement, zero network hop. Does not cross engines. LMCache connector : cluster-scale. Stores blocks in a shared LMCache server (CPU DRAM + Ceph/S3 tier). Blocks are accessible to any engine. 16x H100 benchmarks published. Pick native when a single engine has HBM pressure. Pick LMCache when multiple engines share prefixes (RAG with common system prompts, multi-tenant with shared templates). Idea 4 · Benchmark behavior The 16x H100 (80 GB HBM) spread across 4 a3-highgpu-4g test: Low KV footprint (short prompts, low concurrency): all configs match baseline, LMCache adds ~3-5% overhead. Moderate footprint: LMCache starts to help on prefix reuse across engines. KV exceeds HBM: native CPU offload and LMCache both improve throughput substantially; LMCache larger gain because cross-engine sharing. Idea 5 · When LMCache is decisive Multi-tenant serving where system prompts are shared across tenants. RAG where document chunks repeat across queries. Fine-tuned variants (LoRA) on the same base where base-model KV reuse cuts redundant work. Preemption-heavy workloads: restore from CPU cheaper than re-prefill. Idea 6 · When NOT to enable Small HBM pressure — you pay overhead without benefit. Short contexts (<1K tokens) — transfer time > re-prefill. Single-tenant single-prompt workload — no reuse to capture. Code in : Python (stdlib, toy gateway-routing simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A gateway sits between your apps and model providers. Core features are provider routing, fallback, retries, rate limiting, secret references, observability, guardrails. Market split in 2026: LiteLLM is MIT OSS with 100+ providers, OpenAI-compatible, but breaks down around ~2000 RPS (8 GB memory, cascading failures in published benchmarks); best for Python, <500 RPS, dev/prototyping. Portkey is control-plane-positioned (guardrails, PII redaction, jailbreak detection, audit trails), went Apache 2.0 open-source March 2026, 20- Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Gateway "API broker" Process sitting between apps and providers LiteLLM "the MIT one" Python OSS, 100+ providers, breaks at 2K RPS Portkey "guardrails gateway" Control plane + observability, Apache 2.0 Kong AI Gateway "the scale one" Built on Kong Gateway, benchmark leader Bifrost "Maxim's gateway" Retries + Anthropic fallback recipe Cloudflare AI Gateway "edge managed" Edge-deployed managed gateway, zero-ops PII redaction "data scrub" Regex + NER mask before sending to model Jailbreak detection "prompt injection guard" Classifier on user input Audit trail "regulated log" Immutable record of every LLM call Token-bucket "simple rate limit" Refill-based rate limiter Sliding-window "precise rate limit" Time-windowed rate limiter; better fairness The problem In plain words first An AI gateway is one service that sits between your applications and every model provider. Your code calls the gateway with one API (usually OpenAI's format), and the gateway picks the provider, retries on errors, falls back to another provider when one fails or rate-limits you, enforces per-team limits, fetches credentials from a vault, records cost and traces, and can apply guardrails such as removing personal data. Without it, every service carries its own copy of this logic for every provider. The trade-offs are the extra milliseconds each request spends in the gateway, how well it holds up at high request rates, its licence and whether you must run it yourself for data-residency reasons. LiteLLM, Portkey, Kong, Bifrost and Cloudflare or Vercel's gateways sit at different points of those trade-offs. Your product calls OpenAI, Anthropic, and a self-hosted Llama. Each provider has a different SDK, error model, rate limit, and auth scheme. You want failover (if OpenAI 429s, try Anthropic), a single credential store, unified observability, and rate limits per tenant. Reinventing this at the app layer couples every service to every provider. A gateway layer consolidates it into one process with one API (typically OpenAI-compatible) that fans out to providers. Idea 1 · Seven core features Provider routing — OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, self-hosted, etc. behind one API. Fallback — on 429, 5xx, or quality failure, retry elsewhere. Retries — exponential backoff, bounded attempts. Rate limits — per-tenant, per-key, per-model. Secret references — pull credentials from vault at runtime (never in app). Observability — OTel + GenAI attributes (Phase 17 · 13) + cost attribution. Guardrails — PII redaction, jailbreak detection, allowed-topics filters. Idea 2 · LiteLLM — MIT OSS, Python 100+ providers, OpenAI-compatible, router config, fallback, basic observability. Breaks down around 2000 RPS in Kong's benchmark; 8 GB memory footprint, cascading failures under sustained load. Best fit: Python app, <500 RPS, dev/staging gateways, experimental routing. Cost: $0 for OSS; cloud free tier exists. Idea 3 · Portkey — control plane positioning Apache 2.0 OSS as of March 2026. Guardrails, PII redaction, jailbreak detection, audit trails. 20-40 ms per-request latency overhead. $49/mo for production tier with retention + SLA. Best fit: regulated industries needing guardrails + observability bundled. Idea 4 · Kong AI Gateway — the scale play Built on Kong Gateway (mature API gateway product, lua+OpenResty). Kong's own benchmark on 12-CPU equivalent: 228% faster than Portkey, 859% faster than LiteLLM. Pricing: $100/model/month, max 5 on Plus tier. Best fit: already on Kong; >1000 RPS; willing to license. Idea 5 · Bifrost (Maxim AI) Automatic retries with configurable backoff. Fallback to Anthropic on OpenAI 429 is a canonical recipe. Newer entrant; commercial. Idea 6 · Cloudflare AI Gateway / Vercel AI Gateway Managed, zero-ops. Basic retry and observability. Best fit: Edge-serving JavaScript apps on Cloudflare/Vercel. Limited compared to Kong/Portkey on guardrails and rate limits. Idea 7 · Self-hosted vs managed Data residency is the forcing function. Healthcare and finance default self-host (LiteLLM or Portkey OSS or Kong). Consumer products default managed (Cloudflare AI Gateway) or middle-tier (Portkey managed). Hybrid: self-hosted for regulated tenant, managed for others. Idea 8 · Latency budget LiteLLM: 5-15 ms overhead typical. Portkey: 20-40 ms overhead. Kong: 3-8 ms overhead. Cloudflare/Vercel: 1-3 ms overhead (edge advantage). Gateway latency directly adds to TTFT. For TTFT P99 < 100 ms SLA, Kong or Cloudflare. For P99 < 500 ms, any. Idea 9 · Rate-limit semantics matter Simple token-bucket works up to moderate scale. Multi-tenant requires sliding-window + burst allowance + per-tenant tiering. LiteLLM ships token-bucket; Kong ships sliding-window; Portkey ships tiered. Idea 10 · Gateway + observability + routing compose Phase 17 · 13 (observability) + 16 (model routing) + 19 (gateways) are the same layer in production. Pick one tool that covers all three or wire them carefully: most 2026 deployments combine Helicone (observability) or Portkey (guardrails) with Kong (scale) for split roles. Kong pricing: $100/model/month, 5 max on Plus tier. Cloudflare/Vercel: 1-3 ms overhead at the edge. The same idea as a formula Fallback chains. If providers fail independently with probabilities ​ , f 2 ​ , … , a chain of succeeds unless all fail: ∏ k ​ f i ​ Independence is the weak assumption: a shared region, a shared upstream model or a client-side bug makes failures correlated, and the real gain is smaller. Worked example Three providers, honest numbers Error rates: 3%, 2% and 2%. One provider: 97% success. Two, independent: 1 − 0.03 × 0.02 = 99.94%. Three, independent: 1 − 0.03 × 0.02 × 0.02 = 99.9988%. Now suppose a third of the first provider's failures happen during cloud-region outages that also take down the second (both in the same region). The two-provider chain then fails at least 1% of the time (0.03 × ⅓), success at most 99%, not 99.94%. Put fallbacks in a different region or cloud. Latency: each fallback adds a full failed attempt plus backoff, so fallback requests may take 2–3× longer; set a total deadline. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Estimate it Your SLA is a P99 time to first token under 320 ms. The model alone measures 300 ms at P99. You are choosing a gateway to put in front of it. Which classes of gateway fit in the budget, and what do you do when the one you want does not? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The gateway has at most 20 ms at the tail. An edge-managed gateway at 1 to 3 ms and a high-performance gateway at 3 to 8 ms fit, a lightweight proxy at 5 to 15 ms fits with little margin, and a control-plane gateway at 20 to 40 ms does not. If you need the features of the slow one, split the roles: keep the fast gateway on the request path, run the heavy features out of band, or buy the budget back from the model with a faster first token. The budget. The target is 320 ms and the model takes 300 ms, so the gateway may add 20 ms, and that is at the tail. A P99 target means the gateway's own P99, not its median, and a gateway that is quick when idle can be slow under load. The sum of the two tails is a screening estimate only. Before you commit to the SLA, measure the end-to-end first-token P99 through the gateway under load. The classes. Class Overhead in the lesson Fits edge-managed, zero-ops 1 to 3 ms yes high-performance, built on a mature API gateway 3 to 8 ms yes lightweight open-source proxy 5 to 15 ms with little margin control plane with guardrails and audit 20 to 40 ms no The lesson's rule of thumb matches: for a P99 under 100 ms, pick the edge or the high-performance class. For a P99 under 500 ms, any class works. When you want the slow one. The control-plane class brings PII redaction, jailbreak detection and audit trails. Three ways to keep them inside the budget: Split the roles. Put the fast gateway on the request path and run observability and audit off the path. The lesson notes that production deployments combine an observability tool with a scale gateway in exactly this split. Keep only what must be inline. Redaction has to run before the provider sees the prompt, so it stays on the path. Audit and tracing do not. Buy back budget from the model. Prefix caching lowers the first-token time, and a faster model tier does too. Scale decides as well. The lightweight proxy breaks down around 2000 requests per second with an 8 GB footprint in the published benchmark, and the lesson places it below 500 requests per second. If the traffic will grow past that, the high-performance class is the only one that fits both the latency and the scale. Plausible wrong answers. "Every gateway adds a few milliseconds, pick on features." The lesson's overheads run from 1 to 40 ms, and 40 ms is twice this budget. "Put the gateway behind the model, not in front." The gateway routes and falls back before the model. Behind the model it protects nothing. "Add the gateway's median to the model's P99." Two tails do not add that way. Measure the gateway's own tail under load. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why measure the gateway at P99 and not at its median? Expected: the SLA is a P99, and the gateway's tail adds to the model's tail. (level 3) The slow gateway's value is PII redaction. How do you keep it inside the budget? Expected: keep the redaction inline because it must run before the provider sees the prompt, move observability and audit off the path, and then measure whether the remaining overhead fits. (level 3) Traffic will triple next year. Which class survives? Expected: the lightweight proxy breaks down around 2000 requests per second, so plan the move to the high-performance class before that. Where it is taught. The AI gateways lesson gives the latency overhead per gateway class and the scale ceilings. Defend a design You add a second serving replica to double capacity. Throughput rises, but the first-token time of long chat sessions gets worse, and the cache hit rate on both servers falls. Explain the cause, and design the routing so that the second replica stops undoing the cache. Level 3 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Each replica has its own KV cache, and a router that spreads requests at random or in turn sends turn five of a chat to the replica that never saw turns one to four. That replica prefills the whole history again, which is the prefix miss the cache exists to avoid. Route each conversation back to the replica that holds its prefix with a cache-aware policy that remembers which server saw which text, with a load-balance check in front of it. Then read the hit rate on the servers themselves, because the router's record is a guess. The mechanism. A plain Kubernetes Service spreads requests at random. The in-server data parallel controller of SGLang defaults to round robin, which ignores prefixes. Either way, a conversation's turns land on different replicas, and each replica computes the history that the other one already holds. A field report in the SGLang manual measured the damage: with turn-by-turn routing, 23 percent of input tokens were computed again. One request header that pinned each conversation to one GPU raised the cache hit rate from 64.7 to 92.1 percent and halved the median time to first token. How a cache-aware router picks a server. The SGLang gateway keeps one approximate radix tree per model, over the characters of the request text, so it never tokenizes to route. For each request it does three things in order: It checks balance. When the busiest server's load is more than 64 above the lightest and more than 1.5 times the lightest, the request goes to the least-loaded server. Otherwise it computes the match rate, the share of the request text that matches the tree. Above 0.3, the request goes to the server with the longest match. Below 0.3, it goes to the least-loaded server. Every 120 seconds a background task trims each tree to at most 67,108,864 nodes. The balance check comes first on purpose: a prefix-first policy would pile every long conversation onto one hot server. The tree is a guess. The gateway records where it sent text. It never asks a server what it still holds, and a server can evict the prefix later. So a request can arrive at the server the tree names and still prefill. Check the hit rate on the servers themselves, from their counters over a window, and not only the routing decisions. Pick the policy by traffic. Cache-aware routing for chat and agent traffic, where turns share long prefixes. A power-of-two or round-robin policy for batch traffic with unique prompts, because a match rate under the threshold gives no affinity anyway. Do not put multi-turn traffic behind in-server data parallelism with its round-robin default. The same idea in the vLLM layers. The vLLM manual lists routers that read the engine's metrics to pick a replica, and one that also reads the KV cache events the engine publishes with --kv-events-config , so that a request goes to the replica that holds its prefix. The production stack's router keeps a session on one replica. In the gateway lesson's vocabulary, this is provider routing one level down: the AI gateway routes across providers, and the engine router routes across replicas. Pin the router with the engine. The SGLang manual records an incident where the same engine build gave 132,140 tokens per second with one router version and 69,767 with the next. Benchmark the router and the engine as one system, and pin both versions. Plausible wrong answers. "Add a replica and each server's hit rate stays the same." Each replica has its own cache, and random routing splits every conversation across both. "Hash the user id to a server and be done." It keeps a user on one server and ignores load. The manual's gateway balances first, so a hot user cannot saturate one replica with no relief. "Turn on in-server data parallelism instead of a gateway." Its default method is round robin, which ignores prefixes, which is the problem you are solving. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the router check load balance before the prefix match? Expected: a prefix-first policy would send every long conversation to one hot server. The imbalance test sends the request to the least-loaded server when the gap is large. (level 3) Which traffic should not use the cache-aware policy? Expected: batch traffic with unique prompts. A match rate under the threshold gives no affinity, so a load-based policy does the same work with less state. (level 4) One server's hit rate stays low although the gateway routes its conversations there. Why? Expected: the gateway's tree records where it sent text, not what the server still holds. The server evicted the prefix, so the request prefills. Read the server's own counters. (level 4) You upgrade the router without touching the engine. What do you measure? Expected: throughput and hit rate of the router and the engine as one system, because a router change alone halved throughput in a reported incident. Where it is taught. Enumerate five LLM-specific canary metrics (latency, cost/request, error/refusal, output-length distribution, user feedback). Explain why LLM non-determinism (up to 15%) changes what "stable" means in a rollout. Design a rollback path that takes seconds (policy flip) not hours (redeploy). Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 13 (Observability), Phase 17 · 21 (A/B Testing) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, toy canary-progression simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line LLM rollouts combine the hardest parts of software deployment: no unit tests, diffuse failure modes, delayed signals. The sequence is (1) shadow mode — duplicate prod requests to candidate model, log, compare with zero user impact; catches obvious distribution issues but is not a quality guarantee; (2) canary rollout — progressive traffic shift 10% → 25% → 50% → 75% → 100% with gates at each step; track latency percentiles, cost/request, error/refusal rate, output length distribution, user-feedback rate; (3) A/B testing f Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Shadow mode "duplicate to new" Zero-impact send-to-candidate for logging Canary "progressive traffic" Gradual user-exposed rollout with gates Gates "rollout checks" Metric thresholds that block progression Non-determinism "LLM variance" Irreducible run-to-run differences Policy flag "flag flip rollback" Config-level rollback, seconds not hours Model pin "registry digest" Immutable reference to a model version Argo Rollouts "K8s progressive" Kubernetes-native canary/rollback controller KServe "inference K8s" Model serving with canary primitives Istio weighted "mesh split" Service-mesh traffic splitter The problem In plain words first Changing the model behind a product is a release, and releases go wrong. Three practices make it safe. Shadow mode sends real requests to the new model as well as the old one, but only the old one's answers reach users; you compare cost, length, errors and refusals with no risk. A canary rollout then sends a small share of real traffic (1%, then 10%, 25% and so on) to the new model, and at each step checks gates : latency, cost per request, error and refusal rate, answer length and user feedback. If any gate fails, you roll back , which should take seconds: a feature flag flips traffic back and the model version is pinned. LLMs add a twist: the same input does not always give the same output, so a gate must allow for normal run-to-run noise. You ship a new model. Offline evals show 3% accuracy gain. You flip it on in production. Within 24 hours, cost is up 40%, user thumbs-down is up 8%, three customer tickets report "weird answers." You roll back. Redeploy takes 3 hours. Your weekend is ruined. Every piece of that was avoidable. Shadow mode would have caught the 40% cost spike before any user saw it. Canary would have stopped at 10% when thumbs-down moved. Policy-flag rollback would have taken 30 seconds. The discipline is what fills in the gap between "offline evals look good" and "real users are happy." Idea 1 · Shadow mode Candidate receives the same requests as production; outputs are logged, not returned to users. Zero user impact. Log: Output content (diff against production). Token counts (cost delta). Latency. Refusal and error. Catches: cost blow-ups, length regressions, obvious refusal changes, hard errors. Does NOT catch: quality delta users would perceive. Shadow is a smoke test, not a quality test. Idea 2 · Canary rollout Progressive traffic shift with gates. Typical progression: 1% → 10% → 25% → 50% → 75% → 100%. Gate on 5 metrics at each step: Latency percentiles — P50, P95, P99. Breach: canary has P99 > 1.5x baseline. Cost per request — blended $. Breach: >20% above baseline. Error / refusal rate — 5xx plus explicit refusals. Breach: 2x baseline. Output length distribution — mean + P99. Breach: distributional shift. User-feedback rate — thumbs-down / ticket filings. Breach: 1.5x baseline. Idea 3 · Non-determinism is the new variance Identical inputs produce non-identical outputs. Reasons: GPU FP non-associativity (floating-point reduction order varies by batch). Batch-size variance (same prompt in a batch of 128 vs batch of 16). Sampling (temperature > 0). Measured: up to 15% accuracy variation run-to-run on identical eval sets. "Stable" in a rollout means metrics are within expected variance, not identical to baseline. Set gates above the noise floor. Idea 4 · Cost is a variable A 20% better model can be 3x more expensive per call. Cost/request is one of the five gates. Shipping a "better" model that breaks unit economics is a rollback case. Idea 5 · Rollback is the weapon Policy flag (feature flag system): flip percentage in config; takes seconds. Model pinning (registry digest): pinned model does not auto-upgrade. Rollback = revert flag + set pinned digest to previous. Seconds, not hours. If your stack requires redeploy to rollback, fix that before rolling. Idea 6 · Tooling Argo Rollouts / Flagger — Kubernetes progressive delivery controllers. Integrate with Istio/Linkerd weighted routing. Istio weighted routing — service-mesh-level traffic split. KServe / Seldon Core — model serving with built-in canary. Feature flags — LaunchDarkly, Flagsmith, Unleash. Policy-level flip, no redeploy. Idea 7 · Metrics cadence Canary gates check every 5-15 minutes depending on traffic volume. 1% of 1,000 req/min (10 req/min to the canary) gives 50-150 data points per 5-15 minute window — enough for latency but noisy for user feedback. 10% gives ~10x more. Progressions should pause long enough to accumulate enough samples at each step. Idea 8 · The A/B step is optional If the new model is distinctly different (different behavior, different cost curve, different tone), A/B test it at 50% after canary passes. If it's just an improved version of the same behavior, skip to 100% when canary gates pass. Improved means the offline eval showed the gain. The canary gates do not measure task completion, so the skip trusts the eval for it. Idea 9 · Numbers you should remember Canary progression: 1% → 10% → 25% → 50% → 75% → 100%. Non-determinism ceiling: up to 15% run-to-run variance on identical inputs. Five canary metrics: latency, cost, error/refusal, output length, user feedback. Cost gate: >20% above baseline is a breach. Rollback: seconds, not hours. Worked example How much traffic a gate needs A canary at 1% of 1,000 requests a minute gets 10 requests a minute. The baseline thumbs-down rate is 3%, and you want to detect a rise to 4.5% (1.5×). In 15 minutes the canary sees 150 requests: about 4.5 thumbs-down expected at baseline and about 6.75 if worse. A difference of two events is noise. To tell 3% from 4.5% reliably you need roughly 2,500 requests per arm (standard two-proportion test, 80% power, 5% significance): about 4 hours at 1%, or 25 minutes at 10%. So: gate latency, cost and errors at 1% (plenty of signal), and wait for user-feedback gates until 10–25%. Solutions Solution P1 · Reading the canary runs The clean and the 10%-cost runs both promote: 10% is inside the 20% cost gate. The 25% cost regression should fail the cost gate at the first stage. Check the later scenarios in the output: each regression should stop at the stage where its metric first crosses its gate, and the earliest stages catch the strongest signals. Solution B1 · No cost gate Cost per request was never gated, so a model that writes longer answers, or costs more per token, sailed through. Shadow mode would have shown it before any user saw the model: logged token counts per request against production, with a cost delta of +60%. Add cost per request (breach above +20%) and output length as gates. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design You run a canary for a new model. The team wants a rule that stops the rollout when the canary and the baseline differ on any metric. Design the gates so that they catch a real regression and let a healthy rollout through. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Write each gate as a multiplier above the baseline, never as equality. Gate on five metrics: latency percentiles, cost per request, error and refusal rate, output length distribution and user feedback rate. Put every threshold above the run-to-run variance, which the lesson measured at up to 15 percent on identical inputs, and hold each step long enough to collect the samples the gate needs. Why equality fails. Identical inputs produce different outputs. Floating-point reductions on the GPU run in a different order for each batch shape, the batch size changes between runs, and sampling above temperature zero adds its own randomness. The lesson reports up to 15 percent accuracy variation between runs on the same eval set. "Stable" therefore means inside the expected variance, not identical to the baseline. The five gates. Metric Breach Latency P50, P95, P99 canary P99 above 1.5x the baseline Cost per request more than 20 percent above the baseline Error and refusal rate 2x the baseline Output length, mean and P99 a shift in the distribution User feedback, thumbs-down and tickets 1.5x the baseline Measure the noise floor first. Before the canary, run two arms of the same baseline model and record the spread of each metric between them. That spread is the floor. A gate below it halts every rollout, including a good one. The lesson's exercise asks for the multipliers when the eval noise is plus or minus 7 percent, and the answer is a gate above that band. Hold each step long enough. The progression runs 1, 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent. Gates check every 5 to 15 minutes. At 1 percent of a load of 1,000 per minute, the canary sees 10 requests per minute, which is 50 to 150 data points per window. That is enough to read latency and errors, but one or two samples decide the P99, so the P99 gate must hold for more than one window. It is too few for user feedback. Each step must pause until the gate has its samples. Keep the exit cheap. A halt is only useful when the rollback is fast. Keep the traffic share in a policy flag and the model in a registry with a pinned digest, so that a breach reverts in seconds. Plausible wrong answers. "Stop on any difference from the baseline." Two runs of the same model differ, so that rule stops every rollout. "Gate on the mean latency." A mean hides the tail. Gate on the percentiles. "Allow zero cost increase." A better model can cost more. The lesson sets the breach at 20 percent, and the product decides whether the gain pays for it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) How do you learn the size of the noise before the canary starts? Expected: run two canary arms of the same baseline and record the spread of each metric between them. (level 3) User feedback at the first step is too thin to gate on. What do you do? Expected: gate the early steps on latency, cost, errors and length, and apply the feedback gate from the step that has enough samples. (level 4) A gate fires at one step, and the metric is normal again on the next check. Continue or halt? Expected: halt and look. A gate that flaps sits inside the noise or sees an intermittent regression, and both need a decision before more users see the model. Where it is taught. The progressive delivery lesson lists the five gates, the non-determinism ceiling and the step cadence. Estimate it Your service handles 1,000 requests per minute. The canary opens at one percent, and the gate runs every five minutes. About how many data points does one gate check see, and which gates can you trust at this step? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. One percent of the 1,000 per minute is 10 requests per minute to the canary, so a five-minute window holds about 50 points and a fifteen-minute window about 150. That is enough to read latency and error rates, and far too few to read user feedback. Gate the first step on latency, cost, errors and output length, and apply the feedback gate at a later step. The arithmetic. The lesson's cadence is a gate check every 5 to 15 minutes, depending on volume. At 1 percent of a 1,000 per minute load, the canary receives 10 requests per minute, which gives 50 to 150 data points per window. What each gate needs from those points. Gate At about 50 points Latency P50 and P95 readable, with a wide band Latency P99 one or two samples decide it, so hold more than one window Cost per request every request reports its tokens, so a large shift shows Error and refusal rate a baseline of a few percent gives a handful of events, so it is noisy Output length distribution rough, but a large shift shows User feedback only some users rate an answer, so a window holds a few ratings at most The next step changes the picture. At 10 percent the canary sees about ten times more points per window. The feedback gate becomes usable there. This is why the progression pauses at each step: the pause is not a formality, it is the time the gate needs to collect its samples. Write the dwell rule down. For each step, state the number of windows that must pass with every gate green before the share rises. A gate that needs two windows to confirm a breach doubles the exposure of a real regression, so write that trade-off next to the rule. Plausible wrong answers. "One percent is safe, so the gates work at one percent." The share is safe for users, and most gates are blind at that sample size. "Check every minute for faster detection." A one-minute window at this step holds about ten points, which cannot give a percentile. "Start at 25 percent for better statistics." A quarter of the users see the new model before any gate has fired once. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) At which step does the user feedback gate become usable? Expected: at 10 percent, where the canary sees about ten times more points per window. (level 2) Why does a longer window not fix the first step? Expected: a longer window adds points slowly, and a regression runs for the whole window before the gate can fire. (level 3) Traffic falls to a tenth at night. How does the plan change? Expected: the same share gives about one request per minute, so lengthen the dwell, start at a higher share, or run the ramp during the day. (level 3) A breach must hold for two windows before the gate fires. What does that cost? Expected: a real regression keeps running through both windows until the halt, so the rule trades fewer false alarms for a longer exposure. Where it is taught. The progressive delivery lesson gives the metrics cadence and the sample counts per window. Defend a design Last quarter a bad model launch took three hours to undo, because the only way back was a new deployment. You own the release path now. Design it so that the next time, the way back takes seconds. Name the pieces and say what each one holds. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Separate the policy from the model. Keep the traffic split in a feature flag that a configuration change flips, and keep the model in a registry under a pinned digest that never upgrades on its own. A rollback is then two actions: revert the flag, and point the pin at the previous digest, which also restores the prompt and template version pinned with that model. Nothing is rebuilt and nothing is redeployed. Two things change in a launch. The policy. Which share of traffic goes to which model. It lives in a feature-flag system, and a flip takes seconds. The model. The artifact itself. It lives in a registry with a content digest. A pinned digest does not move when a new build appears. A deployment couples the two: to change the policy you ship a new build. The lesson's rule is blunt: if your stack needs a redeploy to roll back, fix that before you roll anything out. The rollback. Revert the flag, set the pinned digest to the previous one, and restore the gate thresholds that went with it. The lesson puts the whole sequence at seconds, against hours for a redeploy. In its opening story, the redeploy took three hours and the flag flip would have taken 30 seconds. The same flag runs the canary. The canary share lives in the same flag: 1, 10, 25, 50, 75 and then 100 percent. A gate breach sets the share back to zero. That makes the halt and the rollback the same mechanism, so the path you rehearse on every rollout is the path you use in an incident. The tooling shape. A progressive delivery controller on the cluster shifts weights at the service mesh or the ingress. A model-serving platform can carry the canary split itself. A feature-flag service holds the policy. Pick one of each, and keep the old model deployed until the new one has held at 100 percent through the gates. Rehearse it. The lesson's exercise asks for a rollback under 60 seconds end to end. Time it in staging on every release, and treat a slower result as a release blocker. Plausible wrong answers. "Roll back by redeploying the previous image." A redeploy takes hours, and the lesson's point is to separate the rollback from the deployment. "Delete the old model a day after the launch." The old model must stay available until the canary has held at full traffic through every gate. "A fast rollback makes the gates unnecessary." The gates decide when to roll back. The fast path only limits the damage once they fire. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why pin the model by digest and not by tag? Expected: a tag can move to a new build. A digest is immutable, so the rollback target is exactly the model that ran before. (level 2) What else must revert together with the model? Expected: the gate thresholds, and any prompt or template version that shipped with the model. (level 3) How do you know the path works before you need it? Expected: rehearse it in staging on every release and time it end to end, against a target such as the lesson's 60 seconds. (level 3) The new model needs a new engine image. Does the flag still work? Expected: yes, when both images run side by side and the flag chooses between them. The old deployment stays alive until the new one has held at 100 percent. Where it is taught. The progressive delivery lesson separates policy flags from model pins and makes the rollback a configuration change. Take-home Take-home. You receive a candidate model, a baseline model, and one week of production request logs with the latency, the token counts and the user feedback of each request. Deliver a rollout plan and a simulator that executes it: a shadow phase, a canary ramp with gates, and a rollback. Inject at least two regressions and show where the plan halts for each one. The logs hold user feedback only for the responses that users saw, so state how the simulator produces feedback for the candidate. Level 4 of 4 · about 60 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Build a simulator that replays the logs through both models, computes the five gate metrics per step, and advances the ramp only when every gate holds for the required number of windows. Set each threshold above the baseline's own run-to-run variance, which you measure by replaying the baseline against itself. Inject a cost regression and a quality regression, and show the step at which each one halts and the rollback that follows. What a complete submission contains. The noise floor. Replay the baseline against itself and report the spread of each metric. This is the floor under every gate. The gates. Latency percentiles, cost per request, error and refusal rate, output length distribution, and user feedback rate. Write each as a multiplier above the floor. The lesson's defaults are a P99 above 1.5x, a cost more than 20 percent above the baseline, errors at 2x, a shift in the length distribution, and feedback at 1.5x. The shadow phase. The candidate sees every request and returns nothing to a user. Report the cost delta, the length distribution, the refusals and the hard errors against the baseline. The ramp. Steps at 1, 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent. Compute the dwell at each step from the samples per window, so that a gate never decides on a handful of points. The rollback. Model it as the lesson describes: a flag back to zero and a pin on the previous digest. The simulator shows the step and the time it takes. Two regressions. The lesson's exercise injects a 25 percent cost regression, and a strong submission shows it halting at the first step. The second regression lives only in the feedback metric, and the submission shows that it stays invisible at the first step and halts only where the sample is large enough. A written decision. The lesson's second exercise: a candidate with a 3 percent accuracy gain and a cost 18 percent above the baseline. Write both policy paths, ship and do not ship, and name who decides. What the reviewer looks for. The floor is measured, not assumed. The gates are multipliers, and the thresholds sit above the floor. The dwell is computed from samples, not from the clock. The regression that the first step cannot see is shown, not hidden. The rollback is rehearsed inside the simulation. What to keep for production. The gate evaluation code and the noise-floor measurement become the checks of the real canary controller. The replay harness becomes the pre-release test for every future candidate. Plausible wrong answers. "Use the lesson's thresholds as they are." The lesson's numbers are defaults. The floor comes from your own baseline. "Advance the ramp on a fixed schedule." A ramp that moves on the clock ignores whether a gate had enough samples. "Model the rollback as a redeploy." The simulator should model the mechanism you will use, and a redeploy is the mechanism the lesson tells you to remove. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The feedback regression was caught late. Is the plan wrong? Expected: no. It shows the limit of the feedback gate, and the fix is a longer dwell at the step where feedback first has samples, or a proxy metric with more volume. (level 4) The candidate has the same cost and tone as the baseline. What changes in the plan? Expected: skip the A/B step after the canary, which the lesson makes optional for an improved version of the same behavior. (level 4) What from the simulator survives into production? Expected: the gate evaluation code and the noise-floor measurement, which become the canary controller's checks. Where it is taught. The progressive delivery lesson gives the gates, the ramp and the exercises that this take-home extends. Explain the mechanism A teammate wants to skip the canary. The new model ran in shadow for a week with no errors and a flat bill, so they call it proven. What does that week show, and what does it leave open? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Shadow mode copies the production requests to the candidate and logs its outputs, and no user sees them. It shows that the candidate does not crash, does not refuse more often, does not cost more and does not write longer answers. It cannot show that users prefer the answers, because no user read one. Shadow is a smoke test, and the canary is the first quality test. What shadow records. For each request, the candidate output is logged next to the production output: the output text, as a diff against production; the token counts, which give the cost delta; the latency; refusals and hard errors. What it catches. Cost blow-ups, length regressions, a change in the refusal rate and hard errors. These are the failures that make a launch expensive or embarrassing, and shadow finds them with zero user impact. What it misses. A quality change that a user would notice. The candidate output never reaches a person, so there is no thumbs-down, no ticket and no retention signal. A model that gives shorter, cheaper and wrong answers passes shadow. What comes next. A canary exposes a growing share of users to the candidate, with a gate at each step. The lesson gates on five metrics: latency percentiles, cost per request, error and refusal rate, the output length distribution, and the user feedback rate. The progression runs from 1 percent to 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent. The first user feedback appears here, not in shadow. Plausible wrong answers. "Shadow passed, so the quality is fine." Shadow has no user, so it measures cost, length, errors and refusals only. "Shadow is a canary at zero percent." A canary returns the candidate output to real users and gates on their feedback. Shadow never returns an output to a user. "A week in shadow replaces the offline eval." The eval judges correctness on a labeled set. Shadow records behavior on live traffic. They answer different questions. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which signal does shadow give that an offline eval does not? Expected: the behavior of the candidate on the real request mix, including cost and output length per request. (level 2) Shadow shows the cost per request is 40 percent above production. What do you do? Expected: stop before any canary. A cost more than 20 percent above the baseline is a gate breach, and a model that breaks the unit economics is a rollback case. (level 2) Why can shadow not measure user feedback? Expected: no user sees the candidate output, so there is nothing for a user to rate or report. (level 3) Shadow doubles the load on your model service. How do you keep it affordable? Expected: send a fixed share of requests to the candidate instead of all of them, and log the same metrics for that share. Where it is taught. The progressive delivery lesson defines shadow mode, the five canary gates and the rollback path.
