In plain words first The idea in one line Traditional A/B testing was not built for non-deterministic LLMs. The critical distinction: evals answer "can the model do the job?" A/B tests answer "do users care?" Both are required; shipping on vibe checks is over. What to test in 2026: prompt engineering (wording), model selection (GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5 vs OSS; accuracy vs cost vs latency), generation parameters (temperature, top-p). Real cases: a chatbot reward-model variant delivered +70% conversation length and +30% retention; Nextdoor AI subject-line experiments del Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Eval "offline test" Labeled-set evaluation of model capability A/B test "experiment" Live randomized comparison on users CUPED "variance reduction" Pre-period regression to reduce variance Sequential test "peek-ok test" Always-valid procedure allowing early stop Multiple comparison "the family error" Running many tests inflates false positives Bonferroni "tight correction" Divide α by number of tests Benjamini-Hochberg "BH FDR" False-discovery-rate control, less conservative SRM "bad split" Sample ratio mismatch; assignment bug Statsig "OpenAI owned" Commercial all-in-one, acquired 2025 GrowthBook "the OSS one" MIT warehouse-native platform mSPRT "sequential probability ratio test" Classical sequential procedure The problem In plain words first An evaluation checks a model on a fixed, labelled set of examples: can it do the task? An A/B test answers a different question: do real users behave better with the new version? You split users at random into group A (current) and group B (new), measure something that matters (task success, retention, cost per request), and only believe a difference that is too large to be chance. Small effects need huge samples: telling a 3.00% conversion rate from 3.06% takes over a million users per group. Several techniques help: CUPED uses each user's behaviour before the test to remove noise, sequential tests let you look at results early without fooling yourself, multiple-comparison corrections stop twenty tests from producing a "winner" by luck, and an SRM check catches broken randomization. You hand-tuned a system prompt. It feels better. You ship it. Conversion changes by noise. You blame the metric. Or you shipped a new model and conversion didn't move — did the model degrade or was the change too small to detect? You don't know, because you shipped without an A/B. Evals answer whether the model can do a task on a labeled set. They do not answer whether users prefer the output. Only a controlled online experiment answers that, and only if the experiment has enough power, controls for non-determinism, and corrects for multiple comparisons. Idea 1 · Evals vs A/B tests Evals — offline, labeled set, judge (rubric or LLM-as-judge or human). Answer: "Is the output correct / helpful / safe on this fixed distribution?" A/B test — online, live users, randomized. Answer: "Does the new variant move the user-level metric that matters?" Both required. Evals catch regressions before exposure; A/B confirms product impact after. Idea 2 · What to test Prompt engineering — wording, system-prompt structure, examples. Metric: task success, user retention, cost/request. Model selection — GPT-4 vs GPT-3.5-Turbo vs Llama-OSS. Metric: accuracy (task) + cost/request + latency P99. Multi-objective. Generation parameters — temperature, top-p, max_tokens. Metric: task-specific (output diversity vs determinism). Idea 3 · CUPED — variance reduction Controlled-experiments Using Pre-Experiment Data. Regress out pre-period variance before comparing post-period. Typical variance reduction: 30-70%. Effective sample size goes up for free. Implementation: both Statsig and GrowthBook implement. Idea 4 · Sequential testing Classical A/B assumes fixed sample size. Sequential tests ("peek-and-decide") control false-positive rate under repeated looks. Always-valid sequential procedures (mSPRT, Howard's confidence sequences) let you stop early on clear winners. Idea 5 · Multiple-comparison corrections Running 20 A/B tests at 95% confidence produces one false positive by chance. Bonferroni correction tightens α per-test; Benjamini-Hochberg controls false-discovery rate. GrowthBook implements both. Idea 6 · SRM — sample ratio mismatch Assignment hash randomizes users to variants. If 50/50 split delivers 47/53, something is broken — SRM check flags it. Both platforms implement. Idea 7 · Statsig vs GrowthBook Statsig : - Acquired by OpenAI for $1.1B (September 2025). Hosted, SaaS. - Sequential testing, CUPED, held-out populations. - All-in-one: feature flags + experimentation + observability. - Best fit: team already wants a bundled product, doesn't care about OpenAI ownership. GrowthBook : - Open-source (MIT); warehouse-native (reads from Snowflake/BigQuery/Redshift directly). - Multiple engines: Bayesian, Frequentist, Sequential. - CUPED, SRM, Bonferroni, BH corrections. - Self-host or managed cloud. - Best fit: warehouse-SQL shop, data team controls the metric layer, wants OSS. Idea 8 · Non-determinism complicates power Same prompt produces varying outputs. Traditional power calculations assume IID observations. With LLM non-determinism, effective sample size is lower than nominal. Multiply required sample size by ~1.3-1.5x as a safety margin. Idea 9 · Real case outcomes Chatbot reward model variant: +70% conversation length, +30% retention. Nextdoor subject lines: +1% CTR after reward-function refinement. Khan Academy Khanmigo: iterative latency-vs-math-accuracy trade. Idea 10 · The anti-pattern: shipping on vibes Every senior engineer can name a feature that was shipped because "it feels better" with no A/B. Most of them regressed product metrics the team didn't notice for months. A/B is the forcing function. Idea 11 · Numbers you should remember Statsig acquired by OpenAI: $1.1B, September 2025. Solution B1 · A weekend with 6,000 users A 0.1-point difference at 3% needs about 460,000 users per arm to detect; 6,000 per arm gives a result well inside the noise. A weekend is also an unusual population. They shipped noise. They should have computed the sample size first, run for whole weeks, and treated the result as inconclusive. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism Your new prompt scores higher than the old one on your labeled set. A product manager asks why you still want a randomized online test before the full launch. Give the two-minute version. Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. An eval tells you whether the model can do the task on a fixed, labeled distribution. A randomized test with live users tells you whether users notice and care. A prompt can win on the labeled set and move no product metric, or move it the wrong way. You need both: the eval blocks a regression before any user sees it, and the experiment confirms the product effect after. Two different questions. An eval runs offline on a labeled set with a judge, which can be a rubric, a model or a person. It answers: is the output correct, helpful and safe on this distribution? An A/B test runs online with live users assigned at random. It answers: does the variant move the user-level metric that matters, such as retention or task completion? Why one is not enough. Every senior engineer can name a feature that shipped because it felt better, with no experiment. Many of them regressed a product metric that nobody watched for months. The eval cannot see user preference. The experiment cannot catch a regression before exposure. Each one covers the blind spot of the other. What to test online. The lesson names three testable axes: Prompt wording and structure. Metrics: task success, retention, cost per request. Model choice. Metrics: task accuracy, cost per request and latency P99 together. Generation parameters such as temperature and top-p. Metric: task-specific. The order. Eval first. Then shadow and a canary to prove the variant is stable. Then an A/B test at a 50 percent split when the variant is a distinct alternative. When it is only an improved version of the same behavior, the canary can go to 100 percent without the A/B step. Improved means that the eval showed the gain. The canary gates do not measure task completion, so the skip trusts the eval for it. Plausible wrong answers. "The eval set is larger, so it is more reliable." The eval set is fixed and labeled, and it measures correctness, not what users prefer. "Run the experiment and skip the eval to save a week." Without the eval, a regression reaches users before anyone can see it. "If the eval and the experiment disagree, the experiment is wrong." They measure different things. A correct answer that users dislike is a real result. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Name one metric an experiment produces that an eval cannot. Expected: a user-level metric such as retention, conversion or the thumbs-down rate. (level 2) The canary passed, and the experiment shows a small drop in conversion. Ship? Expected: not by default. Write the escalation criterion before the test starts, and treat a negative primary metric as a stop. (level 2) When do you skip the experiment after a canary? Expected: when the new version is an improvement of the same behavior, not an alternative with a different cost curve or tone. (level 3) Why does model non-determinism change the sample size? Expected: identical inputs give different outputs, so the effective sample is smaller than the nominal one. The lesson multiplies the required sample by about 1.3 to 1.5. Where it is taught. The A/B testing lesson separates evals from experiments, and the progressive delivery lesson places the experiment after the canary. Weigh a trade-off A product manager reads the experiment dashboard every morning and wants to end the test on the first day the variant looks significant. Twenty other experiments run this quarter under the same plan. What is wrong with it, and what do you offer instead? Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A fixed-sample test assumes one look at a sample size chosen in advance. Looking every day and stopping at the first significant result gives noise many chances to cross the line, so the false positive rate climbs. Offer a sequential test, which stays valid under repeated looks and still allows an early stop on a clear winner. Across many experiments, correct for multiple comparisons, and reduce variance with pre-experiment data so each test needs fewer samples. The peeking problem. Classical A/B analysis assumes the sample size is fixed before the test. Each extra look is another test, and a stop at the first significant look selects the noise. The manager's plan is not wrong because it looks often. It is wrong because it decides on a procedure that was not built for repeated decisions. Sequential testing. Always-valid sequential procedures, such as the mixture sequential probability ratio test and confidence sequences, control the false positive rate under repeated looks. You can check daily and stop early on a clear winner, and the error rate stays what you set. The lesson's simulator shows the fixed and the sequential boundaries side by side. Twenty experiments. At 95 percent confidence, 20 experiments produce about one false positive by chance. Two corrections exist. Bonferroni divides the error rate by the number of tests, which is strict. Benjamini-Hochberg controls the false discovery rate and is less conservative. Choose by the cost of one false launch against the cost of missing a real win. Variance reduction. CUPED regresses out the variance that pre-experiment data explains. The lesson gives a typical reduction of 30 to 70 percent, which raises the effective sample size at no cost in traffic. That is the honest way to shorten a test. Two more checks. A sample ratio mismatch check catches a broken assignment before you read any result. Non-determinism in model output lowers the effective sample size, so the lesson multiplies the required sample by about 1.3 to 1.5. Plausible wrong answers. "Stopping early is fine when the p-value is small." Under a fixed-sample test, a small p-value on the first day is partly selected noise. Only a sequential procedure keeps that stop valid. "Run all the tests at 95 percent and ship the winners." About one winner is a false positive by chance. Correct for multiple comparisons. "A longer test is always more reliable." Longer helps only if the assignment is sound. Check the sample ratio first. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg for the quarter? Expected: Bonferroni when any false launch is costly, Benjamini-Hochberg when you accept a controlled share of false discoveries in exchange for power. (level 3) What does CUPED need, and what does it give? Expected: it needs a pre-period metric for each unit, and it gives a tighter estimate from the same traffic. (level 4) A new model needs a larger sample than the quarter allows. What do you change? Expected: pick a primary metric with lower variance, apply CUPED, or extend the test. Do not shorten it by stopping early under a fixed-sample procedure. Where it is taught. The A/B testing lesson covers sequential tests, CUPED, SRM checks and multiple-comparison corrections. a1722: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Load Testing LLM APIs — Why k6 and Locust Lie Lesson 17.22 75 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain the two anti-patterns (GIL trap, prompt-uniformity trap) that make generic load testers lie for LLM APIs. Pick a tool for a given purpose: LLMPerf (benchmark run), k6 + streaming extension (CI gate), guidellm (large-scale synthetic), GenAI-Perf (NVIDIA reference). Design four load patterns (steady, ramp, spike, soak) and name the failure mode each catches. Build a realistic prompt distribution using mean + stddev of input tokens rather than fixed length. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 08 (Inference Metrics), Phase 17 · 03 (GPU Autoscaling) Type : Build. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy realistic-prompt generator + latency collector). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Traditional load testers were not designed for streaming responses, variable output lengths, token-level metrics, or GPU saturation. Two traps bite most teams. The GIL trap: Locust's token-level measurement runs tokenization under the Python GIL, which competes with request generation under heavy concurrency; tokenization backlog then inflates reported inter-token latency — your client is the bottleneck, not the server. The prompt-uniformity trap: identical prompts in a loop test one point on the token distribution; real traffic has variable l Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means LLMPerf "the LLM harness" Anyscale benchmark tool, streaming-aware GenAI-Perf "NVIDIA tool" NVIDIA reference harness LLM-Locust "Locust for LLMs" Locust extension fixing GIL trap guidellm "synthetic benchmark" Large-scale synthetic tool k6 Operator "K8s k6" CRD-based distributed k6 GIL trap "Python client overhead" Tokenization backlog inflates reported latency Prompt-uniformity trap "single-prompt lie" Loop with same prompt hits cache, inflates throughput Steady-state "constant load" Flat RPS for N minutes Ramp "linear up" 0 to target over duration Spike "burst test" Sudden multiplier then revert Soak "long test" Hours for leak detection The problem In plain words first A load test sends a server realistic traffic at increasing volume to find where it breaks before users do. LLM servers have two traps that make ordinary load tests lie. The prompt-uniformity trap : if every simulated user sends the same prompt, the server's prefix cache answers almost all of them from memory, and you measure a cache, not a model. The GIL trap : Python load tools such as Locust tokenize responses in the same process that sends requests, so at high concurrency the client slows down and its timing numbers include its own delays. A good LLM load test samples prompts from a realistic distribution of lengths and contents, uses a tool that does not bottleneck itself (LLMPerf, k6, GenAI-Perf, LLM-Locust), and runs four shapes of traffic: steady, ramp, spike and soak. You k6-tested your LLM endpoint at 500 concurrent users. It held. You shipped. In production at 200 actual users the service fell over — P99 TTFT exploded, GPUs pinned. Two things happened. First, k6 sent 500 identical prompts — your request-coalescing and prefix caching made it look like you were handling 500 concurrent decodes when you were actually handling one. Second, k6 doesn't track inter-token latency on streaming responses the way the eye experiences it; it sees one HTTP connection, not 500 tokens arriving at varying intervals. Load testing for LLMs is its own discipline. Idea 1 · The GIL trap (Locust) Locust uses Python and runs tokenization client-side under the GIL. Under high concurrency the tokenizer queues behind request generation. Reported inter-token latency includes client-side tokenization backlog. You think the server is slow; it's the test harness. Fix: LLM-Locust extension moves tokenization to separate processes, or use a compiled-language harness (k6, LLMPerf using tokenizers.rs). Idea 2 · The prompt-uniformity trap All known load testers let you configure one prompt. In a loop test of 10,000 iterations the exact same prompt sends each time. Server sees the same prefix every time — prefix cache hits approach 100%, throughput looks great. Fix: sample from a prompt distribution. LLMPerf uses --mean-input-tokens 500 --stddev-input-tokens 150 — diverse lengths, diverse content. Idea 3 · Four load patterns Steady-state — constant RPS for 30-60 min. Catches: baseline performance regressions. Ramp — linearly increase RPS from 0 to target over 15 min. Catches: capacity breakpoint, warm-up anomalies. Spike — sudden 3-10x RPS for 2 min then back. Catches: autoscaling latency, queue saturation, cold-start impact. Soak — steady-state for 4-8 hours. Catches: memory leaks, connection-pool drift, observability overflow. Idea 4 · 2026 tool mapping LLMPerf (Anyscale) — Python but Rust-backed tokenization. Mean/stddev prompts. Streaming-aware. Best default for performance runs. NVIDIA GenAI-Perf — NVIDIA's reference. Uses Triton client; comprehensive metric coverage. Note its ITL excludes TTFT; LLMPerf's includes it. Two tools produce different TPOT for the same server. LLM-Locust (TrueFoundry) — Locust extension that fixes the GIL trap. Familiar Locust DSL + streaming metrics. guidellm — large-scale synthetic benchmarking. k6 v2026.1.0 + k6 Operator 1.0 GA (Sept 2025) : - k6 itself (Go, compiled, no GIL) added streaming-aware metrics. - k6 Operator uses TestRun / PrivateLoadZone CRDs for Kubernetes-native distributed testing. - Best for CI/CD gates and SLA testing. Vegeta — Go, simpler than k6. Constant-rate HTTP saturation. Not LLM-aware but good for gateway / rate-limit testing. Locust 2.43.3 stock — has the GIL trap for LLM. Only with LLM-Locust extension. Idea 5 · SLA gate in CI Run k6 on the PR with: 30-50 iterations each at baseline RPS. Gate: P50/P95 TTFT, 5xx < 5%, TPOT under threshold. Break the build on breach. Idea 6 · Realistic prompt distribution Build from real traffic samples (if you have them) or from published distributions (e.g., ShareGPT prompts for chat, HumanEval for code). Feed the mean + stddev to LLMPerf. Avoid loop-with-one-prompt at all costs. Idea 7 · Numbers you should remember k6 Operator 1.0 GA: September 2025. k6 v2026.1.0: streaming-aware metrics. Typical LLMPerf run: 100-1000 requests at concurrency X. Typical CI gate: 30-50 iterations per PR. Four patterns: steady, ramp, spike, soak. Worked example What a uniform test hides Suppose prefill costs about 0.4 ms per prompt token on a miss and the cached path about 80 ms flat. Uniform test: 500 requests, all with the same 2,000-token prompt. 499 are cache hits: TTFT about 80 ms every time. P99 = 80 ms. Realistic test: prompt lengths with mean 500 and standard deviation 150, mostly unique content. Cache hits only where a system prompt is shared; a 2,000-token unique prompt takes about 800 ms. The P99 in production is set by the long, unique prompts: about 800 ms, ten times what the uniform test reported. The same mistake hides concurrency effects: with one cached prefix there is no real prefill load, so the GPU never saturates. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ A loop over one prompt mostly measures the prefix cache. ✗ Stock Locust is a good harness for streaming LLM latency at high concurrency. Its client-side tokenization runs under Python's GIL and inflates the latency it reports. ✓ A soak test of 4–8 hours finds memory leaks a 10-minute test misses. ✗ Load-testing at your expected peak is enough. Spike tests at 3–10× catch autoscaling and queueing failures. Solutions Solution P1 · Uniform against realistic In code/main.py the gap is entirely in the tail: P50 is 80 ms for both, but P99 is 80 ms with uniform prompts and 800 ms with realistic ones, because 499 of 500 uniform requests are cache hits against 421 for the realistic mix. The concurrency levels are identical because the toy has no queueing model. Solution B1 · A gate that lied (1) One fixed prompt: after the first request everything came from the prefix cache, so the gate measured cache latency. (2) No realistic length distribution: production's long prompts set the P95. A third common cause: the test ran against a warm, otherwise idle server, while production also has cold replicas and mixed traffic. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism Two engineers benchmark the same server on the same day and report numbers that differ by a few percent. Both used standard benchmark clients. Before you look at the server, what about the clients could explain the gap, and what rules would you set for the team? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The client is part of the measurement. On one vLLM server the SGLang client read a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher and an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower than the vLLM client, the two clients sent different random prompts, and temperature 0.7 raised the time per token by 10 to 13 percent at one user against temperature 0. The rules: one client, one temperature, one prompt length distribution with the range ratio stated, a flush and a new seed per run, the clock recorded, and all of that written next to every number. Three clients on one server. The manual ran the SGLang client, vllm bench serve and its Rust version against one vLLM server with Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B, with a cache reset before every run and the clients alternated over two rounds. Output tokens per second at 64 users: Temperature SGLang client vllm bench vllm bench, Rust 0 359, 348 379, 377 371, 365 0.7 331, 343 360, 363 356, 353 The two vLLM clients agreed within the noise at 1, 16 and 64 users. The SGLang client read a slower server: a median first token 3 to 10 percent higher, and at 16 and 64 users an output throughput 2 to 8 percent lower. The two clients send different prompt tokens from their random datasets, so part of a small gap can come from the prompts. Temperature 0.7 raised the median time per token over temperature 0 by 10 to 13 percent at one user and 3 to 6 percent at 16 and 64 users. Four defaults that change the result. The SGLang client makes choices before it measures anything: Setting Default What it does to the result --random-range-ratio 0.0 each length is drawn from 1 to the length you asked for, so the average prompt is about half of it ignore_eos on every request generates exactly the output length you asked for --request-rate inf all requests are sent at time 0, and only the concurrency cap holds them back --warmup-requests 1 one request runs before the clock starts The first row is the trap. With the default ratio, an input length of 512 gives an average prompt near 256 tokens, and the report says 512. Pass 1.0 or write the length distribution next to the result. With 1.0, 32 prompts of 512 tokens give an input total of 16384 in the report. Fixed lengths form waves. With the ratio at 1.0 every request has the same length, so requests that start together finish together and their replacements arrive together. At 16 users on the L4, fixed lengths gave a median time to first token of 1,996 ms and a P99 ITL of 82 ms; mixed lengths gave 291 ms and 300 ms. The two settings measure two different servers. Fixed lengths measure bursts, with a slow first token and smooth tokens. Mixed lengths measure steady traffic, with a fast first token and stalls in the stream. Keep 1.0 to compare two builds, and run your real length mix before you set a latency target. The client's own queue. The SGLang client sends every request from one Python process. A 2026 study found that such a client adds its own queue at high request rates and then reports a first token and a time per token higher than the server gave. Before you trust a number at a high rate, compare one client process with two processes that each send half the rate. The lesson names the same trap for a general load tester: tokenization under the interpreter lock in the client inflates the reported inter-token latency, and one prompt sent in a loop hits the prefix cache on almost every request and inflates the throughput. Hand-written scripts. One report measured 13 tokens per second for a large model on eight GPUs against 60 from a hosted API. The script counted words split on spaces and included the first-token time in the rate. A word is not a token, and TTFT is not decode time. Use the benchmark client, which counts tokens and keeps TTFT and TPOT apart. The rules. One client, one version, named in every result. One temperature, named in every result. --random-range-ratio 1.0 , or the length distribution written down. A flush and a new seed before every run, and the cached tokens recorded. The GPU clock recorded and the hot runs set aside. Throughput reported only together with the median and P99 TTFT and TPOT at the same cap. Plausible wrong answers. "Both are standard clients, so the numbers are comparable." On one server the SGLang client read 3 to 10 percent higher first-token times and 2 to 8 percent lower throughput than the vLLM client; a gap of a few percent can come from the client alone. "Temperature does not change speed." Temperature 0.7 raised the median time per token 10 to 13 percent at one user and 3 to 6 percent at 16 and 64 users over temperature 0. "Set the input length to 512 and the prompts are 512 tokens." With the default range ratio of 0.0 the average prompt is about 256 tokens; pass 1.0 or state the distribution. "A load tester that handles HTTP handles model traffic." A generic tool sends one prompt in a loop, which hits the prefix cache almost every time, and it does not read the token gaps of a stream; use a client that samples prompt lengths and counts tokens. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the default range ratio describe half the work? Expected: each length is drawn from 1 to the length asked, so the average prompt is about half of it; with 1.0 every prompt has the full length and the input token total in the report confirms it. (level 3) Fixed lengths gave a late first token and a steady stream, mixed lengths the opposite. Which do you use? Expected: fixed lengths to compare two builds, because they repeat exactly; your real length mix before you set a latency target, because the two shapes measure two different servers. (level 3) A teammate's hand-written timing loop reads 13 tokens per second where a hosted API reads 60. What is wrong with the loop? Expected: it counted words split on spaces and included the first-token time in the rate; a word is not a token and TTFT is not decode time, so use the benchmark client. (level 4) At 16 requests per second the client reports a first token you do not believe. How do you check the client itself? Expected: a single-process client adds its own queue at high rates; run two client processes that each send half the rate and compare, and record the CPU use of the client. Where it is taught. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 13 (Observability), Phase 17 · 24 (Chaos Engineering) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy multi-agent incident triage simulator). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line AI SRE uses LLMs grounded in infrastructure data (logs, runbooks, service topology) via RAG to automate investigation, documentation, and coordination phases. The 2026 architecture pattern is multi-agent orchestration — specialized agents (logs, metrics, runbooks) coordinated by a supervisor; AI proposes hypotheses and queries, humans approve judgment calls. Datadog Bits AI and Azure SRE Agent ship this as managed products. Runbooks are evolving: NeuBird Hawkeye uses adversarial evaluation (two models analyze the s Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means AI SRE "agent for on-call" LLM-backed incident investigation + coordination Supervisor agent "the orchestrator" Top-level agent breaking incidents into sub-queries Specialized agent "domain agent" Sub-agent with tool access (logs, metrics, runbooks) Auto-remediation "AI fixes it" Narrow pre-approved action; NOT broad re-architecture Operational memory "vector runbooks" Post-mortems + runbooks in vector DB for RAG Adversarial eval "two-model check" Independent analyses; agreement = confidence NeuBird Hawkeye "the adversarial one" Product with adversarial-eval + memory pattern Bits AI "Datadog's SRE agent" Datadog-managed AI SRE Pre-incident prediction "early detection" 10-15 min lead time on outage prediction The problem In plain words first SRE (site reliability engineering) is the work of keeping services up: alerts, on-call, incident response, post-mortems. Much of the first half-hour of an incident is searching: grouping error logs, checking metrics, looking at recent deploys and finding the runbook that matches. AI SRE gives that search to agents. A supervisor agent splits the incident into questions, specialist agents query logs, metrics and runbooks with their own tools, and the supervisor presents ranked hypotheses with evidence to the human on call. Agents may also act, but only inside a narrow, pre-approved set (restart a pod, revert a deploy, scale within limits). Anything broader stays with people. Two models analysing the same incident independently, and escalating when they disagree, is a cheap way to catch confident mistakes. An on-call engineer gets paged at 3 a.m. "High error rate in checkout." They check Datadog, Loki, three runbooks, the deploy log. 30 minutes later they realize the root cause is a vLLM OOM from a KV cache spike. They restart the pod; error clears. In 2026 the first 20 minutes of that investigation are automatable. Grouping logs by service, correlating to recent deploys, matching against runbooks — all are RAG + tool-use. A supervised agent can do first-pass triage and present a hypothesis before the human opens Datadog. Fully autonomous remediation is a different problem. Restart pod: safe. Scale GPU pool: safe if policy allows. Re-architect the service: absolutely not. The discipline is drawing the narrow line. Idea 1 · Multi-agent architecture Copy Supervisor breaks the incident into sub-queries. Specialized agents have tool access (log search, PromQL, doc retrieval). Supervisor synthesizes, presents hypothesis + evidence to human. Human approves or redirects. Idea 2 · Auto-remediation scope Safe (narrow) : restart pod, revert specific deploy, scale pool within pre-approved bounds, enable pre-approved feature flag. Not safe (broad) : change service topology, modify resource limits, deploy new code, change IAM, alter databases. Anyone selling "set it and forget it" is overselling. The safe set grows as AI SRE matures, but the boundary is real. Idea 3 · Adversarial evaluation (NeuBird Hawkeye) Two models independently analyze the same incident. If they agree on root cause, confidence is high. If they disagree, escalate to human with both hypotheses visible. Simple pattern, effective filter against hallucinated root causes. Idea 4 · Operational memory Team turnover is the silent kill of traditional SRE — tribal knowledge leaves. AI SRE stores runbooks + post-mortems in a vector DB; agents retrieve on every new incident. When new engineers join, the AI has full history. Idea 5 · Pre-incident prediction MIT 2025 research: LLM trained on historical logs, GPU temperatures, API error patterns predicted 89% of outages 10-15 minutes before they happened on the test set. Reality check: predictions without actuation are dashboards. The operational question is "when we predict, what do we do?" Pre-emptive drain? Pager? Auto-scale? The answer is policy-specific. Idea 6 · Products in 2026 Datadog Bits AI — managed SRE copilot inside Datadog. Azure SRE Agent — Azure-native. NeuBird Hawkeye — adversarial eval + operational memory. PagerDuty AIOps — triage + deduplication. Incident.io Autopilot — incident commander + coordination. Idea 7 · Runbooks as code Runbooks evolve from Confluence pages to versioned markdown with structured sections (symptom, hypothesis, verify, act). Structured runbooks feed better RAG retrieval. Start any AI-SRE rollout by turning unstructured runbooks into structured. Idea 8 · Numbers you should remember MIT early-detection: 89% of outages, 10-15 min lead time. Multi-agent triage: supervisor + (logs, metrics, runbooks) + human. Safe auto-remediation set: restart pod, revert deploy, scale within bounds. Adversarial eval: two models independent; agreement = confidence. Worked example Turning a runbook into something agents can use A Confluence page says "If checkout errors spike, it's usually the GPU box running out of memory; restart it and maybe lower the memory setting." Symptom : error rate on /checkout/generate-summary above 2% for 3 minutes, log pattern kv_cache_allocation_failed . Hypothesis : vLLM KV cache out of memory under burst concurrency. Verify : DCGM_FI_DEV_FB_USED at or above 97% in the 5 minutes before onset; preemption counter rising. Act (pre-approved) : restart the affected pod; set --gpu-memory-utilization to 0.85. Escalate if errors persist 10 minutes after. Each field is now something an agent can retrieve, test with a tool and report on, and the action is narrow enough to allow without a human. Solutions Solution B1 · Confidence is not permission The missing rule is an action allow-list: what an agent may do must be fixed in advance, independent of how confident it is. Changing connection limits across services is a broad, cross-system change and should have been proposed to a human with its evidence, not executed. Confidence decides whether to escalate, not what is permitted. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Weigh a trade-off A vendor demo shows an operations agent that repairs incidents on its own. Your director asks which actions you would let such an agent take on the model service without a person in the loop. Draw the line and defend it. Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Allow a narrow set that was approved in advance: restart a pod, revert one named deployment, scale a pool inside approved bounds, and flip an approved feature flag. Keep everything that changes the shape of the system behind a person: topology, resource limits, new code, access rights and databases. The agent proposes, a person approves the judgment calls, and the safe set grows only as the agent builds a record. The two sets. Safe, automated Not safe, human only restart a pod change the service topology revert one specific deployment modify resource limits scale a pool within pre-approved bounds deploy new code enable a pre-approved feature flag change access rights alter a database What makes an action safe. It is reversible, its blast radius is bounded in advance, and it matches a step in a runbook that a person wrote. The lesson's example incident is a KV cache spike that pushed a serving engine out of memory. A pod restart clears it, and a restart is on the safe list. Raising the memory limit might also clear it, and that change alters how every pod runs from then on, so it stays with a person. How an action earns automation. Write the runbook in structured form: symptom, hypothesis, verify, act. Give the action a success criterion and a verify step that runs after it. Record every proposal and every human decision. Promote the action from proposed to automatic after a run of incidents where the proposal matched what the person chose. The approval gate stays. The architecture is a supervisor over log, metric and runbook agents, a hypothesis with evidence, a human approval, and then an action from the narrow set. Even when two independent models agree on the cause, the approval stays for anything outside the safe set. The lesson is direct about vendors who sell a system that needs no supervision: they are overselling. Plausible wrong answers. "If the agent is accurate enough, let it do everything." Accuracy on past incidents does not bound the damage of one wrong broad action. "No automation until the agent is perfect." A restart and a revert are safe today, and they remove the first part of most investigations. "An approval step makes the agent useless at night." The agent still does the investigation. The person approves one proposed action instead of starting from the dashboards. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is a scale-up inside bounds safe while a resource limit change is not? Expected: the bounds were approved in advance and the action reverses cleanly. A limit change alters how every pod runs and can trigger the next incident. (level 3) What has to be true before the agent may run an action unsupervised? Expected: a structured runbook, a verify step with a success criterion, an audit record, and a record of proposals that matched the human decision. (level 4) The agent restarted the busiest pod during a load spike because a probe failed. Was that inside the rules? Expected: the action was allowed and the trigger was wrong. A restart under load drops the running requests, so the rule needs a condition on load and on the probe type, not only on the action. Where it is taught. The SRE for AI lesson draws the line between narrow and broad remediation and keeps the human approval gate. Defend a design A model trained on your logs, GPU temperatures and error patterns predicts most outages ten to fifteen minutes before they happen. The team wants to ship it as a dashboard panel. Design what the system does with a prediction, and defend the design. Level 4 of 4 · about 15 minutes to answer well. Short answer. A prediction with no action is a dashboard, and nobody watches a dashboard at three in the morning. Write a policy per prediction class: page the on-call, drain the suspect node or pool before it fails, or scale within approved bounds, and record every prediction with its outcome. Start with the page, measure the precision on live incidents, and promote a class to an automatic drain only when its false alarm rate is acceptable and a person has approved that drain as a pre-approved action in the runbook. The result and its limit. The lesson cites a research result: a model trained on past log lines, GPU temperature readings and API error patterns predicted 89 percent of outages 10 to 15 minutes early on its test set. The lesson's reality check follows at once. Predictions without actuation are dashboards. The operational question is what you do when the prediction fires. The design. Classify the prediction. Which failure is coming: a memory exhaustion, a thermal slowdown, a provider error burst. Attach the confidence. Map each class to an action. The lesson's safe set is narrow: restart a pod, revert a deploy, scale within pre-approved bounds. A drain is not on that list, so it needs approval before it runs on its own. Drain the pod from the load balancer and restart it before it falls over. Scale the pool within approved bounds. Page a person with the prediction and the evidence. Fit the action into the lead time. A drain plus a replacement must complete inside the ten to fifteen minutes, so the replacement has to be warm already. A cold start of a large model takes minutes and can eat the whole window. Record outcomes. Every prediction, its class, the action taken and whether the outage happened. Precision and recall per class come from this log, not from the paper. Guard the blast radius. Never run two automatic drains in the same pool at once, and never drain under a load spike without a warm spare. Why page first. A page costs sleep. A false drain costs capacity for the drain time. A false scale-up costs money. Until the precision per class is measured in production, the cheapest wrong action is the page. Promote a class to automatic action when its record justifies it, the same ladder the lesson uses for remediation. Plausible wrong answers. "Ship the panel and let on-call decide." At night nobody watches a panel. The lesson's point is that a prediction without an action is a dashboard. "Automate the drain for every prediction from day one." A false alarm then costs capacity, and nothing has measured the false alarm rate on your traffic. "The research number means we will prevent most outages." The number was on a test set. Your precision in production is unknown until you measure it. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does a false alarm cost under each policy? Expected: a page costs sleep, a drain costs capacity for the drain time, and a scale-up costs money. Pick the policy per class from that cost against the cost of the outage. (level 4) The lead time is ten minutes and a replacement replica takes longer to warm. What changes? Expected: keep a warm spare or act earlier on a weaker signal. A drain with no warm replacement moves the outage instead of preventing it. (level 4) How do you know the predictor still works after the service changes? Expected: track precision and recall per class on live incidents, and retrain when the input distribution shifts. Where it is taught. The SRE for AI lesson reports the early-detection result and asks what the system does when it predicts. Explain the mechanism An incident triage agent proposes a root cause for every alert. The on-call team stopped trusting it after several confident wrong answers. Which pattern from the SRE lesson raises the trust in its output, and what does the team do when the pattern says the agent is unsure? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Run two models independently on the same incident. When they agree on the root cause, confidence is high. When they disagree, the system escalates to a person with both hypotheses and their evidence visible, instead of picking one. The pattern filters invented root causes at a low cost, and the disagreement itself tells the responder that the incident is uncertain. Adversarial evaluation. The lesson names the pattern after a product that ships it: two models analyze the same incident on their own. Agreement is confidence. Disagreement is an escalation with both hypotheses shown. It is simple, and it is an effective filter against a confident wrong answer, because two independent analyses rarely invent the same cause. Where it sits in the architecture. A supervisor splits the incident into sub-queries. Specialized agents with tool access search the logs, run the metric queries and retrieve the runbooks. The supervisor assembles a hypothesis with evidence and shows it to a person, who approves or redirects. Only then does an action run, and only from a narrow approved set. The two-model check sits at the hypothesis step, before the person sees it. What the person does on a disagreement. Reads both hypotheses and the evidence that each one cites. Picks one, redirects the agents, or starts the manual investigation with two leads instead of none. The lesson's division of labor holds: the agent proposes hypotheses and queries, and the person makes the judgment call. What the agents remember. Runbooks and postmortems live in a vector store, and both models retrieve from it on every incident. Operational memory survives team turnover, and a new engineer's first incident has the full history behind it. The limit of agreement. Two models that share training data can agree and be wrong together. Agreement raises confidence, it is not proof. Require every hypothesis to cite the log lines and the metric queries behind it, so that the responder can check the evidence and not the eloquence. Plausible wrong answers. "Ask one model twice at temperature zero." A repeat of the same model shares its blind spots. The pattern needs independent analyses. "Let an agreed hypothesis trigger the fix on its own." Agreement raises confidence. The person still approves the action, and only narrow actions are automated at all. "Disagreement proves the agent is useless." It means the incident is uncertain, which is exactly when a person should look. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why is a split verdict useful to the responder? Expected: it marks the incident as uncertain and gives the responder two candidate causes with their evidence. (level 3) Both models agree and both are wrong. How do you catch it? Expected: require each hypothesis to cite evidence that the responder can check, and keep the human approval before any action. (level 3) What does the pattern cost? Expected: two model runs per incident plus the latency of the slower one, which is small next to the first twenty minutes of a manual investigation that the lesson says are automatable. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Chaos engineering for LLMs is its own discipline in 2026. Prerequisites before running experiments in production: defined SLI/SLO, trace+metric+log observability, automated rollback, runbooks, on-call. Architecture has four planes: control (experiment scheduler), target (services, infra, data stores), safety (guards + abort + traffic filters), observability (metrics + traces + logs), feedback (into SLO adjustments). Guardrails are mandatory: burn-rate alerts pause experiments if daily error-budget burn > 2x expected; suppression windows + trace-ID corr Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means SLI / SLO "service targets" Indicator + objective; required prerequisite Blast radius "scope" Set of services / users affected by experiment Burn-rate alert "budget gate" Fires when error-budget burn rate > 2x expected Game day "monthly drill" Scheduled cross-team chaos exercise LitmusChaos "CNCF workflow" Graduated CNCF Kubernetes chaos tool Chaos Mesh "CNCF CRD" CNCF sandbox Kubernetes-native chaos Harness CE "commercial AI-assisted" Harness chaos with AI recommendations Malformed prompt "tokenizer bomb" Input that stalls tokenization KV eviction storm "preemption cascade" Mass eviction triggering re-prefills The problem In plain words first Chaos engineering means breaking parts of your own system on purpose, in a controlled way, to see whether it survives as designed. You kill a server, cut a network link or make a dependency fail, and watch whether traffic reroutes, fallbacks kick in and alerts fire. LLM stacks have failure modes ordinary services do not: a provider returning "too many requests" for minutes, a KV cache that overflows under long prompts, a strange prompt that stalls the tokenizer. Chaos is only safe with guardrails. You need a defined error budget (how many failures your objective allows), a burn-rate guard that stops an experiment when it eats that budget too fast, a limited blast radius (how much traffic an experiment can touch) and a way to roll back. Chaos testing in traditional stacks is established. LLM stacks add new failure modes. A 4K-token prompt with a poison character stalls the tokenizer for 12 seconds. An upstream provider 429s; your gateway retries; your service OOMs on retry-amplified concurrency. A KV cache eviction storm under burst load causes re-prefill cascades that saturate compute. None of these show up in unit tests. Chaos engineering is how you discover them before users do. Idea 1 · Prerequisites Don't run chaos in production without: SLI/SLO — defined service-level indicators and objectives. Observability — traces, metrics, logs, wired to dashboards. Automated rollback — Phase 17 · 20 policy-flag rollback. Runbooks — structured, Phase 17 · 23. On-call — someone to respond. Missing any means chaos becomes real incident. Idea 2 · Four planes + feedback Control plane — experiment scheduler (Litmus workflow, Chaos Mesh schedule, Harness UI). Target plane — services, pods, nodes, load balancers, data stores. Safety plane — kill switch, suppression windows, blast-radius limits, error-budget gates. Observability plane — normal metrics + trace-ID correlation to distinguish chaos-induced from natural failures. Feedback loop — findings feed back into SLO adjustment, runbook updates, code fixes. Idea 3 · Guardrails are mandatory Burn-rate alert : pause experiment if daily error-budget burn exceeds 2x expected. Suppression windows : silence non-experiment alerts in the blast radius during experiment. Trace-ID correlation : all experiment-induced errors carry a tag so on-call can dedupe. Idea 4 · Five LLM-specific experiments Memory overload — force a KV cache preemption storm by sending long-context requests with high concurrency. Observe: does the service gracefully shed or crash? Network failure — cut connectivity between inference gateway and provider. Observe: does fallback kick in within SLA? (Phase 17 · 19) Provider outage simulation — 100% 429 from OpenAI. Observe: does routing failover to Anthropic? (Phase 17 · 16, 19) Malformed prompt — inject tokenizer-stalling payload (e.g., deeply nested unicode, huge UTF-8 codepoint). Observe: does a single request lock up a worker? KV eviction storm — force eviction by saturating vLLM block budget. Observe: does LMCache recover or does service degrade? Idea 5 · Cadence Weekly — small canary experiments in staging, maybe 5% prod. Monthly — scheduled game day on a specific scenario; cross-team attendance; postmortem. Quarterly — cross-team resilience audit; dependency map update. Idea 6 · Tooling Harness Chaos Engineering — commercial; AI-derived experiment recommendations; blast-radius downscaling; MCP tool integration. LitmusChaos — CNCF graduated; Kubernetes workflow-based. Chaos Mesh — CNCF sandbox; Kubernetes-native CRD style. Gremlin — commercial; broad support. AWS FIS / Azure Chaos Studio — managed cloud offerings. Idea 7 · Starting small First experiment: pod-kill one decode replica under steady traffic. Observe rerouting and recovery. If this works and looks safe, graduate to network chaos. First LLM-specific experiment: inject one provider 429 for 5 minutes. Observe fallback. Most teams discover their fallback wasn't fully tested. Idea 8 · Numbers you should remember Four planes: control, target, safety, observability. Burn-rate pause: 2x expected daily budget burn. Cadence: weekly canary, monthly game day, quarterly audit. Five LLM experiments: memory, network, provider, malformed prompt, KV storm. The same idea as a formula Error budget and burn rate. An objective of availability allows a failure rate (for 99.9%, ). If an experiment produces failure rate on the traffic it touches, the e ​ says how many times faster than allowed the budget is being spent. A burn rate of 30 empties a 30-day budget in a day, if it applies to all traffic. Worked example How much budget does a 5-minute experiment spend? Objective 99.9% (budget 0.1% of requests). Service: 1,000 requests a minute, so 1,440,000 a day and a daily budget of 1,440 failed requests. Provider-429 experiment: touches 30% of traffic for 5 minutes = 1,500 requests; 1.5% fail = 22 failures. Burn rate on that slice: 1.5 / 0.1 = 15× (on the whole service: 0.45 / 0.1 = 4.5×). Budget spent: 22 of 1,440, about 1.5% of the day's budget. Without a working fallback, 100% of that slice fails for 5 minutes: 1,500 failures, more than the whole day's budget. That is what the burn-rate guard is for: abort within a minute and the cost stays near 300. Solutions Solution P1 · Reading the experiment runner In code/main.py the provider-429 experiment aborts (30× burn on a 30% blast radius) while the malformed-prompt experiment completes despite an 80× burn, because its blast radius is only 10%. The gate requires both a high burn rate and a large blast radius, so small experiments may run hot briefly; large ones are stopped. Solution B1 · Three skipped guardrails (1) Blast radius: start with a few per cent of traffic, not all of it. (2) A burn-rate abort: stop automatically within a minute when the budget burns faster than 2× expected. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design You run a chaos experiment in production. One model provider returns rate-limit errors for part of the fleet, so that you can watch the fallback. Alerts start to fire while it runs. Design the safety plane that keeps this from turning into an incident, and explain how on-call tells an experiment failure from a natural one. Level 4 of 4 · about 18 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Three guards sit in the safety plane: a burn-rate alert that pauses the experiment when the daily error-budget burn passes twice the expected rate, suppression windows that silence the non-experiment alerts inside the blast radius, and a tag on the trace id of every error that the experiment causes. On-call reads the tag. An untagged error inside the window is natural and gets the normal response. The planes. The lesson splits the system into a control plane that schedules the experiment, a target plane of services, pods and data stores, a safety plane with the kill switch, suppression windows, blast-radius limits and error-budget gates, and an observability plane that correlates every error with a trace id. The findings feed back into the SLO, the runbooks and the code. The three guards. Burn-rate pause. The experiment is allowed to spend error budget, because that is what a controlled failure does. The gate fires when the daily burn exceeds 2x the expected rate, and it pauses the experiment on its own. Suppression windows. Alerts that the experiment is designed to trigger are silenced for the blast radius and the duration. Nothing outside the radius is silenced. Trace-id correlation. Every experiment-induced error carries a tag, so that on-call can separate it from natural failures without a conversation. The kill switch is a fourth, manual control. It stops the experiment at once and belongs to on-call, not to the scheduler. How on-call reads an alert during the window. A tagged error inside the blast radius is the experiment working. It is logged, not paged. An untagged error inside the window is natural. It takes the normal response. An error outside the blast radius is natural, because the experiment did not touch it. If the burn continues after the pause, the cause is natural, or the experiment broke something that does not recover alone. Run the incident response and roll back the last change. What this experiment should teach. The lesson notes that most teams discover their fallback was never fully tested. Record the time from the first rate-limit error to the first successful fallback, and compare it with the SLA. Record whether the gateway's retries amplified the load before the fallback engaged. Size the blast radius. Choose a share of the fleet small enough that the fallback capacity on the other providers covers it, and write that share into the experiment definition. A larger share tests more and risks a real outage when the fallback is slower than you believed. Plausible wrong answers. "Silence all alerts during the experiment." A natural incident in the same window goes unseen. Silence only the blast radius, and keep tagged errors visible. "Run it in staging, so no safety plane is needed." Staging cannot show the fallback under real traffic. The safety plane is what makes production acceptable. "The burn-rate alert is the kill switch." The alert pauses the experiment. The kill switch stops it at once, and it should be a separate manual control. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why gate at twice the expected burn and not at any burn? Expected: the cause is natural, or the experiment broke something that does not recover on its own. Run the incident response and roll back the last change. (level 4) How do you pick the blast radius for a provider outage experiment? Expected: a share small enough that the fallback capacity covers it, written into the experiment definition and reviewed with on-call. Where it is taught. Explain the mechanism A new team wants to run its first chaos experiment against the model service next week. What do you check for before you agree, and what goes wrong when one piece is missing? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Five things have to be in place: service level indicators with objectives, observability with traces, metrics and logs, an automated rollback, structured runbooks and an on-call owner. Each one lets you measure the experiment, stop it or repair the damage. When one is missing, the experiment is not a test. It is an incident that you scheduled. The five prerequisites. SLI and SLO. Without a target you cannot say whether the experiment hurt anything. Observability. Traces, metrics and logs on a dashboard. You must see the effect while it happens. Automated rollback. The policy-flag rollback from the progressive delivery lesson. A rollback that needs a redeploy is too slow for an experiment. Runbooks. Structured sections: symptom, hypothesis, verify, act. The on-call reads them under pressure. On-call. Someone who responds when the experiment finds something. The first experiments. Start with one pod kill of a decode replica under steady traffic, and watch the rerouting and the recovery. If that looks safe, graduate to network chaos. The first model-specific experiment is one provider returning rate-limit errors for a few minutes, to see the fallback engage. Most teams learn here that their fallback was never fully tested. The cadence. Weekly small experiments in staging or on a small share of production. Monthly game day on one scenario with a postmortem. Quarterly cross-team audit with a dependency map. Plausible wrong answers. "Skip the prerequisites and learn by doing." Without an SLO, a rollback and an on-call owner, the experiment is an outage that you caused on purpose. "A dashboard is observability." Chaos needs traces, metrics and logs with trace-id correlation, so that you can tell experiment failures from natural ones. "Run the biggest experiment first to find the biggest risk." Start with one replica kill, then grow the blast radius. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Which experiment goes first, and why? Expected: kill one decode replica under steady traffic, because it tests rerouting and recovery with a small blast radius. (level 2) Name one failure a generic network chaos tool cannot reproduce for a model service. Expected: a KV cache eviction storm under burst load, or a prompt that stalls the tokenizer. (level 2) Why does the rollback matter more than the dashboard during an experiment? Expected: the dashboard shows the harm, and the rollback stops it. Without the rollback the harm continues until someone fixes it by hand. (level 3) The team wants staging only. When is production the right place? Expected: when staging cannot reproduce the traffic shape, the cache state or the provider behavior, and only with the safety guards in place. Where it is taught. The chaos engineering lesson lists the five prerequisites, the four planes and the first experiments. a1725: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Security — Secrets, API Key Rotation, Audit Logs, Guardrails Lesson 17.25 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Enumerate the four secret-management anti-patterns (config files in VCS, hardcoded env, spreadsheets, static keys) and name their replacements. Explain the AI-gateway-pulls-from-vault pattern as 2026 production standard. Implement a PII scrubber with consistent tokenization (same value → same placeholder) so semantics survive. Name the 2026 Vercel supply-chain incident and what it taught about CI/CD credential hygiene. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 19 (AI Gateways), Phase 17 · 13 (Observability) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy PII-scrubber + audit-log writer). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Eliminate secret sprawl via centralized vaults (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault). Never store credentials in config files, env files in VCS, spreadsheets. Use IAM roles over static keys; OIDC for CI/CD. The AI-gateway pattern is the 2026 solution: apps → gateway → model provider, with gateway pulling credentials from vault at runtime. Rotate in vault and all apps pick up in minutes — no redeploys, no Slack "who has the new key" messages. Rotation policy ≤90 days; scan with TruffleHog / GitGuardian / Gitleak Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Vault "secrets store" Centralized credential management service IAM role "identity-based auth" Role assumed by app; returns short-lived creds OIDC for CI/CD "cloud-issued tokens" No static keys in CI — identity via OIDC TruffleHog / GitGuardian / Gitleaks "secret scanners" Commit-time secret detection RBAC / ABAC "access control" Role-based vs attribute-based PII scrubbing "data masking" Remove or tokenize sensitive entities Consistent tokenization "stable placeholders" Same value → same token each time Mesh approach "Mesh tokenization" Semantic-preserving tokenization pattern Egress whitelist "outbound allowlist" Only permitted domains reachable Audit log "immutable history" Append-only record for compliance The problem In plain words first An LLM service leaks in three typical ways. Secrets leak: an API key committed to git stays in its history even after deletion. Personal data leaks: a user types a social security number or a diagnosis into a prompt, and it travels to an outside provider. Data leaves the network : a compromised service sends information to an attacker's server, sometimes hidden in DNS lookups. The defences match. Keep secrets in a vault and let services fetch them with their cloud identity, rotating them regularly; scan every commit for secrets. Scrub personal data before a prompt leaves your systems, replacing each value with a consistent placeholder. Allow outbound traffic only to an allow-list of hosts. And keep an audit log of every call, so afterwards you can prove what happened. An intern commits .env with API keys. They delete it quickly. The keys are already in git history — GitGuardian scan catches it, your rotation process is "Slack the team, update 40 config files, redeploy all services." 8 hours later, half your services are live and half are waiting for deploy windows. Separately, user prompts include "My SSN is 123-45-6789." Prompt goes to OpenAI. You have a BAA but your internal policy is to mask PII before forwarding. You didn't. Separately, your EKS cluster's LLM pod can reach any internet host. Someone exfils data via DNS lookup to an attacker-controlled domain. Nothing blocked it. Security for LLM services has to address all three vectors and prove it afterwards. Vault-backed credentials. PII scrubbing. Network egress filtering. Audit logs as the evidence trail. Idea 1 · Centralized vault + IAM-role pull Vault : HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager. One source of truth. IAM role : app/gateway authenticates via its IAM identity, not a static key. Vault returns the secret for the lifetime of the token. The AI-gateway pattern : gateway pulls OPENAI_API_KEY from vault at request time. Rotate in vault; next request gets the new key. No redeploys. Idea 2 · Rotation policy ≤ 90 days All API keys, vault root tokens, CI/CD credentials. Automated rotation where possible. Manual rotation logged and tracked. Idea 3 · Secret scanning TruffleHog — regex + entropy on commits. GitGuardian — commercial, high accuracy. Gitleaks — OSS, runs in CI. Run on every commit. Block PR if new secret detected. Idea 4 · Zero-trust posture MFA required on all accounts. SSO via SAML/OIDC. RBAC (role-based) or ABAC (attribute-based) for fine grained access. Short-lived tokens (hours, not days). Device posture — only corp devices with disk encryption. Idea 5 · PII / PHI scrubbing Before the prompt leaves your infra: Entity recognition (spaCy NER, Presidio, commercial). Mask matched entities: "My SSN is 123-45-6789" → "My SSN is [SSN_TOKEN_A3F]" . Consistent tokenization (Mesh approach): same value maps to the same placeholder so the LLM preserves relationships. Optional reverse mapping for LLM response. Static regex filters catch basic patterns; NER catches more. Use both. Idea 6 · Input + output guardrails Input: block known jailbreaks, forbidden topics; rate-limit per-user. Output: regex scrub for leaked secrets (API key patterns, email patterns in refusal contexts), classifier for policy violations. Idea 7 · Network egress whitelist LLM services in a dedicated subnet: - Whitelist: api.openai.com , api.anthropic.com , vector DB endpoints, vault endpoints. - Everything else: drop. - DNS via allowlist-only resolver (avoid DNS-tunneling exfil). Idea 8 · Audit log Immutable log of every LLM call with: - Timestamp. - User / tenant. - Prompt hash (not raw prompt for privacy). - Model + version. - Token counts. - Cost. - Response hash. - Any guardrail trips. Retain per regulatory requirement (SOC 2 1 year, HIPAA 6 years). Idea 9 · The 2026 Vercel incident Supply-chain attack: compromised CI/CD credentials exfiltrated env vars across thousands of customer deployments. Lesson: CI/CD credentials are prod-equivalent. Store in vault. Scope narrowly. Rotate aggressively. Idea 10 · Numbers you should remember Rotation policy: ≤ 90 days. Scan on every commit: TruffleHog / GitGuardian / Gitleaks. Vercel 2026: CI/CD creds compromised → thousands of customer env vars leaked. Audit log retention: SOC 2 = 1 year, HIPAA = 6 years. Worked example Consistent placeholders keep meaning A user writes: "My SSN is 123-45-6789. Please update the account for 123-45-6789 and email jane@example.com." Naive masking: "My SSN is [SSN]. Please update the account for [SSN] and email [EMAIL]." Fine here, but with two different numbers the model could not tell them apart. Consistent tokenization: "My SSN is [SSN_001]. Please update the account for [SSN_001] and email [EMAIL_001]." The model sees that both mentions are the same value. A second user's SSN becomes [SSN_002], so relationships across a conversation survive. The mapping table stays inside your systems; if the answer contains [EMAIL_001], you can map it back before showing it to the user. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ Deleting a committed key does not remove it from git history; rotate it. ✗ Regex filters catch all personal data. They catch fixed formats; names and addresses need entity recognition as well. ✓ Restricting DNS to an allow-list resolver blocks DNS-tunnelling exfiltration. ✗ Audit logs should store raw prompts so investigations are easy. Store hashes and metadata; raw prompts are themselves sensitive. Predict before you run Before running the code below: the scrubber below uses three regexes. Which of these will it miss: an SSN written with spaces ("123 45 6789"), a phone with brackets, or a name? See it drawn A small scrubber with consistent placeholders Copy What you should see Copy Copy Reading this output The dashed SSN, the email and both phone formats become stable placeholders, and the repeated SSN maps to the same one. The names "Jane Doe" and "Bob" pass through, and so does the SSN written with spaces. That is why production scrubbers combine patterns with entity recognition (Presidio, spaCy) and test against real samples of what users type. What design removes this problem? (Solution B1.) Recap What to keep from this lesson Secrets: one vault, pulled at runtime with the service's identity; rotate at least every 90 days. Scan every commit (TruffleHog, GitGuardian, Gitleaks) and block on findings. Scrub personal data before prompts leave; use consistent placeholders. Allow outbound traffic only to known hosts, including DNS. Keep an immutable audit log of hashes and metadata. Solutions Solution B1 · Rotation without redeploys Store the key in a vault and let the gateway (or each service) fetch it at request time using its cloud identity. Rotation is then one change in the vault: the next request gets the new key, no service needs a config change, and the old key can be revoked immediately. Code in : (Python, TypeScript optional: compliance is policy + process, not code). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Multi-framework coverage is table stakes for 2026 enterprise deals. EU AI Act : in force since August 1, 2024. Most high-risk requirements were due August 2, 2026, but the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendment (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) postponed them: 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems, 2 August 2028 for AI inside regulated products. Virginia simila Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means SOC 2 Type II "audited controls" Controls operating over 6-12 months, independently attested HIPAA BAA "healthcare contract" Business Associate Agreement; required for PHI GDPR "EU privacy" Real-time PII redaction is the defensible 2026 standard EU AI Act "EU AI rules" High-risk enforcement December 2027 (postponed from August 2026); €15M / 3% (high-risk obligations) — €35M / 7% (prohibited practices) Colorado AI Act "US AI state law" June 30, 2026 effective (delayed by SB25B-004); impact assessments ISO 42001 "AI governance" Emerging framework for AI risk + transparency ISO 27001 "security ISMS" Information Security Management System baseline Conformity assessment "EU AI doc package" High-risk requirement: docs, testing, logging Cross-framework mapping "one control, many frames" Single policy satisfies multiple framework controls The problem In plain words first Enterprise customers buy software only after checking it against compliance frameworks : rule sets for security and data handling. SOC 2 Type II shows an auditor watched your controls work for 6–12 months. HIPAA governs US health data and requires a signed BAA (business associate agreement) before patient data reaches any vendor, including your model provider. GDPR governs EU personal data. PCI-DSS covers card data. ISO 27001 and the newer ISO 42001 are international standards for security and AI governance. The EU AI Act classifies AI systems by risk; most chat and copilot products are "limited risk" (transparency duties), while hiring, credit or medical uses are "high risk" with documentation, logging and assessments. Many controls (access logs, change management, encryption, secrets) satisfy several frameworks at once, so you build each control once and map it. An enterprise customer's procurement asks for SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, HIPAA BAA, ISO 27001, and "EU AI Act compliance statement." Your team has SOC 2 Type I. You're six months from Type II and haven't started GDPR Article 30 records. Multi-framework coverage is not an LLM problem — it's an enterprise-SaaS problem, with LLM-specific overlays. Procurement teams in 2026 want a matrix with a row per framework and a column per control, not a PDF. Idea 1 · The seven frameworks Framework Scope LLM-specific requirement SOC 2 Type II B2B SaaS baseline Process controls audited over 6-12 months HIPAA US healthcare BAA required; PHI cannot leave infrastructure without signed agreement GDPR EU users Real-time PII redaction; data subject rights; Article 30 records PCI-DSS Payment data Configuration + contracts for AI touching payment EU AI Act Serving EU users Risk tier classification; high-risk systems: conformity assessment, documentation, logging Colorado AI Act Serving CO residents Impact assessments; right to appeal ISO 42001 AI governance Emerging; pairs with ISO 27001 Idea 2 · EU AI Act timeline August 1, 2024: in force. February 2, 2025: prohibited-AI practices enforced. August 2, 2026: the original date for high-risk obligations, now postponed by the 2026 Digital Omnibus amendment. December 2, 2027: stand-alone high-risk systems (Annex III: hiring, credit, education and so on) enforced: conformity assessment, documentation, logging. August 2, 2028: high-risk AI in products under harmonized legislation (Annex I). Risk tiers: Unacceptable (banned), High-risk (conformity + logging), Limited-risk (transparency), Minimal-risk (no constraint). Most B2B LLM SaaS is limited-risk; high-risk kicks in for employment, credit, education, law enforcement, migration, essential services. Fines (Article 99): up to €15M or 3% global annual turnover for breaches of high-risk-system obligations (Art. 99(4)); up to €35M or 7% for prohibited AI practices (Art. 99(3)); whichever higher applies. Idea 3 · GDPR — real-time redaction is the standard Post-processing cleanup (redact PII after the LLM sees it) is not a defensible posture — the model already saw the data. Real-time inference-layer redaction is the 2026 standard: Entity recognition before the LLM call. Consistent tokenization (Mesh approach) preserves semantics. Store only redacted prompts + consented opt-in raw. Recent enforcement: €30.5M against Clearview AI (Dutch DPA, Sept 2024) is the largest documented AI-specific GDPR fine to date; €15M against OpenAI (Italy's Garante, Dec 2024) is the largest LLM-specific fine, though it was overturned on appeal in March 2026 and the ruling remains under further review. Post-processing claims have failed at audit. Idea 4 · HIPAA — BAA is not optional You cannot send PHI to external AI services without a signed Business Associate Agreement. All three hyperscaler LLM platforms (Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Vertex) offer BAAs. OpenAI direct API offers BAA. Anthropic direct API offers BAA. Confirm before sending PHI. Idea 5 · SOC 2 Type II Type I: controls designed and documented. Type II: controls operate effectively over 6-12 months. B2B procurement in 2026 defaults to Type II. Type I is a starter; Type II is the gate. Common audit drivers: access logs (who saw what), change management (how was it deployed), risk assessments (quarterly), incident response (tested?). Audit log from Phase 17 · 25 is directly reusable. Worth the cost at scale. Idea 7 · ISO 42001 — emerging Published late 2023. Growing procurement requirement alongside ISO 27001. Framework for AI governance including risk management, data quality, transparency, human oversight. Idea 8 · OpenAI's reference profile OpenAI maintains SOC 2 Type 2, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, ISO/IEC 27701:2019, GDPR/CCPA/HIPAA (BAA)/FERPA, PCI-DSS for ChatGPT payment components. That is roughly the enterprise table stakes in 2026. Idea 9 · Numbers you should remember EU AI Act fines: up to €15M / 3% (high-risk obligations, Art. 99(4)); up to €35M / 7% (prohibited practices, Art. 99(3)). EU AI Act high-risk enforcement: December 2, 2027 (stand-alone systems) and August 2, 2028 (in regulated products), after the 2026 Digital Omnibus postponement. Largest documented AI-specific GDPR fine: €30.5M, Clearview AI (Dutch DPA, Sept 2024). Largest LLM-specific GDPR fine: €15M, OpenAI (Italy's Garante, Dec 2024; overturned on appeal March 2026). SOC 2 Type II window: 6-12 months of operated controls. Colorado AI Act effective date: June 30, 2026 (delayed from February 2026 by SB25B-004). Worked example Which frameworks does one deal need? A US hospital network wants your LLM note-summarizer, used by its staff in the US and in its Dublin office. Dublin staff and EU patients → GDPR : redaction before inference, records of processing, data-subject rights. B2B procurement → SOC 2 Type II (a Type I report will not pass).
