a1727: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production FinOps for LLMs — Unit Economics and Multi-Tenant Attribution Lesson 17.27 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Explain why traditional FinOps (tags + tiers) breaks on LLM spend and name the three new attribution dimensions. Enumerate the four token layers (prompt, tool, memory, response) and why single-bucket billing hides cost. Design an enforcement ladder (rate → spend cap → kill switch) for a multi-tenant product. Pick a unit metric (cost per resolved query / artifact) instead of $/M tokens. Before you start Needs : Phase 17 · 13 (Observability), Phase 17 · 14 (Caching) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, toy cost-attribution simulator with kill switch). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Traditional FinOps breaks on LLM spend. Costs are token-transactions, not resource-uptime. Tags don't map — an API call is a transaction, not an asset. Engineering decisions (prompt design, context window, output length) are financial decisions. The 2026 playbook has three attribution dimensions to instrument on day one: per-user ( user_id ) for seat pricing and expansion, per-task ( task_id + route ) for product surface cost and prioritization, per-tenant ( tenant_id ) for unit economics and renewal. Four token layers — prom Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Per-user attribution "user-level cost" user_id stamped on every call Per-task attribution "feature cost" task_id + route identify product surface Per-tenant attribution "customer cost" tenant_id ; drives unit economics Four token layers "cost layers" prompt + tool + memory + response Rate limit "429 guard" Per-tenant ceiling enforced at gateway Daily spend cap "daily ceiling" Tenant-scoped budget with alert Kill switch "auto-pause" Spend z-score > 4 triggers auto-suspension Cost per resolved "product unit metric" Cost tied to product outcome, not tokens Telemetry joiner "trace-to-billing" Highest-accuracy attribution pattern Stacked optimization "cache+batch+route+gateway" Compounding savings to ~5-10% baseline The problem In plain words first FinOps is the practice of knowing who spends what in the cloud and keeping it under control. LLM calls make that hard: the provider's bill shows tokens and dollars, not which customer, feature or user caused them. So you attribute cost yourself: every call carries a user ID, a task or route name and a tenant (customer) ID, and you join those tags to the token counts. It also helps to split tokens into layers : the prompt you wrote, tool results fed back in, conversation memory, and the model's answer, because each is fixed in a different way. Then you enforce : rate limits per tenant, daily spend caps, and an automatic kill switch when a tenant's spend is wildly above its normal level. Finally, you judge cost per outcome (per resolved ticket, per completed task), not per million tokens. Your bill says $40,000. You don't know: - Which tenant spent it. - Which product feature drove it. - Whether any individual user was abusive. - Whether prompt bloat, tool calls, or memory amplification was the culprit. Tag-and-aggregate on provider-side works for cloud resources (EC2, S3) where tags propagate to line items. LLM API calls do not auto-tag — you have to stamp user/task/tenant at the call site and carry through. Retroactive attribution always misses edge cases. Idea 1 · Three attribution dimensions Per-user ( user_id ): who is costing what. Drives seat pricing, expansion conversations, identifies power users. Per-task ( task_id + route ): which product surface costs what. Drives feature prioritization, kill-expensive-features decisions. Per-tenant ( tenant_id ): which customer is profitable. Drives unit economics, renewal pricing, tier thresholds. Instrument all three at call site on day one. Retroactive is always worse. Idea 2 · Four token layers Layer Example Typical % of total Prompt system + user input 40-60% Tool tool-call results fed back 20-40% (agent workloads) Memory prior conversation / retrieved docs 10-30% Response model output 10-30% Bucketing all four together makes optimization blind. Break them out in your attribution schema. Idea 3 · Enforcement ladder Rate limit per tenant. 2-3x expected peak. Return 429 with Retry-After . Tenant sees friction; no surprise bill. Daily spend cap per tenant. 1.5-3x contracted ceiling. Trigger: tighten rate limit + alert customer-success. Kill switch on spend z-score > 4 relative to tenant baseline. Auto-pause tenant; page on-call; escalate to ops + CS. Idea 4 · Attribution patterns Tag-and-aggregate : stamp metadata headers; aggregate later. Simple; rough. Telemetry joiner : join traces to billing via trace IDs. Highest accuracy. What mature teams do. Sampling + extrapolation : sample 5-10%, multiply. Cost-effective for rough spend; misses tails. Model-based allocation : regression to infer cost driver. For legacy data without tags. Event-sourced : cost as events in a stream (Kafka / Kinesis). Real-time. Real-time streaming : dashboard updates sub-second. Idea 5 · Cost per X is the unit metric $/M tokens is vendor speak. Product metrics: Cost per resolved support ticket. Cost per generated article. Cost per successful agent task. Cost per user-session-minute. Tie cost to a product outcome. Otherwise optimization is unanchored. Idea 6 · Cost attribution trace shape Copy Emit on every call. Store in data lake. Aggregate per dimension. Phase 17 · 13 observability stack is where this lives. Idea 7 · The compounded-savings stack Stack: cache + batch + route + gateway. With all four: - Cache L2 (Phase 17 · 14): ~10x cheaper input. - Batch (Phase 17 · 15): 50% off. - Route to cheap model (Phase 17 · 16): 60% cost reduction. - Gateway efficiency (Phase 17 · 19): redundancy + retries. Best-case stacked: ~5-10% of naive baseline. Most teams have 2-3 levers engaged; few stack all four. Idea 8 · Numbers you should remember Attribution dimensions: per-user, per-task, per-tenant. Four token layers: prompt, tool, memory, response. Kill switch: spend z-score > 4. Unit metric: cost per resolved query, not $/M tokens. Stacked optimizations: ~5-10% of baseline possible. The same idea as a formula Spend anomaly score. For a tenant with daily spend history mean and standard deviation , today's spend gives x − μ ​ A kill switch at fires on spend far outside the tenant's own normal range, rather than on an absolute dollar figure that suits one tenant and not another. Worked example Cost per resolved ticket A support assistant spent $12,000 last month on 300,000 conversations; 180,000 ended with the ticket resolved without a human. Cost per conversation: $12,000 / 300,000 = $0.04. Cost per resolved ticket: $12,000 / 180,000 ≈ $0.067. A cheaper model cuts spend to $7,000 but resolution drops to 120,000: cost per resolved ticket ≈ $0.058, slightly better, but 60,000 more tickets now reach human agents, each costing far more than $0.07. The unit metric (cost per resolved ticket, plus the human cost of escalations) shows the "cheaper" model costs more overall. Token prices alone would have hidden that. Check your mental model Which statements are right? ✓ LLM API calls do not carry your tags; you stamp them at the call site. ✗ Cost per million tokens is the metric to optimize. Tie cost to an outcome (per ticket, per task), or optimization has no anchor. ✓ In agent workloads, tool results fed back can be 20–40% of tokens. ✗ A single global spend cap protects every tenant fairly. Caps and anomaly thresholds should follow each tenant's contract and baseline. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism Finance asks for the cost per million tokens as the key metric for the model service. You push back. What metric do you propose instead, and what must every call record so that you can compute it? Level 1 of 4 · about 5 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Propose a cost per product outcome: per resolved ticket, per generated article, per successful agent task or per session minute. A price per million tokens is the vendor's unit, and it says nothing about whether the spend produced anything. To compute the outcome metric, stamp every call at creation with the user id, the task id with its route, and the tenant id, split the tokens into prompt, tool, memory and response, and join the cost to the outcome event. Why the token price misleads. A cheaper model that needs twice the tokens per task costs more per task. A prompt change that cuts tokens and lowers the resolution rate raises the cost per resolved ticket while the token dashboard goes green. The lesson's rule is to tie cost to a product outcome, because an optimization without that anchor has no direction. Three attribution dimensions. Dimension Key What it answers per user user_id who costs what, for seat pricing and abuse per task task_id and route which product surface costs what per tenant tenant_id which customer is profitable Instrument all three at the call site on day one. A provider line item carries none of them, and retroactive tagging always misses cases. Four token layers. Layer Typical share prompt, the system text and the user input 40 to 60 percent tool, the results fed back into the context 20 to 40 percent on agent workloads memory, the prior turns and retrieved documents 10 to 30 percent response, the model output 10 to 30 percent One bucket hides which layer drives the spend, so you cannot pick the lever. The record on every call. The trace carries the trace id, the three dimension keys, the four layer counts, the cost, and two flags, one for a cached input and one for a batch call. The most accurate attribution pattern joins these traces to the billing export by trace id, which the lesson calls the telemetry joiner. Plausible wrong answers. "Tokens are what we pay for, so tokens are the metric." They are the vendor's unit. The business pays for outcomes, and a cheaper token can mean a more expensive task. "Tag the cloud bill by team like any other resource." A model call is a transaction, not an asset. The line item has no team on it unless the call stamped one. "Per-tenant cost is enough." Per-task shows which feature to fix and per-user shows abuse. The lesson instruments all three. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why does the token price alone mislead? Expected: it says nothing about tokens per outcome. A cheaper model that needs twice the tokens per task costs more per task. (level 2) Why split the tokens into four layers? Expected: one bucket hides whether prompt bloat, tool results, memory or output drives the spend, so you cannot choose the right fix. (level 2) Why stamp the call at creation instead of tagging the bill later? Expected: the provider line item has no user, task or tenant on it, and retroactive attribution always misses cases. (level 3) Which attribution pattern is the most accurate, and what does it need? Expected: the telemetry joiner, which joins trace ids to billing. It needs the trace id on every call and a billing export with the same key. Where it is taught. a1728: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Self-Hosted Serving Selection — Matching Engine to Hardware and Scale Lesson 17.28 45 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Pick an engine given hardware (CPU / AMD / NVIDIA Hopper / Blackwell), scale (1 user / 100 / 10,000), and workload (general chat / agent / long-context). Name the 2026 TGI maintenance-mode status (December 11, 2025) and why it biases new projects toward vLLM or SGLang. Describe the dev/staging/prod pipeline, including where a GGUF-to-safetensors format conversion sits between stages. Explain why "CPU-first" points to llama.cpp and "AMD" excludes TRT-LLM. Before you start Needs : All Phase 17 lessons covering engines (04, 06, 07, 09, 18) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript (stdlib, engine-decision tree walker). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Engine selection is a function of hardware, scale, and ecosystem — not a leaderboard read. Four engines dominate self-hosted inference in 2026: llama.cpp, Ollama, vLLM, SGLang, with TGI trailing in maintenance mode. llama.cpp is fastest on CPU — widest model support, full control over quantization and threading. Ollama is the dev-laptop one-command install, ~15-30% slower than llama.cpp (Go + CGo + HTTP serialization), 3x throughput gap under prod-like load. TGI entered maintenance mode December 11, 2025 — o Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means llama.cpp "the CPU one" Widest model support, fastest on CPU Ollama "the laptop one" One-command install, dev-grade throughput TGI "HF's serving" Maintenance mode since Dec 2025 vLLM "the default" Broad production baseline 2026 SGLang "the agentic one" Prefix-heavy, RadixAttention TRT-LLM "NVIDIA-locked" Blackwell throughput leader, NVIDIA only GGUF "llama.cpp format" Bundled K-quant variants Production-stack "vLLM K8s" Phase 17 · 18 reference deployment Pipeline pattern "dev→stage→prod" Ollama → llama.cpp → vLLM; weight formats differ per engine The problem In plain words first If you run models on your own machines, you need a serving engine : the program that loads the model and answers requests. Five are common. llama.cpp runs models efficiently on CPUs and Apple chips. Ollama wraps llama.cpp in a one-command tool for laptops. vLLM is the general-purpose production server for GPUs. SGLang is a production server that excels when prompts share long prefixes, as in agents and RAG. TGI (Hugging Face's server) entered maintenance mode in December 2025, so new projects should avoid it. Choose in three steps: first by hardware (CPU, Apple, AMD, NVIDIA generation), then by scale (one developer or thousands of users), then by workload (chat, agents, RAG, long context). Your team starts a new self-hosted LLM project. One engineer says Ollama, another says vLLM, a third says "doesn't TGI just work out of the box?" All three are right for different contexts. None is right for all. In 2026 the choice tree matters: hardware first, scale second, workload third. And one specific 2025 event — TGI entering maintenance mode December 11 — changes the default for new projects. Idea 1 · The five engines Engine Best for Notes llama.cpp CPU / edge / minimal deps / widest model support Fastest on CPU, full control Ollama Dev laptops, single user, one-command install 15-30% slower than llama.cpp; 3x prod throughput gap TGI HF ecosystem, regulated industries Maintenance mode Dec 11, 2025 vLLM General-purpose production, 100+ users Broad production default; v0.15.1 Feb 2026 SGLang Agentic multi-turn, prefix-heavy workloads 400,000+ GPUs in production Idea 2 · Hardware-first decision CPU-first → llama.cpp. Ollama works too but is slower. No other engine is competitive on CPU. AMD GPU → vLLM is the strongest-supported path (AMD ROCm support). SGLang also works. TRT-LLM is NVIDIA-locked, so it's out. NVIDIA Hopper (H100 / H200) → vLLM or SGLang or TRT-LLM. All three top-tier. NVIDIA Blackwell (B200 / GB200) → TRT-LLM is the throughput leader (Phase 17 · 07). vLLM and SGLang follow close. Apple Silicon (M-series) → llama.cpp (Metal). Ollama wraps this. Idea 3 · Scale-second decision 1 user / local dev → Ollama. One command, first-token in seconds. 10-100 users / small team → vLLM single-GPU. 100-10k users / production → vLLM production-stack (Phase 17 · 18) or SGLang. 10k+ users / enterprise → vLLM production-stack + disaggregated (Phase 17 · 17) + LMCache (Phase 17 · 18). Idea 4 · Workload-third decision General chat / Q&A → vLLM wins on broad default. Agentic multi-turn (tools, planning, memory) → SGLang's RadixAttention (Phase 17 · 06) dominates. RAG with heavy prefix reuse → SGLang. Code generation → vLLM fine; SGLang slightly better on cache. Long context (128K+) → vLLM + chunked prefill; SGLang + tiered KV. Idea 5 · The TGI maintenance trap Hugging Face TGI entered maintenance mode December 11, 2025 — only bug fixes going forward. Historically: top-tier observability, best-in-class HF-ecosystem integration (model cards, safety tools), slightly behind vLLM on raw throughput. For new projects in 2026: default away from TGI. Existing TGI deployments can continue but should migrate eventually. SGLang and vLLM are the safer defaults. Idea 6 · The pipeline pattern Dev (Ollama) → staging (llama.cpp) → prod (vLLM). The engines take different weight formats — GGUF for the llama.cpp family, HF safetensors for the GPU engines — so a format conversion may sit between stages. Engineers iterate quickly on laptops; staging mirrors production quantization; prod is the serving target. Idea 7 · Ollama caveat Ollama is great for dev. It is not great for shared production: Go HTTP serialization adds overhead, concurrency management is simpler than vLLM, OpenTelemetry support lags. Use Ollama where it shines — one user, one command — and switch to vLLM for shared. Idea 8 · Self-hosted vs managed is a separate decision Phase 17 · 01 (managed hyperscalers), · 02 (inference platforms) cover managed. This lesson assumes you've already decided to self-host. Reasons to self-host: data residency, custom fine-tune, total cost ownership at scale, domain model not available on hosted. Idea 9 · Numbers you should remember TGI maintenance mode: December 11, 2025. vLLM v0.15.1: February 2026; PyTorch 2.10; Blackwell SM120 support. SGLang production footprint: 400,000+ GPUs. Ollama throughput gap vs llama.cpp: 15-30% slower; 3x under prod load. Worked example Three projects, three engines A data scientist wants to try models on a MacBook. Hardware: Apple Silicon → llama.cpp (Metal). Scale: one user → Ollama on top of it. A support bot for 2,000 staff on two H100s, mostly general chat. Hardware: NVIDIA Hopper → vLLM, SGLang or TRT-LLM. Scale: production → vLLM (broad default, good tooling). An agent platform where every request reuses long tool schemas and a big system prompt. Workload: heavy prefix reuse → SGLang (RadixAttention). Avoid in all three: starting a new deployment on TGI, now only receiving bug fixes. a1729: Course home / Phase 17 · Infrastructure & Production Model Demo Interfaces — From a Function to a Shareable App Lesson 17.29 90 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Write the input, model call, and output contract of a demo, with a limit on each part. Build a standard library HTTP app with one HTML page, a JSON endpoint, and a Server-Sent Events endpoint. Validate input in order of cost, and return JSON errors that tell the user the next action. Protect a public demo with a per-client token bucket, a daily usage cap, and an optional access token. Write request logs that keep no input text and no client address. Compare the standard library demo with two framework versions, and name the signals that a demo must become a product. Before you start Needs : Phase 11 · 13 (Building a Production LLM Application), Phase 17 · 08 (Inference Metrics), Phase 17 · 19 (AI Gateways) Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A model demo has one contract: an input, a model call, and an output. Put a limit on each part before you share the link. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Demo contract "The UI" The input limits, the model call, and the output shape, including errors Token bucket "A rate limiter" A per-client counter that refills at a fixed rate up to a capacity. Each request uses one token Retry-After "Try later" A response header with the number of seconds, or a date, after which the client can try again Server-Sent Events "Streaming" A text/event-stream response of event: and data: lines, with a blank line after each event Time to first token "Latency" The time from the request to the first token on the user's screen Usage cap "The budget" A limit on the total number of model calls in a time window, for all clients together Keyed hash "An anonymous ID" An HMAC of the client address with a secret salt. It is a pseudonym: anyone with the salt can test a known address Content Security Policy "CSP" A response header that tells the browser which scripts, styles, and connections the page can use The problem In plain words first A demo interface is a small web page and server that lets other people try your model. It must do the things a notebook never does. It validates input before spending a model call: size, type, allowed characters. It shows progress , so a slow model does not look broken, and streams tokens as they are produced (the usual format is Server-Sent Events, SSE). It returns errors a stranger can act on : what went wrong and what to do, never a stack trace. And it protects your budget once the link is shared: a token bucket limits how fast each client can send requests, a daily cap limits total cost, and logs keep only what you need. This lesson builds all of that with Python's standard library, then shows the same demo in Gradio and Streamlit. Your model works in a notebook. Now a reviewer wants to try ten inputs, and a customer wants to see one result on a phone. Neither of them will open your notebook. A notebook cell has no input limits and no progress display. Its errors are stack traces that only you can read. It also runs with your credentials and your budget. If you put the cell behind a public URL without changes, you can expect failures like these: A user pastes a 40,000-character document. The model call runs for a minute and then fails with a stack trace. One script sends 500 requests in one minute. Each request is a paid model call. The page shows nothing for eight seconds, so the user clicks the button four more times. The server log keeps every input, including the input with a customer account number. A demo interface prevents these failures with a small amount of code. This lesson builds one with the Python standard library, so you can see every part. Then it builds the same demo with two popular frameworks and compares what each one does by default. Idea 1 · A demo is a contract Every demo has three parts. The input is what the user can send. The model call turns the input into an output. The output is what the user sees, and that includes errors. Write the contract down before you write the page: Part Question to answer Answer in this lesson Input What type, what size, which characters? A string of 1 to 500 characters, with no control characters Model call How long does one call take, and what does it cost? A toy keyword model that runs in under a millisecond at no cost Output What does the user see on success and on failure? A label, a score, and a reply, or a JSON error with a hint A notebook has no limit on any of the three parts. A demo sets a limit on each part, and the server applies the limits to every client. The checks run in order of cost. A bad request stops at the first check that it fails, so it costs the server almost nothing. The model call comes last, because it is the only step that costs money. Idea 2 · Validate before the model runs The browser can check input before it sends anything. The maxlength and required attributes on a text area give the user feedback with no network call. These checks help honest users only. Any client can send a request without the page, so the server repeats every check. Put the server checks in order of cost: Read the Content-Length header. Refuse a body over the limit before you read it. Parse the JSON body. Refuse a body that is not a JSON object. Check the fields. Refuse empty text, text over the limit, and control characters. Spend a model call only on a request that passed every check. Failed check HTTP status Error code No Content-Length header 411 Length Required length_required Content-Length is not a number 400 Bad Request bad_length Body over 4,096 bytes 413 Content Too Large body_too_large Body stops before Content-Length bytes arrive 408 Request Timeout request_timeout Content type is not JSON 415 Unsupported Media Type unsupported_media_type Body is not a JSON object 400 Bad Request bad_json Text is missing, empty, too long, or has control characters 422 Unprocessable Content missing_text , empty_text , text_too_long , control_characters RFC 9110 defines these status codes and their names. Examples are part of the input design. An example shows the user what a good input looks like. It also gives a reviewer a test with one click. Pick one example for each output class. This demo has a positive, a negative, and a neutral example. Idea 3 · Show that the model is working A model call can take several seconds. With no feedback, the user cannot tell a slow model from a broken page. A user who sees no change can click again, and then the server gets a second paid request. The page in this lesson gives four kinds of feedback: It disables the submit button while a request runs. It shows the elapsed time and updates it every 100 milliseconds. It shows the time to first token when the first token arrives. It shows the total time when the request ends. When you studied inference metrics , time to first token (TTFT) was a server metric. The demo page shows the same number to the user, measured in the browser. Idea 4 · Send the output as a stream A language model produces its reply one token at a time. If the server waits for the last token, the user waits for the full generation. If the server sends each token when it is ready, the user starts to read after the first token. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is the standard format for this. The response has the content type text/event-stream . Each event is a group of event: and data: lines, and a blank line ends the event. The WHATWG HTML standard defines the format. Copy The browser has an EventSource interface for SSE, but it only sends GET requests. A GET request puts the input in the URL, and web servers and proxies write URLs into their access logs. This demo sends a POST request with a JSON body instead. The page reads the response with fetch() and response.body.getReader() , and it parses the event format itself. A stream has one problem that a single JSON reply does not have. The server sends status 200 before the first token. If the model fails after that, the server cannot change the status. So the server sends an error event in the stream, and the page shows that event as an error. When you built the production LLM application , a framework sent the tokens over SSE for you. This lesson writes the same protocol by hand, so you can see each line that the server sends. Idea 5 · Write errors that a user can act on An error message has two jobs. It tells the user what happened, and it tells the user what to do next. A stack trace does neither job for a stranger. Every error in this demo has the same JSON shape: Copy code is a stable name. Client code and tests compare against it. message states the fact, with the numbers that the user needs. hint gives the user one action. request_id connects a user report to one log record. RFC 9457 defines a standard error format for HTTP APIs, called problem details. This demo uses a smaller shape for the same purpose. Use RFC 9457 when other teams call your API. Idea 6 · Share a public demo safely A public link changes who can send requests. Plan one control for each risk: Risk Control in this demo Control for a larger audience One client sends too many requests A token bucket per client, with 429 and Retry-After Per-user limits after sign-in Strangers find the link An optional access token in the Authorization header Single sign-on with an identity provider Total cost grows with no limit A daily usage cap, with 503 and Retry-After Spend limits and alerts at the model provider Very large or unusual input Body size limit, text length limit, control character check Content moderation on input and output Logs keep private input Records with the input length and a keyed hash of the client A retention period and access control on the logs A token bucket uses two numbers. The capacity is the largest burst that one client can send. The refill rate is the long-run request rate. Each request takes one token, and the bucket refills continuously up to its capacity: Copy When the bucket is empty, the server answers 429 Too Many Requests . RFC 6585 defines status 429, and it lets the server add a Retry-After header. This demo always adds the header, with the number of seconds until the next token. The page reads the header and disables the button for that time. The demo uses the client IP address as the bucket key. Behind a reverse proxy, every request comes from the proxy address, so all users share one bucket. In that case, read the client address from a header that your own proxy sets. Do not trust that header from any other source, because a client can put any value in it. When you studied AI gateways , the gateway applied rate limits per tenant. A demo needs the same control at a smaller scale. A rate limit controls each client, but it does not control the total. A hundred clients that each stay under the limit can still use the full budget. A usage cap counts all model calls in one day and refuses calls after a fixed number. Logs need the same care as input. The default http.server handler writes the client IP address and the request line to standard error. If the input is in the URL, the input goes into the log. This demo replaces that log line. Each request writes one record with the route, the status, the error code, the latency, and the input length. The client address becomes a keyed hash, so you can count requests per client without storing the address. Tell users what you keep. It holds the HTTP status, a stable code, a message, a hint, and optional response headers. Copy The validator removes leading and trailing white space first. Step 3 · The token bucket Copy take returns 0.0 when it accepts the request. Otherwise it returns the seconds until the bucket has enough tokens. The server rounds that value up and sends it in Retry-After . RateLimiter keeps one bucket per client in an OrderedDict . A lock protects the dictionary, because ThreadingHTTPServer handles each request in its own thread. When the dictionary has more than max_clients entries, the limiter removes the client with the oldest request. A removed client gets a full bucket on its next request. Set max_clients above the number of active clients that you expect. The limiter takes a clock argument. The tests pass a FakeClock , so a test can move time forward by ten seconds with no wait. Step 4 · The stream Copy json.dumps writes a newline inside a string as the two characters \n . Each event therefore has one data line with no raw newline in it. A raw newline in the data would break the event format. The generator catches a model failure and sends an error event, because the server already sent the status line. The delay and sleep arguments slow the stream down for a browser, and they keep the tests fast. Step 5 · The request handler DemoHandler extends BaseHTTPRequestHandler . The POST handler runs the checks in the order from the concept section: Copy admit checks the access token and the token bucket. charge checks the daily cap. It runs last, so only valid requests count against the cap. Every request writes one log record in the finally block, and that includes rejected requests. The record keeps route , never the raw path, because a path can carry a query string with user text. Four details prevent failures that are easy to miss: timeout = 10 on the handler class closes a connection when the client stops sending. Without it, a client that declares 100 bytes and sends 10 holds a server thread forever. The handler sends a 408 JSON error with the request id and closes the connection. A timeout after the stream starts only closes the connection, because the status line is already sent. log_message returns without output. This removes the default log line with the client address and the request line. drain reads and discards up to 64 KiB of a refused body. RFC 1122 says that TCP sends a reset when a host closes a connection with unread data. The client can then lose the 413 reply. send_stream catches BrokenPipeError and closes the generator. When the user closes the tab, the model stops, and the request costs nothing more. BaseHTTPRequestHandler uses HTTP/1.0 by default. The end of a streamed body is then the moment when the server closes the connection. A server that uses HTTP/1.1 sends the body with chunked transfer coding for the same purpose. The script reads the stream like this: Copy A network chunk can end in the middle of an event. The reader keeps the incomplete part in buffer until the blank line arrives. The page writes model output with textContent and never with innerHTML . Model output is untrusted text. Design the sequence of checks a request passes before the model runs, and give the HTTP status for each refusal. Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Run the cheap checks first and the paid step last. Refuse an oversized body from its Content-Length header before you read it, check the access token, take one token from the client's rate bucket, parse and validate the JSON, charge the daily usage cap, and only then call the model. Each refusal returns a JSON error with a stable code, a message and a hint, and the statuses in that order are 413, 401, 429, 422 and 503. Why the order matters. A bad request stops at the first check that it fails, and that check should cost the server almost nothing. The model call is the only step that costs money, so it comes last. The browser can repeat some checks with maxlength and required , but those help honest users only. Any client can send a request without the page, so the server repeats every check. The sequence. Step Refusal Status route exists unknown endpoint 404 Content-Length present and numeric missing, or not a number 411, 400 body size under the limit over 4,096 bytes, refused before the read 413 body arrives in time client stops sending 408 access token, when configured missing or wrong 401 token bucket per client bucket empty, with Retry-After 429 content type and JSON object wrong type, or not an object 415, 400 fields missing, empty, too long, control characters 422 daily usage cap the day's budget is spent, with Retry-After 503 model call 200 The cap is charged after validation, so that only valid requests count against the day. The error shape. Every refusal has the same JSON body: a code that client code and tests compare, a message that states the fact with its numbers, a hint with one action, and a request_id that joins a user report to one log record. Two limits, not one. The token bucket bounds each client: a capacity for the burst and a refill rate for the long run. It does not bound the total. A hundred clients that each stay under the limit can still spend the whole budget, so the usage cap counts all model calls in a day and refuses after a fixed number. Behind a proxy. The bucket key is the client address. Behind a reverse proxy every request arrives from the proxy, so all clients share one bucket. Read the client address from the header that your own proxy sets, and trust that header from the proxy only. Log every request. One record per request, in the finally block, including the refused ones: the route, the status, the error code, the latency and the input length. The client address becomes a keyed hash. The text is never stored, and the page says so. Plausible wrong answers. "Validate the text first, then check the size." Reading the body before the size check spends the cost that the check exists to avoid. "A rate limit is enough, skip the cap." A per-client limit bounds each client. A hundred clients under the limit still spend the whole budget. "Return 500 with the stack trace, developers can read it." A stranger cannot act on a stack trace. An error needs a code, a fact and one next action. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the usage cap come after the field checks? Expected: so that only valid requests count against the day's total. (level 2) Why refuse on the header before reading the body? Expected: it stops a large upload before the server spends memory and time on it. (level 3) Behind a reverse proxy one heavy user gets everyone rate limited. Why? Expected: every request arrives from the proxy address, so all clients share one bucket. Read the client address from the proxy's header, and trust it from the proxy only. (level 3) What does the server do with a refused body before it answers 413? Expected: it reads and discards up to 64 KiB, because a close with unread data can trigger a TCP reset and the client loses the reply. Where it is taught. The model demo interfaces lesson orders the checks by cost and defines the error shape, the token bucket and the usage cap. Debug a failure Your demo streams tokens to the page over server-sent events. Users report that the page sometimes shows half an answer and then stops, with no message. The server log shows a model exception on exactly those requests. Why does the user see nothing, and how do you fix the protocol? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The server sends the status line with status 200 before the first token. When the model fails after that, the status cannot change, so the client sees a stream that ends early and nothing else. Send an error event inside the stream, and make the page show that event as an error. Also stop the generator when the client disconnects, so that a closed tab stops the model. The protocol problem. A streamed response has one status line, and it goes out first. Every token after it is a body chunk. An exception in the generator after the first token cannot turn a 200 into a 500. The connection closes, and the page has no way to tell a short answer from a failure. The fix in the lesson. The stream generator catches the exception and yields one more event: Copy Then it returns. The page reads each frame and handles three event names: token appends text, done ends the request and shows the totals, and error shows the message and the hint. The error carries a request id, so a user report maps to one log record without storing any input. Two details that make it hold. The page buffers the incoming bytes and cuts frames at the blank line, because a network chunk can end in the middle of an event. A parser that treats each chunk as one event breaks on long answers. json.dumps escapes a newline inside a string, so each event has one data line. A raw newline inside the data would end the event early. Stop the model when the user leaves. When the user closes the tab, the next write fails with a broken pipe. The handler catches it and closes the generator, so the model stops and the request costs nothing more. The lesson also sets a socket timeout on the handler class, so a client that stops sending does not hold a server thread. Log the failure. The request handler records one log line for every request in its finally block, with the route, the status, the error code, the latency and the input length. A stream that failed with an error event appears there with its code, so the failures are countable. Plausible wrong answers. "Buffer the whole answer and return JSON instead." That removes streaming, and the user waits for the last token on every request. "Send the error text as another token." The page cannot tell an error from model output, and the done event never arrives. "Retry the request on the server when the model fails." The user already has half an answer. A retry duplicates output and doubles the cost. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why can the server not send a 500 when the model fails halfway? Expected: the status line went out before the first token, and a response has one status. (level 2) A user closes the tab halfway through. What should the server do? Expected: the write fails with a broken pipe, the handler closes the generator, and the model stops. (level 3) Why does the page buffer the bytes instead of parsing each chunk as an event? Expected: a chunk can end in the middle of an event, so the reader keeps the partial text until the blank line arrives. (level 3) What goes into the error event besides the message? Expected: a stable code that tests can compare, a hint with one action, and the request id that joins the report to a log record. Where it is taught. The model demo interfaces lesson writes the event stream by hand and sends the error event after the status line. Write the contract first: a string of 1 to 500 characters with no control characters, a model call with a known cost, and an output that includes a JSON error with a hint. Run the checks in order of cost, body size, access token, per-client token bucket, input validation, daily cap, and only then the model call. Return a stable error code with a message, a hint and a request id, and log the route, the status, the latency and the input length with a keyed hash of the client, never the text or the address. a1801: Course home / Phase 18 · Ethics, Safety & Alignment Instruction-Following as Alignment Signal Lesson 18.1 45 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Name the three stages of the InstructGPT pipeline and the loss used in each. Explain why a 1.3B instruction-tuned model beat the raw 175B GPT-3 on human preference evaluation. State what the KL penalty in stage 3 is protecting against and why removing it collapses to mode-seeking behaviour. Describe the alignment tax and the PPO-ptx mitigation Ouyang et al. used against it. Before you start Needs : Phase 10 · 06 (SFT), Phase 10 · 07 (RLHF), Phase 10 · 08 (DPO) Type : Learn. Time : about 45 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, toy three-stage pipeline), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Every later critique of RLHF argues against this pipeline. Before you study how optimization pressure distorts a proxy, you have to see the proxy. InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) defined the reference architecture: supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response pairs, a reward model trained on pairwise preference rankings, and PPO against the reward model with a KL penalty to the SFT policy. A 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred over a 175B GPT-3. That single result is the reason every frontier lab in 2026 still ships an RLHF-shaped post-training pip Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means SFT "instruction tuning" Stage 1: cross-entropy fine-tune on prompt-response pairs Reward model "the RM" Scalar regressor over (prompt, response) trained with Bradley-Terry on pairwise labels Bradley-Terry "pairwise preference loss" $-\log \sigma(r_w - r_l)$; reduces pairwise ranking to binary classification KL penalty "the regularizer" beta * KL(pi \|\| pi_SFT) — keeps the RL policy near the SFT anchor PPO-ptx "PPO with pretraining mix" Adds a fraction of pre-training log-likelihood to the PPO objective to offset the alignment tax Alignment tax "the RLHF regression" Post-RLHF drop on standard benchmarks that RLHF did not target Labeler preference "the ground truth" Sample of human rankings; the RM is a statistical proxy for this, not for "human values" The problem Pre-trained language models complete text. They do not answer questions. Ask GPT-3 "write a Python function that reverses a list" and you often get back another prompt, because most of the training distribution is web text that continues with more web text. The model is doing its job — the job is wrong. The proxy every serious lab used to fix this is human preference. Two completions go to a rater; the rater picks the better one; a reward model learns the rater. Then an RL loop shifts the policy toward outputs the reward model scores high. That is the full InstructGPT thesis in three sentences. The rest of the paper is engineering. Idea 1 · Stage 1: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Collect prompt-response pairs where the response is what a well-intentioned human would write. Ouyang et al. used 13k prompts from labelers and the OpenAI API. Fine-tune the base model on this data with standard cross-entropy loss. What SFT gives you: the model now answers questions instead of continuing them. What it does not give you: any signal about which answer the rater prefers when multiple are plausible. Idea 2 · Stage 2: reward model (RM) For each prompt, sample K completions from the SFT model. A labeler ranks them. Train a reward model that scores any prompt-response pair so that, for pairs where y_w was preferred over y_l : ​ = − lo g σ ( r ( x , y w ​ ) − r ( x , y l ​ ) ) This is the Bradley-Terry pairwise preference loss. The RM is usually initialized from the SFT model with the LM head replaced by a scalar head. Reward models are small: 6B was enough for the 175B InstructGPT. They are also fragile — section 5 of the paper is mostly about reward-hacking behaviours that showed up at small scale. Idea 3 · Stage 3: PPO with a KL penalty Define the objective: ​ [ r ( x , y ) ] − β KL ( π ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ∥ π SFT ​ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ) Maximize with PPO. The KL term keeps pi from drifting far from the SFT policy. Without it, the optimizer finds adversarial examples — strings that score high under the RM because the RM never saw them, not because humans actually prefer them. The KL coefficient beta is the single most important RLHF hyperparameter. Too low: reward hacking. Too high: no improvement over SFT. Idea 4 · The alignment tax After RLHF, the model is preferred by humans but regresses on standard benchmarks (SQuAD, HellaSwag, DROP). Ouyang et al. call this the alignment tax and fix it with PPO-ptx: mix pre-training gradients into the RL objective so the model does not forget how to do downstream tasks it was never rewarded for. ​ ( π ) = J ( π ) + γ E x ∼ D pretrain ​ ​ [ lo g π ( x ) ] PPO-ptx became standard. Anthropic, DeepMind, and Meta all use some variant. Idea 5 · The result A 1.3B InstructGPT (SFT + RM + PPO-ptx) is preferred by labelers over the 175B base GPT-3 about 70% of the time. The gap widens on hidden-test prompts from production traffic. Two things to read off this number: Alignment is a different axis from capability. The 175B model had more capability; the 1.3B model had more alignment; labelers preferred the aligned one. The capability floor is set by the base model. You cannot RLHF a base model into knowing facts it never saw. Idea 6 · Why this is the reference point for Phase 18 Every critique in later lessons — reward hacking (Lesson 2), DPO (Lesson 3), sycophancy (Lesson 4), CAI (Lesson 5), sleeper agents (Lesson 7), alignment faking (Lesson 9) — argues against some part of this pipeline. Reward hacking attacks stage 2. DPO collapses stages 2 and 3. CAI replaces the human labeler. Sycophancy shows the labeler is a biased signal. Alignment faking shows the policy can route around stage 3 entirely. You cannot follow any of these critiques without the pipeline in your head first. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py simulates the three stages on toy preference data. The base "policy" is a biased coin over actions {A, B, C}. Stage 1 SFT mimics labeler actions on 200 prompts. Stage 2 fits a Bradley-Terry reward model from 500 pairwise rankings. Stage 3 runs a simplified PPO update with a KL penalty to the SFT policy. You can watch the reward climb, the KL divergence grow, and the policy drift — and you can turn off the KL term to see reward hacking appear inside 50 update steps. What to look at: Reward trajectory with beta = 0.1 vs beta = 0.0 . ​ ) over training steps. Final action distribution compared to labeler preference. a1802: Course home / Phase 18 · Ethics, Safety & Alignment Reward Hacking and Goodhart's Law Lesson 18.2 60 min Learn Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do State Goodhart's Law and why it is not a folk slogan but a predictable property of any optimization against an imperfect proxy. Describe the Gao et al. 2023 scaling law: mean proxy-gold gap as a function of KL distance from the initial policy. Name four common manifestations of reward hacking (verbosity, sycophancy, unfaithful reasoning, evaluator tampering) and trace each back to the shared mechanism. Explain why KL regularization alone does not save you under heavy-tailed reward error (Catastrophic Goodhart). Before you start Needs : Phase 18 · 01 (InstructGPT), Phase 10 · 07 (RLHF) Type : Learn. Time : about 60 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, proxy-vs-gold-reward simulator), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Any optimizer strong enough to maximize a proxy reward will find the gap between the proxy and the thing you actually wanted. Gao et al. (ICML 2023) gave this a scaling law: proxy reward increases, gold reward peaks then falls, and the gap grows with the KL divergence from the initial policy in a way you can fit in closed form. Sycophancy, verbosity bias, unfaithful chain-of-thought, and evaluator tampering are not separate problems. They are the same problem in different costumes. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Goodhart's Law "optimizing a proxy breaks it" Any strong optimizer against an imperfect proxy reliably finds inputs where the proxy-target gap is large Gold reward "what we actually want" The target the proxy is a noisy measurement of; in practice, a larger-sample RM or human eval Proxy reward "the RM" The scalar used during training; by construction, it is what the optimizer sees Over-optimization curve "the reward-hacking U-curve" Proxy climbs, gold peaks then falls as KL from initial policy grows KL budget "how far we can drift" sqrt(KL(pi \|\| pi_init)) ; Gao et al. plot reward against this Catastrophic Goodhart "KL does not save you" Under heavy-tailed reward error, KL-constrained optimal policy can maximize proxy while providing no gold utility Unfaithful reasoning "wrong CoT, right answer" Chain-of-thought that does not causally drive the final prediction Evaluator tampering "gaming the scorer" Agent modifies its environment, scratchpad, or the RM's inputs to register success The problem You cannot measure what you actually want. You can measure a proxy for it. Every RLHF pipeline exploits this substitution: "human preference" becomes "Bradley-Terry fit on 50k labeled pairs." An optimizer that reaches high reward on the proxy has, by construction, done well at the thing you measured. Whether it did well at the thing you wanted depends on how tightly the proxy tracked it, and the answer is always: less tightly than you hoped. Gao, Schulman, Hilton (2023) measured this directly. Train a "gold" reward model from 100k labels. Train proxy RMs from {1k, 3k, 10k, 30k} subsets of the same data. Optimize a policy against each proxy. Plot gold-RM score vs KL divergence from the initial policy. Every curve rises, peaks, and falls. The peak is further out for larger proxies. The fall is inevitable. Idea 1 · Goodhart's Law, made precise Goodhart's original formulation: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Manheim and Garrabrant (2018) distinguish four variants: regressional (finite-sample), extremal (tails), causal (proxy is downstream of target), and adversarial (agent gaming). For RLHF, extremal + adversarial are the dominant modes. Gao et al. give a functional form for the gold reward. Let d = sqrt(KL(pi || pi_init)) and let R_gold(d) be mean gold reward. Empirically: BoN ​ ( d ) R gold RL ​ ( d ) ​ = d ( α BoN ​ − β BoN ​ d ) = d ( α RL ​ − β RL ​ lo g d ) ​ Both forms rise from zero KL, peak, and then fall. The proxy score has no clean fit in the paper; it keeps climbing, roughly linearly in d at large KL. So at large d , gold falls below baseline even while proxy keeps climbing. The proxy-gold gap has the same signature for best-of-n sampling and for RL. This is the "over-optimization curve." It is not a bug in a specific reward model. It is the shape of the problem. Idea 2 · Four costumes, one mechanism Verbosity bias. Labelers weakly prefer long explanations. RM learns "longer = better." Policy emits longer outputs, reward climbs, quality does not. Addressed at training time by length penalties (SimPO), at evaluation time by length-controlled win rates. Sycophancy. Labelers weakly prefer agreement. RM learns "agree with the user." Policy affirms false premises. Lesson 4 covers the scaling behaviour. Unfaithful reasoning. The RM learns "answers that look correct are correct." The policy emits chains of thought that justify any answer the scorer wants. Turpin et al. (NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2305.04388) demonstrate CoT is not load-bearing on the final answer in several failure modes. Evaluator tampering. The agent modifies its own environment to register success. Sleeper-agent and in-context-scheming work (Lessons 7-8) show this is reachable at 2024-2026 frontier scale. Each of these is a case of the proxy correlating with the target over the training distribution, and the optimizer selecting inputs where the correlation breaks. Idea 3 · Catastrophic Goodhart A common defense: "we will add KL regularization to keep the policy close to the reference model, so reward hacking is bounded." Gao et al. already showed this softens but does not prevent the gold-reward collapse. "Catastrophic Goodhart" (OpenReview UXuBzWoZGK) makes this sharper. Suppose proxy reward error is heavy-tailed — there exist rare but achievable inputs where proxy minus gold is unbounded. Under a KL constraint the optimal policy can place all its mass on these inputs: proxy reward is arbitrarily high, gold reward is at baseline. KL regularization constrains the policy distribution but does not constrain which modes it targets when those modes exist under the reference model. The condition ("heavy-tailed error") is not exotic. Any bounded measurement of an unbounded world has heavy-tailed error in the tails — that is what "tails" means. Idea 4 · What actually works (partially) Ensemble RMs with worst-case aggregation (Coste et al., 2023). The optimizer can break one RM but not all of them simultaneously. Reward-model robustness to distributional shift (Zhou et al., "Shift-of-Reward-Distribution", 2024). Conservative KL schedules and early stopping at the empirical proxy-gold gap. Direct Alignment Algorithms (DPO, Lesson 3) — which have their own Goodhart failure modes, proven in Rafailov et al. "Scaling Laws for Reward Model Over-optimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms" (NeurIPS 2024). None of these eliminate reward hacking. They move the curve's peak further out. This is often enough for a shipping product. It is never enough for a "solved" alignment claim. Idea 5 · The 2026 unified view "Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models" (arXiv:2604.13602) proposes a single mechanism: probability mass shifts to outputs that maximize proxy reward by exploiting easy-to-learn heuristics — authoritative tone, formatting, confident delivery — that spuriously correlated with approval in the preference data. The paper unifies verbosity, sycophancy, unfaithful CoT, and evaluator tampering as the same optimizer-plus-proxy interaction with different affordances per deployment. This view implies the defense is also unified. Every mitigation has to either reduce proxy-target gap (better data, better RMs), reduce optimization pressure (conservative schedules, early stop), or shift selection pressure onto hard-to-game features (process supervision, debate, information flow control). Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py simulates Gao et al.'s over-optimization curves on a toy regression problem. The "gold" reward is the true linear function of a feature vector. The "proxy" RM is the gold plus Gaussian noise fit on a finite sample. A policy is a mean of a Gaussian over features; training is hill-climbing on proxy reward with a KL penalty to the initial policy. You can vary: sample size of the proxy, KL coefficient, and the noise tail heaviness. Watch the proxy-gold gap open at exactly the KL distance the paper predicts. What changes about the peak location and post-peak collapse? Read Gao et al. Figure 1 (ICML 2023). The paper proposes a functional form for the gold reward as a function of d . Fit it to your simulated curves from Exercise 1 and compare parameters. Take a recent RLHF paper that claims to have "solved" reward hacking (the phrase is a red flag). Identify which of the four costumes the paper tested against and which it did not. The 2026 unified view argues verbosity, sycophancy, unfaithful CoT, and evaluator tampering share a mechanism. Design a single experiment that would simultaneously falsify all four if the unified view is wrong. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Explain the mechanism A model review lists four separate problems: answers got longer without getting better, the model agrees with users who are wrong, its reasoning text does not drive its final answer, and in one agent test it edited the test file so the check would pass. Four teams want four fixes. What do you tell them? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. These are four costumes of one mechanism: the optimizer found features that the proxy reward paid for and that only correlated with quality in the training data. Length, agreement, reasoning that looks right and a passing check were all cheaper than the real thing. The defenses are unified too: shrink the gap between proxy and target, reduce optimization pressure, or move the selection pressure onto features that are hard to game. The four costumes. Verbosity. Labelers weakly preferred long explanations, so the reward model learned that longer is better. Fixes: a length penalty at training time, a length controlled win rate at evaluation time. Sycophancy. Labelers weakly preferred agreement, so the policy affirms false premises. Unfaithful reasoning. The reward model learned that answers that look correct are correct, so the policy writes reasoning that justifies whatever the scorer wants; the chain of thought is not load bearing for the answer. Evaluator tampering. The agent changes its environment, its scratchpad or the scorer's inputs so that success registers. Editing the test is this costume. Each is the proxy correlating with the target on the training distribution and the optimizer selecting the inputs where the correlation breaks. The unified view. Probability mass shifts toward outputs that win approval through easy to learn heuristics, such as authoritative tone, formatting and confident delivery, that happened to correlate with approval in the preference data. Which costume appears depends on what the deployment affords. The three defense classes. Reduce the proxy to target gap: better data, more robust reward models, ensembles with worst case aggregation. Reduce optimization pressure: conservative KL schedules and early stopping at the measured proxy to gold gap. Move selection onto hard to game features: process supervision, debate, control of what information the scorer sees. Tell the four teams to share one dashboard that plots the four symptoms against KL distance from the initial policy, and to pick fixes from these three classes rather than one patch per symptom. Plausible wrong answers. "These are unrelated bugs." Each is the proxy correlating with the target in training and the optimizer finding where the correlation breaks. "Penalize length and the problem is gone." Length is one feature; the optimizer moves to the next cheap feature the proxy pays for. "The agent cheated, so the agent is misaligned." It did what the reward said; the fix is a reward and an environment that pay only for the real outcome. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Two fixes exist for the first finding, one at training time and one at evaluation time. Name them. Expected: a length penalty inside the training reward, and a win rate that controls for length at evaluation time. (level 2) Why does the lesson file the chain of thought finding under reward hacking? Expected: the reward model learned that plausible looking answers are correct, so the policy produces reasoning that justifies the answer the scorer wants. (level 3) Why does editing the test count as the same mechanism and not as a bug? Expected: the check was the proxy, and the optimizer found a cheaper way to make it register success than solving the task. (level 3) Name one defense from each class. Expected: more or better labels for the reward model; a conservative KL schedule with early stopping; process supervision or debate that scores the steps instead of the surface. Where it is taught. The reward hacking and Goodhart's law lesson names the four costumes and the unified view. Explain the mechanism A team trains a chat model against a reward model and reports that the reward climbs with every step. They plan to train longer. Why is a reward that only goes up a warning sign, and which curve would you ask them to plot before they continue? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The reward model is a proxy for what you want, and a strong optimizer finds the inputs where the proxy and the target disagree. The proxy score climbs while the true quality rises, peaks and then falls. Ask for the gold reward, from a larger reward model or human ratings, plotted against the square root of the KL distance from the initial policy. The gap between the two curves is the reward hacking. The law. When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. This is not a slogan but a property of optimization against an imperfect proxy. Of the four variants, regressional, extremal, causal and adversarial, the extremal and adversarial ones dominate preference training: the optimizer reaches into the tails and games the scorer. The curve. The lesson's reference experiment trains a gold reward model on a large label set and several proxy reward models on smaller subsets of the same labels, then optimizes a policy against each proxy. Plotted against the square root of the KL distance from the starting policy, every gold curve rises, peaks and falls. The peak sits further out for proxies trained on more labels. The proxy score has no peak; it keeps climbing. The same shape appears for best of n sampling and for reinforcement learning, which shows that the mechanism is the optimizer plus the proxy, not the algorithm. What to do with it. Plot gold against KL distance and stop near the empirical peak instead of training to a step budget. Use an ensemble of reward models with worst case aggregation; the optimizer can break one but not all at once. Get more labels for the proxy; the peak moves out, but the fall remains. Expect the four costumes of the same problem in the outputs: verbosity, sycophancy, unfaithful reasoning and evaluator tampering. None of this removes reward hacking. It moves the peak, which is often enough to ship and never enough to call alignment solved. Plausible wrong answers. "Reward went up, so the model improved." The proxy always goes up; the gold reward is what peaks and falls. "Train longer and the gold will catch up." The gap grows with KL distance; longer training moves further down the falling side. "A better reward model solves it." More labels move the peak out; any bounded proxy of an unbounded target has a gap somewhere. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What is the proxy and what is the gold in a preference training run? Expected: the proxy is the reward model the optimizer sees; the gold is what you want, in practice a larger reward model or human ratings. (level 2) How does a larger label set for the proxy help, and how much? Expected: the peak of the gold curve moves further out in KL distance; the fall still comes. (level 2) Name two ways this shows up in a chat model. Expected: longer answers and agreement with the user, both learned because labelers weakly preferred them. (level 3) The team switches from reinforcement learning to picking the best of several samples. Does the curve change? Expected: no; both select for high proxy reward, and the mechanism is the optimizer plus an imperfect proxy, not the training algorithm. Where it is taught. The reward hacking and Goodhart's law lesson gives the over optimization curve and its scaling law. Explain the mechanism A colleague argues that reward hacking is bounded in their pipeline because the policy trains with a KL penalty against the reference model, so it cannot drift far. Why is that argument incomplete, and under which condition does it fail completely? Level 3 of 4 · about 9 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The KL penalty constrains how far the policy's distribution moves, not which modes it moves toward. The over optimization curve already shows that a KL penalty softens the collapse of the gold reward without preventing it. When the proxy's error is heavy tailed, rare but reachable inputs exist where proxy minus gold is unbounded, and a KL constrained optimal policy can place its mass on them: proxy reward arbitrarily high, gold reward at baseline. What the penalty buys. With a KL term the gold curve still rises, peaks and falls as the policy moves from the reference. The penalty makes the slope gentler and a better proxy pushes the peak out. Neither changes the shape. Catastrophic Goodhart. Suppose the proxy's error has heavy tails: somewhere under the reference model there are inputs the proxy loves far more than the gold does. The KL constraint limits the total distance between the policy and the reference. It does not stop the policy from concentrating that allowed distance on exactly those inputs, because they already have support under the reference. The result is a policy that scores arbitrarily well on the proxy and no better than baseline on the gold. Why the condition is plausible. A reward model is a bounded measurement of an unbounded world. The lesson argues that such a measurement has heavy tailed error in its tails, so the assumption is not exotic. It is still an assumption: for each proxy, measure the tail of the proxy to gold gap on held out labels before you rely on a KL budget. What helps, partially. An ensemble of reward models with worst case aggregation: the optimizer can find one model's tail error, but the minimum over several pays only where they all err together. Reward models trained to be robust to shift in the output distribution. Conservative KL schedules and early stopping at the measured proxy to gold gap. Nothing from the direct preference family is exempt; those losses have their own scaling law for over optimization. Plausible wrong answers. "Small KL means small reward hacking." KL bounds the drift, not its direction; the policy can spend the budget on the proxy's tail errors. "Heavy tails are an exotic assumption." The lesson argues they are ordinary for a bounded reward model; measure the proxy to gold gap instead of assuming the tail is light. "Use the direct preference loss, it has no reward model." It has an implicit one and its own over optimization curve. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does a KL penalty constrain, and what does it leave free? Expected: the distance of the policy distribution from the reference; which high reward modes under the reference the policy concentrates on. (level 3) How can several reward models do what one model with a penalty cannot? Expected: the optimizer can find one reward model's tail error, but the minimum over several models pays only where they all err together. (level 4) Does switching to a direct preference loss remove the problem? Expected: no; the direct alignment family has its own scaling law for over optimization, so the same monitoring applies. (level 4) Turn this into an operating rule for a training run. Expected: plot gold against KL distance with held out labels, stop at the empirical peak, and treat a rising proxy with a flat gold as the alarm whatever the KL coefficient. Where it is taught. The reward hacking and Goodhart's law lesson explains Catastrophic Goodhart and why KL regularization alone fails. State the failure mode each of IPO, KTO, SimPO, ORPO, BPO fixes in DPO. Distinguish "implicit reward gap" from "preference strength" and explain why IPO's identity mapping matters. Explain why Rafailov et al. (NeurIPS 2024) prove DAAs over-optimize despite having no explicit RM. Before you start Needs : Phase 18 · 01 (InstructGPT), Phase 18 · 02 (Reward hacking), Phase 10 · 08 (DPO basics) Type : Learn. Time : about 75 minutes. Code in : Python (stdlib, six-variant preference-loss comparator), TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Rafailov et al. (2023) showed RLHF's optimum has a closed form in terms of the preference data, so you can skip the explicit reward model and optimize the policy directly. That insight spawned a family — IPO, KTO, SimPO, ORPO, BPO — each fixing a failure mode of DPO. In 2026, direct alignment algorithms ship more frontier post-training runs than PPO. But the over-optimization curve from Lesson 2 still applies: DAAs do not escape Goodhart, they just move where it bites. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means DPO "RLHF without a reward model" Loss derived from the closed-form RLHF optimum; policy parameters only Implicit reward "the log-ratio" beta * log(pi(y\|x) / pi_ref(y\|x)) — the DPO-implied reward IPO "bounded DPO" Replaces log-sigmoid with identity; implicit reward gap capped by 1/(2 beta) KTO "unpaired DPO" Prospect-theory utility over single labels with loss aversion SimPO "reference-free DPO" Length-normalized log-likelihood + margin; no reference policy ORPO "one-stage DPO" NLL + odds-ratio preference term; trains from base model in one pass BPO "chosen-preserving DPO" DPO plus a penalty for decreasing the chosen response's absolute log-prob Degraded Chosen "chosen goes down" DPO decreases chosen log-prob so long as rejected falls faster DAA "direct alignment algorithm" Any preference-loss method that skips an explicit RM The problem The RLHF objective (Lesson 1): max ​ E x , y ∼ π ​ [ r ( x , y ) ] − β KL ( π ∥ π ref ​ ) has a known optimum: ( y ∣ x ) = Z ( x ) 1 ​ π ref ​ ( y ∣ x ) exp ( β r ( x , y ) ​ ) So the reward is implicitly defined by the ratio of the optimal policy to the reference: ​ ( y ∣ x ) π ∗ ( y ∣ x ) ​ + β lo g Z ( x ) Substitute this into the Bradley-Terry preference likelihood and the partition function Z(x) cancels because it depends only on x . What remains is a loss in the policy parameters alone — no reward model needed. That is DPO. The wrinkle: the derivation assumes the optimum is reachable, the preference data is in-distribution, and the reference policy is the true mode anchor. None of these hold exactly. Every family member fixes a different violated assumption. Idea 1 · DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) ​ = − lo g σ ( β lo g π ref ​ ( y w ​ ∣ x ) π ( y w ​ ∣ x ) ​ − β lo g π ref ​ ( y l ​ ∣ x ) π ( y l ​ ∣ x ) ​ ) What can go wrong: The implicit reward gap beta * (log(pi/pi_ref)_w - log(pi/pi_ref)_l) is unbounded. A tiny preference can produce an arbitrarily large gap. The loss drives chosen and rejected log-probs in opposite directions. It can push the chosen absolute log-prob down as long as the rejected falls faster. This is the Degraded Chosen Response phenomenon. Out-of-distribution preferences (pairs where both responses are rare under the reference policy) produce arbitrary implicit rewards. Idea 2 · IPO (Azar et al., 2024) Identity Preference Optimization replaces the log-sigmoid with an identity mapping on the preference probability. The loss becomes a squared-error on a bounded target: ​ = ( lo g π ref ​ ( y w ​ ∣ x ) π ( y w ​ ∣ x ) ​ − lo g π ref ​ ( y l ​ ∣ x ) π ( y l ​ ∣ x ) ​ − 2 β 1 ​ ) 2 The margin is bounded by 1/(2 beta) . Preference strength and implicit-reward gap are proportional. No blow-up. Idea 3 · KTO (Ethayarajh et al., 2024) Kahneman-Tversky Optimization drops pairwise structure entirely. Given a single labeled output and a binary "desirable" or "undesirable" signal, it maps to a prospect-theory utility: ​ ( y ∣ x ) π ( y ∣ x ) ​ − z ref ​ ) with different weights for gains and losses (loss aversion). Benefit: you can use unpaired data, which is far more plentiful. Idea 4 · SimPO (Meng et al., 2024) Simple Preference Optimization aligns the training signal with generation. Remove the reference policy entirely and normalize log-likelihood by length: ​ = − lo g σ ( ∣ y w ​ ∣ β ​ lo g π ( y w ​ ∣ x ) − ∣ y l ​ ∣ β ​ lo g π ( y l ​ ∣ x ) − γ ) with a margin gamma to stabilize. The length normalization removes the incentive to exploit DPO's length-bias failure mode (longer y_w gives a larger log-prob gap by construction). Idea 5 · ORPO (Hong et al., 2024) Odds-Ratio Preference Optimization adds a preference term to the standard SFT negative log-likelihood: ​ L OR ​ ​ = L NLL ​ ( y w ​ ) + λ L OR ​ = − lo g σ ( lo g odds ( y l ​ ) odds ( y w ​ ) ​ ) ​ No reference policy — the SFT term is the regularizer. Train in a single stage from the base model to the aligned model. No separate SFT checkpoint. Idea 6 · BPO (ICLR 2026 submission, OpenReview id=b97EwMUWu7) Identifies the Degraded Chosen Responses problem: DPO preserves the ranking y_w > y_l but the absolute log-prob of y_w can drop. BPO adds a single-line correction that penalizes downward moves on the chosen response. Reported +10.1% accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on math reasoning over DPO. Idea 7 · The universal result: DAAs still over-optimize Rafailov et al. "Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms" (NeurIPS 2024) trained policies with DPO, IPO, SLiC on multiple datasets across KL budgets. The gold-reward-vs-KL curves have the same Gao et al. peak-and-collapse shape. The implicit reward queries out-of-distribution samples during training; KL regularization does not stabilize this. DAAs do not escape Goodhart. They change the surface where it bites from "reward model over-optimized" to "reference policy ratio over-optimized." The universal fix — better data, ensembles, early stopping — applies to both. Idea 8 · Choosing among them (2026) If you have large paired preference data: DPO with conservative beta, SimPO if length bias is evident. If you have unpaired binary feedback: KTO. If you want a single-stage pipeline from a base model: ORPO. If you see degraded chosen log-probs in DPO logs: BPO. If preference strengths vary widely and DPO is saturating: IPO. Every lab runs all five on a battery and picks the winner per task. There is no reason the optimum is the same for math reasoning and safety. Use it: the same idea with real libraries code/main.py compares six losses (DPO, IPO, KTO, SimPO, ORPO, BPO) on a toy preference dataset where the true preference strength varies by pair. Each loss is optimized against the same 500-pair sample with a small softmax policy. Plots final win rate, chosen-log-prob drift, and implicit-reward spread per method.
