Read the code A decode loop keeps keys and values in a preallocated cache and attends one query over the stored prefix. Generation always stops one token short of the configured context length, and the first tokens of a long prompt attend to extra zero rows. The cache code is: python class KVCache: def __init__(self, max_len, d_k, d_v): self.k = np.zeros((max_len, d_k)) self.v = np.zeros((max_len, d_v)) self.n = 0 def append(self, k, v): k = np.atleast_2d(k) v = np.atleast_2d(v) self.n += k.shape[0] if self.n >= self.k.shape[0]: raise ValueError("cache full") self.k[self.n - k.shape[0]:self.n] = k self.v[self.n - k.shape[0]:self.n] = v def keys(self): return self.k Explain the two symptoms from the code and fix them. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The capacity test rejects an append that ends exactly at the capacity, so the last slot is never used and generation stops one token early. The counter is also updated before the test, so a refused append leaves the length wrong. The accessor returns the whole buffer rather than the filled prefix, so attention sees the empty zero rows. Check that the length plus the new steps does not exceed the capacity before touching the counter, and return views of the first n rows. Defect one: the boundary. An append that fills the cache to its capacity is valid. The test must refuse only when the new length would exceed the capacity. With the strict comparison the last row is dead, and a generation loop that sizes the cache from the context length stops one token short. Defect two: the counter. Adding to the length before the check means a failed append leaves the cache claiming steps it never stored. The next call then writes past the real data or refuses a valid append. The rule from the practice is that a refused append changes nothing. Defect three: the view. keys() returns every row of the buffer, filled or not. The query then attends over zero rows that carry weight after the softmax, which dilutes the output for short prefixes. Return the first n rows only. The corrected class. Copy The copy into the buffer also protects the cache from later changes to the caller's arrays. How this meets the generation loop. The assembly lesson's generator keeps the active window inside the context length by dropping the oldest tokens when the prompt plus the generated tokens would exceed it. A cache with a fixed capacity needs the same rule one level down: either refuse the append and let the loop slide the window, or evict the oldest rows. The practice pins the refusing version so the boundary is explicit. Plausible wrong answers. "Use greater-or-equal so the cache never overflows." It also rejects the exact fill and wastes the last slot. "Return the full buffer; the zero rows have no effect." Zero keys still get softmax weight and pull the output toward the zero values. "Update the count first so the slice indices are simpler." A refused append then corrupts the length. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does the decode step do with the stored keys? Expected: it scores one query against every stored key, divides by the square root of the key size, takes a softmax and weights the stored values. (level 3) A second bug writes every append at row zero. What is the symptom? Expected: new steps overwrite old ones, so attention only ever sees the latest append and the model loses its context. (level 4) Where does a paged cache change this design? Expected: the capacity becomes a pool of fixed-size blocks shared by requests, so an append that needs a new block can wait or preempt instead of failing the request. Where it is taught. The GPT assembly lesson bounds generation to the context length with a sliding window, and the KV cache practice pins the capacity rule and the filled-prefix views. Read the code The assembly lesson says that swapping the activation and replacing LayerNorm with RMSNorm turns its model into the next open model family. A candidate submits this RMSNorm: python def rms_norm(x, weight, eps): mean = x.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True) var = ((x - mean) ** 2).mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True) return weight * (x - mean) / np.sqrt(var) + eps What is wrong, and what does the correct function compute? Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. This is a LayerNorm without a shift, not an RMSNorm, and it adds epsilon after the square root instead of inside it. RMSNorm does not subtract the mean. It divides the input by the root of the mean of the squares over the last axis, with epsilon inside the root, and multiplies by a learned weight. The two normalizations. Copy LayerNorm centers and scales each token vector, then applies a learned scale and shift. RMSNorm keeps the direction of the vector and only fixes its magnitude. It has no mean subtraction and no shift, which saves one reduction per token and one parameter vector per layer. The epsilon. Epsilon exists to keep the division defined when the variance or the mean square is near zero. Inside the root it bounds the denominator from below. Outside the root it does nothing for a zero variance and shifts every output by a constant, which is wrong in both cases. The practice task has one mutant for each of these placements. Over which axis. Both normalizations reduce over the last axis, the feature axis, independently for every token in every batch element. Reducing over the batch axis turns the layer into a batch statistic, which changes with batch composition and breaks single-example inference. Biased variance. LayerNorm uses the biased variance, the mean of the squared deviations over the feature count. The unbiased estimate with one fewer in the denominator is a statistics convention that does not belong here and makes the output disagree with every standard library version by a factor that depends on the width. Why the swap is safe in the assembly. The final normalization sits between the last block and the tied head, and both functions take and return the same shape. Swap the class, drop the shift parameter, and the head, the embedding and the generation loop are untouched. Plausible wrong answers. "RMSNorm is LayerNorm with the shift removed." It also removes the mean subtraction; without that difference it would not be a different layer. "Epsilon placement does not matter for normal inputs." It matters exactly for the inputs it exists for, the ones with near-zero variance. "Use the unbiased variance, it is more correct." Standard library versions use the biased form; the choice is a contract, not a statistics question. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) What does the caller's epsilon argument control, and what happens if the function ignores it? Expected: the floor on the denominator; ignoring it and using a fixed constant makes a reference comparison fail when the caller passes a different value. (level 3) Why does RMSNorm have no shift parameter? Expected: it does not center the input, so there is no mean to restore; the next linear layer's bias can absorb a shift if one is needed. (level 4) A pretrained checkpoint has LayerNorm scales and shifts and you swap in RMSNorm. What breaks? Expected: the shift has nowhere to load and the scale was learned on centered inputs, so the loaded model no longer matches the trained function. Where it is taught. The GPT assembly lesson places the final LayerNorm and names the RMSNorm swap, and the normalization practice checks both functions. Take-home The reference small GPT configuration uses a learned position embedding of shape 1024 by 768. Replace it with a sinusoidal table computed at construction time, add it to a batch of token embeddings, and tell me by how much the parameter count changes and why the model still forwards. Level 2 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Build a table with one row per position and one column per feature, where column 2i holds the sine and column 2i + 1 holds the cosine of the position divided by the base raised to 2i over the model width. Register it as a buffer, slice the first T rows at each forward and add them to the token embeddings without changing the caller's array. The table has the same shape as the learned one, so the forward pass is unchanged, and the count drops by 786,432 parameters because the table is no longer learned. The table. Copy The exponent is 2i over the width, so the frequencies fall from one down to one over the base across the columns. The columns alternate between sine and cosine; putting all sines in the first half and all cosines in the second is a different layout and does not match the reference. Positions start at zero. An odd width has no pair for its last column, so that column stays zero. The table is built once with numpy and stored as a torch buffer, so it moves to the device of the model and the add sees two tensors on the same device. Why the forward pass is unchanged. The assembly adds a position vector to each token vector before the first block. Nothing downstream knows whether that vector came from a learned table or a fixed one. The shape contract is the same, so the blocks, the final LayerNorm and the tied head run unchanged. The parameter count. The learned table holds 1024 rows of 768 values each. Removing it from the parameter list drops the unique parameter count by 786,432. The parameter counter must count unique tensors, so that the tied language model head is not counted twice, and it must not count buffers. Two mistakes to avoid. Adding the table in place with += changes the caller's embeddings, which the training loop still holds. Dividing the exponent by the width of the even part instead of the full width gives an odd width the frequencies of a narrower model. Plausible wrong answers. "Register the table as a parameter so the optimizer can refine it." Then it is a learned table again and the count does not drop. "Start positions at one so the first row is not all zeros and ones." The reference starts at zero; row zero is the code of position zero. "Use the same exponent for sine and cosine columns but a different base." Both columns of a pair share one angle; only the function differs. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why interleave sine and cosine rather than put them in two halves? Expected: a checkpoint trained with the interleaved layout expects each pair of neighbor columns to form one rotation, and the two layouts are not interchangeable. (level 2) What does the base control? Expected: the lowest frequency, and so the longest position range before the slowest columns repeat. (level 3) Which position scheme does the assembly lesson say turns this model into the next model family? Expected: a rotary scheme applied inside attention replaces the additive table and leaves the block and the head unchanged. (level 3) A fixed table has no parameters; what does the model lose? Expected: the ability to learn position features from data, in exchange for a table that extends to any length at construction. Where it is taught. The GPT assembly lesson sets this swap as an exercise and gives the parameter delta, and the sinusoidal encoding practice checks the interleaved layout. Explain the mechanism Write the one line that applies a sampling temperature to a vector of logits, then tell me what happens to the distribution as the temperature goes toward zero, equals one, and goes above one. Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Divide the logits by the temperature before the softmax. Near zero the division stretches the gaps between logits, so the largest one takes almost all the mass and sampling becomes greedy. At one the model's own distribution is used, and above one the gaps shrink, the distribution flattens, and rare tokens are drawn more often. The line. Copy The order matters in a full sampler: the generation loop reads the final position's logits, divides by the temperature, applies any top-k or top-p filter, takes the softmax, and draws one token. Three regimes. Temperature Effect on the gaps between logits Behavior Toward zero Gaps grow without bound Argmax; the same token every time Equal to one Unchanged The model's natural distribution Above one Gaps shrink Flatter distribution, more surprise, more errors Why division and not multiplication. Multiplying the logits by the temperature does the opposite of what people expect: a higher value sharpens the distribution. The practice lab has a mutant that makes this mistake, and the sign of the effect is the first thing its tests check. Reading the effect. Two measurements show what a temperature did: the probability of the top token, and the entropy of the distribution. As the temperature rises the top probability falls and the entropy rises. A sweep over temperatures on fixed logits makes both curves visible without a model in the loop. Plausible wrong answers. "Temperature scales the probabilities after the softmax." Scaling probabilities and renormalizing changes nothing; the division happens on the logits. "A higher temperature makes the model smarter." It only flattens the distribution, which trades repetition for more mistakes. "Temperature one means no sampling." It means sampling from the unchanged distribution; greedy is temperature zero or argmax. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) Why does temperature zero need a special case in code? Expected: division by zero; implement it as argmax rather than dividing. (level 2) A product wants deterministic output. Is temperature zero enough? Expected: it removes sampling randomness, but ties and numeric differences across batches can still change the argmax. (level 2) How does temperature interact with a top-p cutoff? Expected: the cutoff must run on the temperature-scaled probabilities, otherwise it cuts the distribution at temperature one and the setting does less than expected. Where it is taught. The GPT assembly lesson describes the three temperature regimes in its generation loop, and the temperature lab sweeps them on fixed logits. Take-home Given the logits of the last position, a temperature, a value of k and a seeded random generator, write the function that draws the next token. State the order of the operations, how ties are broken, and how the draw uses exactly one random number. Level 2 of 4 · about 20 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Divide the logits by the temperature, keep the k largest and set the rest to negative infinity, take the softmax, and draw one index from the result. Ties keep the lower index. The draw calls the generator once, takes the cumulative sum of the probabilities in vocabulary order, and returns the first index whose cumulative value exceeds the random number. The code. Copy The order. Temperature first, then the filter, then the softmax. The filter has to see the scaled logits, because the scale changes which tokens hold the mass when a top-p cutoff is added later. The softmax runs last so that a removed token has probability exactly zero and the kept ones renormalize. Ties. Sorting the negated logits with a stable sort keeps the lower index first among equal values. Sorting ascending and reversing the result flips that, so the higher index wins and the output differs from the reference on every tie. One random number. A seeded generator gives reproducible samples only if every call consumes the same number of draws. The function reads one uniform number, compares it with the cumulative sum, and returns the first crossing. Rounding can leave the last cumulative value a hair below one, so the fallback returns the last token with positive probability instead of failing. Do not change the input. The filter writes into a new array. Writing negative infinity into the caller's logits destroys the values that the next step, or a log, still needs. Plausible wrong answers. "Call the generator's choice function with the probabilities." It works, but it consumes draws differently across versions and breaks the one-draw contract that the tests pin. "Apply the temperature after the filter." The filter then selects tokens at temperature one and the setting changes less than intended. "Sort descending by reversing an ascending sort." Equal logits then keep the higher index, which contradicts the tie rule. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does top-k one produce? Expected: greedy decoding, the argmax every time. (level 2) Why must the filter run before the softmax and not after? Expected: zeroing probabilities after the softmax leaves a distribution that does not sum to one unless it is renormalized; masking the logits does that for free. (level 3) The assembly lesson keeps the context inside a fixed length during generation. How? Expected: when the prompt plus generated tokens exceed the context length, the oldest tokens are dropped so the active window fits. (level 3) How do you make two runs with one seed produce the same text? Expected: the same generator, one draw per step, the same tie rule and the same temperature; any extra draw shifts every later token. Where it is taught. The GPT assembly lesson describes the generation step as temperature, top-k mask, softmax and multinomial draw, and the sampling practice pins the order, the tie rule and the single draw. Debug a failure A nucleus filter is reviewed because a product team says small values of p give an empty distribution on some prompts: python def top_p_filter(logits, p): probs = softmax(logits) c = np.cumsum(probs) out = np.where(c <= p, logits, -np.inf) return out Find the two bugs and explain how the filter must interact with the temperature in the full sampler. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The cumulative sum runs in vocabulary order instead of in order of decreasing probability, so the kept set is not the most probable prefix at all. The comparison also drops the token that makes the sum reach p, which for a small p leaves nothing and yields an empty distribution. Sort by probability first, keep the shortest prefix whose sum reaches p including the crossing token, and run the filter on the temperature-scaled logits. Bug one: the order. Nucleus sampling keeps the smallest set of most probable tokens whose mass reaches p. That requires sorting by probability, highest first, before the cumulative sum. In vocabulary order the sum crosses p at an arbitrary place and the kept set is a prefix of the vocabulary, not of the ranking. Bug two: the crossing token. The token whose addition makes the cumulative sum reach p is part of the nucleus. A strict comparison excludes it. When the top token alone carries more mass than p, nothing passes and the softmax of all negative infinities is NaN. Keep the prefix up to and including the first index where the sum is at least p, and if rounding keeps the sum from ever reaching p, keep every token. The fix. Copy The stable sort on the negated probabilities keeps the lower index first on ties. Temperature comes first. The full sampler divides by the temperature, applies top-k, applies top-p to that result, and takes the softmax last. If the temperature is applied after the filters, the nucleus is chosen at temperature one and a hot or cold setting changes less than the user asked for. The assembly lesson lists nucleus sampling as the extension of its top-k generation loop, with the check that the kept probabilities sum to at least p. Plausible wrong answers. "Use a strict comparison so you never exceed p." The definition is the smallest prefix that reaches p; excluding the crossing token breaks it and can leave an empty set. "Take the cumulative sum in index order; the vocabulary is already sorted by frequency." Token ids are not sorted by probability for a given context. "Apply the temperature after the filter so the nucleus is stable." The nucleus is then chosen at the wrong temperature and the knob loses most of its effect. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the filter return logits with negative infinity rather than probabilities? Expected: so the final softmax renormalizes the kept tokens and gives removed tokens exactly zero, and so top-k and top-p compose. (level 3) What does p equal to one keep? Expected: every token, unless rounding leaves the sum short, in which case the rule to keep all tokens applies. (level 4) Top-k and top-p are both set. Which one acts first and why does it matter? Expected: top-k first, then top-p on the survivors; the reverse order can keep a different set because the nucleus mass is computed over different candidates. Where it is taught. The GPT assembly lesson adds nucleus sampling next to top-k in its exercises, and the sampling practice pins the crossing token and the order of operations. a1936: Course home / Phase 19 · Capstone Projects Training Loop and Evaluation Lesson 19.36 90 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Build a training loop that computes cross entropy loss with the correct input and target alignment for next token prediction. Configure AdamW with weight decay applied to weight tensors and not to LayerNorm or bias tensors. Implement a learning rate schedule with linear warmup and cosine decay, and read the resulting LR over time. Evaluate on a held out split with evaluate_model so the eval loss is comparable across runs. Generate a qualitative sample every K steps with generate_and_print_sample to catch divergence before the loss curve does. Persist per step loss to JSONL so you can reload, plot, and ship the training log as a deliverable. Before you start Needs : Phase 19 lessons 30 to 35 Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line A loop that does not measure is a loop that lies. This lesson builds the training loop that drives the GPT model: AdamW with weight decay split, a warmup plus cosine learning rate schedule, a calc_loss_batch helper, an evaluate_model pass on held out data, a generate_and_print_sample qualitative probe every K steps, and a JSONL log of losses you can plot after. The same skeleton trains every decoder LLM you will ever build. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Loss alignment "Shift by one" Input tokens at positions 0..T-1, target tokens at positions 1..T; cross entropy is computed on flattened shapes Decay split "Two groups" AdamW receives matrix shaped tensors with weight decay and scale or bias tensors with none Warmup "Ramp" The learning rate climbs from zero to its target over a fixed number of steps so the optimizer state can populate Eval batches "Held out batches" A fixed slice of the validation token tensor, sliced once at script start, used identically every probe Qualitative probe "Sample print" A short generation from a fixed prompt printed every K steps to catch failure modes loss alone hides The problem A training script that prints the loss but does nothing else fails three ways. It cannot tell you if the loss is decreasing for the right reason (the model could overfit the training set and never learn). It cannot tell you if a divergence is starting (the loss can spike for one step and recover, or one step and crash). It cannot tell you what the model has learned (loss is a scalar; a generated sample is a paragraph). All three failures hide unless the loop measures. The loop in this lesson measures three ways. Loss on the training batch every step. Loss on a held out batch every K steps. A generated continuation from a fixed prompt every K steps. The training log lands in JSONL so the artifact is the loop's testimony. The idea The two non-obvious pieces are the loss alignment and the AdamW decay split. Idea 1 · Loss alignment The model predicts the next token at every position. If the input batch is tokens [t0, t1, t2, t3] , the target batch must be [t1, t2, t3, t4] . Cross entropy is computed on the flat shape (batch * seq, vocab) against the flat target (batch * seq,) . Forget the shift and you train the model to predict itself, which converges to zero loss while learning nothing useful. Idea 2 · AdamW decay split Weight decay regularizes weight tensors but not normalization scales or biases. Putting decay on the LayerNorm scale slowly drives the scale to zero and breaks normalization. Putting decay on a bias is mathematically harmless but a waste of cycles. The standard split is: matrix shaped tensors (linear weights, embedding tables) get decay, anything that looks like a scale or shift does not. Idea 3 · Warmup plus cosine schedule Warmup ramps the learning rate from zero to the target over a few hundred steps so the optimizer state has time to populate. Cosine decay drops the learning rate back toward zero over the remaining steps so the final phase fine tunes the weights at a small step size. The combination is the most common schedule in open weights LLM training because it removes most of the brittle moments in the first thousand steps and the last thousand steps. Idea 4 · Held out evaluation evaluate_model runs a fixed number of batches from the validation split, accumulates loss, divides by the batch count, and returns. No gradient. No dropout. The number is reproducible across runs given the same seed and the same split. Reporting the held out loss next to the training loss is how you spot overfitting. Idea 5 · Qualitative sampling as an early signal A model whose training loss drops nicely but whose generated samples are all the same token is broken. A model whose loss curve looks flat but whose generated samples sharpen into coherent words is learning. The qualitative probe runs faster than reading the full curve and catches modes the scalar misses. Build it code/main.py implements: make_batches(token_ids, batch_size, context_length) which slices a long token tensor into input and target pairs. calc_loss_batch(model, inputs, targets) which forwards, flattens, and returns the scalar cross entropy. evaluate_model(model, val_loader, max_batches) which iterates a fixed number of validation batches with no grad and returns the mean loss. generate_and_print_sample(model, prompt, max_new_tokens) which runs the lesson 35 generation function on a fixed prompt and prints the result. build_param_groups(model, weight_decay) which produces the two-group AdamW parameter list. cosine_with_warmup(step, warmup_steps, total_steps, max_lr, min_lr) which returns the LR at a given step. train(...) which runs the loop, persists outputs/losses.jsonl , and prints the eval loss and a sample every eval_every steps. A demo that trains a tiny model on synthetic data for a small number of steps, writes a JSONL log, and prints the eval loss and a sample at the probe points. The demo runs in well under a minute on CPU. Run it: Copy Output: per step loss line, eval loss every probe step, a generated sample every probe step, and a final outputs/losses.jsonl you can load with json.loads per line. Stack torch for autograd, optimizer, and modules. main.py reimplements the lesson 35 GPTModel and supporting modules locally. Production patterns in the wild Three patterns turn the textbook loop into something you can leave running overnight. Gradient norm clipping is non negotiable. A bad batch (anomalous data, an LR spike, a numerical edge case) produces a huge gradient that wipes out hours of training. torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(params, max_norm=1.0) after backward and before step keeps the optimizer in a safe range. The clipping value is a free parameter; one is the default that survives most setups. Resumable JSONL logging, not pickled state. Per step loss records as {"step": int, "train_loss": float, "lr": float} lines in JSONL are durable: any crash leaves a readable artifact, you can grep, you can plot with thirty lines of Python, and you can resume training by reading the last step. Pickled state ties you to the exact module layout that produced the file, which is brittle across refactors. Eval batches drawn from a fixed slice. The validation tokens get sliced into batches at script start, not on the fly. Reproducibility depends on the eval batches being identical from run to run; otherwise comparing eval loss between two runs measures the batch shuffle as much as the model. Use it: the same idea with real libraries The loop in this lesson is the same skeleton that trains a 124M model on real data. Swap the synthetic token tensor for a datasets -style loader and the loop runs unchanged. The JSONL log is the deliverable that turns a training run into evidence. The next lesson uses one to compare a freshly trained checkpoint with a pretrained one. The qualitative sample probe is the catch-all that scalar loss cannot replace. Exercises Add weight_decay_groups() unit tests that confirm scale and bias parameters land in the no decay group and linear and embedding weights land in the decay group. Replace synthetic random tokens with bytes from a small text file so the demo trains on something legible. Verify the generated sample uses characters present in the file. Add a min_lr floor of 10 percent of max_lr to the cosine schedule and re-plot. Save a checkpoint every eval_every steps in addition to the JSONL log. Add a resume_from flag that reloads model state and optimizer state. Log per step throughput (tokens per second) next to the loss and confirm it stays in a steady band. Practice and reference One-page references from the source repository that cover this lesson, with commands, defaults and fixes in one place. TL Cheat sheet · Train and Load a GPT from Scratch Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Read the code A hand-written optimizer step is labeled AdamW. Review it: python def adam_step(params, grad, m, v, t, lr, beta1, beta2, eps, weight_decay): grad = grad + weight_decay * params m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * grad v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * grad * grad m_hat = m / (1 - beta1 ** t) v_hat = v / (1 - beta2 ** t) return params - lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps), m, v Is this AdamW? What changes, and why does it matter for a language model? Level 2 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. No, this is Adam with an L2 penalty folded into the gradient. AdamW applies the decay directly to the parameters, scaled by the learning rate, outside the adaptive step. When the penalty goes through the gradient it is divided by the second-moment estimate, so parameters with large gradients get almost no decay and the regularization becomes uneven across the model. The corrected step. Copy The decay term is added to the update, not to the gradient. It never passes through the moment estimates. What the difference changes. Adam normalizes every coordinate by its running gradient magnitude. A penalty that enters as part of the gradient is normalized too, so a weight with a large, noisy gradient is barely decayed while a weight with a tiny gradient is decayed hard. Decoupled decay shrinks every weight by the same fraction per step, which is what the regularizer was meant to do. Language model recipes use the decoupled form, and the loop in the training lesson builds its parameter groups around it. Three more details the practice pins. The step counter starts at one. With t = 0 the bias correction divides by zero, and with t + 1 the first step acts as the second. Epsilon sits outside the square root. Inside it, tiny gradients give a much smaller step than intended. The function returns new state arrays. Updating m and v in place changes the caller's state and breaks checkpoint resume. Where the decay should not go. Even with the correct form, the decay belongs on matrix-shaped weights only. Normalization scales and biases get no decay, which is the subject of the parameter group split. Plausible wrong answers. "L2 and weight decay are the same thing." They coincide for plain gradient descent, not for an adaptive optimizer that normalizes the gradient. "Put epsilon inside the square root for stability." It changes the step size for small gradients; the reference form adds it after the root. "Start the step counter at zero like an index." The bias correction then divides by zero on the first step. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) What does the bias correction fix in the first steps? Expected: the moment estimates start at zero and are biased low early; dividing by 1 - beta**t rescales them. (level 2) Why return new arrays instead of updating in place? Expected: a pure function keeps the caller's state intact, so a step can be retried or compared and a checkpoint stays consistent. (level 3) How does the learning rate schedule interact with decoupled decay? Expected: the decay is multiplied by the current learning rate, so warmup and cosine decay also scale the regularization over training. Where it is taught. The training loop lesson configures AdamW with its decay split, the cosine schedule lesson pairs it with warmup and decay, and the Adam practice checks the decoupled form. Take-home Write a training loop for a table of next-character logits: one row per context character, one column per next character. Train it with gradient descent on a text, under a fixed step budget and a seeded generator, until its held-out NLL is lower than a model that ignores the context. Tell me what the held-out check must look like for the comparison to mean anything. Level 3 of 4 · about 30 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Build the pairs so that the current character is the context and the following character is the target, compute the log-softmax over each row, and descend the mean of the negative target log-probabilities over the training pairs within the step budget. The held-out check scores a fixed split that training never saw, with the same loss definition for the bigram and the unigram baseline, and the model only passes when its held-out value is lower than the baseline's. Reproducibility comes from drawing the initial table from the generator that the caller passes, not from a global one. The model and the loop. Copy The pair direction is the whole model: context first, target second. Reversing them trains a model that predicts the previous character, and counting each next character as its own context trains nothing about what follows what. The gradient sign. The update subtracts the gradient. Adding it climbs the loss, which is visible on the first evaluation, and is the first mutant the practice checks. The held-out check. The loop lesson's rule is that evaluation runs on a fixed held-out slice with no gradient, and the number must be comparable across runs. For this task that means three things. The split is fixed before training and never touched by the loop. The unigram baseline, which assigns each character its frequency in the training text regardless of context, is scored on the same held-out characters with the same loss definition. The bigram passes only when its held-out value is strictly lower. A model that wins on the training text and not on the held-out text has memorized the training text. The budget. A step budget is part of the contract. A loop that runs more steps than the budget may reach the target but fails the task, and in a real run it is the difference between a planned job and an overrun. Plausible wrong answers. "Evaluate on the training text to save time." The comparison then measures memorization and the baseline comparison means nothing. "Draw the initial table from the global random state." Two runs with one seed then differ, and the test for reproducibility fails. "Train until the loss stops improving." The budget is part of the contract and an open-ended loop hides a slow or stuck run. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why return log-probabilities and not raw logits from the scoring function? Expected: the loss needs a normalized distribution per row; raw logits are not comparable across contexts. (level 3) The model beats the baseline on training text and loses on held-out text. What happened? Expected: it memorized the training pairs; a held-out split exists to catch exactly that. (level 4) How does this toy loop map onto the full training loop in the lesson? Expected: the pair construction is the shift-by-one, the row lookup is the forward, the held-out check is the fixed evaluation, and the budget is the step count of the schedule. Where it is taught. The training loop lesson sets the rules for held-out evaluation and loss alignment, and the character bigram practice trains the smallest model under a step budget. Read the code A training run looks healthy for the first few thousand steps, then the loss starts to climb and samples degrade. The optimizer is built with one parameter group: python optimizer = AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay) Write the function that builds the parameter groups correctly and explain which tensors must be excluded from decay and why. Level 3 of 4 · about 10 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Decay belongs on matrix-shaped tensors, which are the linear weights and the embedding tables, and not on normalization scales or biases. A decayed LayerNorm scale drifts toward zero over thousands of steps until normalization stops working, which matches the late failure. Split the parameters by shape into a decay group and a no-decay group and pass both to the optimizer. The split. Copy A two-dimensional or larger tensor is a weight matrix or an embedding table. A one-dimensional tensor is a scale or a shift, which includes LayerNorm parameters and every bias. The rule by dimension is simple and matches the standard recipe. Why decay on a scale is harmful. Weight decay pulls every decayed parameter toward zero on every step. A linear weight has gradient pressure in many directions and the pull acts as regularization. A LayerNorm scale has one job, to set the magnitude of the normalized activations, and a steady pull toward zero shrinks the residual stream of every block until the signal is too small for the layers that follow. The effect accumulates slowly, which is why the run looks fine at first. Why decay on a bias is waste. Decaying a bias is mathematically harmless but spends update cycles on a parameter that regularization does not need to control. The split excludes it along with the scales. How to test the split. A unit test can walk the named parameters and assert that each scale and bias landed in the no-decay group and each linear and embedding weight landed in the decay group. The loop lesson lists exactly this test as its first exercise. Plausible wrong answers. "Weight decay applies to all weights by definition." The standard recipe excludes normalization and bias tensors; applying it everywhere breaks normalization over time. "Decide by parameter name, excluding anything called bias." Names vary across implementations; the dimension rule is robust. "Lower the weight decay until the run is stable." A smaller value slows the drift but keeps the pull on the scales. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) The language model head is tied to the token embedding. Which group is it in, and how many times? Expected: once, in the decay group, because it is the same tensor as the embedding table. (level 3) A model uses RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm. Does the rule change? Expected: no; the RMSNorm weight is one-dimensional and stays out of the decay group. (level 4) Why does the problem appear late rather than at the start of training? Expected: the decay shrinks the scale by a small fraction per step, so the damage compounds over thousands of steps before the activations become too small. Where it is taught. The training loop lesson defines the two-group AdamW split and the test for it, and the Adam practice implements the decoupled decay the groups feed into. Read the code Two evaluation runs on the same checkpoint and the same fixed validation batches report different losses. The dropout layer is: python def dropout_forward(x, p, rng, training): mask = rng.random(x.shape) >= p if training: return x * mask / (1 - p), mask return x * (1 - p), mask Find every problem with the inference path and explain what the evaluation function expects. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Inverted dropout scales the kept units during training so that inference is the identity, but this inference path multiplies the input by one minus p, which belongs to the non-inverted form and shrinks every activation. It also draws from the generator in inference mode, which changes every later random number in the run, such as the next training mask and the next probe sample. Inference must return the input unchanged and must not touch the generator. The two bugs. Scaling at inference. With inverted dropout the division by one minus p happens in training, so the expected activation already matches the no-dropout value. Scaling again at inference halves the signal at a rate of one half and damages every layer that follows. Drawing at inference. The mask is sampled before the branch. Evaluation consumes random numbers, so the generation sample after the probe, and any later training step, sees a different stream than a run without the probe. The fix. Copy At inference the layer returns a copy of the input and a mask that is true everywhere, and it does not draw. Keep an entry when the random number is at or above p, so the complement rule is right, and divide the kept entries by one minus p. The backward pass multiplies the incoming gradient by the same mask and divides by the same factor. What evaluation expects. The training loop's evaluation function runs a fixed number of validation batches with no gradient and no dropout, and the number must be reproducible across runs given the same seed and split. Any randomness inside the model during that pass breaks the comparison between two runs, because the difference measures the random stream rather than the model. The assembly lesson's model has an embedding dropout of 0.1, so this layer sits in the path of every evaluation. Plausible wrong answers. "Scale down at inference as the original dropout paper did." That form skips the scaling in training; mixing the two forms shrinks the activations. "Re-seed the generator before every evaluation." It hides the extra draws but still changes the training stream afterwards; the inference path should not draw at all. "Keep an entry when the random number is below p." That keeps a fraction p and drops the rest, the complement of the intended mask. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why divide by one minus p during training at all? Expected: so the expected value of each activation is the same with and without the mask, which makes inference the identity. (level 2) Why must the backward pass use the same mask? Expected: the gradient must flow only through the units that were kept, with the same scale, otherwise the gradient does not match the forward computation. (level 3) The evaluation is reproducible but still differs from a run that skipped the probe. What else draws? Expected: the sampled generation at the probe step consumes draws from the shared generator; give the probe its own generator. Where it is taught. The training loop lesson requires that evaluation skip gradients and dropout, the GPT assembly lesson places the embedding dropout, and the inverted dropout practice checks the identity at inference. Read the code A colleague reports that their language model reaches a loss near zero very early in training, and the generated samples are garbage. The batch code is: python def calc_loss_batch(model, tokens): logits = model(tokens) return cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, logits.shape[-1]), tokens.reshape(-1)) What went wrong, and what does the correct version look like? Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The targets are the inputs, so the model learns to predict the token it was just given, which is trivial and converges to zero loss while learning nothing. The target at position t must be the input at position t + 1 . Slice the inputs to drop the last token and the targets to drop the first, then flatten both to batch times time by vocabulary and batch times time. The alignment. For input tokens t0, t1, t2, t3 the targets are t1, t2, t3, t4 . Every position predicts the next token, which is why one training example covers the context length plus one raw id. The batch maker produces the two tensors already shifted, or the loss function shifts them: Copy with inputs = window[:-1] and targets = window[1:] . Why the flatten. Cross-entropy takes a matrix of rows by classes and a vector of class ids. Flattening batch and time into one axis turns the three-dimensional logits into that matrix and the two-dimensional targets into that vector, and the mean over rows is the mean over every predicted position. Flattening is not the bug; the missing shift is. Why the symptom is a near-zero loss. Predicting the current token from the current token needs only an identity through the embedding and the output head, which a tied head gives for free. The loss collapses, the eval loss collapses too, and only the qualitative sample shows that nothing was learned. That is why the training loop prints a generated continuation at every probe step and not only the two losses. The numeric side. The practice task also checks that the cross-entropy is computed from a shifted softmax, so that large logits do not overflow, and that the loss is the mean over examples rather than the sum. Plausible wrong answers. "The learning rate is too high." A high learning rate diverges or oscillates; a collapse to zero loss points at a leak in the objective. "Flattening mixes the batch and time axes." The flatten is required; the rows are independent predictions and their order does not matter to the mean. "The model overfits the training set." Overfitting shows a gap between training and validation loss; here both collapse. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Which signal in the training loop catches this bug first? Expected: the generated sample at the probe step; both losses look excellent. (level 2) The validation loss is also near zero. Why does held-out data not catch it? Expected: the target leak is in the loss definition, which is the same on both splits. (level 3) How does the sliding-window dataset avoid this at the source? Expected: it returns a window of context length plus one and splits it into input and target in the dataset itself, so the loop never sees unshifted pairs. (level 3) Your supervised fine-tuning data masks the instruction tokens. Where does the mask go relative to the shift? Expected: after the shift, so the ignored positions line up with the shifted targets. Where it is taught. The training loop lesson explains the loss alignment and the qualitative probe, and the softmax and cross-entropy practice checks the batched loss. Map each pretrained parameter name onto a parameter inside the lesson 35 GPT model. Handle the two name conventions that differ between published GPT-2 weights and the model in this track: wte/wpe/h.N.attn.c_attn/c_proj and mlp.c_fc/c_proj versus the locally named tok_embed/pos_embed/blocks.N.attn.qkv/out_proj and mlp.fc1/fc2 . Before you start Needs : Phase 19 lessons 30 to 36 Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Training a 124 million parameter model from scratch is a budget decision; loading a published checkpoint is a Tuesday. This lesson loads pretrained GPT-2 style weights from a safetensors file into the exact architecture from lesson 35, walks the parameter name mapping piece by piece, and sanity generates a continuation to prove the load worked. No network, no third party loaders, no opaque magic. Terms you'll hear Term What people say What it actually means Name map "Key remapping" The function from pretrained tensor names to local parameter names; usually a literal dict with one entry per layer index expanded over a loop Shape mismatch "Bad shape" The pretrained tensor exists under the mapped name but its dimensions disagree with the local parameter; the loader refuses to assign and logs the pair Transpose-on-load "Conv1d layout" Published GPT-2 stores attention and MLP projections in the transpose of what nn.Linear expects; the loader transposes during assignment Weight tying alias "Shared LM head" Setting model.lm_head.weight = model.tok_embed.weight so the head and embedding share storage; the head is not in the file because of this Load report "Coverage summary" A small dataclass that tracks loaded, missing, unexpected, and shape_mismatch lists; printing it is how you tell whether the load succeeded The problem Published weights are not packaged for your architecture. They carry the names the original implementation used. The pretrained file has transformer.h.0.attn.c_attn.weight of shape (2304, 768) ; your model expects blocks.0.attn.qkv.weight of shape (2304, 768) (which is the same matrix in a different layout convention) or your model uses nn.Linear which stores the matrix transposed. The same parameter shows up with three subtly different identities (name, shape, byte layout) and the loader has to reconcile all three. A loader that copies blindly puts the right tensor in the wrong place and you get a model that generates nonsense. A loader that refuses to copy when the shape differs but logs nothing leaves you guessing which tensor failed to land. The loader in this lesson is explicit: every assignment is logged, every shape is checked, and a LoadReport summarizes hits, misses, and shape mismatches so you can read what happened. The idea The name mapper is just a function from string to string. The shape check is one if. The assignment happens inside torch.no_grad() so autograd does not track the load. The report holds the outcome of every name. Idea 1 · The GPT-2 naming convention Published GPT-2 weights live under names like: Pretrained name Shape Meaning wte.weight (50257, 768) Token embedding wpe.weight (1024, 768) Position embedding h.N.ln_1.weight (768,) LayerNorm 1 scale at block N h.N.ln_1.bias (768,) LayerNorm 1 shift at block N h.N.attn.c_attn.weight (768, 2304) Fused QKV linear weight h.N.attn.c_attn.bias (2304,) Fused QKV linear bias h.N.attn.c_proj.weight (768, 768) Attention output projection h.N.attn.c_proj.bias (768,) Attention output projection bias h.N.ln_2.weight (768,) LayerNorm 2 scale h.N.ln_2.bias (768,) LayerNorm 2 shift h.N.mlp.c_fc.weight (768, 3072) MLP fc1 weight h.N.mlp.c_fc.bias (3072,) MLP fc1 bias h.N.mlp.c_proj.weight (3072, 768) MLP fc2 weight h.N.mlp.c_proj.bias (768,) MLP fc2 bias ln_f.weight (768,) Final LayerNorm scale ln_f.bias (768,) Final LayerNorm shift Two surprises to plan for. The c_attn , c_proj , c_fc linears are stored with the matrix transposed relative to what nn.Linear.weight expects. The loader transposes during assignment. The LM head is not in the file at all; the model relies on weight tying with wte , so the head is set by aliasing once wte lands. Idea 2 · The local naming convention The model in this track uses descriptive names: Local name Meaning tok_embed.weight Token embedding pos_embed.weight Position embedding blocks.N.ln1.scale LayerNorm 1 scale at block N blocks.N.ln1.shift LayerNorm 1 shift blocks.N.attn.qkv.weight Fused QKV blocks.N.attn.qkv.bias Fused QKV bias blocks.N.attn.out_proj.weight Attention output projection blocks.N.attn.out_proj.bias Output projection bias blocks.N.ln2.scale LayerNorm 2 scale blocks.N.ln2.shift LayerNorm 2 shift blocks.N.mlp.fc1.weight MLP fc1 blocks.N.mlp.fc1.bias MLP fc1 bias blocks.N.mlp.fc2.weight MLP fc2 blocks.N.mlp.fc2.bias MLP fc2 bias final_ln.scale Final LayerNorm scale final_ln.shift Final LayerNorm shift The mapping is a fixed function. The lesson ships it as a dict that the loader iterates. Idea 3 · The stub fixture Real GPT-2 weights are 0.5 GB. The demo does not download them; it generates a small safetensors fixture at first run, with the exact GPT-2 naming convention and shapes appropriate to a 12-block model at d_model 192 instead of 768. The fixture has the right structure to exercise every code path in the loader. Swap the fixture for the real file and the loader works without modification. Build it code/main.py implements: A small replica of the lesson 35 GPTModel so this lesson is self contained. make_pretrained_to_local(num_layers) which expands the per-layer entries. load_safetensors(model, path) which iterates names, maps them, checks shape, transposes the conv1d-style weights, and assigns under torch.no_grad() . Returns a LoadReport . make_stub_safetensors(path, cfg) which generates a fixture file with the exact pretrained naming convention. A demo that creates outputs/gpt2-stub.safetensors on first run, builds a fresh model, captures one generated continuation from random init, loads the stub, captures another continuation, prints both, and verifies the two are different (the load actually changed the model). Run it: Copy Output: the fixture path, a per-name load log, a LoadReport summary, a continuation before the load, a continuation after the load, and a shape mismatch on a single intentionally bad tensor injected into the fixture so the failure path is exercised. Stack safetensors for the on disk format and a streaming reader. torch for the model and the assignment math. No transformers , no huggingface_hub , no network calls. Production patterns in the wild Three patterns make the loader survive contact with weights you did not create. Always validate the file before any assignment. Open the file, list every tensor name with its dtype and shape, run the full mapping with shape checks, and only on success start assigning. Half-loaded models are silent failure machines. Log every assignment with the source name and the destination name. When something looks wrong, the log tells you which tensor landed where; the alternative is reading hexdumps. The LoadReport dataclass in this lesson tracks loaded , missing , unexpected , and shape_mismatch lists and prints a summary at the end. The LM head is a weight tying alias, not a separate copy. Setting model.lm_head.weight = model.tok_embed.weight after loading tok_embed is the canonical pattern. Copying the embedding matrix into a fresh lm_head.weight parameter breaks tying and quietly doubles your parameter count. Use it: the same idea with real libraries The loader works for any safetensors file that uses the pretrained naming convention. Real GPT-2 files (small / medium / large / xl) work without code changes; only the model config differs. The same pattern extends to LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen weights once you update the name map. The shape checks and the report stay identical. Sanity generation after a load is a quick gate: if the post-load samples look like the pre-load samples, the load did not change the model, which means the mapping silently missed every tensor. Plug the loader into the lesson 35 generation function and produce two side by side samples: one from random init, one from the loaded fixture. Add an export path: write the current model state into a fresh safetensors file using the pretrained naming convention. Round trip the loader and confirm the report has zero shape mismatches. a1938: Course home / Phase 19 · Capstone Projects Capstone Lesson 38: Classifier Fine-Tuning by Head Swap Lesson 19.38 90 min Build Completed Lesson goals What you will be able to do Replace a language-model head with a classification head without re-initialising the body. Implement two training regimes: frozen body (head-only) and full fine-tuning, sharing one training loop. Build a tokeniser-aware data pipeline that pads, masks padding, and pools attention output. Compute precision, recall, F1, and a confusion matrix from raw logits. Reason about the trade-off between parameter count, training time, and head-room. Before you start Needs : Phase 19 lessons 30-37 (NLP LLM track: tokenizer, embedding table, attention block, transformer body, pre-training loop, checkpointing, generation, perplexity) Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python (torch, numpy). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Track B's first capstone. A pretrained language model is a stack of self-attention blocks ending in a token-prediction head. When you want spam vs ham, the head is wrong but the body is mostly right. This lesson rips the head off, glues a two-class linear layer onto the pooled representation, and trains the classifier two different ways: final-layer only, and full fine-tuning. The eval is precision, recall, and F1 on a held-out split. You learn what each strategy buys you and what it costs. The problem You pre-trained a small transformer on a generic corpus. The output head projects the last hidden state to a 1000-token vocabulary. You now have 800 SMS messages labelled spam or ham and you want a binary classifier. Three options exist. The wrong option is to train a fresh classifier from scratch on 800 examples. The body of the pretrained model already encodes useful structure: word identity, position, simple co-occurrence. Throwing it away wastes the compute that built it. The two right options are head swap with the body frozen, and head swap with the body trainable. Head-only training is fast, almost free in memory, and rarely overfits with this little data. Full fine-tuning is slower, can overfit on small data, but reaches higher accuracy when the downstream domain drifts from the pretraining corpus. This lesson builds both, so you can compare them on the same fixture. The idea The model is a function f_theta(tokens) -> hidden_states . The head is a function g_phi(hidden) -> logits . Swapping heads means keeping theta and replacing g_phi . The body's parameters are the expensive part. The head is a single linear layer. Two trainable parameter sets matter: theta (the body): tens of thousands of weights per attention block. phi (the head): hidden_dim * num_classes weights plus a bias. In head-only training you compute gradients against phi and zero them against theta . PyTorch lets you do this by setting requires_grad=False on body parameters. The optimiser then sees only the head and the body stays frozen. In full fine-tuning you let gradients flow back through the whole stack. The body's weights drift to fit the classification objective. The risk is catastrophic forgetting on small data: the body's pretraining gets washed out by overfitting noise. The Pooling Question A classifier needs one vector per sequence, not one vector per token. Three common choices: Mean pool : average the hidden states across the sequence, weighted by the attention mask. CLS pool : prepend a special token and use only its output. This is what BERT does. Last-token pool : use the last non-padding token. This is what GPT-class classifiers do. This lesson uses mean pooling with explicit attention-mask weighting. It is the simplest, gives a stable signal across sequence lengths, and does not require pretraining a CLS token. The Data Eight hundred SMS messages, balanced 400 spam and 400 ham, are generated deterministically in code/main.py . The generator uses a fixed seed, picks templates and substitutes slot fillers, and emits messages between 5 and 25 tokens long. Real datasets have noise this fixture does not. The point of the fixture is reproducibility. The data splits 80/20: 640 train, 160 test. Splits are stratified so the test set keeps the 50/50 balance. A held-out set with a known balance lets precision and recall be read as honest numbers. The Metrics Binary classification with class 1 as the positive class (spam). Counts are: TP : predicted spam, was spam. FP : predicted spam, was ham. FN : predicted ham, was spam. TN : predicted ham, was ham. The three headline metrics: precision = TP / (TP + FP) . Of the messages flagged spam, what fraction actually are? recall = TP / (TP + FN) . Of the actual spam, what fraction did the model flag? F1 = 2 * P * R / (P + R) . The harmonic mean of the two. A confusion matrix prints the four counts as a 2x2 grid. The demo writes this to stdout for both training regimes. Architecture The body is a deliberately tiny transformer: vocab 260, hidden 64, 4 heads, 2 blocks, max sequence 32. It is small enough to train both regimes to convergence inside ninety seconds on CPU. It is not pretrained in the lesson; instead, the pretrain_quick helper does five epochs of LM training on the same fixture's text to give the body a non-trivial starting point. This keeps the lesson self-contained. What you will build The implementation is one main.py plus one test module ( code/tests/test_main.py ). ByteTokenizer : maps bytes to ids, reserves a pad id. Block : a transformer block with multi-head attention and a feed-forward layer. Pre-norm. LMBody : token + position embeddings plus a stack of blocks. Returns hidden states. MeanPool : mask-weighted average over the sequence axis. Classifier : body, pool, linear head. The body is the same instance across regimes. freeze_body and unfreeze_body : toggle requires_grad on body parameters. train_classifier : one shared loop. Accepts the model and an optimiser configured for whichever parameter group is trainable. evaluate : runs the test set and returns Metrics(precision, recall, f1, confusion) . run_demo : pretrains the body briefly, then trains and evaluates head-only, then full, prints both reports, and exits zero. Why the comparison matters The head-only regime usually trains faster and underfits more gracefully. On this fixture you typically see precision near 0.9 and recall near 0.85 after twenty epochs of head-only training. Full fine-tuning takes about three times longer and lands within a couple of points either way, depending on the random seed. The lesson does not pick a winner. It teaches you to read the numbers and the cost. On 800 examples and a tiny body, head-only is the right call. On 80,000 examples and a bigger body, full fine-tuning starts to pay off. The contract you take from this lesson is the API: the same train_classifier function handles both, and the toggle is one call. Stretch goals Add a third regime that unfreezes only the last block. This is sometimes called partial fine-tuning. It costs less than full FT and learns more than head-only. Add a learning-rate scheduler. A cosine schedule on the head plus a smaller constant rate on the body is a common production setup. Replace mean pooling with a learned attention pool: a small attention layer with one learned query. This often beats mean pool on longer sequences. The implementation gives you the hooks. The tests pin the contract. The numbers are yours to push. Do you train only a new classification head, or do you update every weight? Defend the choice. Level 1 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Swap the language-model head for a two-class linear layer and start with the body frozen. Head-only training is fast, costs almost no memory, and rarely overfits on this little data. Unfreeze the body only when the frozen run leaves accuracy on the table and the domain is far from the pretraining text. Two regimes, one loop. The body maps tokens to hidden states and stays as it is. The head maps a pooled hidden state to two logits and is new. Head-only training sets requires_grad=False on the body, so the optimizer sees only the head. Full fine-tuning lets the gradient flow through the whole stack, and the body drifts toward the classification objective. What each one buys. On the fixture in the capstone lesson, head-only training reached a precision near 0.9 and a recall near 0.85 after twenty epochs. Full fine-tuning took about three times longer and landed within a couple of points either way, depending on the seed. With 800 examples the body has little to learn from the labels, and a lot to forget. Pooling. A classifier needs one vector per sequence. Mean pooling weighted by the attention mask is the simplest choice and gives a stable signal across lengths. A CLS token needs pretraining of that token. Last-token pooling is what decoder-style classifiers use. Read the numbers, not one accuracy. Report precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix on a held-out split with a known balance. On 80,000 examples and a larger body, the body has enough signal to move without overfitting, and a domain shift can justify the cost. A middle path unfreezes only the last block. Plausible wrong answers. "Train a fresh classifier from scratch, the model is small anyway." The pretrained body already encodes word identity, position and co-occurrence; a new model from 800 examples throws that away. "Updating every weight is always more accurate, so do it." On 800 examples it lands within a couple of points of the frozen run and costs about three times the training time, with a real risk of overfitting. "Report accuracy, the classes are balanced." Precision and recall tell you which error you make, and the confusion matrix shows the counts behind the score. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does requires_grad=False on the body do to the optimizer? Expected: the optimizer receives only the head parameters, so the body weights never change. (level 2) Why mean pooling and not the last hidden state? Expected: mean pooling with the mask is stable across lengths and needs no special token; last-token pooling suits decoder models that saw that pattern. (level 2) Why keep the test split stratified? Expected: a known class balance lets you read precision and recall as honest numbers. (level 3) The full update scores lower than the frozen run on this data. What happened? Expected: the body overfit the small set and lost pretrained structure; lower the body learning rate, unfreeze fewer blocks, or stay with the head. Where it is taught. The classifier fine-tuning capstone builds both regimes on one training loop and reads precision, recall and F1 for each. Weigh a trade-off You have a small pretrained language model and 800 labeled text messages, half spam and half not. Design the classifier: what you keep, what you replace, which of two training regimes you choose, how you split and evaluate, and when the other regime would win. Level 2 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Keep the pretrained body and replace the vocabulary head with a linear layer to two classes over a mean-pooled, mask-weighted sequence vector. With 800 examples, train the head only with the body frozen: it is fast, light on memory and rarely overfits, and on this fixture it reaches about 0.9 precision and 0.85 recall after twenty epochs. Full fine-tuning takes about three times longer and lands within a couple of points either way; it starts to pay off at the scale of 80,000 examples or when the domain drifts far from the pretraining text. What to keep and replace. The body already encodes word identity, position and co-occurrence. Training a fresh classifier from scratch on 800 examples throws that away. The head is the wrong part: it projects to the vocabulary. Replace it with one linear layer from the hidden width to two logits over a pooled vector, and train with cross-entropy against the label. Pooling. A classifier needs one vector per message. Mean pooling weighted by the attention mask is the simplest stable choice across lengths and needs no special token. The alternatives are a leading class token, which the body would have to be pretrained with, and the last non-padding token, which decoder-style classifiers use. Two regimes, one loop. Regime Trainable set Cost Risk Head only The linear head Fast, almost free in memory Underfits when the domain is far from pretraining Full fine-tuning Head and body About three times longer Overfits and forgets on small data Both run through the same training function; the toggle flips requires_grad on the body parameters, so the optimizer sees only the head in the first regime. Data and evaluation. Split 80/20, stratified so the test set keeps the 50/50 balance: 640 train, 160 test. Report precision, recall and F1 for the spam class with the confusion matrix, so the numbers can be read as honest estimates. The fixture is balanced and generated, so real data will be noisier. The decision. On 800 examples and a tiny body, head only is the right call. On 80,000 examples and a bigger body, full fine-tuning starts to win. A middle path unfreezes only the last block, which costs less than full tuning and learns more than the head alone. The contract is the API, not the winner: one training function, one toggle. Plausible wrong answers. "Train a small classifier from scratch; the model is tiny anyway." That wastes the pretraining and 800 examples are too few to learn the language from zero. "Always fine-tune everything for the best accuracy." On small data full tuning overfits and forgets, for a result within a couple of points of the head alone at three times the cost. "Use the last token's hidden state without a mask." Padded sequences then pool a padding position; the mask must select the last real token or weight the mean. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the frozen body rarely overfit here? Expected: only the head's few parameters move, so the model cannot memorize 640 examples through the body. (level 2) Why stratify the split? Expected: so the test set keeps the class balance and precision and recall mean what they say. (level 3) Precision matters more than recall for this product. What changes in the design? Expected: the decision threshold on the spam logit, chosen on a validation split held out from the 640 training messages to trade recall for precision, so the 160 test messages stay untouched for the final numbers; the training regime stays the same. (level 3) The messages are in a domain the body never saw. Which regime and why? Expected: full or partial fine-tuning, because the frozen features do not carry the domain and the head alone underfits. Where it is taught. The classifier fine-tuning lesson builds both regimes on the 800-message fixture and compares their precision, recall and cost. Build a collate function that masks instruction tokens so cross-entropy only counts response tokens. Train a tiny transformer body under the SFT objective and watch the eval metric move. Implement greedy and temperature-sampled generation that respects the response-start boundary. Compute held-out exact-match on generated completions. Before you start Needs : Phase 19 lessons 30-37 (NLP LLM track: tokenizer, embedding table, attention block, transformer body, pre-training loop, checkpointing, generation, perplexity) Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python (torch, numpy). The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A pretrained base model can extend a sequence but cannot follow an instruction. Supervised fine-tuning is the smallest change that fixes this: feed the model paired examples of an instruction and a desired response, and train the body to predict the response tokens. The trick is that you only want the loss to count the response, not the instruction. This lesson builds an Alpaca-style SFT loop with a custom collate function that masks instruction tokens with ignore_index=-100 , trains on 200 instruction-response pairs, and e The problem A base model trained on next-token prediction has no idea what an instruction is. Show it the string "What is the capital of France?" and it will continue the question or invent a new sentence. The model has the language but not the format contract. The SFT contract is a string template. Every training example becomes a single sequence with three regions: Copy The boundary tokens are special tokens reserved at training time. The model learns that everything after <RESP> is the response and the response is what gets graded. The base model's next-token objective still applies; it is just trained on a corpus where every example has this shape. But there is a catch. If you feed the entire sequence to a vanilla cross-entropy loss, you are training the model to also predict the instruction tokens. The instruction is given. You want zero gradient on those positions. The fix is the mask. The idea ignore_index is a feature of torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy . Any target position equal to ignore_index contributes zero loss and zero gradient. The convention in PyTorch is -100 . The collate function builds two tensors per example: input_ids (the full sequence) and labels (a copy of input_ids with the instruction positions overwritten by -100 ). The model sees the whole sequence during the forward pass; attention can attend to the instruction. The loss only counts response tokens. This is exactly what you want: condition on the instruction, predict the response. The Data Two hundred instruction-response pairs are generated deterministically in main.py . They cover six task types: factual single-shot (capital of X) arithmetic list extraction one-sentence summary code (print, sort) definition Each task has a templated instruction and a deterministic response. This is intentionally simple. Exact-match is brittle, and the lesson uses a fixture where the right answer is one specific string. Real SFT datasets need fuzzy metrics; the principle is identical. Splits are 160 train, 40 test. The test set covers all six task types so per-category exact-match can be reported. Tokenisation and Padding The tokeniser is byte-level with three reserved specials: INST_ID = 256 : marks the start of the instruction region. RESP_ID = 257 : marks the boundary between instruction and response. PAD_ID = 258 : padding for variable-length batches. The sequence is [INST] inst_bytes [RESP] resp_bytes [PAD]* . The collate function: Tokenises each example. Pads every example in the batch to the longest sequence in the batch. Builds labels = input_ids shifted by one (causal LM target), with: - The instruction region replaced by -100 . - The padding region replaced by -100 . - The RESP_ID boundary position itself replaced by -100 (you do not train the model to predict the boundary token; it predicts what follows). The shift is the standard causal trick: position i of input_ids predicts position i+1 , so labels[i] = input_ids[i+1] (with the final position dropped from the input and the first dropped from the target). The mask is applied after the shift to land on the right positions. Training The loop is the standard PyTorch SFT loop. Adam, learning rate around 3e-4 to 1e-3, ten to twenty epochs on this fixture, no scheduler. The model is small enough (hidden 96, 2 blocks, max length 64) to train to convergence on CPU inside two minutes. Every fifth epoch the loop runs a tiny eval pass on the held-out set and prints exact-match. Watching exact-match go from 0.0 at epoch one to something like 0.85 at epoch fifteen is the lesson's payoff: you can see the model learning the format and the answers at the same time. Generation At eval time the model gets the instruction prefix [INST] inst_bytes [RESP] and generates tokens until either: the sequence reaches max_len , or the model emits a special stop heuristic: two consecutive sentence-ending bytes ( . , ! , ? ). The lesson ships greedy decoding plus an optional temperature sampler. Exact-match uses greedy because temperature would make the metric stochastic. Real systems often sample, then judge fuzzily; that pipeline is lesson 41. Exact-Match Evaluation Exact-match is the strictest text metric. The predicted response string is normalised (lowercase, strip whitespace, collapse double spaces) and compared to the reference response, normalised the same way. The metric is either 1 or 0 per example. The aggregate is the mean. Real SFT pipelines complement exact-match with token-level F1 (lesson 41) and a judge model. Exact-match remains useful because it is unambiguous; if it says 0.7, exactly 70 percent of test instructions produced the gold response character for character. What you will build The implementation is one main.py plus tests. InstructionTokenizer : byte-level encoder with reserved specials. Encodes either an instruction prefix or a full pair. make_dataset : generates 200 pairs across six task types with a fixed seed. SFTDataset : returns (input_ids, labels) per example, already mask-prepared. sft_collate : dynamic padding, builds the batch tensor, sets -100 on instruction and pad positions. TinyGPT : transformer body plus tied or untied LM head. train_sft : the SFT loop, with per-epoch eval hooks. generate : causal decode from a prefix, greedy or sampled, with the stop heuristic. exact_match : normalised string comparison, returns float in [0, 1] . run_demo : builds the data, trains for twenty epochs, evaluates, prints a per-category breakdown, exits zero on success. Why the mask matters Without the mask, the loss treats instruction tokens as targets. The model learns to predict the instruction. This is a different objective and produces a worse model in two ways. First, model capacity is wasted reconstructing inputs the user always provides. Second, the response loss is smaller in the gradient sum because instruction tokens outnumber response tokens in most batches; the optimiser's effective learning rate on the part you care about is lower than you intended. The mask is not a polish; it is the objective. Stretch goals Add a learning-rate warmup followed by cosine decay. SFT is more sensitive to LR than pretraining. Add per-token loss logging and plot the loss curve over training. Notice that early epochs are dominated by template tokens ( <RESP> , common prefixes) and later epochs are dominated by the actual answer tokens. Extend the eval to BLEU-1 or chrF. Exact-match underestimates models that produce a paraphrase with the same answer. Add a chat template with multi-turn formatting and train on a fixture that includes follow-ups. The implementation gives you the format contract, the mask, and the loop. The objective change from base model to instruction follower is one collate function.
