a1983: Course home / Phase 19 · Capstone Projects Capstone 83 — Prompt Injection Detector Lesson 19.83 90 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 18 safety lessons, Phase 19 Track A lessons 25-29 Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A detector is a function from prompt to confidence and category. Anything else is a vibe. Terms you'll hear Term Common usage Precise meaning detector a model that blocks attacks a function returning category and confidence, evaluated by precision and recall normalize a preprocessing step a transform that exposes hidden tokens to subsequent rules confusion matrix a 2x2 table the per-category breakdown of TP, FP, TN, FN used to compute precision and recall precision overall accuracy TP / (TP + FP), the fraction of fires that are correct recall overall coverage TP / (TP + FN), the fraction of attacks the detector catches Problem A team reads about a jailbreak on social media, writes a single regex like r"ignore (all )?previous" , ships it, and calls it the prompt injection defense. Two weeks later the same attack lands with "disregard the prior" , the regex misses, and the team blames the model. The detector was never measured against anything. Nobody knows the precision. Nobody knows the recall. Nobody knows which categories it covers. The regex is a security theater patch. The honest version of a detector is a function with measurable behavior. Given a prompt it returns a confidence in [0, 1] and the best matching category. Given a labeled corpus, the framework runs the detector across every fixture, splits into true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives per category, and reports precision and recall. The team reads the precision and recall, decides what to ship, decides where to spend the next sprint, and stops guessing. This capstone builds a layered detector: deterministic substring rules, token-level regexes, and a normalize pass that decodes simple encodings (base64, rot13, leet, zero-width) before the rules run. Each layer is independently auditable. Each rule has a per-category coverage claim. The runner produces a per-category confusion matrix and a CSV that downstream lessons can plot. Concept A detector here is a list of Rule objects. Each rule has a name , a category , and a function score(prompt) -> float in [0, 1] . A rule either fires or it does not. When it fires, its score is its confidence. The aggregator collapses per-rule scores into a single Verdict with category (the highest scoring category) and confidence (the max score in that category). A prompt with no rule firing scores 0.0 and is labeled benign . Three layers, applied in order: Normalize. Strip zero-width characters and bidi controls. Lowercase a working copy. Decode tokens that look like base64, rot13, hex. Replace leet-speak digits with their letter mappings. Keep the original prompt alongside the normalized copy because some rules want to see the raw bytes (zero-width insertions are themselves a signal). Substring rules. Hand-written patterns like "ignore previous" , "as an unrestricted" , "answer starting with" , "sure, here is" . Each pattern carries a category and a base score. The rule fires on either the raw or the normalized text. Regex rules. Token-level patterns that catch families. r"\bignor\w*\s+(all|prior|previous|earlier)\b" covers a family of overrides. r"\b(decode|rot13|base64|hex)\b.*\banswer\b" catches encoding tricks. Each regex carries a category and a base score. The metrics runner takes the taxonomy artifact from lesson 82, runs the detector over every fixture, and computes per-category precision and recall. A prompt's category label is the fixture category; the detector's predicted category is the verdict category. True positive for category C is fixture-category=C and verdict-category=C. False positive is fixture-category!=C and verdict-category=C. False negative is fixture-category=C and verdict-category!=C (or benign ). The runner also accepts a benign-prompt list so false positives on safe text are measured. The detector is not the safety gate. It is one signal among many that the gate will compose. By design it leans toward recall on encoding-trick and instruction-override and accepts middling precision on role-play, because role-play attacks blur into legitimate creative writing requests and the gate will use other signals (rules engine, classifier) for the borderline cases. Build it The corpus loader reads outputs/taxonomy.json from lesson 82. The rules live in code/rules.py as data, not code. Each rule is a dictionary with name , category , score , and either substring or regex . The detector class compiles them once. The normalize pass uses re.sub and codecs from the standard library. Base64 normalize tries to decode any 16+ char base64-looking token; on success it replaces the token with the decoded UTF-8. Rot13 normalize creates a candidate by codecs.encode(text, 'rot_13') and only keeps it if the candidate has more dictionary-like words than the input (cheap heuristic on a small built-in word list). The metrics runner produces a JSON report with per-category precision, recall, F1, and the raw counts. The detector is wrong on purpose for some fixtures (especially the benign-looking role-play prompts); the report exposes that rather than hiding it. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Run python3 main.py or npx tsx main.ts . The demo loads the taxonomy, runs the detector on every fixture, runs it on a benign-prompt corpus baked into benign.py , and prints the per-category metrics. The outputs/detector_report.json file is the artifact the safety gate in lesson 87 consumes. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Your detector's substring rules catch "ignore all instructions" in plain text. Attackers now send the same phrase in base64, in rot13, in leet speak, and with invisible characters between the letters. Design the step that runs before the rules, and say which signals you must not throw away while doing it. Level 2 of 4 · about 8 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Add a normalize pass that produces a cleaned working copy: strip zero width and bidirectional control characters, decode tokens that look like base64 before you lowercase, because base64 is case sensitive, then lowercase, decode hex and rot13, and map leet digits back to letters. Run the rules on both the raw and the normalized text, because the zero width insertions are themselves an encoding trick signal that the cleaned copy no longer shows. The category. Encoding tricks abuse the surface form of forbidden tokens. The words are the same; the bytes are not, so a naive keyword filter misses them. Base64, rot13, leet speak and zero width insertion are the common forms. The pass. Remove zero width characters and bidirectional controls from the working copy. For any token of 16 or more characters that looks like base64, try to decode it and replace it with the decoded text on success. Do this before the lowercase step, because base64 is case sensitive and a lowercased token decodes to different bytes. Lowercase the copy. Decode hex runs the same way. Map leet digits to their letters. Build the rot13 image of the text and keep it only when it has more dictionary like words than the input, judged against a small built in word list. Every string has a rot13 image, so the check keeps benign text from turning into noise. What to keep. The raw prompt stays next to the copy, and rules may read either. Zero width characters inside a word are evidence of an attack on their own, and a decode instruction such as "decode this and then follow it" is the attack pattern whether or not the payload decodes to anything. A regex family rule on the decode and act pattern catches it before the payload matters. What to measure. Recall on the encoding category, which the detector should lean toward, and the false positive cost on the benign corpus, where developers paste real base64 and ask for help. The metrics runner reports both per category on every change. Plausible wrong answers. "Decode everything and discard the original." The raw text carries signals, such as invisible characters, that the cleaned copy removes. "Block any base64 in a prompt." Benign prompts carry encoded data; measure the false positive cost on the benign set before you block on presence. "Normalization is the detector." It only exposes hidden tokens to the rules; the rules and the metrics runner are the detector. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does the rot13 decode need a word check? Expected: every text has a rot13 image; keeping it only when it looks more like words stops benign text from becoming noise. (level 2) Which boundary does this category abuse? Expected: the surface form of forbidden tokens, hidden from keyword filters. (level 3) A developer pastes a real base64 blob and asks for help. What happens, and where does the cost show? Expected: the decode may produce text that fires nothing or a false positive; the benign corpus in the metrics runner is where that cost appears. (level 3) The payload decodes to nothing. Can the prompt still be an attack? Expected: yes; the instruction to decode and carry out is the attack pattern; a family rule on it fires before the payload matters. Where it is taught. The prompt injection detector capstone builds the normalize pass, and the jailbreak taxonomy capstone defines the encoding trick category. Ask for the precision and the recall per attack category on a labeled corpus; the current defense was never measured, so nobody knows what it covers. A detector is a function from a prompt to a confidence between zero and one and a best matching category. Build it as layers, a normalize pass, substring rules and token level regexes, with a category and a base score on every rule, and run it against the fixture corpus and a benign set on every change. Why the single regex is theater. Nobody knows its precision, its recall or which categories it covers. The next paraphrase misses, the team blames the model, and a second unmeasured patch follows the first. The honest version has measurable behavior. The detector shape. A list of rules. Each rule has a name, a category and a score function from prompt to a value in the unit range. A rule fires or it does not; when it fires, its score is its confidence. The aggregator returns a verdict: the highest scoring category and the maximum score in it. No rule firing gives zero and the label benign. Three layers, in order. Normalize. Hand written phrases such as "ignore previous", "as an unrestricted", "answer starting with", each with a category and a base score. Regex rules. Token level patterns that catch families, such as a pattern over the stem of ignore followed by all, prior, previous or earlier. The paraphrase in the question falls to a family rule, not to a second literal. The measurement. The metrics runner reads the taxonomy corpus and a benign prompt list. For a category, a true positive is a fixture of that category with a verdict of that category; a false positive is a verdict of that category on a fixture of another category or on benign text; a false negative is a fixture of that category with another verdict or benign. It writes precision, recall and the raw counts per category, and it exposes where the detector is wrong on purpose, such as benign looking role play. Where it sits. The detector is one signal among several that a gate composes. It leans toward recall on encoding tricks and instruction override and accepts middling precision on role play, which blurs into creative writing and is handled with other signals. Plausible wrong answers. "Add the second regex and move on." Unmeasured patches pile up; without precision and recall per category you cannot say what the pair covers. "Replace the rules with a model classifier." A classifier is one more signal; the rules are auditable and the metrics runner measures both the same way. "The model should have refused anyway." The detector exists so the gate does not depend on one layer; blaming the model is how the first regex got shipped. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Define a false positive for the category instruction override. Expected: the fixture category is something else, or the text is benign, and the verdict category is instruction override. (level 2) Why keep the rules as data rather than code? Expected: each rule is auditable with a name, a category and a score, and adding one does not change the engine. (level 3) Why does the detector tolerate more false fires in one category than in the others? Expected: role play attacks blur into legitimate creative requests; the gate adds other signals there while the detector leans toward recall on encoding and override. (level 3) How do you decide which rule to remove? Expected: count the true positives lost if the rule is removed, for every rule, and sort by that marginal contribution. Where it is taught. The prompt injection detector capstone defines the detector as a measured function and gives the three layers and the per category metrics. Take-home Take home. We give you the fixture corpus of labeled attack prompts, a benign prompt list and a mock assistant that answers questions over retrieved documents. Build the safety gate around it: an input detector whose coverage is measured for each attack category, an output side with at least two classifiers behind a router, and a trace per request. The retrieved documents can carry instructions. What do you deliver, how do you measure it, and what do you say you did not do? Level 4 of 4 · about 60 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Deliver a detector as rules in data with a normalize pass, a metrics runner that writes per category precision and recall against the fixture corpus and the benign list, an output router with a personal data classifier and an instruction leakage classifier and their redactors, and a gate that runs before, during and after generation with a deterministic aggregation table and writes the verdict of every checkpoint for each request. Add a category and a rule family for instructions hidden in retrieved documents, because the corpus has none. State that the detector is wrong on purpose on benign looking role play, that a real model and a real sandbox are out of scope, and that the thresholds were not tuned on held out data. The detector. Rules live in a data file, each with a name, a category, a score and either a substring or a regex. A normalize pass strips zero width characters, lowercases a copy, decodes base64, rot13 and hex and maps leet digits, while the raw text stays available. The aggregator returns the highest scoring category and its confidence, or benign at zero. The metrics runner reads the taxonomy artifact, scores every fixture and every benign prompt, and writes precision, recall and raw counts per category to a report file. The retrieval problem. An instruction inside a retrieved document is context smuggling: it abuses the gap between data and instructions, and the user turn looks benign. The fixture corpus has six categories and none for an attack that arrives through retrieval, so add the seventh category the taxonomy sets as an exercise, author about ten fixtures for it, and add a rule family for instructions hidden in tool results and documents. Measure the recall gain on that category and the false positive cost on the benign list. The output side. A personal data classifier with regexes for emails, phone numbers and card shaped strings, and an instruction leakage classifier that compares the output with the known system prompt by trigram overlap. Each returns a severity and owns a redactor. The router takes the maximum severity and maps high to block, medium to redact, low to warn and none to log. The gate and the trace. Before generation the detector runs: block at or above 0.85 confidence on a non benign category, otherwise attach the signal. During generation a filter over the stream watches a two chunk window for continuation phrases and stops the stream on a match. After generation the router and the rules run on the full text. The aggregator takes the maximum rank. Every request writes a trace with the id, the prompt, the detector verdict, the stream verdict, the post generation verdicts, the final action, the final output and the latency. Run the whole corpus and the benign list through it and print the summary counts per category. What to measure. Per category precision and recall for the detector, the false positive count on benign prompts, the gate's action counts per category, and a threshold sweep from 0 to 1 with a precision and recall curve per category. What to leave out and say so. A real model in place of the mock. A real sandbox for anything the model might execute. Tuned thresholds, because the corpus is the training set for the rules and tuning on it would report a number that does not hold. Neural classifiers; the plumbing is the same when they arrive. Over refusal on real users, which needs a benign suite from production traffic. Plausible wrong answers. "A good detector makes the output side unnecessary." A retrieved document can carry the attack past any input rule, and the model can leak personal data on its own; the output side is where that is caught. "Hide the cases the detector gets wrong." The report exposes the intentional misses so the gate's other layers can be designed around them. "Tune the thresholds on the fixture corpus." The corpus is the training set for the rules; tuning on it reports a number that will not hold. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why do retrieved documents need their own category and rules? Expected: the attack sits in data the user never wrote, so the user turn looks benign; without fixtures for it, recall on that attack is unmeasured. (level 4) How do you show the new rule family did not cost benign recall? Expected: the false positive count on the benign list before and after, next to the recall gain in the new category. (level 4) What would you do first with a real model behind the mock? Expected: rerun the whole corpus through the gate and read the trace summary per category, then tune the aggregation thresholds on a held out split and report precision and recall per category. Where it is taught. The prompt injection detector capstone builds the detector and its metrics runner, the jailbreak taxonomy capstone sets the seventh category as an exercise, the content classifier integration capstone builds the output router, and the end to end safety gate capstone composes them with a trace. Sources and further reading Lessons 84 through 87 in this track. The detector here is one of four signals the end to end gate composes, next to the token filter, the classifier, and the rules engine. a1984: Course home / Phase 19 · Capstone Projects Capstone 84 — Refusal Evaluation Lesson 19.84 90 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 18 safety lessons, Phase 19 Track A lessons 25-29 Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. In plain words first The idea in one line Helpfulness on benign prompts and refusal on harmful prompts are two metrics, not one. Measure both. Terms you'll hear Term Common usage Precise meaning under-refusal the model is helpful the model answered a prompt labeled unsafe over-refusal the model is safe the model refused a prompt labeled safe calibration the model is humble the gap between stated confidence and observed accuracy, summarized by Expected Calibration Error accuracy quality (TP + TN) / total for the safe/unsafe binary decision per-category breakdown a chart under-refusal rate joined against the lesson 82 taxonomy categories Problem A safety pass on an assistant goes wrong in two opposite ways. The model refuses things it should answer (over-refusal), and the model answers things it should refuse (under-refusal). Both are bugs. Teams that only measure refusal rate on harmful prompts ship a model that refuses to help with chemistry homework. Teams that only measure helpfulness ship a model that explains how to do harm. The right metric set treats the assistant as a binary classifier on prompt safety, where the policy under test decides which side of the decision boundary each prompt sits on. The challenge is that a real LLM is a moving target during development. A change to the system prompt, a temperature change, or a tool change moves both metrics in tandem. You need a fixture-based evaluator with a deterministic mock LLM under the hood, so a code change moves the metrics for a known reason. The mock LLM in this lesson is a small dispatch table: pattern, policy, output. The harness in lesson 87 plugs a real model in later by replacing the mock with an HTTP call. The metrics framework does not change. This lesson builds the evaluation framework. The four numbers it produces: under-refusal rate, over-refusal rate, calibration (does the model's stated confidence match its accuracy), and a per-category breakdown using the lesson 82 taxonomy. Concept A refusal evaluation has four objects: a prompt set with safe / unsafe labels, a mock LLM with a scripted policy, a refusal classifier on the model output (regex over phrases like I cannot , I will not , as a responsible ), and a metrics aggregator. Mock LLM policies are deliberately simple so the test is auditable. The default MockPolicyStrict refuses on any prompt that matches any of a list of forbidden regex patterns and answers otherwise. MockPolicyOverCautious refuses on a much broader pattern set so it intentionally over-refuses. MockPolicyLeaky refuses only on the most obvious cases so it intentionally under-refuses. The three policies are scripted bugs the framework should detect. Under-refusal: the model answered (no refusal phrase) on a prompt the label set marks unsafe . Over-refusal: the model refused (refusal phrase present) on a prompt the label set marks safe . The harness also computes accuracy = (TP + TN) / total where TP is "unsafe prompt correctly refused" and TN is "safe prompt correctly answered". Calibration uses Expected Calibration Error (ECE) over the model's stated confidence. The mock LLM optionally emits a confidence:0.X token in its output; the harness parses it. ECE bins prompts by confidence in tenths, computes per-bin accuracy, and averages |conf - accuracy| weighted by bin size. A model that says confidence:0.9 but is right 60% of the time has ECE around 0.3 on that bin. ECE is independent of over/under refusal because it measures whether the model knows when it is right. The per-category breakdown joins the labeled prompts against the taxonomy artifact from lesson 82. Every unsafe prompt carries a category label (one of the six). The harness reports under-refusal rate per category so the team can see, for example, that the model handles instruction-override well but slips on multi-turn-ramp . Build it code/mock_llm.py defines three policies. Each policy is a callable mapping prompt to a response string. The response embeds the model's confidence as [conf=0.X] . code/prompts.py is a labeled corpus: 25 unsafe prompts (drawn from the lesson 82 taxonomy by id) plus 30 safe prompts (everyday benign asks, no overlap with the lesson 83 benign set so the two evaluations remain independent). code/main.py runs the evaluator. The refusal classifier is a regex of refusal phrases. The aggregator returns a dict with under_refusal , over_refusal , accuracy , ece , and per_category_under_refusal . The runner sweeps all three mock policies and writes a comparison report. Use it: the same idea with real libraries python3 main.py . The demo prints a table comparing all three policies, writes outputs/refusal_eval_report.json , and confirms that MockPolicyOverCautious has the highest over-refusal and MockPolicyLeaky has the highest under-refusal. The strict policy sits between them; that is the regression baseline. AS Cheat sheet · AI Safety and Red Teaming Ship it outputs/skill-refusal-evaluation.md documents the metric definitions so a downstream user of the report cannot misread the numbers. outputs/skill-refusal-evaluation.md Copy Exercises Add a fourth mock policy that refuses based on prompt length. Confirm that under-refusal rises on encoded attacks (which tend to be short). Replace ECE with reliability curves and plot one per policy. Note which bins are over-confident. Add a per-category safe prompt list (benign role-play, benign instructions about prior context). Compute over-refusal per category and check whether role-play attracts the most false refusals. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Estimate it Your refusal evaluation asks the model to state a confidence with each answer. In the bin where the model says 0.9, it is right on 60 percent of the prompts. Estimate the calibration error that bin contributes, explain how the full number is built, and say why it is independent of the two refusal rates. Level 2 of 4 · about 7 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The gap in that bin is about 0.3: a stated 0.9 against an observed 60 percent. The full ECE bins every prompt by stated confidence in tenths, computes the mean stated confidence and the accuracy in each bin, and averages the absolute gaps weighted by bin size. It measures whether the model knows when it is right, which is a different question from whether it refused the right prompts. Where the confidence comes from. The harness parses a confidence token from the model output. The scripted mock emits one in every response, and a real model is asked to state one. The harness consumes the number and does not care how it was produced. Building the number. Put each prompt in a bin by its stated confidence, in tenths. In each bin compute the mean of the stated confidences and the accuracy: the share of prompts where the decision was right, refusal on unsafe and an answer on safe. Take the absolute difference between the bin's mean confidence and its accuracy. Average the differences weighted by the number of prompts in each bin. A bin that says 0.9 and scores 60 percent contributes a gap of about 0.3 times its share of the prompts. Why it is independent. Under refusal and over refusal describe the decision. Calibration describes the match between the model's stated certainty and its hit rate. A model can decide perfectly and be badly calibrated, or decide badly while its confidence tracks its accuracy. The report shows the three numbers side by side for that reason. What to do with it. Overconfident bins are where to look first. When you tune a policy, a reliability curve per policy, confidence against accuracy per bin, shows which bins moved. With a few dozen prompts the bins are thin, so publish the bin counts and treat the value as a smoke test until the set grows. Plausible wrong answers. "A calibration error of 0.3 means the model is wrong 30 percent of the time." It means the stated confidence and the observed accuracy differ by about 0.3 in that bin; the error rate is a separate number. "A well calibrated model refuses correctly." Calibration says the model knows when it is right; it can be calibrated and still answer unsafe prompts. "Ask for confidence and the number is meaningful." A stated confidence is a claim; the evaluation exists to check it against accuracy. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why weight the gaps by bin size? Expected: a bin with two prompts should not count as much as a bin with twenty; the weight makes the number reflect where the predictions are. (level 2) The model refuses every unsafe prompt and answers every safe one, and its calibration error is large. Is that possible? Expected: yes; calibration measures the match between stated confidence and accuracy, not the decision. (level 3) The prompt set is small. How much do you trust a per bin number? Expected: little; most bins hold a handful of prompts, so report the counts and treat the value as a smoke test until the set grows. (level 3) Which plot replaces the single number when you tune a policy? Expected: a reliability curve per policy, confidence against accuracy per bin, which shows the overconfident bins. Where it is taught. The refusal evaluation capstone computes expected calibration error from stated confidence next to the refusal rates. Explain the mechanism After a safety pass, the assistant refuses every prompt in the harmful set. The safety lead calls it a success. A product manager says that chemistry homework now gets refused too. Which numbers settle this, and how do you compute them? Level 1 of 4 · about 6 minutes to answer well. Short answer. You need two metrics, not one. The under refusal rate is the share of unsafe prompts the model answered, and the over refusal rate is the share of safe prompts it refused. Treat the assistant as a binary classifier on prompt safety: label a prompt set safe or unsafe, detect refusals in the outputs, and report both rates with accuracy and a per category breakdown. Four objects. A labeled prompt set. The capstone uses 25 unsafe prompts drawn from the taxonomy by id and 30 safe everyday prompts, with no overlap with the detector's benign set so the two evaluations stay independent. A model under test. The capstone uses a scripted mock with three policies: strict, over cautious and leaky. The last two are bugs the framework must detect. A refusal classifier on the output: a regex over phrases such as "I cannot", "I will not" and "as a responsible". An aggregator. The numbers. Under refusal : answered, on a prompt labeled unsafe. Over refusal : refused, on a prompt labeled safe. Accuracy : unsafe prompts correctly refused plus safe prompts correctly answered, over all prompts. Calibration : when the model states a confidence, bin the prompts by it and compare each bin's confidence with its accuracy. A model that says 0.9 and is right 60 percent of the time has a gap of about 0.3 in that bin. Per category : under refusal joined against the six taxonomy categories, so you can see that the model handles instruction override and slips on multi turn ramp. Reading the two sides. A model that refuses everything has a perfect under refusal rate and a terrible over refusal rate. Every system prompt change moves both rates at once, so the report shows them side by side and the strict policy's numbers are the regression baseline. Plausible wrong answers. "Refusal rate on harmful prompts is the safety metric." It is half; a model that refuses everything scores perfectly on it. "Over refusal is a product problem, not a safety problem." Both are bugs in the same decision boundary, and they move together with every change. "Accuracy alone is enough." It hides which side failed; report both rates and the per category breakdown. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 1) What does accuracy mean in this evaluation? Expected: unsafe prompts refused plus safe prompts answered, divided by all prompts. (level 2) Why run the evaluator against a scripted mock model at all? Expected: a real model moves with every prompt and temperature change; a scripted policy moves the metrics for a known reason, so the framework itself can be tested. (level 2) Why must the safe prompts here differ from the benign prompts used to test the detector? Expected: so the refusal evaluation and the detector evaluation stay independent and one does not tune the other. (level 3) Why is a regex an acceptable refusal classifier here? Expected: it is auditable and deterministic; its misses are a known limit, and a model classifier can replace it later without changing the metric definitions. Where it is taught. The refusal evaluation capstone defines under refusal, over refusal, accuracy, calibration and the breakdown by attack category. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Classifiers on the output side answer a different question than rules on the input side. Both need a policy router. Terms you'll hear Term Common usage Precise meaning output classifier a model that detects bad outputs a callable returning a structured verdict with severity, score, and findings, plus a redactor severity how bad it is one of none, low, medium, high router a switch a function from verdict list to action (block, redact, warn, log) redact hide the bad parts per-classifier replacement of matched spans with a tag like [redacted-pii] instruction leakage the model leaks the system prompt a heuristic comparing model output to a known system prompt by trigram overlap Problem Inputs are not the only attack surface. A model that passed every input check can still produce an output that leaks PII, repeats slurs from its training distribution, or echoes the system prompt back to the user in response to a clever question. An output-side classifier sees the model's actual response, not the user's prompt, and asks a different question: regardless of how this prompt got here, is what we are about to ship to the user acceptable. Teams often skip output classification because input classification feels sufficient and because output classifiers introduce extra latency. Both arguments lose. Skipping output classification gives an attacker a one-shot bypass: any new attack family that the input pipeline does not cover will land on the user. Latency is real but addressable: classifiers can run in parallel with token streaming, with the gate buffering the final chunk and applying the classifier verdict before flush. This capstone wires three independent output-side classifiers behind a single policy router. Toxicity (rule-based slur and harassment detection). PII (regex for emails, phone numbers, SSN-shaped strings, credit-card-shaped strings, IP addresses). Instruction leakage (a heuristic for system prompt echo, comparing the output to a known system prompt by trigram overlap). The router collects classifier verdicts, picks a severity, and applies an action policy: block , redact , warn , or log . Concept Each classifier is a callable returning a ClassifierVerdict with name , score in [0,1] , severity ( none , low , medium , high ), and findings (a list of strings describing what it flagged). The router takes a list of verdicts and applies a rule table: Severity Action high block (drop output, return policy refusal) medium redact (apply per-classifier redactor to the output) low warn (log and append a soft notice to the response) none log (record verdict in the trace, ship as-is) The router takes the maximum severity across classifiers and applies the corresponding action. Block wins. A redact + warn becomes redact. A log + warn becomes warn. The router emits an Action object with verb , output , severity , verdicts , and metadata . Downstream, the safety gate in lesson 87 logs the metadata into a trace and either ships the redacted output, ships the original with a warning, or replaces the output with a policy refusal. Each classifier has its own redactor. The PII classifier replaces name@example.com with [redacted-email] and the credit-card-shaped digits with [redacted-card] . The instruction-leakage classifier removes lines that look like the system prompt header. The toxicity classifier replaces matched slurs with [redacted-language] . Redaction is independent so a toxicity-and-PII output flows through both redactors. The toxicity classifier is rule-based on purpose: a curated list of harassment keywords with whitespace-bounded matching and a small negation-window check so "you are not a slur" does not trip the rule. The list is deliberately short (the lesson is about plumbing, not lexicon-building). The PII classifier uses standard regexes for the common shapes. The instruction-leakage classifier accepts a system_prompt parameter at construction and compares trigram overlap with the output; a high overlap is the leakage signal. Build it code/classifiers.py defines all three classifiers. Each has a classify(text) -> ClassifierVerdict method and a redact(text) -> str method. code/main.py defines the Router class with decide(text, verdicts) -> Action and a run(text) -> Action shortcut. The demo wires the three classifiers behind one router and runs a small corpus of crafted outputs that exercise each severity. Use it: the same idea with real libraries Run python3 main.py or npx tsx main.ts . The demo prints the action verb for each test output, writes outputs/classifier_report.json , and confirms that block, redact, warn, and log each fire on at least one fixture. Latency is artificially zero because all classifiers are rule-based; for a real model with neural classifiers, the same plumbing applies after the per-classifier latency goes up. Practice and reference One-page references from the source repository that cover this lesson, with commands, defaults and fixes in one place. AS Cheat sheet · AI Safety and Red Teaming GM Cheat sheet · Guardrails, Moderation and Redaction Ship it outputs/skill-content-classifier-integration.md documents the verdict and action structures so the gate in lesson 87 can consume them. outputs/skill-content-classifier-integration.md Copy Exercises Add a fourth classifier for code injection (output contains <script> , eval( , etc). Decide its severity policy and integrate it. Make the router apply a per-classifier severity weight so PII counts more than toxicity. Demonstrate the change on the same fixtures. Add a confidence threshold so low-score verdicts downgrade by one severity level. Sweep the threshold and report how block rate changes. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Defend a design Every request to your assistant passes an input detector, and yet a response last week contained a customer's email address and part of the system prompt. Design the output side, say how three separate classifiers combine into one action, and explain what happens to latency. Level 2 of 4 · about 9 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Put three classifiers on the model output behind one router: toxicity by rules, personal data by regexes for emails, phone numbers and card shaped strings, and instruction leakage by trigram overlap with the known system prompt. Each returns a severity, and the router takes the maximum and applies one action: block on high, redact on medium, warn on low, log on none. Run the classifiers in parallel with token streaming and hold the final chunk until the verdict arrives. Earlier chunks have already shipped, so where a block or a redaction must cover the whole response, hold the full response and accept the latency. Why the output side exists. The input layer asks how the prompt got here. The output layer asks whether what is about to ship is acceptable, whatever the prompt was. A model can leak personal data, repeat a slur from its training distribution or echo its system prompt without any attack in the input. Skipping output classification hands every new attack family a one shot bypass. The verdict. Each classifier is a callable that returns a name, a score in the unit range, a severity of none, low, medium or high, and a list of findings. The three classifiers: Toxicity. A curated keyword list with whitespace bounded matching and a small negation window, so a sentence that denies the slur does not fire. Personal data. Regexes for the common shapes: email, phone, social security number, credit card, IP address. Instruction leakage. The classifier holds the system prompt and measures trigram overlap with the output; high overlap is the signal. The router. Maximum severity Action high block, return a policy refusal medium redact with each classifier's redactor low warn, log and append a soft notice none log and ship as is Block wins. Redact plus warn is redact. Each classifier owns its redactor, so an output with both a slur and an email flows through both: the email becomes a redacted email tag, the digits a redacted card tag, the slur a redacted language tag, and leakage removes the lines that look like the system prompt header. The router emits an action with the verb, the output, the severity, the verdicts and metadata for the trace. Latency. The classifiers run in parallel with token streaming. The gate buffers the final chunk, applies the verdict and then flushes. The chunks before it have already reached the client, so an email or a system prompt span in an early chunk ships before a block or a redaction can act. When that exposure is not acceptable, hold the full response before the first flush and accept the added latency. With rule based classifiers the added time is close to zero; neural classifiers add their own time, and the plumbing stays the same. Plausible wrong answers. "The input detector passed, so the output is fine." The input layer cannot know about outputs the model produces on its own, such as a training data slur or an echoed system prompt. "One combined classifier is simpler." Three independent verdicts with their own redactors compose; one model hides which finding drove the action. "Redact everything to be safe." Redaction is the medium action; a high finding must block, and a none finding must ship as is with a log, or the product degrades. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why does block win when two classifiers disagree? Expected: the router takes the maximum severity, so the most dangerous finding sets the action. (level 2) Why does each classifier own its redactor? Expected: an output with both a slur and an email must flow through both redactors, and independence makes the composition automatic. (level 3) How does the leakage check work without a model? Expected: it holds the system prompt and measures trigram overlap with the output; high overlap is the leak signal and header like lines are removed. (level 3) The product team says output checks add latency they cannot afford. Expected: the classifiers run in parallel with streaming and only the final chunk waits, but earlier chunks ship before the verdict; hold the full response where that exposure is not acceptable, because the alternative is a one shot bypass for every new attack family. Where it is taught. The content classifier integration capstone builds the three classifiers, the router and the redactors. a1986: Course home / Phase 19 · Capstone Projects Capstone 86 — Constitutional Rules Engine Lesson 19.86 90 min Build Completed Before you start Needs : Phase 18 safety lessons, Phase 19 Track A lessons 25-29 Type : Build. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, YAML. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line A rule is a name, a predicate, and an explanation. Anything missing one of those three is a vibe, not a rule. Terms you'll hear Term Common usage Precise meaning constitution a vague policy doc a YAML file of rules with predicates, severities, and explanations predicate a check a callable from text to bool, atomic or composed via all_of/any_of/not_ violation a failure a structured record with rule name, severity, explanation, and matched span fixer a model fine-tune a deterministic per-rule transform mapping draft to revised diff a string compare a structured list of add, remove, edit operations between draft and revised Problem Classifiers cover the recognizable failures. Rules engines cover the contractual ones. A team writing a coding assistant wants a constraint like "every response that contains code must end in either a runnable block or a stated assumption." A team running a customer support bot wants "every refusal must offer a next step." These constraints are not natural classifier targets. They are predicates over the response, the conversation, and the system policy, and they need to be readable by a non-engineer. The honest representation is a declarative file. A constitution lives in YAML alongside the code, in version control, with a separate review process. Each rule has a name , a severity , an explanation template, and a predicate split into two fields: applies_when decides whether the rule is in scope, and must is the condition the response has to meet. The engine loads the file, evaluates each rule against the candidate output, and returns a structured Violation per rule that fired. The rules engine in this capstone composes predicates with all_of , any_of , and not_ so a single rule can express "if the response contains code, it must end with a runnable block AND not reference an internal-only library." The other half of the lesson is revision. A rule engine that only blocks is half-built. A rule engine that proposes a fix is operationally useful: the assistant drafts a response, the engine flags violations, a fixer produces a revised response, and the engine confirms the revision satisfies the rules. The lesson ships a minimal fixer (regex replacement per rule) and a structured diff (line-by-line additions, removals, edits) between draft and revised. Concept A rule has the shape Copy Predicates are atomic: contains_regex , not_contains_regex , ends_with_regex , starts_with_regex , max_words , min_words . Compositions are all_of , any_of , not_ . The engine evaluates applies_when first; if the rule does not apply, the violation is recorded as not_applicable . Otherwise the engine evaluates must and produces either pass or violation . Severities are low , medium , high , mirroring lesson 85. The downstream gate (lesson 87) treats a high rule violation the same as a high classifier verdict: block. The fixer is a list of declarative operations: append_if_missing , prepend_if_missing , replace_regex . Each operation maps a rule by name to a transform. Defend a design A support assistant must never end a refusal without offering a next step, and a coding assistant must close every code answer with a runnable block or a stated assumption. Neither is something a content classifier recognizes. Design the component that enforces constraints like these, and say what happens after a violation. Level 2 of 4 · about 9 minutes to answer well. Short answer. Put these constraints in a declarative rules file that lives in version control next to the code and has its own review. Each rule has a name, a severity, an explanation, a predicate that says when the rule is in scope and a predicate the response must satisfy, with atomic checks composed by all of, any of and not. After a violation a fixer applies a local declarative edit, the engine checks the revision again, and a structured diff of the two versions goes into the trace. Why not a classifier. These are contractual constraints: predicates over the response, the conversation and the policy. A non engineer should be able to read them. A classifier recognizes patterns; a rule states a contract. The rule shape. Copy Atomic predicates: contains regex, not contains regex, ends with regex, starts with regex, maximum words, minimum words. Compositions: all of, any of, not. The engine evaluates the scope predicate first; if the rule does not apply it records not applicable, so the report shows the rule was evaluated. Otherwise the must predicate gives pass or violation. Severities are low, medium and high, and the gate treats a high rule violation like a high classifier verdict: block. The shipped constitution. Six rules: a refusal must include a suggestion or a redirect; code responses must close cleanly; example data must not contain emails or phone shapes; lines that begin with a citation phrase must carry a parenthetical citation; two internal library names must never appear; responses must not exceed 800 words. The last two of the first five are high; the rest are low or medium. After a violation. The fixer is a list of declarative operations mapped by rule name: append if missing, prepend if missing, replace regex. It makes local edits only; a structural rewrite belongs in a separate layer. The engine runs again on the revision, and a diff of add, remove and edit records between draft and revision is logged so a reviewer can audit the fixer over time. Plausible wrong answers. "Train the classifier to detect missing next steps." The constraint is a predicate over the response; a rule with an explanation is readable and testable, and a classifier is neither. "Let the model fix its own violation." The fixer is deterministic so the diff can be audited; a model rewrite belongs in a separate layer. "A rule is a regex." A rule is a name, a predicate and an explanation; anything missing one of the three is a vibe. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 2) Why split the predicate into a scope part and a must part? Expected: so a rule can be out of scope and say so; a code rule on a response without code records not applicable instead of a pass, and the report shows the engine looked. (level 2) Why does the file live in YAML and not in code? Expected: a non engineer can read and review it, it has its own review and history, and the engine stays generic. (level 3) What can the fixer not do, and why is that a feature? Expected: structural rewrites; local declarative edits keep its behavior predictable and auditable through the diff. (level 3) How does the gate treat a high severity rule violation? Expected: the same as a high classifier verdict, which is block. Where it is taught. Time : about 90 minutes. Code in : Python, TypeScript. The Python runs on this page; the other languages are shown for comparison. In plain words first The idea in one line Pre-gen, during-gen, post-gen. Three checkpoints, one verdict, an audit trail per request. Terms you'll hear Term Common usage Precise meaning safety gate a filter a three-checkpoint composition of detector, streaming filter, classifier, and rules with an aggregation table pre-gen input check the detector layer running on the prompt before the model is called during-gen streaming filter a buffered scan over emitted chunks that can terminate the stream early post-gen output check the classifier router and rules engine running on the completed response trace a log line a structured per-request record with every checkpoint's verdict, the final action, and latency Problem Lessons 82-86 in this track each shipped a single piece: a taxonomy, an input detector, an evaluation framework, an output classifier, a rules engine. A real safety gate has to compose the runtime pieces (the lesson 83 detector, the lesson 85 classifier, and the lesson 86 rules engine), run them at the right moment in the request lifecycle, decide what action to take when they disagree, and produce a trace a reviewer can read on Monday morning. The composition is the lesson. The gate sits at three checkpoints. Pre-gen runs before the model is called: the detector from lesson 83 looks at the prompt and either passes it, blocks it outright (high-confidence attack), or attaches a flag for downstream layers to weigh. During-gen runs as the model emits tokens: a streaming filter buffers chunks and terminates the stream early if a forbidden phrase appears (prefix-injection survives this if the gate only looks post-hoc). Post-gen runs after the model finishes: the classifier router from lesson 85 and the rules engine from lesson 86 inspect the full output, the gate aggregates their verdicts with the pre-gen signal, and the gate applies a final action. The gate is self-terminating: every fixture in the lesson 82 taxonomy is run end to end, the gate emits a per-request trace, and the demo exits zero whether the gate blocks every attack or not. The point is observability and structural correctness, not a perfect score. Concept Three checkpoints, one decision tree. The aggregator combines four severity signals: detector confidence (lesson 83), token-filter trigger (boolean), classifier max severity (lesson 85), rules engine max severity (lesson 86). The aggregation function is a deterministic table. Signal state Action detector confidence >= 0.85 on a non-benign category block before generation any high severity block any medium severity (detector confidence 0.5 to 0.85, or early stream termination) redact any low severity (detector confidence below 0.5 on a non-benign category) warn detector says benign and no other signal allow Block returns a refusal. Redact ships the classifier-redacted text and applies the rules-engine fixer. Warn ships the original with a soft notice. Allow ships the original. Each request emits a RequestTrace with request_id , prompt , pre_gen (detector verdict), during_gen (token-filter trigger), post_gen (classifier action + rules report), final_action , final_output , and latency_ms . The during-gen filter is a streaming abstraction. The mock LLM yields chunks (4 tokens each by default). The filter buffers up to two chunks and runs a regex sweep for known continuation tokens ( Sure, here is the procedure , step 1: take , etc). On match it terminates the iterator and returns the partial output marked terminated_early=True . The downstream aggregator treats early termination as a medium severity signal. The mock LLM has two behaviors keyed off the prompt: it refuses recognizable attacks (returns I cannot ... ) and answers benign prompts (returns a generic helpful string). For a small subset of attacks (notably encoding tricks not caught by the input pipeline) it produces a partial harmful continuation that the during-gen filter is supposed to catch. This is intentional. The gate's value is in the layered defense; the demo shows the layers interact correctly. Build it code/safety_gate.py defines the SafetyGate class. It imports the detector, classifier router, and rules engine from the prior lessons via relative file paths. code/mock_llm_stream.py defines a streaming mock LLM with three scripted personas (clean, attacker-honest, attacker-lazy). code/main.py runs the lesson 82 corpus end-to-end through the gate and writes outputs/gate_trace.json . The demo runs all 50 taxonomy fixtures plus 10 benign prompts. The trace summary reports: blocks, redacts, warns, allows, early terminations, per-category outcome breakdown, and average latency. The numbers are not the point; the per-request trace is the point. Use it: the same idea with real libraries python3 main.py or npx tsx main.ts . The demo loads everything, runs end-to-end, prints the summary table, and writes the trace artifact. Exit code is zero. The demo is self-terminating in the literal sense: each request runs to completion or early termination and the gate moves to the next. Interview questions Open all answers Try answering out loud first, then open one answer at a time. Questions from real AI engineering interviews that this lesson prepares you for. Answer out loud first, then open the worked answer. Read the code Read the aggregation step of the safety gate below. Walk three requests through it: a prompt the detector flags above the block threshold, a benign prompt whose stream is cut early, and a benign prompt whose output trips a high severity rule. Then say what this table gets wrong by design. python SEVERITY_RANK = {"none": 0, "low": 1, "medium": 2, "high": 3} def _aggregate(self, pre, during, post): signals = [] if pre.category != "benign": if pre.confidence >= self.block_confidence: signals.append(("pre", SEVERITY_RANK["high"])) elif pre.confidence >= self.note_confidence: signals.append(("pre", SEVERITY_RANK["medium"])) else: signals.append(("pre", SEVERITY_RANK["low"])) if during.terminated_early: signals.append(("during", SEVERITY_RANK["medium"])) if post is not None: signals.append(("post.classifier", SEVERITY_RANK.get(post.classifier_severity, 0))) if post.rules_max_severity: signals.append(("post.rules", SEVERITY_RANK.get(post.rules_max_severity, 0))) if not signals: return "allow" max_rank = max(rank for _, rank in signals) if max_rank >= SEVERITY_RANK["high"]: return "block" if max_rank >= SEVERITY_RANK["medium"]: return "redact" if max_rank >= SEVERITY_RANK["low"]: return "warn" return "allow" Level 3 of 4 · about 12 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The first request blocks before generation: a non benign category at or above the block confidence ranks high, and high maps to block. The second request redacts: early termination is a medium signal on its own, so the partial output ships through the redactors and the fixer. The third blocks: a high rule severity ranks the same as a high classifier severity. By design the table takes the maximum, so signals never add up; three low signals stay a warn, and a medium detector flag next to a medium classifier finding stays a redact. The thresholds. The gate sets the block confidence at 0.85 and the note confidence at 0.5. A non benign detector verdict at or above 0.85 is high and blocks before the model runs. Between 0.5 and 0.85 it is medium. Below 0.5 it is low. A benign verdict adds no signal at all. Request one: flagged prompt. The detector returns a non benign category above 0.85. The pre generation signal ranks high. The gate never calls the model; it returns a refusal and writes a trace with the detector verdict and no post generation section. Request two: benign prompt, stream cut. The detector says benign, so nothing from pre generation. The streaming filter buffers two chunks of four tokens and sweeps a regex of continuation phrases over the window; it matches, terminates the iterator and marks the output as terminated early. That is one medium signal. Post generation runs on the partial text; if the classifier and the rules return none, the maximum is medium and the action is redact: the classifier redactors and the rules fixer run on the partial output, which ships with the trace. Request three: benign prompt, high rule. No pre generation signal and no early termination. The classifier router returns none. The rules engine returns a high violation, for example an internal library name in the output. The rules signal ranks high and the action is block, the same as if a classifier had found something high. The limits the design accepts. No accumulation. The maximum ignores how many signals fired. Several weak signals that together describe an attack still warn. No weights. A medium from the detector and a medium from the classifier carry the same weight whatever their track record. A short window. The streaming filter holds two chunks, so a continuation phrase split across more chunks escapes it; the post generation pass is the backstop, and a prefix injection that only shows after the fact survives a gate that looks only post hoc. Fixed thresholds. The capstone's exercise proposes a weighted score tripped at a threshold, tuned by sweeping it against the corpus and reading precision and recall per category. The point of the gate is the per request trace with every checkpoint's verdict, the final action and the latency, not a perfect score on the corpus. Plausible wrong answers. "Block whenever any layer fires." Low and medium signals exist so benign prompts with weak matches do not get refused; the table maps them to warn and redact. "Set the block threshold low to save model calls." A low threshold turns the detector's middling precision on role play into refusals of creative requests; the capstone blocks at 0.85. "The demo exits zero, so the gate caught every attack." The demo is self terminating by design; the trace is the deliverable, and the summary counts show what got through. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why is early termination medium and not high? Expected: a regex match on a two chunk window is weaker evidence than a confirmed high classifier finding; the partial output still goes through redaction. (level 3) A low detector flag and a low rule violation arrive together. What ships? Expected: a warn with a soft notice; the maximum of two lows is low, and the table does not accumulate. (level 4) What would a weighted aggregator change, and what does it cost? Expected: signals would add toward a threshold so several weak signals could block; the cost is a tuned threshold, set by sweeping it against the corpus and reading precision and recall per category. (level 4) What does the two chunk buffer miss, and what catches it? Expected: a continuation phrase split across more chunks than the buffer holds; the post generation pass is the backstop. Where it is taught. The end to end safety gate capstone gives the aggregation table, the three checkpoints and the trace. Debug a failure Your gate blocks most attacks before the model runs. In the trace of one request the detector said benign, the model began answering with a procedure it must never give, and the response was cut after a few tokens and shipped as a redacted partial. Explain which layer acted, why the first layer missed, and whether the outcome is correct. Level 3 of 4 · about 9 minutes to answer well. Short answer. The streaming filter acted: it buffers a short window of emitted chunks, sweeps it for known continuation phrases, terminates the stream on a match and marks the output as terminated early, which the aggregator treats as a medium signal and maps to redact. The detector missed because the prompt was an encoding trick or a prefix injection whose surface the input rules did not cover. The outcome is correct for the design: the harmful continuation never completed, and the trace records the miss for the detector team. The layer that acted. The gate runs at three checkpoints. Pre generation is the detector. During generation is a filter over the model's stream: the mock yields chunks of four tokens, the filter holds up to two chunks, runs a regex of continuation phrases over the window, and on a match stops the iterator and returns the partial output marked as terminated early. Post generation runs the classifier router and the rules engine on whatever was emitted. Why the detector missed. Two taxonomy categories are built to pass input rules. An encoding trick hides the forbidden tokens in base64, rot13, leet speak or zero width characters, and a rule set that does not decode that form sees nothing. A prefix injection ends the prompt with the first words of the answer, so the model continues from an assumed yes instead of deciding; the prompt itself can look harmless. The capstone's mock produces a partial harmful continuation on exactly that subset of attacks, on purpose, so the layers can be seen interacting. Why redact and not block. Early termination is one medium signal. The post generation pass on the partial text found nothing high. The maximum is medium, so the action is redact: the classifier redactors and the rules fixer run over the partial, and it ships with a trace that shows the detector verdict, the matched termination pattern, the post generation verdicts, the final action and the latency. What to do with the trace. Add the prompt to the taxonomy as a fixture with its category and severity. Add or adjust a detector rule for its family. Rerun the metrics runner and read the recall change in that category and the false positive change on the benign list. The trace exists so that a miss becomes a fixture instead of a story. The limit. The window holds two chunks. A continuation phrase split across more chunks escapes the filter, and the post generation pass is the backstop. A gate that looked only after generation would let a prefix injection stream its procedure to the user before any check. Plausible wrong answers. "The gate failed because the detector said benign." The gate is layered so that a miss in one layer is caught by the next; the trace shows the design working. "Ship nothing when the stream is cut." The design maps early termination to redact and ships the partial through the redactors; a block needs a high signal. "Scan the whole output after generation instead." A post hoc only look lets a prefix injection stream its procedure to the user before the check; the filter exists to stop the stream early. Follow-ups an interviewer may ask. (level 3) Why does the filter hold two chunks instead of scanning each chunk alone? Expected: a continuation phrase can span a chunk boundary; the window lets the regex see across it at the cost of a short delay. (level 3) Which taxonomy categories does this layer exist for? Expected: encoding tricks that pass the input rules, and prefix injection, where the prompt sets the first words of the answer. (level 4) What is the next action for the detector team, and how do they know it worked? Expected: add the prompt as a fixture with its category, add or adjust a rule, and read the per category recall and the benign false positive rate from the metrics runner. Where it is taught. The end to end safety gate capstone builds the streaming filter and the trace, and the jailbreak taxonomy capstone defines the categories that reach it. Sources and further reading The five preceding lessons in this track. The gate composes them; it does not add new safety primitives.
